units.la: QVIN sit immensum Dei erga genus humanum beneficium, vera sacrosancti Euangelij restitutio, quæ nostris hisce temporibus à Patre luminum, cùm aliis populis, tum præsertim toti Hollandiæ oblata est, nemo, non dico Christianus, sed sanus mente diffiteri, Viri præstantissimi, potest.Nam si terræ in qua habitamus fæcunditas, si agrorum vbertas, si messis copia, si pax & tranquillitas vitæ, si Sol ipse, & lux hæc quam intuemur oculis, sunt summæ Dei erga nos mortales benignitatis testimonia: quantò illa sunt maiora, per quæ, non terram, sed cœlum: non terrenum, sed cœlestem animi victum: non cum hominibus tantùm, sed cum Deo ipso conscientiarū nostrarum pacem: non denique hanc corpoream, sed illam spiritualem salutis æternæ lucem obtinemus? Quæ omnia Dei certè quidem eximia dona tunc accipimus, quum inenarrabili ipsius beneficio ac incōprehensibili bonitate, puram illam benedicti Euangelij doctrinam ac praedicationem nobis ab eo restitutam habemus. Est enim illa penè visibilis faciei Dei aspectus: est Dei nobiscum suaue colloquium ac familiaritas, est denidenique ipsamet Dei nobiscum cohabitatio, ex qua summa nostra etiam in hac vita, nedum in cœlis fœlicitas pendet, vt præclarè docet Dauid psal. 4. his verbis. Multi dicunt, quis efficiet vt videamus bonum? Attolle super nos lucem faciei tuæ, Iehova, indideris lætitiam animo meo maiorem, quàm temporis, quo frumentum & mustum aucta sunt. In pace cubabo. Atque hoc tantùm Dei beneficium Hollandiæ, vobis, vestræque ciuitati, Viri Ornatiff. hac nostra ætate, atque adeo non ante septeniũ diuino plane munere, (οὐ ϑὲ κύλος τὰ ἀνθρώπινα) & miraculo contigit. Quam obrem eò maiori sunt odio digni, qui illud Dei munus vel vobis inuidentes, conantur vi nobis eripere: vel quale, quantumque sit pro dignitate non æstimantes, nituntur illius vos in contemptum adducere: vel denique qua ratione idem à vobis conseruari possit, & debeat, ignorantes, assi-duè scriptitando, declamandóque student cœtus illos Christianos (in quibus vera ac sincera illa diuini & Euangelici verbi prædicatio, & explicatio à legitimis pastorib. extat) omnino tollere, vel in odium ho-minum, ne ab vllis frequententur, rapere. Verùm vt eos prætermit-tam, qui vel armis Euangelium op-pugnant : vel sannis suis & con-temptione irrident.(quoniâ vtro-rumq; est manifesta impietas) de illo tertio dūtaxat hominū genere nunc dicam, qui sacros illos & E-uangelicos conuentus (qui sunt verissima Dei in his terris sedes,seu Ecclesia visibilis) vel damnant, vel aspernandos docent. Qui si animi morbo solo çontradicendi studio hoc dicunt, sunt à nobis, tanquam deplorati homines, & qui veritate ipsam Dei oderint, planè relinquendi. Sin verò id faciunt, q̃ nondum illis ipsis sanctis congressionibus interfuerint, itáque quanta sit Dei donorum in ijs congregationibus copia, quámque suauis illorum sensus, nondum gustarint, ad eas accedant ipsi, & nobiscum illis Dei donis amicè fruantur. Eos enim ad eandem nobiscum participationem, ad eandem Dei domum, ad Ecclesiam visibilem ecce benignè inuitamus, vt ipsa experientiâ nunc intelligant, Quàm bonum, & quàm iucundum sit, habitare ac conuenire fratres etiam vnà, vt est in Psal.133. adeò vt nullius, quantumuis pretiosi ac suaueolentis vnguenti odor, sit suauitate ac fragrantia cum hoc sacro hominum in Dei nomen visibiliter conuenientium confseffu, comparandus.Intelligent illos coetus visibiles esse domum illam Dauidis, in qua perennis aquae fons sit apertus, qua peccata hominum delentur, & immunditiae purgatur, vt ait Zacharias c.13. Intelligent quāobrem idē Dauid Dei propheta, quum & patriasuauissima,& vxore charissima, & bonis omnibus in exilio tristfsimo careret, vnum tamen illum visibilem Ecclesiae coetum (à quo tunc aberat) magis,quàm illa omnia desiderarit,seque illi reddi cum tantis suspirijs exoptarit, exclamans psal.84. Quàm amabilia sunt tabernacula tua Domine exercituum: Desiderio afficitur, etiamque deficit anima mea, veniendi ad atria tua. Denique intelligent illud esse verissimum, quod consentienter Dei verbo scripsit Augustinus Sermone 108. de
units.tr: Most distinguished gentlemen, no one who is sound of mind, I will not say no Christian, can deny that the true restoration of the most holy Gospel is an immense benefit of God toward the human race. In our times the Father of lights has offered it, not only to other peoples, but above all to the whole of Holland. If the fertility of the land we live in, the richness of the fields, the abundance of the harvest, peace and the calm of life, the sun itself and this light we see with our eyes are signs of God's great kindness toward us mortals, how much greater are those gifts through which we obtain, not an earthly land but heaven, not earthly sustenance but the spiritual life of the soul, not only peace with men but peace of conscience with God himself, and finally not this bodily light but the light of eternal salvation? We certainly receive all these as God's outstanding gifts when we have, by his unspeakable kindness and incomprehensible goodness, the pure preaching of the blessed Gospel restored to us. For this is almost a visible sight of God's face: it is the sweet converse and familiarity of God with us, and finally God's own dwelling with us, on which our highest happiness depends, not only in heaven but even in this life. David teaches this clearly in Psalm 4, in these words: Many say, who will show us good? Lift up over us the light of your face, O Jehovah; you have put gladness in my heart, greater than when their grain and wine increased. I will lie down and sleep in peace. This great benefit of God has come to Holland, to you and to your city, in our own age, and not even seven years ago, by a gift and miracle that is plainly divine (not as the wheel of human affairs turns by chance [οὐ τύχῃ κυλίει τὰ ἀνθρώπινα]). Therefore those who are the more deserving of hatred are those who, either envying you, try to snatch that gift from you by force, or who, not valuing how great it is and how worthy of esteem, strive to bring you into contempt for it, or finally who, ignorant of how it may and must be kept by you, labour by constant writing and declaiming to destroy altogether those Christian assemblies (in which the true and sincere preaching and exposition of the divine and evangelical Word is found under lawful ministers), or to snatch them away, out of hatred of men, so that no one may attend them. But to pass over those who attack the Gospel with arms, or who mock it with their sneers and contempt (since the impiety of both is plain), I will speak now only of that third kind of men who either condemn or teach that to be despised those holy and evangelical gatherings, which are the truest seat of God on this earth, that is, the visible Church. If they say this out of a sickness of mind, from a mere zeal for contradiction, they are to be left by us as hopeless men who hate the very truth of God. But if they say it without having taken part in those holy meetings, and so have not yet tasted how great is the abundance of God's gifts in those assemblies and how sweet is their savour, let them come to them themselves and enjoy those gifts of God with us in friendship. For we kindly invite them to the same sharing with us, to the same house of God, to the visible Church, so that by experience they may now understand how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell and meet together, as is said in Psalm 133, so that the fragrance of no ointment, however precious and sweet-smelling, can be compared in sweetness and fragrance with this sacred gathering of men who visibly come together in the name of God. They will understand that those visible assemblies are that house of David in which a fountain of living water is opened, by which the sins of men are washed away and uncleanness is cleansed, as Zechariah says in chapter 13. They will understand why David, the prophet of God, when he lacked his most beloved homeland, his dearest wife, and all his goods in a most sorrowful exile, nevertheless longed for that one visible assembly of the Church (from which he was then absent) more than all those things, and with such sighs wished to be restored to it, crying out in Psalm 84: How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs, yes, faints, for the courts of your house. Finally they will understand that what Augustine wrote in agreement with God's Word is most true: in Sermon 108 on the Times [...]

units.la: Temp. Ecclesia visibilis est torcular fontis æterni, in qua cælestis vitis fructus exundat. Item Serm. 109. Duo parentes genuerunt nos ad mortem, duo ad vitam. Ad mortem, Adam, & Eua. Ad vitam, Christus, & Ecclesia. Atque vt id lubentius faciant, sub nomine vestro mortalibus omnibus gratissimo Consules, Senatoresq; Ornatis. eos hoc libello ad visibilem Dei Ecclesiam ingrediendā amicissimè prouocamus. Et certè iustissima nominis vestri hîc appellandi causa mihi datur. Nam quum ante paucas septimanas recusus fuerit tanquā crābè bis recoēta hîc libellus, qui prius scriptus à quodam tenebrione (suppresso videlicet nomine) Sckuenfeldianorum insana deliria reuocat, damnat omnes Ecclesiasticos conuentus, & si quis sese ad eos adiungat, eum hominum seruum appellat, nihil est æ-quius, quàm vt αὐτιδοτον huic pe-stilentissimo libello opponatur. Caeterum quum is mihi à fratribus plurimùm in Christo obseruandis, Pastoribus vestris vigilantissimis fuisset oblatus, quem pro ratione mei muneris examinarem, quod ipsi partim mole negotiorum quae in tam ampla ciuitate (qualis vestra est) quotidie incidunt, obruerentur: partim propter gregis sui varios morbos corporis, in ouium suarum aegrotantium consolatione toti occuparentur: onus mihi ab illis iniunctum recusare non potui. Itaque scriptum illud non modo legi relegíque, quanuis ineptum & leuidense: sed etiam, quoniam erat blasphemum, confutaui. Hoc enim & ad Dei gloriam, & ad Ecclesiae ipsius aedificationem pertinere mihi visum est. Porrò Responsum meum vobis, præsertim viri Amplissimi, dedicare volui, à quorum ecclesiæ Pastoribus libellum illum examinandum acceperam, vt quemadmodum vestrorum Pastorum vigilantia ac diligentia maturè venenum fuit animaduersum: ita huius laboris quoque mei (per quem subsidiariam tantum operam illis præstiti) laus secundum Deum Optimum Maximum, ad vos rediret: vt quemadmodum dignitate cæteras Hollandicas ciuitates superatis, sic in vera Christi doctrina conseruanda exemplo vestro aliis omnibus præluceatis. Et quidem ad illud non modò temporis huius ratio (quo tristissima ecclesiæ facies multis in locis appareret) sed etiam magna (quibus nunc abundatis) ad id adiumeta, quæ Deus vobis singularia sua misericordia, summininstrat, vos exhortantur. Nam ut prætermittam insignem illum vestrum Consulem, & in afflictionibus pro Christi nomine toleradis propemodum Heroem, Bardesium, ea est ecclesiæ vestræ felicitas, ea Pastorum vestrorum diligentia & doctrina, ea Presbyterij cum reliquo corpore Ecclesiæ concordia, ut reliquæ urbes bona vestra merito sibi optent, ac mirentur. Sed nec ipse, quum hanc tam iustam vos in defendenda Ecclesiæ visibilis causa oblatam cohortandi occasionem haberem, prætermittere (utpote qui vos plurimi semper fecerim, faciámque) eam potui. Illi certè libello fuit obuiam eundum, & quidem statim ac maturè, dum adhuc effet recens vulnus. Præclarè enim Augustinus Sermone ne 102. de Temp. Calidis vulneribus solent medicamenta celerius subuenire. Quando in corpore vulnus accepimus, si statim medicamenta requirimus, cito sanitatem recipere poterimus. Si moram fecerit, necesse est, ut ad sanitatem tardius plaga ipsa redeat, aut aliqua foeda cicatrix remaneat. Si haec in corpore facimus, quanto magis animae vulneribus remedium adhibere debemus, vbi ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei facti sumus? Hæc Augustinus sapientissimè.
units.tr: The visible Church is the winepress of the eternal fountain, in which the fruit of the heavenly vine overflows. Likewise in Sermon 109: Two parents begot us to death, and two to life. To death, Adam and Eve. To life, Christ and the Church. And so that they may do this more willingly, I, under your name, most acceptable to all mortals, most distinguished Consuls and Senators, call them most warmly by this little book to enter the visible Church of God. And indeed a most just reason for naming you here is given to me. For a few weeks ago this book was reprinted here, like a crab cooked twice over, though it was first written by a certain obscure fellow (with his name naturally suppressed), who recalls the mad delusions of the Schwenckfeldians, condemns all ecclesiastical assemblies, and calls anyone who joins them a slave of men. Nothing is more fitting than that an answer be set against this most pestilential book. Moreover, when it had been brought to me by our most esteemed brothers in Christ, your vigilant ministers, so that I might examine it as my office required (since they were partly overwhelmed by the burden of business that daily arises in so large a city as yours, and partly wholly occupied with comforting the various bodily illnesses of their flock), I could not refuse the task laid on me by them. So I not only read and re-read that writing, though it was silly and frivolous, but also, because it was blasphemous, I refuted it. For this seemed to me to pertain both to the glory of God and to the building up of the Church itself. Furthermore, I wished to dedicate my Answer to you, especially to you, most distinguished gentlemen, from whose church's ministers I had received that libel to examine. My aim is that, just as the vigilance and diligence of your ministers noticed the poison early, so too the praise of this labour of mine (through which I have given them only supporting help) may, under God, the Best and Greatest, return to you. Thus, as you surpass the other Dutch cities in dignity, so you may also shine before all others as an example in preserving the true doctrine of Christ. Indeed, not only the character of this time, when the saddest face of the Church appears in many places, urges you to this, but also the great aids which you now enjoy, and which God in his singular mercy supplies to you. For, to pass over your famous Consul Bardesius, who is almost a hero in bearing afflictions for the name of Christ, such is the happiness of your church, such the diligence and learning of your ministers, such the harmony of the elders with the rest of the body of the Church, that the other cities rightly wish for your blessings and marvel at them. But I myself, since I had this so just an opportunity to exhort you in defending the cause of the visible Church, could not pass it by (since I have always held you in high regard, and shall continue to do so). That libel had to be met, and indeed at once and promptly, while the wound was still fresh. For Augustine wisely says in Sermon 102 on the Times: Medicines usually help hot wounds more quickly. When we receive a wound in the body, if we seek remedies at once, we shall be able to recover health quickly. If we delay, the injury must return to health more slowly, or some foul scar will remain. If we do this for the body, how much more ought we to apply a remedy to the wounds of the soul, when we have been made in the image and likeness of God? So wisely Augustine.

units.la: Atque vt hanc meam erga vos obseruantiam, studiúmque vestri nominis & ecclesiæ, æqui boníque interpretemini: denique vt hoc quantulumcunque munus meum benignè accipiatis obnixè vos, vestrásque Dominationes, Viri Grauissimi, oro, obsecróque.
units.tr: And I earnestly beg and entreat you, most distinguished gentlemen, to receive this my respect for you, and my concern for your good name and for the Church, in a fair and kindly spirit, and to accept graciously this gift of mine, however small it is.

units.la: Valete. Deus vos omnes tueatur, & regat, vobis vestræque ciuitati, & Ecclesiæ benedicat.
units.tr: Farewell. May God keep you all and rule you, and bless you, your city and the Church.

units.tr: Before I answer that book which you, my most beloved brothers in Christ, have sent me (praying the Lord God that by his great mercy this labour of mine may serve the glory of himself and the Church of God), I will say a few words about the matter itself on which the dispute is to turn. In this way our replies to the arguments put forward can be understood more easily, and the truth itself, which the author of that book has tried as hard as he could to wrap in thick darkness, may come forth and, like the most brilliant sun, be able to break through the clouds placed in its way.

units.la: A.j. conatus est) emergere, ac velut Sol splendidissimus obiectas nebulas perrumpere queat. Quatuor autem tantum proponam, & eaquidem breuissimè, vt lux aliqua toti huic argumento afferri possit: è quibus illud erit primum, A mundo condito semper inter mortales aliquam Dei ecclesiam extitisse, atque eam etiam ad finem vsque Mundi in his terris futuram esse. Ac quidem eam ab initio Mundi extitisse quis ambigere poterit, si modo vel leui oculo tantùm sacram scripturam percurrerit? Nam statim atque Mundus conditus, atque homo ille primus Adamus vnà cum vxore Eua à Deo creatus fuit purus, sanctus, pius ecquis dubitat, quin duo illi & verè Deum coluerint (quàdiu in illo suo puro statu perstiterunt) & vera Dei Ecclesia eáque etiam visibilis fuerint, nisi quis fortasse neget veram Dei Ecclesiam esse cœtum aliquem, quantumuis exiguum, qui verum Deum syncerè ex ipsius verbo ac voluntate colat? quo tamen modo Paulus Ecclesiam definit. Itaque statim à Mundo condito cœpit in Adamo & Eua esse Dei Ecclesia, quæ etiam omnes hominum politicos cœtus & respublicas origine atque antiquitate præcedit. Et certè hic quoque est finis creationis Mundi, vt esset nimirum Dei ecclesia (id est cœtus hominum verè ac manifestè verum Deum ex ipsius iussu venerantium) potius, quàm vt essent vel familiæ, vel Respublicæ vel regna, vel aliæ hominum politicæ societates, quatenus homo ipse (cuius causa Mun-
units.tr: I will set out only four points, and these very briefly, so that some light may be brought to the whole subject. The first is this: since the world was made, there has always been some Church of God among mortals, and there will be one on this earth until the end of the world. Who could doubt that it existed from the beginning of the world, if he ran through Holy Scripture even with a casual glance? For as soon as the world was created, and that first man Adam, together with his wife Eve, was made by God pure, holy and pious, who doubts that those two truly worshipped God (for as long as they remained in that pure state), and that there was a true Church of God, and a visible one too? Unless perhaps someone denies that the true Church of God is any gathering, however small, which sincerely worships the true God according to his Word and will, which is how Paul defines the Church. So from the creation of the world there began to be a Church of God in Adam and Eve, a Church which also precedes all human political assemblies and commonwealths in origin and antiquity. And certainly this too is the purpose of the creation of the world: that there should be a Church of God (that is, a gathering of men who truly and openly worship the true God at his command), rather than families, commonwealths, kingdoms, or other human political societies. Man himself, for whose sake this world was made,

units.la: Mundus hic à Deo factus est) Dei potius colédi, quàm societatis cum alio homine ineundæ aut tuendę gratiâ à Deo ipso formatus est. Adeo vt qui negat verâ Ecclesiam Dei eámque etiam visibilem ab initio Mundi extitisse, ille proculdubio se vel primæ sacrorum bibliorum paginæ prorsus ignarum fateatur ac ostendat. Certè eodem spectauit Moses,quum nobis certarum familiarum capita & nomina ab Adamo vsque ad Noachum ante diluuium: & post diluuium à Noacho ad Abrahamum vsque descripsit: nimirum vt ostenderet in ijs saltem piis familijs & Dei verum cultum,& Ecclesiam quoq; subsistitisse:atque inibi (quantumuis esset corruptus reliquus Mundus) remansisse. Eodem quoque Apostolus ad Hebræos cap. vndecimo collimauit, dum ab Abele ipsius Adami filio ad sua vsque tempora & pios, & Deum ex vera fide colentes in his terris semper per successiones ætatum fuisse, perpetua quadam serie demonstrat. Quid est enim ecclesia, nisi hominum verè Deum colentium,vti dixi, cœtus? Sed & ipsam eandem ecclesiam ad finem vsque Mundi in his terris perduraturā docet apertissimi sacræ Scripturæ loci, in quibus præclaræ illæ Dei promissiones (quas de futura Ecclesiæ suæ perpetuitate toties inculcauit) continentur, quorum duos tantùm breuitatis gratia proferemus, quum sint tamen pene innumerabiles. Vnus est.Psal. 72. verf.7. alter. Psal. 89. verf.37.38. vbi Dominus Deus pollicetur hoc semen & regnum (quod & Dauidis & suum appellat, éstque ipsius ecclesia, testibus Angelo & Petro Apostolo) fore in his terris tam diuturnum, quàm Sol ipse, & Luna, reliquaque sidera in cœlis lucebunt atque fixa mansura sunt; id autem significat, vsque ad consummationem seculi, & finem huius Mūdi. Dico autem diserte Ecclesiam fore perpetuam & quidem in his terris, quoniam illud ipsum est, de quo multi hodie anxiè quærunt. Nam post vltimam resurrectionem, collectósque pios omnes in cœlo vnà cum Domino nostro Iesu Christo nostro duce, fore etiam in cœlis, non modo diuturnam, sed etiam beatam ac æternam, nemo, meo quidem iudicio, dubitare potest. Et certè quidem toties Christum homines spoliant omni vera dignitate, omni in his terris imperio, omnibus denique ijs præclarissimis epithetis, quibus & Sponsus, & Caput, & Redemptor passim in sacra scriptura nominatur, quoties illi ecclesiam. i. sponsam, corpus, & populum redemptum adimunt, id est, quoties esse ac subsistere in his terris ecclesiam negant, quod est impiissimum & plus, quam exprimi possit, absurdum. Quum enim Christus non in vnum tantum aut alterum seculum, sed perpetuo sit & verè dicatur sponsus. Matth.9. verf. 19. sponsam ergo habeat necesse est. Illa verò est vna Ecclesia, quemadmodum interpretatur Paulus 2. Corinth. 11. verf. 1. Quare Ecclesia quoque aliqua perpetuò sit & existat oportet, adeóque in his terris : quoniam non Angelos aut Homines (qui in cœlo sunt) alloquitur Scriptura, sed nos qui hic in terris viuimus, quando demonstrat esse in his terris populum & cœtum aliquem, veluti sponsam, cuius Christus sit sponsus, vt in eo populo ac cœtu esse studeamus, vt & Christus quotidie in his terris dona sua salutaria tribuit hominibus. Ergo Ecclesiā esse oportet in his quoque terris. Est enim ecclesia cœtus ille hominum, qui salutem ac salutaria illa dona accipiunt à Christo. Qui si nullus est, nullis quoque illa dabit Deus: atque ita erunt inanes pro eo tempore quo non erit Ecclesia, illæ Dei de redimendis hominibus promissiones; quum suum effectum in nullis habeant, quandiu nulla erit Ecclesia. Quum Christus sit hodie, & heri, & in perpetuum (quamdiu erit hic Mundus) quum Christus inquam, sit semper atque etiam in his terris caput, Ephes. 5. verf. 22. Ergo reliqua corporis membra. i. Ecclesiam in his terris habeat necesse est. Neque enim Christus vel totius Mundi vel infidelium hominum séque ab illo prorsus separantium ratione caput est: sed fidelium duntaxat & ecclesiæ suæ: quemadmodum vbique explicat idem Paulus 1.Corinth.12. verf. 27. Vos estis, ait alloquens solos fideles corpus Christi. Quum idem Christus & semper & in his terris sit Dominus & Rex suum quendam populum possidens peculiariter. 1. Pet.2.verf.9. Ergo sit, atque adeo in his terris illa possesio atq; populus illi subditus, necesse est. Ecquis enim vere dicetur possessor absque possessione, Dominus & Rex absque peculiari populo, Grege, ac dominio? Gloria namque regis est populi multitudo, quemadmodum ait Solomo, illa vero possessio ac populus Christo peculiaris est Ecclesia.Act. 20. ver.28, 1.Pet.2. ver.9. Ergo Ecclesia aliqua sit in his terris oportet. Quumq; Christus & sit & dicatur Deus etiam in hoc Mundi statu, Hebr.1. & 2. templum quoque habeat in hoc Mundo necesse est vbi vere colatur. 1. Corinth.5.verf. 6. Neque enim verus Deus sine cultu & templo esse vult. At illud est Ecclesia & quidem sola, quemadmodum ait organum illud Dei selectum Paulus 1. Timoth. 3.verf.15. Ecclesia est, Domus Dei, columna veritatis, in qua nos quoque versari oportere docet. Denique Ecclesiam Dei credimus. Atqui eius rei, quae non est, nulla fides est. Ergo esse Ecclesiam oportet, & quum ille Symboli articulus nostram in his terris fidem ostendat, ergo Ecclesiam quoq; hic aliquâ extare necesse est, manet igitur illud quod propositimus firmum & immotū, Ecclesiā Dei habere verissimas Dei de sua etiā in his terris perpetuitate, ac duratio ne promissionis rationes: in coelo autē de sua etiam æternitate ac felicitate. Atque hoc primum est ex illis quatuor, quod ab omnibus intelligi imprimis cupio, Neque tamen propterea Papistis assentimur, qui Ecclesiam Dei in his terris certo cuidam loco veluti Romæ tanquam glebæ affigunt, & illi perpetuam personarum successionem in eadem cathedra assi-
units.tr: was formed by God to worship God, rather than to enter into or maintain society with another man. So much so that whoever denies that the true Church of God, and a visible one too, has existed from the beginning of the world shows himself, beyond doubt, to be utterly ignorant of even the first page of the sacred books. Moses certainly had this in view when he set down for us the heads and names of particular families, from Adam to Noah before the Flood, and from Noah to Abraham after the Flood. Clearly he wished to show that the true worship of God and the Church also subsisted in those godly families, and remained there, however corrupt the rest of the world was. The Apostle to the Hebrews, in chapter eleven, also aimed at the same thing, when he demonstrates in an unbroken sequence that from Abel, the son of Adam, down to his own times there were always, through successive generations, pious people on earth who worshipped God in true faith. For what is the Church, if not, as I have said, an assembly of men who truly worship God? But the most open passages of Holy Scripture also teach that this same Church will endure on this earth until the end of the world. These passages contain those glorious promises of God, which he so often impressed upon us concerning the perpetuity of his Church. I shall cite only two of them for the sake of brevity, although there are almost countless others. The first is Psalm 72, verse 7; the second is Psalm 89, verses 37 and 38. There the Lord God promises that this seed and kingdom (which he calls both David's and his own, and which is his Church, as the angel and the Apostle Peter bear witness) will last on this earth as long as the sun itself, and the moon, and the other stars shall shine in the heavens and remain fixed. This means, clearly, until the consummation of the age and the end of this world. I say expressly that the Church will be perpetual, and indeed on this earth, because this is precisely the point about which many today inquire anxiously. For that after the final resurrection, when all the godly have been gathered together in heaven with our Lord Jesus Christ, our leader, the Church will also be in heaven, not only lasting but also blessed and eternal, no one, in my judgment, can doubt. And indeed, whenever men strip Christ of all true dignity, of all rule on this earth, and finally of all those most distinguished titles by which he is everywhere named in Scripture (Bridegroom, Head, and Redeemer), that is, whenever they deny that the Church, his bride, his body and redeemed people, exists and subsists on this earth, they do the most impious thing, and something more absurd than can be expressed. For since Christ is not a bridegroom for one or two ages only, but always, and is truly called a bridegroom, he must of necessity have a bride. Matthew 9, verse 15. That bride is one Church, as Paul explains, 2 Corinthians 11, verse 2. Therefore a Church must also always exist and be, and so on this earth as well; for Scripture is not addressing angels or men who are in heaven, but us who live here on earth, when it shows that there is on earth a people and a gathering, as it were a bride, of whom Christ is the bridegroom, so that we may strive to be in that people and gathering, and because Christ daily bestows his saving gifts upon men here on earth. Therefore the Church must also be on this earth. For the Church is that gathering of men who receive salvation and those saving gifts from Christ. If there is none, God will give those gifts to no one; and thus those promises of God concerning the redemption of men will be empty for the time in which there is no Church, since they have no effect in anyone as long as there is no Church. Since Christ is today, and yesterday, and for ever (as long as this world lasts); since Christ, I say, is always, and also on this earth, the Head, Ephesians 5, verse 22, the remaining members of the body, that is, the Church, must of necessity be on this earth too. For Christ is Head not of the whole world, nor of unbelievers who separate themselves wholly from him, but of believers only, and of his Church, as the same Paul explains everywhere, 1 Corinthians 12, verse 27: "You are," he says, addressing believers alone, "the body of Christ." Since the same Christ is always and also on this earth Lord and King, possessing a certain people peculiarly for himself, 1 Peter 2, verse 9, there must of necessity be on this earth that possession and the people subject to him. For who could truly be called a possessor without a possession, or a lord and king without a peculiar people, flock, and dominion? "For the glory of a king is the multitude of the people," as Solomon says; and that possession and people, peculiar to Christ, is the Church. Acts 20, verse 28; 1 Peter 2, verse 9. Therefore some Church must be on this earth. And since Christ both is and is called God even in this present state of the world, Hebrews 1 and 2, he must also have a temple in this world where he is truly worshipped. 1 Corinthians 5, verse 6. For the true God does not wish to be without worship and a temple. But that is the Church, and indeed the only one, as Paul, that chosen instrument of God, says, 1 Timothy 3, verse 15: the Church is "the house of God, the pillar and ground of the truth, in which we too are taught that we ought to dwell." Finally, we believe in the Church of God. But there is no faith in a thing that does not exist. Therefore the Church must exist; and since that article of the Creed shows our faith in this earth, the Church too must of necessity be here in some form. So the point we proposed remains firm and unshaken: the Church of God has the most true reasons, drawn from God's promise, for its perpetuity on this earth, and for its duration, and in heaven for its eternity and happiness. This is the first of those four points, which I especially wish everyone to understand. Yet we do not therefore agree with the Papists, who fix the Church of God in a certain place on this earth, as if to a clod, namely Rome, and assign to it a perpetual succession of persons in the same chair. This is also most absurd, since God gathers his Church freely wherever he wills. Thus what we have said is most true: God wishes his Church to be perpetual on this earth, sometimes in this place, sometimes in that. The second is that there are most certain…

units.la: A. ii. assignant, vti etiam hoc est salsissimum: quum Deus liberrimè vbicunque velit suâ ecclesiam colligat, Ita illud quod diximus est veriffimū, Deum in his terris Ecclesiam suâ perpetuâ esse velle modo hoc, modo illo loco. Alterum est, esse certissimas notas ex quibus illa vera Dei Ecclesia etiam in his terris visibiliter, perspicuè, ac, vt ita loquar, ocula riter agnosci, dignoscíque à cæteris hominum vel prophanorum & prorsus infidelium, vel hæreticorum coetibus atque congregationionibus possit. Hoc quidem mirum & prorsus ἀδύνατον non-nullis videtur, sed est tamen verissimum. Inde enim est, vt non semper vera illa Dei Ecclesia in his terris sit ita visibilis (licet nihilominus in his terris sit aliqua) quoniā illæ certissimæ ecclesiæ Dei notæ non semper à nobis manifestè, euidenter, atque visibiliter in certo cœtu hominum perspici ac obseruari possunt vel potuerunt. Quo fit, vt tunc è terris Ecclesiam illam Dei perijsse arbitremur, quum illa Ecclesiæ symbola nimirum nusquam apparent nobis. Et tamen tunc quoque Deus suam in terris ecclesiam nihilominus habet, quamuis nos ita eã oculis discernere & in aliquo cœtu conuentúque hominum videre minimè possimus, Sic tempore Eliæ nusquam in Regno Israelis putabatur ab ipsomet Dei Propheta esse Dei Ecclesia, quæ tamen, quemadmodum Deus ipse testatur, septem hominum millibus constabat. Sic tempore exilij Ægyptiaci, Babylonicæ captiuitatis, sæuissimi illius dominatus Antiochi in Iudæos, quum per montes & antra & caucrnas laterent viri pij. Sic denique paucis annis ante restitutum hoc nostro seculo Euangelium summa Dei optimi maximi misericordia, dum fratres Waldenses (qui tunc erant penè sola Dei ecclesia) & raro aut nunquam colleƈti, in terræ hiatibus, in syluis, in saxis & rupibus soli vagíque errarent, lateréntque. Quod si nullæ certæ & veræ ad veram Dei Ecclesiam dignoscédam notę essent, certè neque potuissent olim viri pij, vt Elias, neque nunc quoque possent fideles distingue-re tempus illud, quo vera illa Dei Ecclesia in his terris fuit aut est visibilis, & quo eadem illa non est visibilis: sed aut vera Ecclesia perpetuò confunderetur cum falsa: aut ecclesia censeretur semper fuisse vel visibilis, vel inuisibilis. Fateor equidem vera ecclesiam non ita semper fuisse, aut esse visibilem in his terris: fateor quoque non quicunque sunt visibilis ecclesiæ membra, eosdem semper in ecclesia inuisibili censeri debere (multi sunt intus & in Ecclesia visibili lupi ac hypocritæ: verùm in illa inuisibili ecclesia nulli sunt, nisi verè electi Dei, veréque fideles) tamen inde non efficitur, quo minus sint certæ quædam notæ & pignora, quibus vera ecclesia certissimè agnosci atque etiã seceǝrni visibiliter ab infidelium vel hæreticorum hominum cœtibus atque conuentibus possit. Ergo quænam sint illæ notæ, videndum est. In quo non est nobis longa disputatione opus. Vno enim verbo DomiDominus noster Iesus Christus, Doctor ille optimus, docet ecquos pro suis ouibus, ac proinde pro sua veraque Ecclesia in hoc Mundo agnoscat. Nam apud Ioan. cap. 10. ver. 27. Oues meae, inquit Christus, vocem meam audiunt, & ego eas agnosco & sequuntur me. Ioannes ipse in epistola secunda postquam sic scripsisset. Qui manet in doctrina Christi, hic & Patre & Filium habet, addidit, Si quis venit ad vos, & hanc doctrinam non affert, ne recipite eum domum, nec Aue ei dicite. Denique Paulus veritatem Dei ab Apostolis & Prophetis praedicatam constituit fundamentum & quidem verum & solum ecclesiae. Quamobrem in quocunque hominum coetu idololatria abijcitur & vox Christi auditur: in quocunque coetu ea doctrina quae habet Christum, non autem homines caput, sonat: in quocunque doctrina Prophetica & Apostolica pro solo fidei fundamento retinetur, is certe coetus eam notam obtinet, ex qua vera Dei Ecclesia definiri debet. Id quod etiam his rationibus confirmari potest. Primum, quum vera Dei ecclesia sit hominum non quidem omnium, sed fidelium congregatio, ex fide erit dignoscenda discernendaque ea congregatio, videlicet ut quae veram fidem habet, ea certe quidem ecclesia vera nominetur: quae vero vera fide caret, ea nequaquam censeatur Ecclesia Dei. Atqui vera fides solo Dei verbo, eoque scripto, innititur: non hominum commentis, non traditionibus, nec doctrinis: sed, quemadmodum dixi, in
units.tr: assign it, just as this is also most absurd, since God freely gathers his Church wherever he pleases. So what we said is most true: God wills his Church to be perpetual on this earth, now in this place, now in that. The second point is that there are most certain marks by which that true Church of God can be recognised on this earth, visibly, clearly and, as I may put it, to the eye, and distinguished from the other assemblies and gatherings of men, whether profane and wholly unbelieving or heretical. To some this seems a wonder and quite impossible [ἀδύνατον], but it is nonetheless most true. For this is why the true Church of God is not always so visible on this earth (although there is always some Church on earth), because those most certain marks of the Church of God cannot always be seen and observed by us clearly, evidently and visibly in a definite gathering of men, or could not be. Hence we judge that the Church of God has perished from the earth whenever those marks of the Church nowhere appear to us. Yet even then God still has his Church on earth, although we cannot discern it with our eyes in this way and see it in any gathering or assembly of men. So in the time of Elijah, the prophet of God himself thought that there was nowhere in the kingdom of Israel the Church of God, which nevertheless, as God himself attests, consisted of seven thousand people. So too in the time of the Egyptian exile, the Babylonian captivity, and the most savage domination of Antiochus over the Jews, when the godly lay hidden in mountains, caves and dens. So finally, a few years before the Gospel was restored in our century by the great mercy of God, the best and greatest, when the brethren of the Waldenses (who were then almost the only Church of God) were rarely or never gathered together, but wandered alone and lay hidden in the clefts of the earth, in the woods, among the rocks and crags. But if there were no certain and true marks by which the true Church of God could be distinguished, then certainly the godly of old, such as Elijah, could not have done so, nor could the faithful now distinguish that time in which the true Church of God on earth was or is visible from the time in which it is not visible. Rather, either the true Church would be constantly confused with the false, or the Church would be thought to have always been either visible or invisible. I grant indeed that the true Church has not always been, or is not now, visible on this earth. I also grant that not all who are members of the visible Church are to be counted always in the invisible Church (there are many wolves and hypocrites within the visible Church, but the invisible Church contains only those who are truly elect of God and truly faithful). Yet it does not follow from this that there are not certain marks and pledges by which the true Church can be most certainly recognised, and also visibly set apart from the gatherings and assemblies of unbelieving or heretical men. Therefore we must consider what those marks are. In this we need not a long disquisition. For our Lord Jesus Christ, that best of teachers, teaches in one word by what sign he recognises his sheep, and therefore his true Church, in this world. For in John 10.27 Christ says: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. John himself, after writing thus in his second epistle, added: Whoever abides in the teaching of Christ, he has both the Father and the Son. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, nor say to him, Hail. Finally, Paul established the truth of God preached by the Apostles and Prophets as the foundation, and indeed the true and only foundation, of the Church. Wherefore, in whatever gathering of men idolatry is cast out and the voice of Christ is heard; in whatever gathering the doctrine that has Christ, and not men, as its head is sounded; in whatever gathering the prophetic and apostolic doctrine is held as the sole foundation of faith, that gathering certainly bears the mark by which the true Church of God ought to be defined. This can also be confirmed by the following reasons. First, since the true Church of God is a congregation not of all men but of the faithful, that congregation must be recognised and distinguished by faith, so that the congregation which has true faith is rightly called a true Church, while that which lacks true faith is by no means to be counted the Church of God. But true faith rests on the word of God alone, and that written: not on the inventions of men, nor on traditions, nor on doctrines, but, as I have said, it is founded on the word of God alone, revealed through the Prophets and Apostles. Therefore the Church is to be judged by us from that written word of God alone, as from its most true mark, so that the gathering which embraces that written word of God is called the Church, as it truly is.
