units.la: solo Dei verbo per Prophetas & Apostolos reuelato fundatur:ergo ex solo illo Dei verbo scripto Ecclesia est à nobis velut ex verissima sua nota dijudicanda, vt qui illud Dei verbum scriptum amplectitur cœtus, is Ecclesia, vti est, sic appelletur. Itaque & Christus ipse, & Petrus,&Paulus nos ad scripturas sacras reuocant,vt nos verâ fidē sequi doceant, ac proinde esse illud in vera Ecclesia Dei,Christus ait, Scrutamini scripturas. Petrus autē, Habetis sermonem Propheticum, scriptum nempe, cui recte facitis quòd attendatis. Paulus autem, tradidi vobis Christum mortuum esse pro peccatis nostris, secundum scripturas: sepultum item & excitatum tertio die, secundum scripturas. Ergo ex scriptura sacra discernitur quinā verè fideles sint, ac proinde quæ sit vera eorum congregatio, id est, quæ sit vera Ecclesia. Deinde veræ Ecclesiæ secernendæ Christus, & quidem solus, est & nota, & iudex. Nam qui cœtus verum Christum habet, is est vera Dei Ecclesia ex quo fit, vt qui ad eam adducuntur, dicantur ad Christum adduci: Christo lucrifieri qui in ea sunt, & esse in Christo. Quare quū ex solo Dei verbo scripto verus Christus à falso discernatur, eâdem quoq; notâ vera Ecclesia à falsa distinguenda est. Nam qui verbum illud Dei scriptum sequitur, is & verum Christum, & veram Ecclesiā habet,in eáque proculdubio est. Denique quum passim à Prophetis ad legem id est ad scripturā sacrā remittamur, qua Moses ipse testatur Iudæos olim à ceteris populis sepaseparatos, & Dei populum ac Ecclesiâ ex eo merito censitos, quòd Dei verbum scriptum apud fe haberent & conseruarent, vt ait Pau- lus : certè apparet ex eo quod quispiam cœtus habet penes fe verbum Dei scriptum, illudq; audit, ampleCtitur,profitetur, esse veram Dei ecclesiam : ac proinde verissima ecclesiæ Dei notam esse verbi illius diuini seu sacræ scripturæ puram quæ in ea extat prædicationem. Et quoniam sacramenta ab ipso Christo instituta sunt illius doctrinæ symbola, fi gilla atque appendices, certè idem quoque ille hominum cœtus, qui veram Christi doctrinam audiet & sequetur, sacramentorum quoque à Christo præceptorum vsum, quantum poterit, retinebit, féque illis sponte non priuabit. Nam Apostolus Paulus duo illa tanquâ indissolubili nexu coniuncta simul quoque copulauit. Sic de nobis, ait, reputent homines, vt de Ministris Christi,(hoc ad verbi diuini & Christi vocis prædicationem pertinet) & dispensatoribus Mysteriorum Dei. (Hoc autem ad eiusdem etiam Sacramenta referendum est) Et quia omnis hæc Christi doctrinæ Sacramentorumque administratio idcirco à nobis fit, auditur, & suscipitur, vt verum Deum colamus,ac glorificemus, id quod fine vitę sanctitate fieri nequaquam potest (Hæc est voluntas Dei, ait Paulus,sanctificatio vestra. Idcirco ea quoque agendi ratio, in vera Dei Ecclesia instituitur, probatur, ac quantum fieri potest conferuatur, per quam improbi hominum (qui illam Christi vocem audiunt, sacramentis communicat) improbi inquâ, mores vel emendantur: vel pro rei gravitate tum à magistratu, poena civili: tum ab ecclesia ipsa, poena censuráque Ecclesiastica, ex Christi praecepto castigantur: Quam agendi in scelerum emendatione rationem, Disciplinam ecclesiasticam veteres omnes scriptores semper appellarunt. Ergo has tres notas verae Ecclesiae etiam visibiliter in his terris agnoscendae & à reliquis hominum congregationibus dijudicandę secernendaeque luce meridiana clarius iam videmus, Nimirum puram verbi Dei & vocis Christi auditionem ac proinde praedicationem, puram & ex Christi instituto sacramentorum administrationem, denique sanctificationis commendationem cum morum depravatorum in ijs qui se Christianos profitentur, correctione coniunctam. Quod quidem tamen ita procedit, ut ex illis tribus notis prima proculdubio certior, potior, ac maior sit, & reliquarum duarum fundamentū: ut qui coetus illa prima nota careat, etiamsi alias duas retineat, tamen vera Dei Ecclesia ἀπλῶς & simpliciter censeri neque possit, neq; debeat. Iam vero cum illae notae tres perspicuè ac manifestè in multis hominum coetibus hodie in his terris appareant, in ijs nimirum Ecclesijs quę ferió Euangelicae ac Reformatae nominantur, quis iam dubitet, quin eadem illae sint verae Dei Ecclesiae & visibiles, & in his quoque terris existentes? Quod si quis objiciat, ijciat, Non eam esse Reformatarum Ecclesiarum in singulis ipsius membris vel etiam toto corpore sanctitatem, quae prorsus omni labe ac vitio careat? Haud equidem negamus, & hoc ipsum etiam dolemus: & propterea illarum ecclesiarum Pastores in eo maximè dies noctesque laborant, ut qui purum illud Dei verbum & Christi vocem audiunt, quotidie meliores sanctioresque evadant. Verùm ecquis hanc perfectam absolutámque omnibus numeris sanctitatem ac Iustitiam à reformatis ecclesiis exigat, quam ne in suis quidem ecclesiis viderunt ipsimet Apostoli, tot Dei donis ornati, tam egregia miraculorum virtute praediti, in illo etiamnum calente homi-num zelo, & in illo Ecclesiae primitiuae flore? Imo verò sic diserte scribit Ioannes, dilectus ille Christi discipulus, ille, qui totus charitatem & sanctitatem & in vita, & in scriptis spirat, Si dixerimus, ait, nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas Dei in nobis non est. Et tamè illi hominum coetus ab ipsis Apostolis Christo collecti procul dubio Ecclesiae Dei & visibiles, & in his terris erant. Quàm sunt igitur iniqui Iudices ij, qui à nostris ecclesiis eam legem ac perfectam iustitiam requirunt, quam ne in suis quidem ecclesiis, licet verissimis extare posse quandiu hic viuitur, Apostoli ipsi testati sunt: Sic in symbolo Apostolorum confitemur quidem ecclesiam in his terris sanctam, sed non perfectam. Nam aliud est homines sanctos esse debere, aliud plena iustitia perfectos, quando & hæc ipsa est no-stra perfectio, nimirum agnoscere nos imperfectos: adeo vt quos etiam Paulus perfectos vocat (progressus nimirum cuiusdam in pietate argumento) ijs tamen ipsis multa desse ad summam tum vitæ integritatem, tum intelligetiam vel suo exemplo fateatur. Quare non obstat illa vitæ sanctitas imperfecta, quominus, si tres illæ notæ, vel etiam sola illa prima in aliquo cœtu manifeste appareat. Ille cœtus demum vera Dei Ecclesia eáque visibilis dici debeat. Id quod quum in Ecclesijs Euangelicis, reformatisque (si modo nullo odio aut præiudicio ducimur) hodie cernatur, negari certè non potest, quin eædem illæ sint & verè & visibiles adhuc Dei ecclesiæ in his terris. Atque hoc secundum est. Quod ex illis quatuor à vobis intelligi volumus. Tertium est, debere quemlibet pium ac fidele sese illi Ecclesiæ adiungere quæ & vera est & visibilis, id est, ex ijs notis, quas supra diximus, agnosci etiam in his terris poterit. Quum enim Christus sit nobis etiam in his terris quærendus & sequendus, certò ijs adhæreamus oportet, qui suauem illam Christi vocem & salutare (quod faciunt ij cœtus, qui superiores illas tres notas habent) audiunt. Nam oues, quemadmodum ait Christus ipse, Pastorem sequuntur. Iam verò & Christum & Deum in his terris sequi aliter nequimus, quàm si ipsius vocem ac verbum audiamus, vt fusè docet Apostolus. Ergo qui se ab ijs visibilis Ecclesiæ cœtibus separant, rant,in quibus vox Christi sonat, purū Euāge lii prædicatur,verbū Dei est fidei fundamen-tum, ij certè sese à Christo, à Deo, à salutis suæ via & tramite,denique à vera Ecclesia se-iungunt. De huiusmodi enim id est, visibili Ecclesia dicit Christus.Qui vos audit,me audit: Qui vos spernit,me spernit.Quod de visibilis ec-clesiæ cœtu, non autem de ecclesia inuisibili & dictum esse à Christo,& à nobis intelligen-dum apparet ex eo, quòd in ecclesia inuisibili nemo audiri potest, quum is cœtus inuisibilis Ecclesia videri non possit. Itaque in ea nemo homo loquitur, & prædicat: nemo etiam est auditor. Neque enim quisquam auditor ibi esse potest vbi nemo est prædicator, Romano 10.verf. 14. Quamobrem de visibili Ecclesia loquitur Christus, quum ait,Qui vos audit,me audit,&c. Quemadmodum enim nemo extra arcam Noachi è diluuio saluus euasit, sic neque extra huiusmodi Ecclesiam id est,visibilem, si illic est, quisquam æternam salutem consequitur,quanquam in ea Ecclesia salutem istam à Deo per Christum fide apprehensum, non ab ipsa Ecclesia,id est, non ab ipso hominum cœtu obtineat. Cæterum arcam Noachi esse typum Ecclesiæ etiam visibilis,non autem dūtaxat inuisibilis docet Petrus. 1.epistol.cap. 3. verf. 20. 21. qui illam arcam comparat cum eo cœtu, in quo est celebraturque Baptisma. Atqui ille cœtus est certè quidem prorsus visibilis, quoniam quum Ecclesia est inuisibilis, Baptisma nullo modo potest in ea adminístrari aut celebrari. Ex quo fit, vt verissimè fuerit à Patribus orthodoxis dictum, Ille non habet Deum Patrem, qui non habet ecclesiam visibilem matrem. Huiusmodi enim ecclesia id est visibilis ecclesia est, sedes & columna veritatis. vt loquitur Paulus, est Domus seu templum Dei in his terris, vt pote in quo visibiliter & audibiliter (si ita dici potest) verbū Dei prædicatur, & qui sese ab ea separat, is quoq; se à Dei veritate, & à Dei templo plane separat. Erit salus in Sione, ait Propheta: residuum populi illic fructificabit, inquit alter: Zacharias autem, in illa est fons scaturiens aquæ vitæ, illa videlicet pura verbi diuini explicatio atque prædicatio.
units.tr: ...is founded on the Word of God alone, revealed through the Prophets and Apostles. Therefore the Church must be judged by us from that written Word of God alone, as from its most certain mark, so that the assembly that embraces that written Word of God is rightly called the Church, as it truly is. Thus Christ himself, Peter and Paul all call us back to the holy Scriptures, to teach us to follow the true faith. Accordingly Christ says, in proof that this belongs to the true Church of God, Search the Scriptures. Peter says, You have the prophetic word, that is, the written word, to which you do well to attend. Paul says, I delivered to you that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was likewise buried and raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. Therefore it is from Holy Scripture that we discern who are truly faithful, and so what their true assembly is, that is, what the true Church is. Next, Christ alone, and indeed Christ alone, is both the mark and the judge by which the true Church is separated out. For the assembly that has the true Christ is the true Church of God. From this it follows that those who are brought into it are said to be brought to Christ, that those who are in it are gained for Christ, and that they are in Christ. Since, then, the true Christ is distinguished from a false one by the written Word of God alone, the true Church must be distinguished from a false one by the same mark. For whoever follows that written Word of God has both the true Christ and the true Church, and without doubt is in it. Finally, since everywhere we are sent by the Prophets back to the law, that is, to Holy Scripture, by which Moses himself testifies that the Jews were of old separated from other peoples and counted as God's people and Church on this very ground, that they had and kept the written Word of God, as Paul says, it certainly appears from this that any assembly which has the written Word of God among it, hears it, embraces it and professes it, is the true Church of God. Therefore the most certain mark of the Church of God is the purity of that divine Word, or of Holy Scripture, and of the preaching of it which is found in the Church. And since the sacraments were instituted by Christ himself as symbols, seals and appendages of that doctrine, certainly that same assembly of men which hears and follows the true doctrine of Christ will also retain, as far as it can, the use of the sacraments commanded by Christ, and will not of its own accord deprive itself of them. For the Apostle Paul joined these two together, as if bound by an indissoluble tie. Let men so regard us, he says, as ministers of Christ (this pertains to the preaching of the divine Word and the voice of Christ) and stewards of the mysteries of God (this must also be referred to the sacraments of the same). And since all this teaching of Christ and administration of the sacraments is done, heard and received by us so that we may worship and glorify the true God, which can by no means be done without holiness of life (This is the will of God, says Paul, your sanctification), therefore that manner of acting is also established in the true Church of God, approved, and preserved as far as possible, by which wicked men who hear that voice of Christ and share in the sacraments are either corrected in their morals, or, according to the gravity of the matter, are punished by the magistrate with civil punishment, or by the Church itself with ecclesiastical punishment and censure, in accordance with Christ's command. All the ancient writers have always called this manner of correcting sins the church discipline. Therefore we now see more clearly than the midday light that these three marks of the true Church are to be recognised even visibly in this earth and distinguished from other assemblies of men: namely, the pure hearing, and so the preaching, of the Word of God and the voice of Christ; the pure administration of the sacraments according to Christ's institution; and finally the commendation of sanctification joined with the correction of depraved morals among those who profess themselves Christians. Yet it so proceeds that of these three marks the first is without doubt the surest, the most powerful and the greatest, and the foundation of the other two; so that an assembly which lacks that first mark, even if it retains the other two, cannot and ought not to be considered the true Church of God absolutely [ἀπλῶς] and simply. Now, since these three marks appear clearly and plainly today in many assemblies of men in these lands, namely in those churches which are commonly called Evangelical and Reformed, who can doubt that these same are the true and visible Churches of God, existing also in these lands? But if someone objects that the Reformed churches do not have a holiness in their individual members, or even in the whole body, that is wholly free from every stain and fault, we do not indeed deny it, and we ourselves grieve over it; and therefore the ministers of those churches labour day and night chiefly to ensure that those who hear that pure Word of God and the voice of Christ grow better and holier every day. But who would require from the Reformed churches that perfect and absolute holiness and righteousness in every respect, which the Apostles themselves, adorned with so many gifts of God, endowed with such remarkable power of miracles, living in that still fervent zeal of men and in that flower of the early Church, did not find even in their own churches? Indeed, John, that beloved disciple of Christ, who breathes charity and holiness entirely both in his life and in his writings, writes plainly, If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth of God is not in us. Yet those assemblies of men gathered by Christ through the Apostles themselves were without doubt both the Churches of God and visible, and existed in these lands. How unjust judges, then, are those who require from our churches that law and perfect righteousness which the Apostles themselves testified cannot be found even in their own churches, however true, as long as one lives here! So in the Apostles' Creed we confess indeed that the Church on this earth is holy, but not perfect. For it is one thing for men to be bound to be holy, and another to be perfected in full righteousness; and this very thing is our perfection, namely to acknowledge that we are imperfect. So much so that even those whom Paul calls perfect (evidently as an argument of some progress in piety), he nonetheless admits, even by his own example, lack much both of full integrity of life and of understanding. Therefore that imperfect holiness of life does not stand in the way, so that if these three marks, or even the first mark alone, clearly appear in some assembly, that assembly ought finally to be called the true Church of God, and a visible one. Since this is seen today in the Evangelical and Reformed churches (if indeed we are not led by any hatred or prejudice), it cannot be denied that these same are truly and visibly the Churches of God in these lands. And this is the second point, which we want you to understand from those four. The third is that every pious and faithful person ought to join himself to that Church which is both true and visible, that is, which can be recognised even in these lands by the marks we have mentioned above. For since Christ is to be sought and followed by us even in these lands, we must surely adhere to those who hear that sweet voice of Christ and his saving word (which those assemblies do that have the three marks mentioned above). For the sheep, as Christ himself says, follow the shepherd. Now we cannot follow Christ and God in these lands in any other way than by hearing their voice and Word, as the Apostle teaches at length. Therefore those who separate themselves from those visible assemblies of the Church in which the voice of Christ sounds, in which the pure Gospel is preached, and in which the Word of God is the foundation of faith, certainly sever themselves from Christ, from God, from the way and path of their salvation, and finally from the true Church. For Christ speaks of this kind of Church, that is, the visible one: He who hears you hears me; he who rejects you rejects me. That this was said by Christ of the visible assembly of the Church, and not of the invisible Church, and must be understood by us so, appears from the fact that no one can be heard in the invisible Church, since that invisible assembly cannot be seen as a Church. Therefore no man speaks or preaches in it, and there is no one who hears. For no one can be a hearer where there is no preacher (Rom. 10. verse 14). Therefore Christ speaks of the visible Church when he says, He who hears you hears me, and so on. For just as no one escaped from the flood safe outside Noah's ark, so too no one attains eternal salvation outside this kind of Church, that is, the visible one, if it is there; although in that Church he obtains that salvation, apprehended by faith from God through Christ, not from the Church itself, that is, not from the assembly of men. Moreover, that Noah's ark was a type of the visible Church as well, and not merely of the invisible, Peter teaches (1 Peter, chap. 3, verses 20, 21), who compares that ark with the assembly in which Baptism is performed and celebrated. But that assembly is certainly wholly visible, since, if the Church were invisible, Baptism could in no way be administered or celebrated in it. From this it comes about that the orthodox Fathers spoke most truly: He who does not have the visible Church as mother does not have God as Father. For such a Church, that is, the visible Church, is the pillar and ground of the truth, as Paul says, and is the house or temple of God on this earth, inasmuch as in it the Word of God is preached visibly and audibly (if one may so speak), and whoever separates himself from it also plainly separates himself from the truth of God and from the temple of God. Salvation will be in Zion, says the Prophet; the remnant of the people will bear fruit there, says another; and Zechariah, in her there is a fountain of living water springing up, that is, the pure explanation and preaching of the divine Word.

units.la: Quamobrem idem ille Propheta docet quicunque salutem quærent, certatim ad eam venturos esse, Dicet enim quisque proximo suo, Ascendamus in montem Domini. Ille vero mons Domini, est visibilis ecclesia, vocem Christi audiens. Quum vero nostri aduersarij nempe Libertini hos scripturæ locos ad ecclesiā invisibilem referunt, aut restringunt, toto cœlo errāt. Quî enim possemus alios inuitare vt ad eum montem venirent, qui non videretur, ad eam Sione confugerent, quæ cerni nō posset? Quomodo enim ecclesia invisibilis, aut alius quilibet cœtus invisibilis in his terris à nobis in his terris quæri potest? Quomodo fructus in invisibili loco nobis visibilis esse potest? Itaque magna est absurditas hos & similes locos ad ecclesiam invisibilem referre, quod illi faciunt. Verum, quemadmodum dixi in reformatis matis Euangelicisq; visibilibus ecclesijs id fieri, id est, salutem de Dei verbo doceri, proculdubio negari nisi a prorsus cæco surdoue homine non potest. Denique qui ad eam visibilem ecclesiam non venient, minatur Dominus(cui potius,quàm vlli Libertino hæretico, illiúsve scripto credendum est) tandem prorsus esse perituros. Et vt uno verbo dicam, est visibilis Ecclesia vnica illa vinea, quam sibi Dominus ex omnibus arboribus visibiliter decerpsit: est riuus, quæ ex omnibus aquis selegit: est columba, quam ex omnibus auibus dilexit: est ouis, quam ex omnibus pecudibus segregauit: est populus, quem sibi ex omnibus peculiarem conseruauit, vt qui Ecclesiam Dei spernit, nec ad eam sese adiungit, ille & vineam Dei, & lilium, & riuum, & columbam, & ouem, & populum Dei peculiarem aspernetur.Quod qui facit,certè quidem impius merito pronunciari ab omnibus potest. Atqui hæc tam præclara Ecclesiæ epitheta esse tribuenda Ecclesiæ Dei visibili, non autem soli inuisibili (sæpius enim hoc ipsum propter nostrorum aduersariorum, id est, Libertinorum perfrictam frontem repetedum est) apparet ex eo, quòd illa omnia ei cœtui conueniunt, ad quæ Deus nos inuitat, & ad quem vult vt accedamus.eum enim tot laudibus passim in sacra Scriptura ornat. Quomodo verò ad eum cœtum hic inuitarentur qui nusquam in terris est aut videri potest? Vera enim illa veterum sententia, idem de non entibus, & de non apparentibus iudicium à nobis fit, vt frustra ad ea hïc quærenda inuitemur. Ergo de Ecclesia visibili dicuntur. Quamobrem qui verè pius ac Christi seruus esse & manere volet (omnes autem boni velle debebunt)is certè sese illi visibili Ecclesiæ & cœtui debet con iungere qui vocem Christi, exturbata depulsaque nimirum idololatria audit in his terris & ei credit. Atque hoc tertium est quod nos priùs explicare voluimus, quàm susceptam confutationem aggrederemur. Restat igitur quartum & vltimum ex illis quatuor, quæ præmittenda censuimus caput. Est autem huiusmodi. Propter abusum rei, qui ab hominibus manat, nequaquam tamen rem ipsam esse aut damnandam aut tollendam. Exempli gratiâ. Homines ebriosi abutuntur vino ; gulosi, cibis : latrones, syluis ad sua latrocinia perpetranda: ergóne propterea tamen & vinum, & cibus, & syluæ damnanbuntur , vel ex hominum vsu prorsus tollentur ? Nequaquam certè: Nec aliter quisquam ( nisi communi omnium hominum iudicio careat) respondebit. Imò & ipso Dei verbo homines hæretici abutuntur ( quid enim est tam sanctum, quò non perrumpat & quod non polluat hominum væcordia & furor?) quis tamen idcirco vel ipsum Dei verbum condemnabit, vel tollendum extinguendumque fatebitur ? Nemo pius, quod equidem putem, Nemo nisi Atheus plane, & monstrū hóminis ac porcus potius quàm homo. Et certè quidem huius nostræ responsionis manifestissima est ratio Nam res ipsæ à Deo qui nihil malum creat, sunt conditæ. Earum autem abusus ex homi- num vitio manat: Itaq; cibi, ait Paulus, à Deo conditi sunt ad vsum hominis, & cum gra-tiarum actione sumpti, sancti sunt, nedum polluti: at eorum abusus velut ingurgitatio, & ebrietas, ex hominum intemperantia & scele re nascitur. Quamobrem ista duo, Res ipsa nimirum, & eiusdē rei abusus latissimè secer- nenda sunt, nec propter abusum rei de re ipsa malè pronūtiandū est, ne Deum potius quàm nos accusare videamur, qui res eas producit,& quidē semper quatenus res sunt, & tales sunt, bonas.Quid verò, nónne artibus optimis ho- mines scelerati abuti ad suam nequitiam so- lent? veluti, Mercatură, ad auaritiam, & cir- cumueniendos proximos: Scriptură,ad falsum scriptum supponendum: Arte monetaria, ad falsos numos cudendos, conflandos: Medici- na, ad toxica porrigenda? Ergo singulæ illæ artes tam necessariæ damnentur, & è vita ho- minum tollantur necesse est, si ex abusu de re- bus ipsis est semel statuendum ac iudicandum. Quid opidis cöditis commmodius? Et tamen quot modis possunt opidorum monumentis & mœnibus abuti homines scelerati ad sese contra iustum imperium tegendos?Nihil ho- minum societate & rebus publicis constitutis melius, & hominibus salutarius. Verumta- men quot homines hoc prætextu & dum sunt in illa societate, aut ei præsunt, ea tamen abvtuntur ad suum quæstum, aut ambitionem, aut crudelitatem? Ergo tollatur prorsus exstinguaturque omnis hominum societas, omnes Respublicæ & ciuitates funditus euertantur, opida excindantur, si propter rei abusum, res ipsa vel nobis odio esse debet: vel prorsus à nobis fugienda atque damnanda est. Quamobrem de reipsa ex illius abusu iudicare, est, vt iam intelligunt omnes, absurdissimum atq; imprudentissimum. Quod cum cuiuis tam perspicuum sit, vt illud à nemine negari posse exi-stimem, illud generaliter iam concludo, eos pessimè sentire, qui vel verbum Dei, vel veram Ecclesiam quæ in his terris visibilis est, fugiendam aut deserendam esse censent, docent vel contendunt, quoniam sceleratí quidam homines vel verbo Dei ad suos errores & sectas abutuntur: vel Ecclesiæ Dei nomine ac splendore, ad turpis suæ vitæ inquinamenta celanda: vel denique in ea, non quemadmodum oportet, aut ad quem finem à Deo constituta est, versantur. Quæ quatuor quoniam & verissima esse vident omnes, & magnam ad futuram libri (quem ad me misistis) refutationem lucem afferunt, iam ad eam aggrediar, si prius, quàm sit ipsius libri auctor scriptor ineptus, breuiter demonstrauero.
units.tr: Wherefore the same Prophet teaches that all who seek salvation will come eagerly to her, for "each will say to his neighbour, Let us go up to the mountain of the Lord." That mountain of the Lord is the visible Church, which hears the voice of Christ. But when our opponents, namely the Libertines, refer or restrict these passages of Scripture to the invisible Church, they wander entirely from the truth. For how could we invite others to that mountain, if it is not seen, or flee to that Zion, which cannot be perceived? For how could the invisible Church, or any other invisible assembly, be sought by us in this earth? How could fruit in an invisible place be visible to us? Therefore it is great absurdity to refer these and similar passages to the invisible Church, as they do. Indeed, as I have said, that this happens in the reformed, evangelical, visible churches, namely that salvation is taught from the Word of God, can undoubtedly be denied only by a man who is utterly blind and deaf. Finally, the Lord threatens that those who do not come to that visible Church will at last perish utterly (and he is to be believed rather than any Libertine heretic or his writing). And, to say it in one word: the visible Church is that one vineyard which the Lord has plucked for himself visibly out of all trees; it is the brook which he chose out of all waters; it is the dove which he loved out of all birds; it is the sheep which he set apart from all cattle; it is the people which he kept for himself as his own peculiar people out of all. Therefore whoever despises the Church of God and does not join himself to it, despises both the vineyard of God, and the lily, and the brook, and the dove, and the sheep, and the peculiar people of God. Whoever does this may certainly be rightly pronounced impious by all. Yet that these so splendid epithets of the Church must be attributed to the visible Church of God, and not to the invisible alone (for this must often be repeated on account of the brazen forehead of our opponents, that is, the Libertines), is clear from the fact that all those things agree with that assembly to which God invites us and to which he wills that we should come; for he adorns it with so many praises throughout Holy Scripture. But how would we be invited to that assembly here, which is nowhere on earth or can be seen? For the old saying is true, and we make the same judgement of non-beings and non-appearing things: we would be invited in vain to seek them here. Therefore these things are said of the visible Church. Wherefore whoever wishes to be and remain a true, pious servant of Christ (and all good people ought to wish this) must certainly join himself to that visible Church and assembly which hears and believes the voice of Christ in this earth, idolatry having been clearly driven out and cast down. And this is the third point which we wished to explain before we undertook the refutation proposed. There remains, therefore, the fourth and last of those four things which we thought should be set out at the head. It is of this kind: on account of the abuse of a thing, which comes from men, the thing itself is by no means to be condemned or removed. For example: drunkards abuse wine, gluttons abuse food, robbers abuse woods for carrying out their thefts. Are wine, food, and woods therefore to be condemned, or entirely removed from human use? By no means; and no one (unless he lacks the common judgement of all men) will answer otherwise. Indeed, heretics abuse even the Word of God itself (for what is so holy that the folly and fury of men does not break into it and defile it?). Yet who will therefore condemn the Word of God itself, or confess that it should be removed and extinguished? No pious man, as I think; no one but a plain atheist, a monster of a man, a pig rather than a man. And certainly the reason for this our answer is most manifest: for the things themselves were created by God, who creates nothing evil. But their abuse arises from human vice. Thus, as Paul says, foods were created by God for the use of man, and when taken with thanksgiving they are holy, not polluted; but their abuse, such as gluttony and drunkenness, arises from human intemperance and wickedness. Therefore these two things, namely the thing itself and the abuse of that same thing, must be carefully distinguished, and one must not pronounce badly about the thing itself on account of its abuse, lest we seem to accuse God rather than ourselves, who produced those things, and indeed always as far as they are things and such as they are, good. But do not wicked men commonly abuse the best arts for their wickedness? For example: commerce, for avarice and for cheating neighbours; writing, for forging documents; the art of coining, for minting and casting false coins; medicine, for administering poisons. Therefore, if we must once for all decide and judge from the abuse of things, those single arts, so necessary, must be condemned and necessarily removed from human life. What is more useful than founded cities? Yet in how many ways can wicked men abuse the walls and fortifications of cities to shelter themselves against just rule? Nothing is better than human society and constituted commonwealths, and nothing more salutary for men. Yet how many men, under this pretext, and while they are in that society or preside over it, nonetheless abuse it for their gain, or ambition, or cruelty? Therefore let every human society be utterly extinguished, let all commonwealths and states be overturned from the foundations, let cities be razed, if on account of the abuse of a thing the thing itself must be hateful to us or be utterly shunned and condemned by us. Wherefore to judge of the thing itself from its abuse is, as all now understand, most absurd and most imprudent. Since this is so plain to everyone that I think no one can deny it, I now conclude in general that those think very badly who maintain, teach, or contend that either the Word of God or the true Church, which is visible in this earth, is to be fled from or deserted, because certain wicked men abuse the Word of God for their errors and sects, or the name and splendour of the Church to hide the defilements of their shameful lives, or finally because men live in it not as they ought, or to the end for which it was established by God. Since all see that these four things are most true, and they bring great light for the future refutation of the book you sent me, I will now proceed to that, if first, before I go on, I have briefly shown that the author of the book itself is an inept writer.

units.la: In quo non persequar falsas illas verbi Dei allegationes, quibus totum hoc scriptum, quo iure, quáve iniuria, confutum est: esset enim infinitum. quum nullus penè sit in hoc libro depromptus è sacra Scriptura locus, quem iste non detorserit, vel intorserit, vel inepta allegoria inuolucrit. Veluti quum illum Geneseos locum, de Eua vxore Adami interpretatur allegorice de Ecclesia, in qua vnusquisque nostrum est, quasi illa sit vxor nostra: veluti itém quum locum Isaiae cap. 65. verf. 20. de pueris & peccatoribus centenarijs, ad omnes alios, praeterquam ad se vnum, refert, quasi vnus ipse coelestia sapiat, nos reliqui omnes, quotquot nunc in terris viuimus mortales? simus fungi, & stipites, & rerum diuinarum prorsus ignari. Veluti denique (pauca enim de multis breuitatis gratia, delegi) quum nos omnes Balaamo pseudoprophetae similes facit, se autem vnum profitetur superesse in terris tanquam alterum Mosen aut Eliam, qui vera sentiat, & doceat, ita nimirum iste contra Pauli praeceptum magnificè de se, & tamè falso, sentit: ita temerè (quod omnes haeretici faciunt) turget carnis suae sensu. Sed haec, inquam, quanquam grauissima peccata, tamen isti homini phantastico & qui omnem hominum societatem fugit, benignè condonemus (est enim illud verissimum quod habet proverbium, Αὐθάδεια seu Obstinatio opinioque de seipso huiusmodi hominum ἐρημότης ξυνοικος) infirmitates istius hominis, vt iubet Paulus, portemus & subleuemus: Illa verò quae sequuntur praesertim in scriptore qui se Christianam doctrinam tradere pollicetur tolerari non possunt, nimirum quod sibi toties manifestissimè contradicit. Nam veritas sibi ipsi constat semper, neque secum vnquam pugnat. Huius autem rei nonnulla exempla, vt in isto scripto legendo sint homines postea cautiores, afferam. Contradictio est in isto scriptore & absurditas manifesta, quum ait, (siquidem istius verba sunt mihi fideliter expositas, & ea comparatio, similitudoque, qua vtuntur, recte perpendatur, & huic argumento accommodetur.) Dona & gratias Dei esse penes Ecclesiam visibilem, & tamen eam negat esse quærendam: quasi non sit pij hominis officium, thesaurum gratiarum diuinarum illic quærere, vbicunque & apud quoscunque eum Dominus ipse depositum, Contradictio est ibidem & magna absurditas, quum, si modo concedunt eam similitudinem, (qua vtuntur in nostra, vt ipsi fingunt, tyrannide describenda) esse aptam, & suæ menti explicandæ consentaneam, quum, inquam, ait, Illa esse Dona Dei, quæ dare tamen situm est in quorundam hominum, vt ipsi vocant furum potestate. (His enim flosculis hæretici isti nos ornant) vt si velint nemo ea præter sese habeat, velut agros communes quidem, sed à se solis furibus, vt nos isti tamen contumeliose vocant, occupatos. Contradictio est atque absurditas insignis, quum scriptor iste approbat, vt inter homines sit aliqua societas ciuilis, eáque à nobis colatur: at neque concedit neque probat, vt Ecclesiam (quæ est hominum quatenus Christiani sunt, societas) certam habeamus, quasi scilicet minus ad fidem & vitam spiritualem necessarius rius sit Christianis Ecclesiæ (vbi verbum Dei prædicatur) cœtus, quàm ad hanc terrenam conseruandam est necessaria hominum inter se societas. Contradictio est atque absurditas, quod iste vbique Ministerium Euangelicum prorsus tollit, suadetque, quantum potest vt omnino à nobis negligatur: & tamen (sic nimirum cogente veritate) fatetur Pastores, id est, Ministros Euangelicos, ducere ad Christum, testari de Christo, admittitque esse ex ijs nonnullos & bonos, & qui veritatem & charitatem annuntiant. Saltem enim illi Pastores sunt audiendi, qui nos ad Christum adducunt: Saltem in illis, qui veritatem annuntiant, Ministerium Euangelicum est à nobis,& ab eo ipso,vel inuito probandum. Contradictio est apertissimaque absurditas, quod ait, Omnes vana docere & pro suo arbitratu, & tamen se esse audiendum: Nam si omnes errant, & ipse quoque errat: Aut se solum pulcrum, veracem, sapientem magno animi errore & superbia ipse in sua causa iudex pronuntiat. Contradictio est & oratio seipsam cuertens in ipsis terminis, quum ait Iustitiam, qua coram Deo iustificamur, esse imputatam nobis, & tamen intra nos & in nobis impleri. Contradictio est atque absurditas flagris digna, Quod vetat ne quenquam iudicemus, & tamen ipse tanquam pro tribunali sedens, velut auctoritate dictatoria nos omnes condemnat, & Ebrios & Balaamos vocat, & indubitanter in nos trásfert, atque accommodat, quæ in falsos Prophetas passim à sacra Scriptura dicuntur. Nam si nemo iudicare debet, cur ipse nos iudicat? Quod si sibi ipsi licere putat de nobis facere iudicium, cur non & nobis quoque de ipso licebit, & quidem meliori iure, qui eum in plurimis hæreticissimum deprehendamus & postea demonstraturi sumus? Contradictio est, atque absurditas, quam ne ipse quidem negare posset. Quod fatetur esse quædam Sacramenta à Christo ipso præscripta, vt à fidelibus obseruentur; & tamen eadem illa à pijs toto vitæ cursu negligi posse idem iste affirmat ac docet? Quæ, obsecro, & quanta est ista absurditas, fateri aliquid à Christo præceptum seruari, & tamen docere illud ipsum à nobis, bonâ conscientiâ, semper sperni posse, nec curandum, vt illo per totam vitam vtamur? Dicet fortasse, se sic sentire, vt ad tempus fuerint instituta illa Christi Sacramenta, & quæ nunc vsum nullum habere debeant. Sed hoc probet, quod dicit. vti enim nos qui nunc, id est, hoc tempore Dei gratiâ in vera Christi ecclesia viuimus, eodem Christo fruimur, eodemque spiritu regimur, quo Apostoli, & qui verè Apostolis successerunt: ita eadem fide, ijsdemque fidei sigillis nempe sacramentis veluti Baptismo & Cœna Domini salutem nostrā consequimur, ipsiusq; obsignationem accepimus, atque retinere debemus, quemadmodum Apostoli. Imò multo magis sacramentis hodie egemus, quàm illi, quoniam fumus in fide infirmiores, quàm illi, i. Apostoli. Denique (si vera est versio) fatetur tales ritus nos ad Christum adducere, fatetur ad senectutem vsque nos alere & vsque quo in cœlo simus; fatetur esse lac vtile, & & quo verè nutriamur; & tamen tales ritus à nobis negligendos putat. O cor ouis, ô stupidum ingenium hominis, ô insanum, imò blasphemum in Christum ipsum qui illa sacramenta instituit hominis iudicium; contumeliosum in Apostolos qui illa Ecclesiæ tradiderunt: iniuriosum in omnes pios & Dei filios, qui illa tam diligenter postea obseruarunt, & obseruanda docuerunt. Sed quid huic homini tam sibi ipsi contrario, & tam inconstanti facias, nisi vt ipsum relinquas sibi, animaduertásque hominem vertiginis spiritu duci, id quod non nos, sed ipsum illius scriptum manifestè clamat. Atque vt breuiter absque odio vllo (vtpote qui hominem non norim, imò cui bene cupiā ex animo) dicam quod res est. Quicunque istius libri auctor est, certè monstrum esse apparet ex variis hereseon assumetis conflatum. Peccatum originale agnoscit, in ceteris tamen purus putus partim Libertinus, partim Anabaptista est. Swenckfeldianus quoque est, dum Euangelicum Ministerium prorsus tollit, & tamen nonnunquam, vi veritatis coactus, illud probat. Pelagianus est, dum perfectam iustitiam nobis in hac vita tribuit, & tamen alibi fatetur à Deo in nobis esse, non à nobis, velle & perficere ita ni-
units.tr: I will not pursue those false appeals to the Word of God by which this whole writing has been refuted, rightly or wrongly; that would take forever, since there is hardly a passage of Holy Scripture in this book that he has not twisted, stretched, or wrapped in some silly allegory. For example, when he interprets allegorically the Genesis passage about Eve, the wife of Adam, as referring to the Church, in which each of us lives, as if she were our wife. Likewise, when he applies Isaiah 65:20, about the children and the sinners who die at a hundred years, to everyone except himself alone, as if he alone had heavenly wisdom and all the rest of us mortals now living on earth were mushrooms and stumps, utterly ignorant of divine things. Finally (I have chosen a few out of many, for the sake of brevity), when he makes all of us like Balaam the false prophet, and professes that he alone is left on earth, like another Moses or Elijah, to think and teach the truth, he thinks highly of himself against Paul's precept, and falsely. So rashly, as all heretics do, he swells with the sense of his own flesh. But these faults, grave as they are, we may kindly overlook in that man, who is fanciful and shuns all human fellowship (for the proverb is most true: self-conceit and an opinion of oneself such as this man's [Αὐθάδεια] is a companion of solitude [ἐρημότης ξυνοικος]). As Paul bids, we should bear with and support this man's weaknesses. But the things that follow cannot be tolerated, especially in a writer who promises to hand down Christian doctrine. I mean that he contradicts himself so often and so plainly. For truth always agrees with itself and never fights with itself. To make readers more careful when they read this writing, I will give some examples of this. There is a contradiction and a manifest absurdity in this writer when he says (if his words are faithfully set out for me, and the comparison and likeness he uses are weighed correctly and applied to this subject) that the gifts and graces of God are in the visible Church, and yet denies that the Church is to be sought. As if it were not the duty of a godly man to seek the treasure of divine graces there, wherever and with whomever the Lord has deposited it! There is also a contradiction and great absurdity in the same place. If they concede that the likeness he uses to describe our tyranny, as they pretend, is apt and suited to explain his own mind, then, I say, he says that these are the gifts of God, which yet it has pleased God to put in the power of certain men whom they themselves call thieves. (With these little flowers the heretics adorn us.) So that, if they wish, no one may have them except themselves, like common fields occupied by themselves alone, as thieves (which is what they insultingly call us). There is a striking contradiction and absurdity when this writer approves that there should be some civil society among men, and that we should cultivate it, yet neither concedes nor approves that we should have a fixed Church (which is the society of men insofar as they are Christians), as if a gathering of Christians where the Word of God is preached were less necessary for faith and spiritual life than human society among themselves is necessary for preserving this earthly life. There is a contradiction and absurdity in that he everywhere utterly removes the evangelical ministry and urges, as far as he can, that it be wholly neglected. And yet (so truth compels, of course) he confesses that the pastors, that is, the evangelical ministers, lead to Christ, bear witness of Christ, and he admits that some of them are good and proclaim truth and charity. For at least those pastors are to be heard who lead us to Christ; at least in those who proclaim the truth, the evangelical ministry must be approved by us, and by him too, even against his will. There is a contradiction and a most manifest absurdity in his saying that everyone teaches vain things according to his own judgment, and yet that he himself is to be heard. For if all err, he too errs; or else he pronounces himself alone beautiful, truthful, and wise, judging in his own cause with great error of mind and pride. There is a contradiction, and a speech overturning itself in its own terms, when he says that the righteousness by which we are justified before God is imputed to us, and yet is fulfilled within us and in us. There is a contradiction and absurdity worthy of the lash, in that he forbids us to judge anyone, and yet himself, sitting as if on a judgment seat, condemns us all with dictatorial authority, calls us drunkards and Balaams, and without doubt transfers to us and applies to us what Holy Scripture says everywhere about false prophets. For if no one ought to judge, why does he judge us? But if he thinks it lawful for himself to pass judgment on us, why will it not be lawful for us also to judge him, and indeed with better right, since we find him to be most heretical in many respects, as we shall show afterwards? There is a contradiction and absurdity which he himself could not deny: he confesses that certain sacraments were prescribed by Christ himself to be observed by the faithful, and yet this same man affirms and teaches that the godly may neglect those same sacraments throughout the whole course of their life. What, I beg you, and how great is this absurdity, to confess that something commanded by Christ is to be kept, and yet to teach that the same thing may always be scorned by us with a good conscience, and need not be cared for, that we should use it throughout life? Perhaps he will say that he thinks those sacraments of Christ were instituted only for a time, and that they ought now to have no use. But let him prove what he says. For just as we who now live, that is, in this time, by the grace of God, in the true Church of Christ, enjoy the same Christ and are ruled by the same Spirit as the Apostles and those who truly succeeded the Apostles, so by the same faith, and by the same seals of that faith, namely the sacraments such as Baptism and the Lord's Supper, we obtain salvation, have received its confirmation, and ought to retain it, as the Apostles did. Indeed, we today need the sacraments much more than they did, since we are weaker in faith than they, the Apostles. Finally (if the translation is correct), he confesses that such rites lead us to Christ, confesses that they nourish us even to old age and until we are in heaven, confesses that they are useful milk by which we are truly nourished; and yet he thinks such rites are to be neglected by us. O heart of sheep, O stupid mind of man, O insane judgment of a man, or rather blasphemous against Christ himself, who instituted those sacraments; insulting to the Apostles, who handed them down to the Church; injurious to all the godly and children of God, who afterwards observed them so diligently and taught that they were to be observed. But what can one do with a man so contrary to himself and so inconstant, except leave him to himself, and notice that the man is driven by a spirit of giddiness, which his writing itself clearly proclaims, not we. And to say briefly, without any hatred (since I do not know the man, and indeed I wish him well from my heart), what the matter is: whoever the author of this book is, he clearly appears to be a monster put together from various heresies. He acknowledges original sin, but in other respects he is purely and simply partly a Libertine, partly an Anabaptist. He is also a Schwenckfeldian, in that he utterly removes the evangelical ministry, and yet sometimes, compelled by the force of truth, he approves it. He is a Pelagian, in that he attributes perfect righteousness to us in this life, and yet elsewhere confesses that it is God who works in us, not we ourselves, both to will and to perform, in such a way that

units.la: Quaest. 16. minirum omni vento doctrinæ rapitur & iactatur, vt vbi consistere debeat, plane iste polypus omnes hereseon colores induens, nesciat. Porrò his omnibus explicatis iam adipsius libri confutationem veniamus. Huius scriptoris scopus est hæc, & quidem salsissima, docere, Primùm, Nullum esse hodie visibilem hominum cœtum, ac congregationem in his terris, quæ Ecclesia Dei dici possit: ac proinde pios ac fideles non debere hodie vlli Ecclesiæ vel reformatæ, vel alij cuiquam sese adiungere. Secundùm, Sacramentorum à Domino nostro Iesu Christo institutorum (quæ iste per contemptum ceremonias appellat) vsum posse per totam vitam bonâ conscientiâ à pijs & fidelibus contemni, ac per totam vitam negligi. Tertium, Posse quemque domi suæ priuatim, sine Pastore, sine Doctore, sine externo Ministerio Euangelico satis consequi veram verbi Dei intelligentiam; quantùm ipsi & ad salutem, & ad vitam sanctam necessarium est. Quæ tria, licet vel ipso intuitu sint horrenda, tamen iste pertinaciter tuetur, & ex ipsius epistola facile colliguntur esse verus istius scripti scopus. In quo sanè sophistarum morem iste secutus est, qui, quemadmodum Aristoteles docet, scribentes, disputantésque in eo maximè laborant, vti conclusio, quam ex præmissis eficere volunt, auditores, lectoréque lateat. Itaque quum reliqui ingenui scriptores soleant epistolas suas præfigere librorum suorum initijs, scopumq; suum in illis statim patefacere, vt certa sit meta, ad quam toto reliquo scripto lectorcs perpetuò colliment: iste contrâ, & quidem magno sophisticóque astu, illum scopum suum ad finem tamen libri reiecit, & conclusionem (quam ex tot præmissis à se Quæstionibus elicere studet) diligenter vsque ad eum locum celat. Vnde de isto scripto vulgare & tritum illud verè vsurpari potest, In cauda venenum.
units.tr: Question 16. ...is caught up and tossed about by every wind of doctrine, so that he cannot tell where he ought to stand, this polypus wearing every colour of heresy. Now that all these points have been set out, let us come to the refutation of the book itself. The aim of this writer, and a most salty one at that, is to teach: first, that there is today no visible assembly or congregation of men on this earth that can be called the Church of God, and therefore that the godly and faithful ought not today to join themselves to any church, whether reformed or otherwise. Second, that the sacraments instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ (which he contemptuously calls ceremonies) may be despised and neglected throughout life by the godly and faithful with a good conscience. Third, that anyone can, privately in his own house, without a pastor, without a teacher, without the external evangelical ministry, attain a sufficient understanding of the Word of God, as much as is necessary for salvation and a holy life. Although these three propositions are horrible even at first sight, he stubbornly defends them, and from his letter they are easily gathered to be the true aim of this writing. In this he has certainly followed the custom of the sophists, who, as Aristotle teaches, when writing and disputing take great pains to keep the conclusion they wish to draw from their premises hidden from listeners and readers. Thus, whereas other honest writers are accustomed to set their letter at the beginning of their books and to reveal their aim at once, so that the reader has a fixed goal toward which he may keep his eyes through the rest of the work, this man, with great and sophistical cunning, has put off his aim to the end of the book, and carefully hides the conclusion, which he strives to draw from so many premises, until that point. Hence of this writing that common and well-worn proverb may truly be applied: Poison in the tail.

units.la: Certè quod ad primum caput, nempe, Nullam nunc in terris esse visibilem Ecclesiam, cui se fideles adiungere debeant, satis illud à nobis antea in præfatione refutatum est, vbi docuimus, quænam sint verae Ecclesiae Dei dignoscendae & cui te adiungere debeas agnoscendae, notae. Quod ad secundum, nempe Sacramentorum vsum à pijs negligi posse, illud satis euertitur, quòd illa ipsa Sacramenta iubentur obseruari à nobis. Nam de Baptismo dicit, vtens verbo imperandi Christus, Ite, baptizate: De sacra verò Coena distinctis verbis præcipit, Manducate, Bibite. Quinimo illa ipsa sacra Domini nostri Coena instituta est, vt vsum in Ecclesia Dei habeant, donec Christus ipse veniat, vt loquitur Scriptura, id est, vsque ad nouissimum diem & resurrectionis tempus. Quare impunè citraque ipsius Dei conteptum neque Coena, neque Baptismus negligi potest. Deniq; tertiū istius libri caput, nimirū Ecclesiam Dei ac veros fideles carere posse in perpetuū Pastoribus & Doctoribus, apertissimè ex eo refutatur. Primum ꝸ Christus mittens
units.tr: Certainly, as to the first head, namely that there is now no visible Church on earth to which the faithful ought to join themselves, this has already been sufficiently refuted by us in the preface, where we showed what the marks are by which the true Churches of God are recognised and by which you ought to know to which of them you should join yourself. As to the second, namely that the use of the sacraments can be neglected by the godly, this is sufficiently overthrown by the fact that those same sacraments are commanded to be observed by us. For concerning Baptism, Christ, using the language of command, says, Go, baptize; and concerning the holy Supper he commands in plain words, Eat, drink. Moreover, that holy Supper of our Lord was instituted so that it might be in use in the Church of God until Christ himself comes, as Scripture says, that is, until the last day and the time of the resurrection. Therefore neither the Supper nor Baptism can be neglected with impunity and without contempt of God himself. Finally, the third head of this book, namely that the Church of God and true believers can do without pastors and teachers for ever, is most plainly refuted by this: First, since Christ, sending

units.la: 1. Cor. 11. vers. 26. Apostolos difcerte ait, Ite, docete, Non ait, Ite, dicite hominibus vt priuatim tantum ac domi legant: sed ait, Docete. Quod si tum ipsimet Apostoli, tum Apostolorum successores docere debent, Ergo in Ecclesia doctores sint oportet. Si aliqui sunt doctores in Ecclesia, ergo & aliqui discipuli, id est, si qui docere iubentur, nos ergo eos quoque audire ex necessitate correlatiuorum iubemur. Quandoquidem ait etiam Paulus, Fides est ex auditu, non ex lectione priuata. Nam sine discipulo nemo dici vel intelligi possit esse doctor, Ergo si qui in Ecclesia iubentur esse doctores, iubentur & alij quidam in eadem Ecclesia esse auditores & discipuli: atque ita demonstratur ex Dei verbo necessarium esse in Ecclesia pastorum officium. Haec prima est illius tertij capitis huius libri confutatio. Secunda est ex eo, quod Paulus enumerans ordines, quos Deus in Ecclesia sua ad eam edificandam perpetuos esse voluit, diserte recensèt, Pastores ac Doctores. Non est autem frustraneum & inutile vel spernendum mandatum & Dei consilium. Quare Pastores ac Doctores in Ecclesia Dei ad ipsius aedificationem perpetuos esse oportet: ac proinde oportet reliquos fideles esse eorum Pastorum discipulos ac auditores. Quo fit, vt qui Ministerium Pastorum ac Docentium in Ecclesia statuit inutile vel tollendum, ille proculdubio vtilius quippiam Ecclesiae, quam ipsum Solem (cuius luce in his terrenis tatum actionibus dirigimur) adimat, eam verò suae instru-
units.tr: 1. Cor. 11. vers. 26. the Apostles, plainly says, Go, teach. He does not say, Go, tell men, so that they may read privately and at home only; but he says, Teach. If then the Apostles themselves, and the successors of the Apostles, ought to teach, then there must be teachers in the Church. If there are some teachers in the Church, then there are also some disciples, that is, if some are commanded to teach, then we too are by necessity of correlatives commanded to hear them. Since Paul also says, Faith comes by hearing, not by private reading. For no one can be called or understood to be a teacher without a disciple. Therefore, if some in the Church are commanded to be teachers, some others in the same Church are also commanded to be hearers and disciples; and thus it is shown from God's Word that the office of pastors is necessary in the Church. This is the first refutation of that third head of this book. The second is from the fact that Paul, listing the orders which God willed to be perpetual in his Church for its building up, expressly names Pastors and Teachers. But the command and counsel of God is not idle, useless, or to be despised. Therefore pastors and teachers must be perpetual in the Church of God for its edification, and consequently the rest of the faithful must be the disciples and hearers of those pastors. From this it follows that whoever holds that the ministry of pastors and teachers in the Church is useless or to be removed, he undoubtedly takes away from the Church something more useful than the sun itself (by whose light we are directed in all our actions in this earthly life), and he weakens it by his own

units.la: instructionis instrumeto priuet, denique Dei ipsius ordinationem impie abroget, ac conculcet.Caeterum perpetuum apparebit in hoc scriptore illud vitiū, vt ex abusu rei de re ipsa iudicium faciat, & eam propterea tollendam censeat: quod est, quemadmodum diximus, absurdissimum.Sed vt Papistae veram Dei Ecclesiam oppugnant a dextris,dum eam semper in his terris visibilem fuisse,& perpetuam persoñarum successionem habuisse dicunt: sic isti tum ex Donatistis (fuit enim haec Donatistarum, vt Augustinus ostendit,qui illorum temporibus vixit, & cum illis saepe disputauit, fuit inquā, haec Donatistarum haeresis, quòd Ecclesia vollent in his terris esse perfectam,quod & isti Libertini postulant a nobis: quòd propterea sese ab Ecclesias vbi purū Dei verbum annuntiabatur, Donatistae separarent,& seorsim suos coetus habere vellent) hoc & isti: quòd Donatistae clamarent iampridem ex his terris periisse Ecclesiā & desiisse in ipsis Apostolis: perinde & isti. Ergo vt dixi,isti tum ex Donatistis tum ex Swenckfeldianis conflati a sinistris aggrediuntur,dum eā prorsus è Mundo perijsse, & nusquam iam extare cōtendunt.
units.tr: ...instrument of its instruction. Moreover, this writer's perpetual fault will appear: he makes a judgment about the thing itself from the abuse of the thing, and therefore thinks it ought to be abolished, which is, as we have said, most absurd. But just as the Papists attack the true Church of God from the right, while they say that it has always been visible on this earth and has had a perpetual succession of persons, so these men, made up partly of Donatists and partly of Swenckfeldians, attack it from the left. For this was the heresy of the Donatists, as Augustine shows, who lived in their times and often disputed with them: they held that the Church must be perfect on this earth, which these Libertines too demand of us, and for that reason the Donatists separated themselves from the churches where the pure word of God was preached, and wished to hold their own assemblies apart. These men too hold the same view, and the Donatists long ago cried out that the Church had perished from this earth and had ceased to exist in the apostles themselves; so do these men. Therefore, as I have said, these men, compounded partly of Donatists and partly of Swenckfeldians, attack from the left, while they contend that the Church has utterly perished from the world and nowhere still exists.

units.la: Et haec quidem hactenus: iam ipsa libri argumenta singula perpendamus. Breuiter autem illa ordine proponemus, & ad ea respondebimus. illud modo meminerint omnes scopum huius libri esse, vt doceat pios homines nulli Ecclesiae visibili in his terris sese adiungere debere.Quod iste probare ac euincere sic conatur,& quidem in responsione ad primam Quæstionem.
units.tr: So much for these matters for now. Let us now weigh each of the book's arguments themselves, and we shall set them out briefly in order and reply to them. Let everyone only keep in mind that the aim of this book is to teach that pious men ought not to join themselves to any visible church on this earth. This he tries to prove and establish, and indeed he attempts it thus in his answer to the first Question.

units.la: Oportebit pios in his terris respicere ad Deum, non ad homines: Ergo pij in his terris nulli Ecclesiæ visibili sese coniungere debent.
units.tr: The pious must look on this earth to God, not to men. Therefore the pious on this earth ought not to join themselves to any visible church.

units.la: Nego consecutionem. Nam quamuis Ecclesia visibilis in his terris constat hominibus, tamen qui sese Ecclesiæ adiungit, non in homines ipsos respicit, sed in Deum, cui illi serviunt. Quare vt vnâ cum illis ipse quoque Deo seruiat,adhæret illi cœtui.Sic Paulus quærebat sese adiungere discipulis,& Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ, non vt in homines illos respiceret, aut illorum hominū seruus esset, sed vt communi fide, & consensu, & charitate cum illis Deo, Deo inquam,ipsi seruiret & cōmunibus cum iis Sacramentis Hierosolymis vteretur. Sic qui seruus est alicuius Principis domestieus,debet se reliquo seruorum eiusdem Principis cœtui & consortio adiungere, in ipsius palatio versari, & se ad iussa Principis audieda cum aliis sistere,vt verè domesticus esse appareat,& vnà cum cæteris famulis cibum capiat.
units.tr: I deny the consequence. For although the visible Church on this earth consists of men, yet he who joins himself to the Church does not look to the men themselves but to God, whom they serve. Therefore, in order to serve God together with them, he too cleaves to that assembly. Thus Paul sought to join himself to the disciples and to the Church of Jerusalem, not so that he might look to those men or be the servant of those men, but so that, by common faith, consent, and love with them, he might serve God, God I say, himself, and partake with them in the common sacraments at Jerusalem. So too, a servant who belongs to the household of some prince ought to join himself to the company and fellowship of the other servants of the same prince, dwell in the prince's palace, and present himself with the others to hear the prince's commands, so that he may appear to be truly of the household, and take his food together with the other attendants.

units.la: In responsione ad Quæstionem secundam.
units.tr: In reply to the second question.

units.la: Debent verè pij communicare cum Deo: Ergo nequaquam cum Ecclesia visibili.
units.tr: True believers ought to communicate with God; therefore by no means with the visible Church.

units.la: Falsa consecutio. Qui enim cum Ecclesia visibili communicant, iidem illi cum Deo ipso communicant, quoniam nostræ cum Deo communicationis veræ vinculum, ac ratio est fides, cuius initium, ædificatio, ac increincrementum in his terris, est auditio verbi Dei, Sacramentorum participatio, & mutua exhortatio, quæ non nisi in Ecclesia esse & fieri possunt. Ergo qui cum Deo communicare & quærit & cupit, ille ad Ecclesiam, (in qua sola velut in templo suo ad eum finem Deus præsens est) accedat, seque illi adiungat. Sic olim pij & fideles qui Deo per fidem adhærebant, sic quoque Ecclesiæ (vt est in Actis) adiungebant, sic qui ex Principis domesticis & purpuratis censeri vult, eorumque præropatiuis frui, consortio se illorum inscribat necesse est. Qui in numero militum vere censeri vult, ad signa frequens sit, & in castris versetur oportet.
units.tr: A false inference. For those who communicate with the visible Church are the very same people who communicate with God himself, since the true bond and ground of our communion with God is faith. Its beginning, its building up and its growth in this earthly life are the hearing of the Word of God, the participation in the sacraments and mutual exhortation, which can be and take place only in the Church. Therefore whoever seeks and desires to communicate with God should come to the Church (in which alone God is present, as in his own temple, for that purpose) and join himself to it. So in former times the godly and faithful, who adhered to God through faith, joined themselves to the Church (as it is in the Acts). So too, whoever wishes to be counted among the Prince's household servants and to enjoy their privileges must necessarily enrol himself in their fellowship. Whoever wishes to be truly counted among the soldiers should be often at the standards and should live in the camp.

units.la: Qui cum Deo per fidem communicat, habet illud omne quod homines decet commune habere: Ergo spernenda est nostra cum visibilis Ecclesiæ corpore communio.
units.tr: Whoever communicates with God through faith has all that men ought to have in common. Therefore our communion with the body of the visible Church is to be despised.

units.la: Falsa est ista consecutio. Nam qui cum Deo communicat, ille etiam cum Christo prius communicet necesse est. Verùm cum Christo nemo communicat, qui idem cum reliquo Ecclesiæ visibilis corpore non coniungatur: quoniam illa est implementum corporis Christi, vt ait Paulus, 1.Corinth.12.
units.tr: That inference is false. For whoever communicates with God must necessarily first communicate with Christ. But no one communicates with Christ who is not at the same time joined to the rest of the body of the visible Church, since that body is the fullness of Christ, as Paul says, 1 Corinthians 12.

units.la: Quod de visibili quoque Ecclesia esse intelligendum, non tantùm de inuisibili, supra satis demonstrauimus. Nam in illa visibili, in qua purum Dei verbum annuntiatur, Deus est præsens & quidem longè meliori nunc ratione per Euangelij prædicationem, quàm olim in visibili tēplo Salomonis,in quo Deus tamē propter ceremonias rerum futura rum,& quas Euangelium habet,dicebatur esse presens. Deinde cū Paulus,1. Timot. 3. ait,Ecclεsiā esse columnam veritatis,docet illius loci circunstantia de visibili Ecclesia, in qua sint Pastores, à Paulo dici. De ea enim illud affirmat Paulus, cui Pastores, & Diaconi, & Presbyteri creantur, quales illic & eodem capite describit Paulus: Ecclesiæ verò inuisibili nulli Diaconi, Presbyteri, & Pastores creari, dariue possunt,quoniam est inuisibilis. Quare de Ecclesia visibilíquæ est cœtus hominum in Christi nomen cogregatorum & Dei verbum annuntiatum à Pastoribus audientium, intelligatur illa laus Ecclesiæ,quod sit columna veritatis,& implementum corporis Christi:non de inuisibili duntaxat ecclesia, vt Libertini isti somniant. Ergo qui cum Deo communicare vult, cum Ecclesia quoque ipsa visibili communicet necesse est.
units.tr: We have already shown quite sufficiently that this must be understood of the visible Church as well, and not only of the invisible. For in that visible Church in which the pure Word of God is proclaimed, God is present, and indeed now by a far better means, through the preaching of the Gospel, than of old in the visible temple of Solomon, in which God was nevertheless said to be present because of the ceremonies of future things, which the Gospel has. Next, when Paul says in 1 Timothy 3 that the Church is the pillar of the truth, the circumstances of that passage show that he is speaking of the visible Church, in which there are ministers. For Paul affirms that of the church in which deacons, elders and ministers are appointed, such as Paul describes there in the same chapter. But no deacons, elders or ministers can be appointed or given to the invisible Church, since it is invisible. Therefore that praise of the Church, that it is the pillar of the truth and the fullness of the body of Christ, must be understood of the visible Church, which is the assembly of men gathered in the name of Christ and hearing the Word of God proclaimed by ministers, and not of the invisible Church alone, as those Libertines dream. Therefore whoever wishes to communicate with God must necessarily communicate also with the visible Church itself.

units.la: Quum Ecclesia vocatur Cōmunio sanctorum, illa Communio de Deo non de ipsis hominibus intelligenda est. Ergo non est necessaria nostra cum reliquis pijs, id est, cum Ecclesia visibili communicatio, vt simus in communione sanctorum.
units.tr: Since the Church is called the communion of saints, that communion is to be understood as a communion with God, not with men themselves. Therefore our communication with the other godly, that is, with the visible Church, is not necessary in order that we may be in the communion of saints.

units.la: Falsum est antecedens,Id est falsa est illorū verborum , Communio sanctorum interpretatio.Dicitur enim Ecclesia sanctorum Cōmunio, non tantùm, quà fideles cum Deo, sed etiam qua inter se communicant.Habent enim comCommunia hæc inter se, vnum corpus, ergo & vnum cœtum in quo se omnes etiam visibiliter consociant: vnum Spiritum, vnam spem suæ vocationis vnum Deum, vnam fidem, vnum Baptisma, ergo & vnam sacrā Cœ-nam. Vt non sit tam absurdum, ac mirum fratres Cosanguineos adhuc filiosfamilias in vna & eadē vnius Paretis domo simul nō habitate: quàm est offendiculi plenum fratres conspirituales & pios in vnam & eandem Ecclesiæ congregationem non simul conuenire & coniungi, vt etiam docet Dauid, Quàm bonum & quàm iucundum, ait, fratres habitare in vnum! Itaque qui sese ab eo cœtu seiungunt, Scismatici vel Hæretici merito nominantur.
units.tr: The antecedent is false; that is, the interpretation of those words, "communion of saints," is false. For the Church is called the communion of saints not only in so far as the faithful communicate with God, but also in so far as they communicate with one another. For these holy ones have among themselves one body, and therefore also one assembly in which they all associate with one another visibly as well; one Spirit, one hope of their calling, one God, one faith, one baptism, and therefore also one holy Supper. It is therefore no less absurd and strange for brothers of the same blood, while still sons under the father's authority, not to live together in one and the same house of one father, than it is full of offence for brothers in the Spirit and godly men not to gather and be joined together in one and the same congregation of the Church. David also teaches this: "How good and how pleasant it is, he says, for brothers to dwell together in unity!" Therefore those who separate themselves from that assembly are rightly called schismatics or heretics.

units.la: Sese visibili Ecclesiæ adiungere, est homi-num seruum fieri, quales esse non debemus. Ergo nulli Ecclesiæ visibili adhærere oportet.
units.tr: To join oneself to the visible Church is to become a slave of men, which we ought not to be. Therefore one ought to adhere to no visible Church.

units.la: Hoc argumentum isti quidem videtur palmarium. Itaque in epistola & in responsione Act. 3. & 4. Quæstione illud repetit. Verum est omnino futile, imo nihili: Nos igitur non debere in ijs quæ ad fidem pertinent fieri hominum seruos, libenter concedimus: sed negamus eos, qui se adiungunt Ecclesiæ Dei visibili (cuius notas supra descripsimus, & quales notæ extant si non in totū saltem magnam partem in reformatis Ecclesijs) negamus, inquam, qui se ijs Ecclesijs addunt, fieri seruos hominum: imò ex seruis idolorum, hominum aut hærescœn fiunt solius Dei serui, vt diserte docet Paulus, Quomodo conuersi fueritis ad Deu, ait, alloquens Thessalonicenses, qui se Ecclesiae visibili adiunxerant, relictis idolis, vt serviretis Deo viuo.
units.tr: This argument seems to that man to be the strongest of all. And so he repeats it in the letter and in the reply to the third and fourth question. It is entirely futile, indeed worthless. We gladly concede that we ought not to become slaves of men in those things which pertain to faith; but we deny that those who join themselves to the visible Church of God (whose marks we have described above, and which marks are found, if not wholly, at least in a great part, in the reformed Churches) become slaves of men when they join those Churches. Rather, from slaves of idols, of men or of heresies they become servants of God alone, as Paul clearly teaches, addressing the Thessalonians, who had joined themselves to the visible Church: "How you were converted to God," he says, "having left idols, to serve the living God."

units.la: In Responsione ad Quaest.3.
units.tr: In the Answer to Question 3.

units.la: In hac responsione explicat tatum ineptam quandam suam similitudinem, ex qua colligitur contra istius sententiam & tamen ex ista similitudine, vera Dei dona & salutaria esse penes Ecclesiam visibilem, vti agri communes sunt penes eos qui eos, aliis negligentibus, occupaverunt. Ac proinde vt eis Dei donis fruamur, esse ad Ecclesiam visibilem accedendum. Deinde istius hominis imperitia hic apparet, qui confundit, Communionem ipsam & Rem cui communicamus. Appellat enim Deum Comunionem, quum tamen Deus sit ipsum illud, cuius fruitione a multis percepta, nascitur inter eos communio. Vt igitur aliud est res communis, velut domus aliqua communis: aliud ipsum ius communionis, seu ipsum ius commune pluribus in ea ipsa domo, ac re communi: sic aliud est, Deus, aliud communio ipsa Dei, quae sane non potest vel esse vel fingi, nisi plures sint qui communicent Deo, ac proinde aliqua sit Ecclesia, quae Deo fruatur communiter. Ex quo sit, vt huic corpori Ecclesiae sese adiungere debeant etiam visibiliter, quum illud corpus seu Ecclesia visibilis (quales nunc summa Dei gratia, sunt Ecclesiae Dei reformatae) sint ij qui Deo fruantur, illíque communicent.
units.tr: In this answer he explains a rather pointless comparison of his own, from which it follows, against his own position, and yet also from this comparison, that the true and saving gifts of God are found with the visible Church, just as common fields belong to those who have seized them while others have neglected them. Therefore, in order to enjoy those gifts of God, we must join the visible Church. Next, this man's ignorance appears here, since he confuses communion itself and the thing in which we share. For he calls God a communion, though God is that very thing whose enjoyment, received by many, gives rise to communion among them. Just as a common thing, such as some common house, is one thing, and the right of communion itself, or the right held in common by several people in that same house and common property, is another, so God is one thing and the communion of God is another. This communion certainly cannot exist or even be imagined unless there are several who share in God, and therefore some Church which enjoys God in common. From this it follows that they ought to join themselves to this body of the Church also visibly, since those who enjoy God and share in him are that body, or the visible Church (such as, by the highest grace of God, the reformed Churches of God now are).

units.la: In Responsione ad Quaest. 4.
units.tr: In the Answer to Question 4.

units.la: Eua, quod erat adiumetum Adamo datum, illi nocuit. Ergo Ecclesia visibilis nobis nocebit, ne soli simus si illi nos adiungamus.
units.tr: Eve, who was given to Adam as a helper, harmed him. Therefore the visible Church will harm us, so that we will not be alone if we join ourselves to it.

units.la: Quid verò? iste concedit, imò suadet, vt nos adiungamus Ecclesiae inuisibili: Illa vere est etiam adiumentum, vt Eua fuit Adamo ex istius interpretatione, ac proinde noxiū. Ergo neque visibili, neque inuisibili Ecclesiae adhaerere iam iuxta istius sententiam debebimus, quia nimirum nocebit nobis, si quod adiumentum quaerimus. Verum quàm est ista allegoria inepta, quemadmodum ille ipse postea fatetur, quum ait hoc adiutorium, de quo locutus est Deus, ad multiplicandi procreandique generis humani adiutorii & vsum pertinere, non ad huiusmodi quaestiones, ad quas tamen iste trastulit. Ergo inepte fecit dū illam ita produxit. Et certe quidem longe dissimillima est ratio Ecclesiae & Euae. Ecclesia cui accedimus, nos ad Dei verbum reuocat, ac proinde est verissimum nobis adiumentum. Eua vero Adamum a Dei verbo auocauit & abduxit, atque idcirco fuit illi nocumentum. Quare dissimillimas iste res inter se comparat, de quibus idem tamen cocludit.
units.tr: But what? This man concedes, indeed urges, that we join the invisible Church. By his own interpretation, that Church too is a helper, just as Eve was to Adam, and therefore harmful. So, according to his opinion, we ought to cling neither to the visible nor to the invisible Church, since it would harm us, clearly, if we sought any helper. But how foolish this allegory is, as he himself later confesses when he says that the help of which God spoke pertains to the use of multiplying and procreating the human race, not to questions of this kind, to which nonetheless he has transferred it. Therefore he acted foolishly in stretching it this way. And indeed the reason of the Church and of Eve is far from alike. The Church to which we come calls us back to the Word of God, and therefore it is most truly a help to us. Eve, however, drew Adam away from the Word of God and led him astray, and for that reason she was a harm to him. Therefore he compares things that are most unlike each other, yet concludes the same thing about them.

units.la: Etsi tempore Abrahami gentiles non erant in Ecclesia Dei visibili, vt ipsum semen ac familia Abrahami, nihilominus tamen erant in vera ac inuisibili Dei Ecclesia, & ad Deum tanquam filij pertinebant. Ergo etsi in visibili Dei Ecclesia, quæ vera est, non simus, tamen propterea non definimus ad Deum tanquam filij pertinere.
units.tr: Although in Abraham's time the Gentiles were not in the visible Church of God, as the seed and household of Abraham themselves were, nevertheless they were in the true and invisible Church of God, and belonged to God as his children. Therefore, even if we are not in the visible Church of God, which is the true one, we do not on that account cease to belong to God as his children.

units.la: Nego tempore Abrahami, & quamdiu illud inter Circuncisionem & Præputium discrimen ex Dei verbo durauit, Gentes ipsas ad Deum, tanquam ipsius filios, pertinuisse, & in vera ac inuisibili Ecclesia fuisse. Sic enim Apostolus Iesu Christi Paulus scribit ad Ephesios. Propterea mementote vos quondam Gentes in carne (quæ dicebatur præputium ab ea, quæ vocatur circuncisio in carne, & quæ manibus fit) vos, inquam, illo tempore fuisse absque Christo, alienos à Repub. Israëlis, & extraneos à pactis promissionum, spem non habentes, & Dei expertes in Mundo. Ex quo apparet verum esse quod dicimus, falsum autem, quod iste ait: & tamen conatur his tribus argumentis confirmare: Primum, quia Deus promiserat fore, vt gentes essent in Ecclesia, ergo iam tunc erant in ea. Respondeo. Promiserat quidem Deus eas futuras in Ecclesia, quemadmodum postea, id est, post incarnationem Domini nostri Iesu Christi reipsa præstitit: sed tunc nondum in ea erant, id est, ante illum Christi aduentum illam suam promissionem Deus non impleuit. Sic possum tibi quippiam promittere, quod tamen in triennium aut aliud aliquod longum tempus differam. Sic promisit nobis Deus vitam æternam, quam tamen dum hic à Domino peregrinamur nondum reipsa obtinemus. Secundum istius falsæ sententiæ probandæ argumentum est, Deus gentibus vitam dabat, ergo gentes ad eum, tanquam filij, pertinebāt. Respondeo. Multæ sunt species beneuolentiæ ac beneficentiæ Dei, sed duæ imprimis, eæque prorsus distinctæ, & inter se diuersæ, quarum prima esse absque secunda potest: secunda tamen absque prima esse non item: veluti vnum potest esse absque duobus, at duo non possunt esse, quin in sese comprehendant vnum. Duobus igitur modis & res à se creatas amat Deus, & illæ ad eum pertinent, nempe vel iure creationis, quo modo res omnes ad eum pertinent, & pluit super bonos & malos: vel iure redemptionis, quo modo soli illi ad Deum pertinent, quos pro filijs agnoscit. Sic dicitur in psalmis. Non fecit taliter omni natio- ni, & Beatum populum cui sic: Beatus populus cuius Dominus Deus eius. Ergo gentes ad Deum pertinebant tunc etiam iure creationis, id est, vt res ad ipso creatæ: non autem iure redemptionis, id est, velut filij ab eo adoptati, quo modo nepe vnū Abrahami semen ad Deū iam tunc pertinebat.
