Tertium istius hominis argumentum est, vetus adoptio & electio populi Israelitici (de qua fit mentio in scripturis) fuit tantum maior quædam istius populi delinitio, seu blandior tractatio ac appellatio, non autem peculiaris quidam & diuersus fauor, quo se illius duntaxat populi Patrem & redemptorem Deus ostenderet. Ergo etiam tunc gentes ad Dei peculium, quemadmodum & Israelitæ, spectabant. Respondeo. Nihil manifestius aduersus Dei verbum affirmari potest, quàm quod iste hic disertis verbis scribit.Ecce enim Moses istum refutat. Quum pos-sessionem distribueret Excelsus gentibus, ait, quū disparaaret filios Adami, statuit terminos populorum pronumero filiorū Israelis, Quia pars Iehoua est populus eius, Iacob funiculus possessionis eius: & quod nunc afferebamus ex psal.147. Non fecit taliter omni nationi. Item psal. 76. Solum in Iudaea notus Deus. Atqui eorum Deus, id est, Pater non erat, a quibus non agnoscebatur.Ergo illius duntaxat populi proprie & Pater erat & Deus. Ex quo fit, ut apud Ofeam Israelitæ dicantur ij fuisse, qui soli vocabantur Populus meus. Et passim, ea sola gens dicatur gens electa in peculium Dei. Nā quod nos, qui olim eramus Gentes, hodie & sumus & vocamur verus populus Dei, illud factum est, quoniam, vt ait Paulus, Christus veniens in Mundum, vtrosque populos fecit vnum dissesso pariete intergerimo, qui nos à populo Dei segregabat. Ex vtrisque igitur & Iudaeis & Gentibus Christus veniens fecit vnum ouile, quoniam antea non erant gentes ouile Dei, Quin imò, ait idem Paulus, Obduratio nuc obtigit ex parte Israëli tamisper dum plenitudo Gentium introierit. Quare ante Christi aduentū prædicatum qz ab Apostolis Euangeliū, Gentes nō fuerunt populus Dei, sed soli Iudæi, cōtra quā tamē iste & sentit & scribit. Ex quibus apparet, q. falso statuat Ecclesiā Dei inuisibilē fuisse tēpore Abrahami etiā inter Gentes: ergo & falsum nos ea sola inuisibili cōtentos esse debere, spreta hac visibili, quę ex certis ipsius notis dignosci potest. Veniamus ad alia phrenetici istius hominis argumenta.
units.tr: I deny that in Abraham's time, and as long as that distinction between circumcision and uncircumcision lasted by the word of God, the Gentiles themselves belonged to God as his children, or were in the true and invisible Church. For so the apostle Paul writes to the Ephesians: Therefore remember that you, once Gentiles in the flesh (who were called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision in the flesh, which is made by hands), I say, at that time were without Christ, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. From this it appears that what we say is true, and what he says is false; yet he tries to confirm it with three arguments. First, because God had promised that the Gentiles would be in the Church, therefore they were already in it at that time. I reply: God indeed promised that they would be in the Church in the future, just as he afterwards actually fulfilled this, that is, after the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. But then they were not yet in it; that is, before that coming of Christ, God did not fulfil that promise. So I too can promise you something, which I nevertheless postpone for three years or some other long time. So God promised us eternal life, which nevertheless we do not yet actually obtain while we are pilgrims here away from the Lord. The second argument for proving this false opinion is that God gave life to the Gentiles; therefore the Gentiles belonged to him as children. I reply: there are many kinds of God's goodwill and beneficence, but two especially, and these entirely distinct and different from each other, of which the first can exist without the second, but the second cannot exist without the first, just as one can exist without two, but two cannot exist without including one within themselves. In two ways, therefore, God loves the things he has created, and they belong to him: either by the right of creation, by which all things belong to him, and he makes his sun rise on the good and the evil; or by the right of redemption, by which only those belong to God whom he acknowledges as his children. So it is said in the Psalms: He has not done so for any nation, and as for his judgments, they have not known them. Blessed is the people whose God is the LORD. Therefore the Gentiles then belonged to God also by the right of creation, that is, as things created by him, but not by the right of redemption, that is, as children adopted by him, in the way that the one seed of Abraham already belonged to God at that time. The third argument of this man is that the old adoption and election of the Israelite people (which is mentioned in the Scriptures) was only a greater definition of that people, or a more flattering treatment and address, and not a peculiar and distinct favour by which God showed himself to be the Father and redeemer of that people alone. Therefore even then the Gentiles looked to God as his own possession, just as the Israelites did. I reply: nothing can be affirmed more plainly against the word of God than what this man writes here in express words. For Moses refutes him: When the Most High divided the inheritance to the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel. For the LORD's portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance. And what we have just cited from Psalm 147: He has not done so for any nation. Likewise Psalm 76: In Judah God is known. But the one whose God, that is, Father, was not acknowledged by those people was not their Father and God in the proper sense. Therefore he was properly the Father and God of that people alone. From this it comes about that in Hosea the Israelites are called those who alone were called my people. And everywhere that one nation alone is called the nation chosen as God's own possession. For the fact that we, who were once Gentiles, are now both truly the people of God and are called so, has come about because, as Paul says, Christ, coming into the world, made both one, breaking down the middle wall of partition, which separated us from the people of God. Therefore, from both Jews and Gentiles, Christ, coming, made one fold, since before this the Gentiles were not the fold of God. Indeed, the same Paul says: Hardening has in part come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in. Hence, before the coming of Christ and the preaching of the gospel by the apostles, the Gentiles were not the people of God, but the Jews alone; yet he both thinks and writes the contrary. From these things it appears that he falsely asserts that the invisible Church of God existed in Abraham's time, even among the Gentiles; therefore it is also false that we ought to be content with that invisible Church alone, scorning this visible one, which can be recognized by its certain marks. Let us come to the other arguments of this frenzied man.

units.la: Ecclesia visibilis quæ sub Mose fuit, Deo fuit immorigera. Ergo omnes visibiles Ecclesiæ sint Deo immorigeræ
units.tr: The visible Church that existed under Moses was disobedient to God. Therefore all visible Churches are disobedient to God.

units.la: Negamus cōsecutionē. Nec enim magis firma est, q; si quispiā ita argumentetur, Menno-nita quidā Anabaptista anno Domini 1581. expilauit Amsterodami ædes amici sui, & eius familiā trucidauit, Ergo omnes Anabaptistæ Mennonitæ idē faciunt. Quam consecutionem ne iste quidem ipse verā esse admiserit. Ex vno enim ad omnes nulla valet consecutio.
units.tr: We deny the inference. It is no firmer than if someone argued like this: a certain Mennonite Anabaptist in the year of the Lord 1581 plundered the house of his friend in Amsterdam and slaughtered his family; therefore all Mennonite Anabaptists do the same. Even this man himself would not admit that such an inference is valid, for no inference from one to all holds good.

units.la: Omnia scelerum genera & infinitæ rixæ de doctrina in Ecclesijs visibilibus hodie regnāt. Ergo nulla Ecclesia visibilis nobis est quęrēda.
units.tr: Every kind of wickedness and endless quarrels over doctrine now reign in the visible Churches. Therefore no visible Church is to be sought by us.

units.la: Primùm, falsum est q; ait, scelera regnare vel tolerari in reformatis Ecclesijs si modo non ta sunt, itē inter ipsos fideles rixas esse vel permitti, quātū homines mederi possunt. Idcirco enim & disciplina Ecclesiastica & Cosistoriū est institutū, vt ista mala è medio Ecclesiæ tollātur. Nā vel iste nunquā Ecclesias vidit: vel se calūniatorē impudentissimū nunc ostendit, dū hoc nostris Ecclesijs mētiens affingit. Sed quāuis non sint tam sanƈti qui eas sequuntur, Euā geliūmque profitentur, qua optaremus, ex abusu tamen Ecclesiæ non est, vt antea diximus, de re, id est, de ipsa Ecclesia iudicandū, neque Ecclesia visibilis propterea est damnanda.
units.tr: First, it is false that wickedness reigns or is tolerated in the reformed Churches, or that quarrels are rife or permitted among the faithful themselves, beyond what human beings can remedy. For this very reason ecclesiastical discipline and the consistory were instituted, so that these evils might be removed from the midst of the Church. Either this man has never seen Churches, or he now shows himself a most shameless slanderer, lying and attributing these things to our Churches. But although those who follow them, and profess the Gospel, are not as holy as we would wish, nevertheless, as we said before, the Church is not to be judged by its abuse, that is, by the thing itself, and the visible Church is therefore not to be condemned.

units.la: Vera Ecclesia soli Deo nota est, ergo nobis.
units.tr: The true Church is known only to God; therefore it is known only to God and not to us.

units.la: C. iiij. ignota est:ac proinde frustrà à nobis quęritur.
units.tr: C. iiij. It is unknown, and therefore it is sought by us in vain.

units.la: Falsum est, veram Dei Ecclesiam absolutè soli Deo notam esse.Nā supra ostendimus veras notas,ex quibus illa & verè agnosci, & ab aliis hominum vel Ethnicorum vel hæreticorum cœtibus discerni possit.
units.tr: It is false that the true Church of God is known absolutely only to God. For we have shown above the true marks by which it can be truly recognised and distinguished from the assemblies of other men, whether heathen or heretical.

units.la: Ecclesiæ visibiles ab Apostolis plätatæ statim post earum mortem perierunt. Ergo frustra & inutiliter à nobis nunc quæruntur, vt nos illis adiungamus.
units.tr: Visible Churches planted by the Apostles perished immediately after their death. Therefore it is in vain and to no purpose that they are now sought by us, so that we might join ourselves to them.

units.la: Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ dupliciter dicûtur,vel quæ ipso Apostolorų ore & prædicatione vocali collectæ sunt: vel quæ in eorum doctrina (quæ & ipsa est Christi doctrina) sunt fundatæ, excitatæ & congregatæ, eâque doctrinam sequuntur. Concedimus igitur plerasque Ecclesias, quæ primo illo modo vocantur Apostolicæ, periisse, qualis Antiochena, Corinthiaca,Alexādrina &c. sed secūdo modo dictę Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ etiamnum hodie (summâ Dei misericordiâ,qui Euangelij benedicti lucem Mundo restituit)palam multis in locis, extant quæ vulgo reformatæ nominantur velut Amsterodami,Vltraiecti,Delphis,Dordraci,Gandaui, & passim non obscuris per Europā vrbibus,ditionibus regnis,&c.Ergo,qui his Ecclesijs sese minimè adiūgit, ille proculdubio Apostolicas Ecclesias,atq; adeo Christum ipsum spernit. Dixit enim illis Christus. Qui vos spernit, me spernit : & Ioann. 17. Non
units.tr: Apostolic Churches are spoken of in two ways: either those gathered by the Apostles' own mouth and oral preaching, or those founded, raised up and gathered in their teaching (which is itself the teaching of Christ) and that follow this teaching. We therefore concede that most of the Churches called Apostolic in the first sense have perished, such as the Antiochene, Corinthian, Alexandrian and so on. But Apostolic Churches in the second sense still exist today, by the great mercy of God, who has restored to the world the light of the blessed Gospel: they stand openly in many places, which are commonly called reformed, as at Amsterdam, Utrecht, Delft, Dordrecht, Ghent, and in many well-known cities, territories and kingdoms throughout Europe. Therefore whoever does not join himself to these Churches at all, he without doubt spurns the Apostolic Churches, and indeed Christ himself. For Christ said to them: He who despises you despises me; and in John 17: Non

units.la: pro eis (Apostolis) ait idem, rego tantum, sed & pro ijs, qui per sermonem eorum crediturisunt in in me. Denique quàm est impudens & absur-dum, & ex Donatistarum haereticorum sententia repetitum, affirmare, Omnes veras Dei Ecclesias visibiles nunc perijsse, & nullibi gentium iam extare, quum tot veri Pastores, tot verae Ecclesiae, tot sancti coetus reformatarum Ecclesiarum extent, cum quibus ne laruae quidem istae Libertinicae (qui certè sunt primorum qui hoc nostro seculo orti sunt, & verbum Dei scriptum literam mortuam elementaque Mundi à Paulo damnata nominarunt, primorum inquam istorum Anabaptistarum soboles ac propago: licet, ut filij degeneres iam ab Anabaptistis in multis dissentiant, seorsimque sibi magna ambitione nouam sectam fabricati sint, & de suo nomine iam eam appellant.) Ergo cum nostris ne laurae quidem ista contendere sanctitate, vel possint vel audeant, quicquid magnifice de sua illa perfectione & impeccatia (falso tamen & mendaciter) iactent.
units.tr: pro eis (for the Apostles), he says again, I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word. Finally, how impudent and absurd it is, and repeated from the opinion of the Donatist heretics, to affirm that all the true visible Churches of God have now perished and nowhere in the nations still exist, when so many true ministers, so many true Churches, so many holy assemblies of the reformed Churches exist! With these the Libertine phantoms (who are certainly the offspring and progeny of the first Anabaptists who arose in our century, and who called the written Word of God a dead letter and the elements of the world, condemned by Paul; I say, of those first Anabaptists; although these degenerate sons now differ from the Anabaptists in many respects, and by great ambition have fabricated a new sect for themselves apart, and now call it by their own name) cannot and dare not compete in holiness. Therefore, whatever they boast magnificently about their own perfection and freedom from sin, they do so falsely and lyingly.

units.la: Deus pollicetur ip ipse docebit suos: Ergo Mnisterio Euangelico externo nō est nobis op9. Subordinata non pugnant inter se, veluti Deus, & Medicus ad sanationem. Etsi enim sana tio est à Deo, Medicus tamen est à Deo nihilominus ordinatus velut instrumētu ipsius sanationis à Deo consequendae. Sic etiam Deus & Cibus in vita hac terrena conseruanda, non pugnant inter se. Etsi enim vita haec est Dei donū, itemq; illius conseruatio: cibus tamē est à Deo constitutus vti instrumētū & mediū ordinariu huius vitæ tuendæ & coferuandæ. Ergo & qui fanari vult, medicu contemnere non debet, licet à Deo fanari fe agnoscat: & qui hic viuere cupit, cibum minime aspernatur, licet à Deo fe alifciat. Eodē modo Deus, & Ministerii Euangelium externum optimè inter se consentiunt. Quod enim credimus, i, quod cor nostrum fleēitur vt fidem verbo Dei habeamus: quod veritati cœlesti acquiescimus: quod Christum agnoscimus redemptorē, hoc verè opus est Dei: sed q opus nēpe Deus per Ministerium Euangelicum externum veluti per instrumētum à se institutū efficit in nobis. Itaque fides dicitur esse ex auditu, etiā quo tēpore & Deus docebit, & erunt omnes Ɗ. Quomodo verò audient inquit Paulus absque prædicante. i. absq; Ministerio Euagelico externo? Deniq; tunc quoq; quum Deus docebit, dicetur, vel hoc ipso teste, quàm speciosi pedes Euangelizantium pacem, euangelizantiū bona! & nominatim Petrus ipse Pascite (inquit) gregi Domini. Quare illo etiā tēpore quo Dominus docet nos, debēt esse & homines q prædicēt & qui Euagelizēt. Ergo illa promissio & efficacitas Dei nec tollit, nec abrogat Ministerium Euangelicum externum, ac proinde neque Ecclesias visibiles: imò quum in illis solis sit & vigeat illud Ministerium Euagelicū, sunt ꝑ pijs omnibus, qui à Deo doceri volūt, visibiles Ecclesiæ quærendę. Deniq; hoc est illud argumētū Anabaptistarū q iste velut ius vetus nobis recoquit, & reponit, de Spirituali illa doçę di ratione,cui iā millies est à nostris responsū.
units.tr: God promises: They shall all be taught by God. Therefore we have no need of the external evangelical ministry. Subordinate things do not fight with one another, as God and a physician do in healing. For although healing is from God, the physician is nonetheless also appointed by God as the instrument of the healing to be obtained from God. So too God and food do not conflict with one another in preserving this earthly life. For although this life is God's gift, and its preservation likewise, food is nonetheless established by God as the instrument and ordinary means of maintaining and preserving this life. Therefore the one who wishes to be healed ought not to despise the physician, although he acknowledges that he is healed by God; and the one who desires to live here does not at all reject food, although he is nourished by God. In the same way God and the external evangelical ministry agree most well with each other. For that we believe, that is, that our heart is bent so that we have faith in the Word of God, that we assent to heavenly truth, that we acknowledge Christ as Redeemer, this is truly the work of God; but it is a work which God accomplishes in us through the external evangelical ministry, as through an instrument he has instituted. Thus faith is said to come from hearing, even at the time when God shall teach, and all shall be taught by God. But how shall they hear, says Paul, without a preacher? That is, without the external evangelical ministry? Finally, even at the time when God shall teach, it will be said, and by this very witness, How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, who bring good news! and Peter himself names it: Feed (he says) the flock of the Lord. Therefore even at that time, when the Lord teaches us, there must be men who preach and who evangelise. Therefore that promise and the efficacy of God neither takes away nor abrogates the external evangelical ministry, and consequently neither the visible Churches; indeed, since that evangelical ministry is in them alone and flourishes in them, visible Churches are to be sought by all the godly who wish to be taught by God. Finally, this is that argument of the Anabaptists which he, as if recooking an old law, now sets before us again, concerning that spiritual method of teaching, to which our people have already replied a thousand times.

units.la: In responsione ad Quæstionem 5.
units.tr: In reply to Question 5.

units.la: In visibili Ecclesia homines suam non Dei doctrinam tradunt,& stabiliunt: Ergo visibilis Ecclesia nequaquam nobis sequenda.
units.tr: In the visible Church, men hand down and establish their own doctrine, not God's doctrine. Therefore the visible Church is by no means to be followed by us.

units.la: Hoc cum ab isto non probetur, apparet istam obiectionem merā esse aduersus nostras Ecclesias calumniam, quæ eò iustius à nobis non agnoscitur,quò impudentius ab isto nobis impingitur.
units.tr: Since he does not prove this, it is clear that this objection is nothing but a calumny against our churches. It is all the more rightly rejected by us, the more shamelessly he hurls it at us.

units.la: In responsione ad Quæstionem 6.
units.tr: In reply to Question 6.

units.la: In Ecclesia visibili littera scripta prædica-tur:illa autem nō est ipsum Dei verbum.Ergo Dei verbum in Ecclesia visibili non prædicatur : ac proinde Ecclesia visibilis neque quærenda neque sequenda est.
units.tr: In the visible Church the written letter is preached, but that letter is not the Word of God itself. Therefore the Word of God is not preached in the visible Church, and so the visible Church is neither to be sought out nor followed.

units.la: Littera à Prophetis & Apostolis scripta,est ipsum Dei verbum,2.Petr.1.vers.19. Rom.14, vers.15.2.Timot.3.vers.16. ad quod nos Christus ipse & Prophetæ remittunt ac reuocant. Christus,Scrutamini Scripturas,ait, illæ enim testantur de me. Ifaias,Ad Legem & Testimonium. Malachias, Recordamini Legis Mosis serui mei. Quamobrem vbicūque illa littera scripta vere docetur,ac prædicatur, illic ipsum quoque Dei verbum annuntiatur.Quod quum hodie, Dei gratiā, fiat in reformatis ac visibilibus Ecclesiis : ergo illæ sunt à piis, qui verbum Dei discere, cognoscere, ac intelligere volunt , quærendæ & adeundæ. Hæc tantùm differentia est inter ipsum Dei verbum, & scriptam (quam iste per contemptum vocat) litteram, quæ inter contractum tantùm nuncupatum ac conceptum inter partes, vel eundem contractum iam scriptum. Quum enim scribitur aliquis contractus seu pactum, nihil aliud scribitur, quàm quod erat prius inter partes conuentum & nuncupatum: sed tantùm forma visibilis illi additur, vt quæ verba partium prius erant inuisibilia & volantia, iam per scripturam illam fiant quodammodo visibilia & fixa. Sed tamen si substantia tum literæ seu scripturæ, tum cōtractus ipsius & pactionis verbis conceptæ spectetur, idem prorsus in vtroque continetur. Vnde & ipsa quoque scriptura de contractu aliquo facta dicitur esse ipsemet noster contractus & pactum ipsum. Eodem modo, ipsum Dei verbum per se est inuisibile: Sed postquam scriptis mandatum est, illud idem factum est iam quodammodo visibile: idem tamen est vtrobique, id est, & in illa littera quæ scripta est Dei verbo, & in ipsomet Dei verbo. Quamobrem pessimè & ignorantisfimè putat iste aliud esse ratione substantiæ & doctrinæ Scripturam seu litteram Sacram, & ipsum extra Scripturam Dei verbum. Est enim vtrunque quemadmodum docuimus, idem. Et quod ait Paulus, Littera occidit, Spiritus viuificat, alió prorsus pertinet. Hoc enim ostendit, nempe nisi Dei Spiritus reddiderit efficax illud externum ministerium, fore tantùm sonitum, qui neque nos excitare à peccatis, neque cor nostrum pungere possit.
units.tr: The letter written by the Prophets and Apostles is the Word of God itself: 2 Pet. 1, vers. 19; Rom. 14, vers. 15; 2 Tim. 3, vers. 16. To this Word Christ himself and the Prophets send us back and recall us. Christ says, "Search the Scriptures, for they testify of me." Isaiah says, "To the Law and to the Testimony." Malachi says, "Remember the Law of Moses my servant." Wherever that written letter is truly taught and preached, there the Word of God itself is also proclaimed. Since this is done today, by God's grace, in the reformed and visible Churches, those Churches are to be sought out and attended by the godly who wish to learn, know and understand the Word of God. There is only this difference between the Word of God itself and the written letter (which he scornfully calls "the letter"): the difference between a contract that has only been agreed upon and spoken between the parties, and the same contract once it has been written down. When a contract or pact is written, nothing else is written than what was previously agreed upon and spoken between the parties. Only a visible form is added, so that the words of the parties, which were before invisible and fleeting, now become in a way visible and fixed through that writing. But if we consider the substance of both the writing or Scripture and the contract itself, the pact conceived in words, exactly the same thing is contained in each. Hence the writing made about a contract is also said to be our very contract and the pact itself. In the same way, the Word of God is in itself invisible; but after it was committed to writing, it has in a way become visible. Yet it is the same in both: in that letter which is written, and in the Word of God itself. Therefore he thinks very badly and most ignorantly that Scripture or the sacred letter differs from the Word of God outside Scripture in substance and doctrine. For, as we have taught, each is the same. And what Paul says, "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life," pertains to something quite different. For it shows that unless the Spirit of God makes that external ministry effective, it will be nothing but a sound, which can neither rouse us from sins nor pierce our heart.

units.la: Littera scripta corrumpi falsa interpreta-tione potest. Verbum autem Dei non potest. Ergo littera scripta non est Dei verbum.
units.tr: A written letter can be corrupted by false interpretation, but the Word of God cannot. Therefore a written letter is not the Word of God.

units.la: Eodem modo verbum Dei corrumpi potest quo littera scripta. Itaque dum haeretici littera scripta abutuntur, eámve corrumpunt, dicuntur etiam corrumpere ipsum Dei verbum. Verum si proprie loqui volumus, neque sacra Scriptura, neque Dei verbum corrumpi potest: sed tantum potest illi falsus sensus seu sententia ab haereticis hominibus ex animi sui errore affingi, qui tamen sensus illis non inest, ut falsitas & corruptio sit in ipso haeretici animo & mente, non in ipso Scripturae sensu. Sed ipse perturbans omnia confundit vitium interpretis cum vera Scripturae sententia, quae duo putat esse idem, adeoque ipsum interpretis vitium inhaerere in ipsa Scriptura sacra.
units.tr: In the same way, the Word of God can be corrupted just as a written letter can. So when heretics abuse the written letter or corrupt it, they are said to corrupt the Word of God itself as well. But if we want to speak properly, neither sacred Scripture nor the Word of God can be corrupted. Only a false sense or meaning can be fastened upon it by heretical men, from the error of their own minds. That sense, however, is not in the Scripture itself, so that the falsity and corruption lie in the heretic's own mind and understanding, not in the meaning of Scripture. But he confuses everything: he mixes up the fault of the interpreter with the true meaning of Scripture, thinks the two are the same, and so attributes the interpreter's fault to sacred Scripture itself.

units.la: In responsione ad Quaestionem 7.
units.tr: In reply to Question 7.

units.la: Verbum Dei est ipse Deus: Littera scripta non est ipse Deus. Ergo littera non est Dei verbum.
units.tr: The Word of God is God himself; the written letter is not God himself. Therefore the letter is not the Word of God.

units.la: Falsum est, quod affirmat ille, nempe Verbum Dei esse ipsum Deum, id est ipsam Dei essentiam. Quod enim dicunt Rabbini, Deus est suum verbum, & verbum ipsius est ipse, non de essentia Dei est intelligendum, quemadmodum facit ille: sed de ea tantum declara-tione virtutum, ut vocat Petrus, attributorumque divinorum, quae in ipsius verbo habemus, & quae virtutes seu attributa cum eiusdem Dei essentia plane consentiunt, eámque verè nobis explicant. Sicut enim Deus dicitur in suo verbo, Sanctus, Bonus, Misericors, Iustus,&c. Sic reipsa quoq; talis est Deus in sese,& in sua essentia.Ex quo fit,ut consentiat essentia Dei, &verbum ipsius quod nobis illa Dei attributa tradit ac declarat,per quæ Dei essentia aliquo modo,(& eo quidem, qui satis sit nobis ad salutem) intelligi potest. Quum verò littera scripta sit ipsum illud Dei verbū,ex quo discimus Deum esse Sanctum,Bonum, Misericordem,Iustum,Sapientem,&c. Ergo littera quoque scripta tam est ipse Deus, quàm verbum ipsius etiam non scriptum dicitur esse Deus ipse, & totum hoc argumentum est mera sophisticè ex ambiguitate vocis verbum Dei.
units.tr: What he affirms is false, namely that the Word of God is God himself, that is, the very essence of God. What the Rabbis say, "God is his own word, and his word is himself," is not to be understood of the essence of God, as he understands it, but only of that declaration of virtues (as Peter calls them) and of the divine attributes which we have in his Word. These virtues or attributes wholly agree with the essence of God and truly explain it to us. For just as God is called in his Word "Holy, Good, Merciful, Just," and so on, so in himself and in his essence he really is such. From this it follows that the essence of God and his Word, which hands down and declares to us those attributes of God, agree, and through them the essence of God can in some measure be understood (and indeed to the extent that is enough for us unto salvation). But since the written letter is that very Word of God from which we learn that God is Holy, Good, Merciful, Just, Wise, and so on, the written letter is as much God himself as his unwritten word is said to be God himself. This whole argument is nothing but a sophism arising from the ambiguity of the phrase "Word of God."

units.la: 1. Argumentum.
units.tr: 1. The argument.

units.la: Christus est verbum Dei: Littera scripta non est Christus. Ergo littera scripta non est verbum Dei.
units.tr: Christ is the Word of God; the written letter is not Christ. Therefore the written letter is not the Word of God.

units.la: Resp. Hic quoque ludit Sophista iste ambiguitate vocum istarum, verbum Dei. Christus enim dicitur Verbum Dei, & littera scripta dicitur etiam Verbum Dei: sed vtrunque diuersa ratione. Christus,quoniam est ipsum illud Verbum,quod ex Patre ineffabiliter genitū,eandē cum Patre essentiā habet. Itaque est. Verbum Dei ἐνδιάθετος,& velut res ipsa,de qua reliqua omnia, quæ Dei verbum dicuntur (velut Reuelatio, Prædicatio & Scriptura) loquuntur. Scriptura verò & Prædicatio & Reuelatio à Deo facta, dicuntur verbum Dei, quoniam illa hoc Dei verbum, Christum nempe, declarant ac patefaciunt hominibus. Ergo non definit littera scripta esse verbum Dei, licet, non fit Christus ipse, quoniam est Christi annunciatio. Sic ipsa declaratio & praedicatio Euangelij passim dicitur Euangelium. Quare qui audit litteram scriptam, idem ille quoque Christum illius autorem audit, & veram annuntiationem de Christo, quod perinde est atque ipsummet Christum audire & videre.
units.tr: Reply. Here too this sophist plays on the ambiguity of the words Word of God. For Christ is called the Word of God, and the written letter is also called the Word of God, but in two different senses. Christ is so called because he is that very Word which was ineffably begotten of the Father and has the same essence as the Father. Thus he is the Word of God ἐνδιάθετος [inward word], and as it were the very thing of which all the other things that are called the Word of God (such as Revelation, Preaching and Scripture) speak. But Scripture, Preaching and Revelation, being made by God, are called the Word of God because they declare and make manifest to men this Word of God, namely Christ. Therefore the written letter does not cease to be the Word of God, although it is not Christ himself, since it is the announcement of Christ. So too the declaration and preaching of the Gospel is everywhere called the Gospel. Hence whoever hears the written letter hears also Christ its author, and the true announcement concerning Christ, which is just as good as hearing and seeing Christ himself.

units.la: Plerique in littera scripta diu versati verbum Dei nec intelligunt, nec capiunt. Ergo littera scripta non est verbum Dei.
units.tr: Many who have long been conversant with the written letter neither understand nor grasp the Word of God. Therefore the written letter is not the Word of God.

units.la: Aliud est diu in aliqua re versatum esse, aliud autem in eadem bene versatum. Concedimus igitur plerosque diu in litteris Sacris esse versatos, qui tamen, quoniam eas ipsas scripturas (quas quotidie tractant) non intelligunt, dicuntur Dei verbum non intelligere: sed tamen inde non efficitur eas non esse verbum Dei, quoniam qui saepe diu tempus in illis terunt, earum sensum non assequuntur, Imo dicuntur non capere verbum Dei, quoniam eam litteram scriptam non assequuntur: Non assequuntur autem, quoniam in ea non bene versantur, & vt oportet. Est enim Dei donum, illius praesertim scripturae intelligentia. Quare qui se putant assequi eam posse sine diuino Spiritu, prorsus inaniter in ea volvenda laborant, ac tempus consumunt. Verum nihilominus illa manet, ac est verbum Dei. Perinde igitur argumentatur iste, atque si diceret. Plerique in Ciceronis lectione & libris versati, non recte tamen loquuntur Latinè: Ergo vera Latinitas in Ciceronis libris non continetur. Quod quàm sit absurdum, nemo non videt. Vitio enim ingenij illius fit, vt Ciceronem legens, & quidem sæpè, tamen non recte loquatur Latinè: non quòd vera Latinitas in illis Ciceronis libris non comprehendatur.
units.tr: It is one thing to have long been occupied with some matter, and another to have been well versed in the same. We grant, therefore, that many have long been occupied with the Holy Scriptures, yet, since they do not understand those very writings which they handle every day, they are said not to understand the Word of God. But it does not follow from this that those writings are not the Word of God, since those who often spend much time on them do not attain their sense. Indeed they are said not to grasp the Word of God because they do not attain that written letter; and they do not attain it because they are not well and as they ought to be versed in it. For the understanding of that Scripture especially is a gift of God. Hence those who think they can attain it without the divine Spirit labour in vain in turning it over and waste their time. Nevertheless it remains, and is, the Word of God. This man therefore argues as if he were to say: many who are versed and practised in reading Cicero's books nevertheless do not speak correct Latin; therefore true Latinity is not contained in Cicero's books. How absurd this is, everyone sees. For it is the fault of their wit that, although they read Cicero, and often, they still do not speak correct Latin; it is not that true Latinity is not contained in those books of Cicero.

units.la: In responsione ad Quaestionem 9. & 10.
units.tr: In reply to Questions 9 and 10.

units.la: Hîc nihil habuit iste, quod responderet. Itaque seipsum, suúmque hunc librum prorsus iam euertens, vi veritatis coactus concedit Sacramentorum vsum (si modò ad ædificationem vsurpentur) esse retinendum. Quem tamen & in epistola, & postea vbique euertit. Sed videte ineptiam hominis, Qui relinquat fidelibus vsum Sacramentorū,& tamen negat eos debere sese adiungere vlli Ecclesiæ. Vbi igitur erit ille vsus Sacramentorum, si non in Ecclesia? Certè ab vno qui solus & extra omnem coetum erit, Sacramenta participari non possunt. quoniam dicuntur κοινωνία, & vinculum nostræ inter nos ipsos, ac non tantum (quamuis primùm) cum Deo per Christum, vnionis ac coniunctionis. Quomodo autem κοινωνία, si quispiam est & manet solus, sese ab omni Ecclesiæ coetu abstrahens & separans, quemadmodum iste & vult & faciendum suadet? Denique ex abusu vel Baptismi, vel sacræ Cœnæ, quem nonnulli inducunt homines, colligit & Baptismum,& sacrā Cœ- nam Domini prorsus & ab omnibus omit- tendam esse, quod, quemadmodum antea di- ximus, est ineptissimum. Nam alij ijsdem re- bus & Sacramentis recte vti possunt, quibus alij abutuntur. Certè quotiescunque in Dei Ecclesiam Pastorum negligentia aliáve qua- piam ratione obrepsit aliqua corruptio & de- prauatio rei sacrae & praeceptae nobis, non est res illa propterea damnanda & prorsus tollen- da, sed abusus tantum ex ea tollēdus & emen- dandus, vsusque illius rei legitimus reuocan- dus. Sic vestes nostras aut domos, in quibus saepe insunt sordes aut maculae grauissimae propterea tamen non deserimus, aut abijci- mus: sed sordes tantum eas & maculas elui- mus, vestes autem ipsas & domos nostras ni- hilominus retinemus.
units.tr: Here this man had nothing to answer. So, utterly overthrowing himself and this book of his, compelled by the force of truth, he concedes that the use of the sacraments (provided they are employed for edification) is to be retained. Yet in his letter and afterwards everywhere he overthrows this same concession. But see the foolishness of the man: he leaves the faithful the use of the sacraments, and yet denies that they ought to join themselves to any Church. Where then will that use of the sacraments be, if not in the Church? Certainly the sacraments cannot be partaken of by one who is alone and outside every assembly. For they are called κοινωνία [communion], and are the bond of union and conjunction not only (although first) with God through Christ, but also among ourselves. But how can there be κοινωνία, if someone is and remains alone, separating and withdrawing himself from every gathering of the Church, as this man both wishes and urges to be done? Finally, from the abuse of either Baptism or the holy Supper, which some men bring forward, he concludes that both Baptism and the Lord's holy Supper are to be utterly omitted by all; which, as we said before, is most absurd. For others can rightly use the very same things and sacraments which others abuse. Certainly, whenever through the negligence of the ministers, or by some other means, some corruption and depravation of a sacred thing delivered to us has crept into the Church of God, that thing is not on that account to be condemned and utterly abolished, but only the abuse is to be removed and corrected from it, and the lawful use of that thing is to be recalled. So we do not for that reason abandon or cast away our garments or houses, in which there are often very serious filth or stains, but we wash away only that filth and those stains, and nevertheless retain the garments and houses themselves.

units.la: In Respons. ad quaest. II.
units.tr: In reply to Question II.

units.la: Extant exempla in prophetis, vbi propter abusum verorum sacrificiorum, vera sacrificia in Ecclesia Dei fieri desierunt. Ergo quum vi- sibilis Ecclesia, nunc abutatur sacramentis, illa omitti debent.
units.tr: There are examples among the prophets where, because the true sacrifices were abused, true sacrifices ceased to be offered in the Church of God. Therefore, since the visible Church now abuses the sacraments, they ought to be discontinued.

units.la: Negamus totum hoc argumentum. Pri- mum quidem falsum est vera sacrificia fieri desijsse in populo Dei propter eorū abusum, & huiusmodi exempla vsquam reperiri apud Prophetas. Contrā Malachias grauissimè in- crepat populum Dei, quod non ita reuerenter ea faceret, vt decebat. Itaque sacrificia ipsa
units.tr: We deny this whole argument. First, it is false that true sacrifices ceased among the people of God on account of their abuse, and no such examples are to be found anywhere in the Prophets. On the contrary, Malachi severely rebukes the people of God because they did not perform these things as reverently as they ought. So God still commended the sacrifices themselves, even though men abused them.

units.la: D. j. commendabat etsi homines sacrificijs abute-rentur.Sæpe quidem Prophetæ in hypocritas Iudæos inuehuntur, qui istis hostijs terrenis Deum placari quidquid tandé scelerate com-missent,qui sacrificijs istis peccata sua redimi (velut iusto precio) credebant, remiffionemq; peccatorum suorum in illis collocabat, quum neq; tunc quoque, vti neque post Christi ad-uentum Sacramenta homines sanctificarent, vt docet Apostolus ad Hebræos: propter tale tamen abusum Deus nufquâ iussit vt illa cessa-rent, aut à Iudæis omitterentur: imò de illis neglectim peractis grauiter conqueritur, Ne-que etiam vllum exemplum extat scripturæ sacræ, vllibi vbi sacrificia propterea omissa fuisse dicantur. Desijt, fateor,sub Idololatris Iudæorum Regibus velut Achaze, Manasse, vero Deo sacrificari, sed sacrificábatur idolis. Ergo etiam tunc sacrificia ficbant, sed non vero Deo : nec id quidem propterea quod Maiores illorum abusi veris sacrificijs fuissent: sed quoniam huiusmodi reges erant idolola-træ, & verum Deum reliquerant. Quare vel vnum suæ sententiæ exemplum proferat iste ex Prophetis, & vicerit : vel se imperitum sacræ scripturæ fateatur : vel impudentem agnoscat. Hoc igitur primum aduersus istum pernegamus. Negamus quoque fecundo loco, quod iste per calumniam ponit, No-ftras Ecclesias, quæ sunt visibiles Dei Eccle-fiæ, abuti Domini Nostri Iesu Christi sacra-mentis. Nam & ea ex vero Christi instituto retiretinent, & ad ea reuerenter accedunt, & pro fidei suæ sigillis nō pro vanis pompis aut spe-ctaculis, vti Papistæ faciunt, vsurpant. Probet igitur iste suas in nos calūnias (quod nun-quam faciet) & tunc quoque triumphet: sed ne canat ante triumphum victoriam,qua nun-quam potietur.
units.tr: Certainly the Prophets often inveigh against the hypocritical Jews, who believed that God could be appeased by those earthly victims, however wickedly they had sinned, who thought their sins were redeemed by those sacrifices as if for a fair price, and who placed the forgiveness of their sins in them. Yet, just as the sacraments did not sanctify men even then, nor do they after the coming of Christ, as the Apostle teaches to the Hebrews, God nowhere commanded that those sacrifices cease on account of such abuse, nor that the Jews should omit them. Rather, he complains bitterly that they were performed carelessly. Nor is there any example in Holy Scripture where sacrifices are said to have been omitted for that reason. I grant that under the idolatrous kings of Judah, such as Ahaz and Manasseh, sacrifice to the true God ceased, but sacrifice was offered to idols. So sacrifices were still being offered at that time, but not to the true God; and this was not because their forefathers had abused the true sacrifices, but because such kings were idolaters who had forsaken the true God. Therefore let this man produce from the Prophets even one example in support of his view, and he will have won; or let him confess that he is ignorant of Holy Scripture; or let him acknowledge that he is shameless. So, first of all, we flatly deny this against him. Secondly, we also deny what he slanderously asserts, that our churches, which are the visible churches of God, abuse the sacraments of our Lord Jesus Christ. For they retain them according to Christ's true institution, approach them reverently, and use them as seals of their faith, not for empty pomp or spectacle, as the Papists do. Let him therefore prove his calumnies against us (which he will never do), and then let him triumph; but let him not sing victory before the triumph, a victory he will never win.

units.la: Accusantur à Prophetis vt hypocritæ & impij qui ceremonias illas externas in lege Dei præscriptas retinebant. Ergo tales sunt qui hodie in visibili Ecclesia sacramentorum vsum seruant.
units.tr: The Prophets accuse as hypocrites and wicked those who retained those external ceremonies prescribed in the law of God. Therefore those who today keep the use of the sacraments in the visible Church are such people.

units.la: Non vocant Prophetæ eos hypocritas, qui Ceremoniarum illarum veterum vsum, vti Deus iusserat,obstruabāt:sed, qui eo prætextu quasi vili pretio à Deo peccata & fraudes suas redimerent, illas Ceremonias & sacrificia vsurpabant, vti diximus supra.
units.tr: The Prophets do not call hypocrites those who kept up the use of those old ceremonies as God had commanded, but those who, under that pretext, as if they could redeem their sins and frauds from God at a cheap price, used those ceremonies and sacrifices, as we said above.

units.la: Pharizæi & Scribæ obiecerunt Christo vel Stephano potius contemptum Sabbati, Templi,id est, Ceremoniarum, quàm vllū aliquod crimen. Ergo Pharizæis similes sunt, qui de sacramentorum à Christo institutorum cōtemptu conqueruntur, & alios accusant.
units.tr: The Pharisees and Scribes charged Christ, or rather Stephen, with contempt of the Sabbath and the Temple, that is, of the ceremonies, rather than with any other crime. Therefore those who complain of contempt for the sacraments instituted by Christ, and accuse others of it, are like the Pharisees.

units.la: Si vel Christus vel Stephanus Sabbatum, vel templum, vel ritus à Deo institutos reipsa contempsissent, merito certè à Pharizæis accusati ac damnati fuissent: atqui videmus quemadmodum vterque sanctè, & sicut Deus iubebat, reuerenter ritus in lege Dei institutos coluerit. Veniebat in festo Paschatis Iesus Hierosolymam, quia sic iussum erat à Deo in
units.tr: If Christ or Stephen had actually despised the Sabbath, or the Temple, or the rites instituted by God, they would certainly have been rightly accused and condemned by the Pharisees. But we see that both of them kept the rites instituted in God's law, reverently and holily, as God commanded. Jesus went up to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover, because this was commanded by God in

units.la: Deutronomio. Quid multis opus est? Dicitur Christus & factus sub lege, & impleuisse legem pro nobis (quod procul dubio de tota lege & Morali, & Ceremoniali, & Politica intelligendum est.) Ergo ritus legales non contempsit, sed obseruauit Christus. Fuit ergo hæc aperta Pharizæorum & Scribarū in Christum ac Stephanum calumnia, dum eos accusant damnantque contemptarum earum Ceremoniarum, quæ à Deo fuerunt institutæ. Cæterum quum Christus ipse omnis virtutis ac pietatis nobis propositum à Deo exemplar, sacrificia, sacramenta, & ritus à Deo præceptos non prætermiserit sed in vsu habuerit, debent tanto magis pij omnes (qui Christum imitari volet) sacramenta in Nouo Teftameto à Deo præscripta vsurpare: diligeter reuerenterq; ijs vti. Non autem, vt iste omnibus modis suadere conatur, ea contemnere. Alibi nobis reponit velut cramben hoc idem argumentum: tam videtur illud palmarium!
units.tr: Deuteronomy. Why say more? Christ is said to have been made under the law and to have fulfilled the law for us (which without doubt must be understood of the whole law, moral, ceremonial and civil). Therefore Christ did not despise the legal rites, but observed them. So this was a manifest calumny of the Pharisees and Scribes against Christ and Stephen, when they accused and condemned them of despising those ceremonies which were instituted by God. Moreover, since Christ himself, the example set before us by God of all virtue and piety, did not neglect the sacrifices, sacraments and rites prescribed by God, but kept them in use, all the godly who wish to imitate Christ ought all the more to use the sacraments prescribed by God in the New Testament, and to use them diligently and reverently. They ought not, as he tries in every way to persuade us, to despise them. Elsewhere he serves up this same argument to us again, like reheated cabbage, as if it were his trump card!

units.la: Sabbatū propter hominem, nō homo propter Sabbatum conditus est. Ergo Sacramenta sunt pro arbitrio nostro spernenda. Hæc enim est vera istius loci mens absque circuitione, & tergi uersatione, quam fortassis iste quaret aut captabit.
units.tr: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore the sacraments are to be spurned at our pleasure. For this is the true meaning of that passage, without circumlocution or evasion, which perhaps he will seek out and seize upon.

units.la: Quum dixerit Christus Baptizate, de Baptismo agens: & de Cœna sacra Comedite, Bibite, proculdubio non est in nobis situm illa sacramenta sumere si volumus, vel non sumere: sed iusta causa subesse debet vt ab ijs, quæ Deus ita disertè fieri præcipit, pro tempore abstiabstineamus. Etsi enim non propter ista conditi sumus, quatenus illa sunt signa terrena & actio quaedam externa in his terris: tamen propter ea conditi sumus, quae illa signa demonstrat nobis, nempe propter nostra cum Deo communionem, quam illa Sacramenta significant, & nobis obsignant.
units.tr: Since Christ said Baptize, speaking of Baptism, and of the Lord's Supper Eat, drink, it is undoubtedly not left to us whether we take those sacraments or not, if we wish. A just cause must exist for us to abstain from those things which God so plainly commands to be done, for a time. For although we were not created for these things, insofar as they are earthly signs and certain external actions in this world, yet we were created for those things which these signs show us, namely our communion with God, which these sacraments signify and seal to us.

units.la: In Responsionem ad Quaestionem 12.
units.tr: In the Reply to Question 12.

units.la: Sacramenta Noui Testamenti velut Baptismus ac Coena Domini sunt umbrae ac Ceremoniae aeque ac Iudaeorum Ceremoniae & legales ritus. Ergo Sacramenta Noui testamenti, id est, Baptismus & Coena Domini aeque ac veteres Iudaeorum ceremoniae, ac signa cessare nunc debent.
units.tr: The sacraments of the New Testament, such as Baptism and the Lord's Supper, are shadows and ceremonies, just as the ceremonies and legal rites of the Jews were. Therefore the sacraments of the New Testament, that is, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, like the old ceremonies of the Jews and their signs, ought now to cease.

units.la: Imo dixit Christus ipse alloquens Nicodemum, qui verum regni Dei amplectendi, profitendique modum a Christo ipso quaerebat, dixit inquam, illi Christus de Baptismo. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & spiritus, non poterit introire in regnum Dei. In quo tamen Christus aqua (id est, signum cum Spiritu sancto regenerante) Re signata coniungens, non vult, (quemadmodum ex aliis sacrae scripturae locis facile intelligi potest) eandem esse vim ac necessitatem signi ac rei significatae ad salutem aeternam consequendam, ne videlicet salutis nostrae gloria, & causae ipsis externis signis alligentur. Dixit idem Christus de sacra Coena sua, Mortem Domini (per eam Coenam) Annuntiabitis donec veniat, id est, vsque ad fine Mundi.
units.tr: Indeed Christ himself said to Nicodemus, who was asking Christ about the manner of embracing and professing the truth of the kingdom of God, speaking to him about Baptism: Unless one is born again of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. In these words Christ joins the water (that is, the sign) to the Holy Spirit who regenerates (the thing signified). He does not wish (as can easily be understood from other passages of Holy Scripture) that the sign and the thing signified should have the same force and necessity for obtaining eternal salvation, lest the glory of our salvation and its causes be bound to the outward signs themselves. The same Christ said of his holy Supper: You will proclaim the death of the Lord (through that Supper) until he comes, that is, until the end of the world.

units.la: {a}Quamobrem, vt in regnum Dei apparenter hic tum his terris intremus, & vt mortem Domini in terris viuentes annunciemus, debet tum Baptismus, tum Cœna Domini perpetuum in Ecclesia Dei vsum ac locum habere. Id quod eorum abrogationem (quam ipse tamen nunc inducit velut essent ceremoniæ legales) prorsus oppugnat. Verum, ait, sacramenta illa duo, Baptismus & Cœna Domini sunt signa, & vmbræ, non res ipsa, ergo sunt iam abrogata. Nego omnino. Quoniam non omnia signa inter pios sunt à Deo nunc quoque abrogata. Arcus cœlestis est signum à Deo datum nunquam deinceps futuri diluuij, quod etiamnum hodie durat. Quænā igitur signa rerum cœlestium seu Christi sunt antiquata? Ea nimirum duntaxat, quæ Christum incarnandum, passurum pro peccatis nostris, & pro nostra iustificatione resurrectu rum designabant. Id quod veteris legis sacrificia, sacramenta, ritus, ac ceremoniæ legales denotabant. Itaque quoniam illa omnia legalia in Christo suum implementum habuerunt, planè iam in Ecclesia Dei cessant, ac cessare in æternum debent. At verò quæ signa sunt nobis Christi pro nobis & incarnati, & passi, & excitati obsignationes ac sigilla (qualis est Baptismus à Christo institutus, & sacra Cœna:) illa nequaquâ cessant, aut ante extremum Dei iudicium in Ecclesia Dei cessabunt, & a pijs vsurpari desinent. Ergo non sunt nostra hæc sacramenta illis Iudæorum similia, vt
units.tr: {a}Wherefore, so that we may enter the kingdom of God visibly here, and while living on earth proclaim the death of the Lord, both Baptism and the Lord's Supper ought to have a perpetual use and place in the Church of God. This flatly opposes their abrogation, which he now introduces as though they were legal ceremonies. But he says: those two sacraments, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, are signs and shadows, not the thing itself; therefore they are already abrogated. I deny this entirely. For not all signs given by God among the godly have now been abrogated. The rainbow is a sign given by God that there will never again be a flood, and it still endures today. What, then, are the signs of heavenly things or of Christ that have been made obsolete? Certainly only those that designated Christ's incarnation, his suffering for our sins, and his resurrection for our justification. These the sacrifices, sacraments, rites and legal ceremonies of the old law signified. Therefore, since all those legal things found their fulfilment in Christ, they have clearly now ceased in the Church of God, and they ought to cease forever. But those signs that are for us Christ's seals and pledges, given for us as incarnate, suffering and risen (such as Baptism instituted by Christ, and the holy Supper), by no means cease, nor will they cease in the Church of God before the final judgment of God, and the godly will not stop using them. Therefore our sacraments are not like those of the Jews, so that

units.la: 1. Cor. 11. verf. 26.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11. vers. 26.

units.la: Coloss. 2. verf. 16.
units.tr: Col. 2. vers. 16.

units.la: Galat. 3.
units.tr: Gal. 3.

units.la: Matt. 26.
units.tr: Matt. 26.

units.la: Luc. 22. vt æque & perinde atq; illa cesscnt, quod tamē iste,sed impijssime,putat:quoniam illa Iudeorum Christi venturi in hunc Mundum & crucifigendi,nostra vero iam exhibiti, & pro nobis crucifixi symbola sunt ac sigilla, quibus fidem nostram de vita æterna nobis in Christo promissa confirmamus.
units.tr: Luke 22. so that they cease equally and in the same way as those do, which this man thinks (most impiously). For those Jewish things were symbols and seals of Christ who was to come into this world and be crucified, whereas ours are symbols and seals of him already revealed and crucified for us, by which we confirm our faith in the eternal life promised to us in Christ.

units.la: Quædam Apostolicæ ordinationes nunc cessarunt:Ergo & sacramenta à Christo instituta debent nunc cessare.
units.tr: Some apostolic ordinances have now ceased. Therefore the sacraments instituted by Christ must also now cease.

units.la: Non est cadē vtriusq; rei ratio.Nā quæ or- dinationes Apostolorū iā cessarūt,eæ in rebus indifferentibus positæ erant,veluti abstinere à suffocato,tecto capite orare : At Sacramenta à Christo instituta non sunt res indifferētes, sed pars diuini cultus,& res sacræ à Deo vt obseruētur præceptæ.Itaque abrogari non possunt.
units.tr: The reasoning is not the same for both. For those ordinances of the apostles that have ceased were concerned with indifferent matters, such as abstaining from what is strangled, or praying with the head covered. But the sacraments instituted by Christ are not indifferent matters; they are part of divine worship, and holy things commanded by God to be observed. Therefore they cannot be abrogated.

units.la: Paulus se misssum dicit nō vt baptizaret, sed vt Euangelizaret. Ergo Baptismus cessare debet in Ecclesia Dei.
units.tr: Paul says that he was sent not to baptize but to preach the gospel. Therefore Baptism ought to cease in the Church of God.

units.la: At iste neque iam in Ecclesia Euangelizari vult quum Ministerium Euangelicum externum, quantum quidem in se est, tollat:neque etiam baptizari.Ergo nihil reliquum facit Ecclesiæ. Sal tē relinqueret illud, ad quod se missum profitetur Paulus, nempe in Ecclesia euangeliza- rent Pastores. Verum enimuero illud Pauli proculdubio comparatè est intelligendū, Nimirū se potius missum fuisse à Christo ad prædicandum vbiq; gentium,quod proprium erat Apostolorū,q ad baptizandū, quod magis videtur proprium esse Pastorum qui certe Ecclesiæ
units.tr: But this man does not want the gospel to be preached in the Church any more, since he removes, so far as he is able, the outward evangelical ministry, and he does not want people to be baptized either. So he leaves the Church nothing. Yet at least he would leave what Paul professes he was sent for, namely that ministers should preach the gospel in the Church. But surely that saying of Paul must be understood comparatively: that he was sent by Christ chiefly to preach to the nations everywhere, which was the proper task of the apostles, rather than to baptize, which seems more properly the task of ministers, who are certainly assigned and appointed to particular congregations.

units.la: D, iiij. sunt afscripti & assignati. Nam si simpliciter illud Pauli intellexerimus, proculdubio non reperietur Paulus fidelis dispensator, qualis tamen fuit, sed vsurpator, vtpote qui eodem illo loco fateatur se, & quidem Corinthi baptizasse, Gaium, Crispum, & Stephanæ familiam.
units.tr: D, iiij. For if we understood that saying of Paul simply, Paul would undoubtedly not be found a faithful steward, as he was, but a usurper, since in the same place he confesses that he baptized at Corinth Gaius, Crispus, and the household of Stephanas.

units.la: Sacramenta, id est, signa Noui Testamenti, velut Baptismus & sacræ Cœnæ signa, non sunt res ipsæ ab ipsis significatæ.Ergo iam nunc cessare debent.
units.tr: Sacraments, that is, the signs of the New Testament, such as Baptism and the signs of the holy Supper, are not the things themselves that they signify. Therefore they must now cease.

units.la: Pessimè, atque contra apertissimum Dei verbum iste colligit, vti in hac ipsa responsione ad Argumentum primum ostendimus. Docuimus enim ex sacra scriptura Christum velle, vt & Baptismus & sacra Cœna in perpetuum durent in Ecclesia Dei vsque ad consummationem seculi. Ergo cessabunt illa quidem, sed post Mundi huius plenam instaurationem. Etsi autem sacramenta quatenus elementis, id est, aqua, pane, vino constant, sint resin sese mere naturales, non minus tamen veritatis ipsius exhibitionem habent illa etiam: adeoque in eo præcipua ipsorum dignitas est constituta.
units.tr: This man draws a wicked conclusion, and one directly against the plain word of God, as we have shown in this very reply to the first argument. For we have taught from Holy Scripture that Christ wills both Baptism and the holy Supper to endure forever in the Church of God until the consummation of the age. Therefore they will indeed cease, but only after the full restoration of this world. Although the sacraments, insofar as they consist of elements, that is, water, bread and wine, are in themselves merely natural, they nonetheless also exhibit the truth itself, and their chief dignity lies in this.

units.la: Caduca & peritura non pertinent ad regnum Christi, quod est æternum. Signa hæc Sacramentorum sunt caduca & peritura. Ergo ad regnum Christi non pertinent.
units.tr: Things perishable and transitory do not belong to the kingdom of Christ, which is eternal. These signs of the sacraments are perishable and transitory. Therefore they do not belong to the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Non pertinent hæc signa ad regnum Christi per se, sed propter significationem illis à Christo adiunctam. Ergo quatenus aqua Baptismi est Aqua, Panis & vinum sacrae Coe-nę, sunt terrena Elementa, nō sunt æterna, nec in regno Dei erunt: sed res ipsæ per illa significatæ, & exhibita Christus ipse totus, nobis vt saluificus sic & viuificus, manebunt in æternum: quare non quatenus res sunt, sed quatenus donorum Dei symbola nobis à Deo præscripta sunt, nunc, atque etiámque dum nostra hæc infirmitas durabit, illa ad regnum Dei pertinebunt.
units.tr: These signs do not belong to the kingdom of Christ in themselves, but because of the signification that Christ has attached to them. So insofar as the water of Baptism is water, and the bread and wine of the holy Supper are earthly elements, they are not eternal, nor will they be in the kingdom of God. But the things themselves signified and exhibited by them, Christ himself wholly, who is for us both Saviour and Life-giver, will remain forever. Therefore it is not insofar as they are things, but insofar as they are symbols of God's gifts, prescribed to us by God, that they now belong to the kingdom of God, and will belong to it for as long as our present weakness lasts.

units.la: Pueri sunt & serui & Mercenarij, & sub tutoribus, nō autē liberi qui ista signa ac elementa retinent. Atqui non fiunt vitæ æternæ participes qui sunt eiusmodi. Ergo qui ista signa seu sacramenta, nempe Baptismum & Coenam Domini retinent, vita æterna carebunt.
units.tr: Those who keep these signs and elements are children, slaves and hired servants, under guardians, and not free. But those who are of this kind do not become partakers of eternal life. Therefore those who keep these signs or sacraments, namely Baptism and the Lord's Supper, will lack eternal life.

units.la: Plane liberi sunt, non serui, & sui iuris, & extra tutelam, denique minimè mercenarij, qui Christo ex ipsius præscripto & verbo seruiunt, résque ab eo ad suum cultum institutas, sequuntur, ac seruant. Iussit autem Christus vt homines baptizarentur. Baptizate, ait. Iussit vt sacra Coena celebraretur à suis, Edite & Bibite ex eo omnes, inquit idem. Ergo qui haec faciunt ex precepto Christi vti fit in reformatis Ecclesijs, illi sunt verè liberi, & spontanei Dei serui, & vitam æternam, quia Deo parent, obtinebunt. Quod autem iste eos per cōtemptum pueros vocat, qui sacramentorum Christi vsum retinent: fatemur cum Paulo quandiu hic viuimus, id est, in his terris ac in hoc mortali corpore, nos ex parte manere adhuc pueros.Hic enim videmus,& cognoscimus ex parte & non perfecte: & ænigmate seu per fidē & non per aspectum.Itaq; nobis opus esse his sacramentis,(quemadmodum opus est spectullis ijs qui sunt imbecilli oculorum visu.) quibus res cœlestes & æternas facilius videamus,melius intelligamus,& rectius credamus,quādoquidem per sacramenta habemus earū ipsarū rerū cœlestiū testes ipsos corporis nostri sensus.Cæterum quū erim’ in cœlo,nō egebimus istis externis adiumētis, quoniā Deus tūc erit omnia in omnibus,inquit Paulus.Sed quid vervbis opus est?Iste in hac ipsa respons.& pag.seipsum statim aperte refutat, quum scribit hęc ipsa sacramenta alere nos vsq; ad senectutē, & vsquequo ad Deum adducamur. i. in cœlū recipiamur.Ergo retinenda sunt si modo alii volumus cibo Spirituali. Et tamē hoc argumētū tam ineptū in responsione ad seq.Quęst. 13.repetit,sui oblitus,& vertiginis spiritu abreptus.
units.tr: Those who keep them are plainly free, not slaves, and their own masters, outside guardianship; in short, by no means hired servants, since they serve Christ according to his own prescription and word, and follow and keep the things instituted by him for his worship. Christ commanded that people be baptized: Baptize, he says. He commanded that the holy Supper be celebrated by his people: Eat and drink of it, all of you, says the same Christ. Therefore those who do these things by the precept of Christ, as is done in the reformed Churches, are truly free and willing servants of God, and they will obtain eternal life, because they obey God. But as for his contemptuously calling those who keep the use of Christ's sacraments children: we agree with Paul that as long as we live here, that is, in this earth and in this mortal body, we remain in part still children. For here we see and know in part and not perfectly, and we see through a glass darkly, that is, by faith and not by sight. Therefore we need these sacraments (just as those who are weak in eyesight need spectacles), so that by them we may see heavenly and eternal things more easily, understand them better, and believe them more rightly, since through the sacraments we have the very senses of our body as witnesses of those heavenly things. Moreover, when we are in heaven we will not need these outward aids, since God will then be all in all, as Paul says. But why use many words? This man in this very reply and page immediately refutes himself, when he writes that these same sacraments nourish us until old age and until we are brought to God, that is, received into heaven. Therefore they must be retained, if we wish to be fed with spiritual food. And yet he repeats this argument, so foolish, in his reply to the following Question 13, forgetful of himself and carried off by a spirit of giddiness.

units.la: Homo non est creatus propter externos cultus. Ergo non propter sacramenta, quæ sunt externus Dei cultus.
units.tr: Man was not created for external forms of worship. Therefore he was not created for the sacraments, which are the external worship of God.

units.la: Supra respondimus huic argumnento 3. argumento quæst. 11. ad quem locum remitto lectorem.Certe quum ad Deum colendum sit homo creatus, oportet eum illa omnia vsurpare, in quibus tum internus, tū externus Dei cultus ex ipsius verbo est positus.Verum,quęnam est ista,quæso, vis argumēti ! Non sumus propter quidpiā velut finē creationis nostrę nati, ergo illius vsum retinere minimē debemus. Non fumus certè propter cibos nati: & tamen si viuere volumus, ciborum vsus est nobis necessarius, atque retinendus.
units.tr: We answered this argument above, as the third argument of question 11, and I refer the reader to that place. Certainly, since man was created to worship God, it is necessary that he make use of all those things in which both the internal and the external worship of God is set down by God's own word. But what, I ask you, is the force of this argument! We were not born for anything as the end of our creation; therefore we ought by no means to keep its use. Certainly we were not born for the sake of food; and yet, if we wish to live, the use of food is necessary to us and must be kept.

units.la: In responsione ad Quaestionem 13.
units.tr: In reply to Question 13

units.la: Hic nugatur tantum iste sophista, non respondet ad Quaestionem propositā: neq; soluit argumentum ipsi obiectum, quia non potest, imo fatetur Sacramenta esse lac nobis nutriendis idoneum ac consentaneum. Cur non igitur illis vtemur, praesertim quum id, sicuti prius docuimus, nobis praeceperit Christus? Porrò quod addit iste, in fine istius responsionis, si sacramenta Noui Testamenti adhuc retinemus, nos esse in eorum puerorum numero, quos damnat sacra Scriptura, censendos, & supra refutatum est in argumento 6. superioris responsionis, & ipsum per se falsum est. Nec enim quoduis puerorum genus condemnat sanctus Spiritus, quādoquidem idem ipse vult vt simus pueri malitiā: sed eos duntaxat pueros damnat, qui ignorantia voluntaria & praefracta pueri in Ecclesia Dei permanent. Ac certè velit, nolit iste, faleatur necesse est, omnes sanctos etiam perfectissimos (praeter vnum tamen Dominū nostrum Iesum Christum) vt olim fuisse, sic nunc quoq; esse in hoc mundo (quod ad res aeternas & caelestes) pueros & infirmos & imbecilles. Itaq; adiumētis auxiliisq; praesertim a Deo institutis, id est, Sacramentis opus habere. Quid enim obsecro, & de se, & de aliis fidelib. ingenuè, & verè fatetur Paulus, ille, inquam, Paulus qui arcana Dei homini ineffabilia viderat. Videmus, ait, in ænigmate. Ecclesia illa Dei Apostolica, & verè, si vnquâ aliâs, perfecta Ecclesia, & arcanorum Dei callentissima, vt se in Dei promissionibus de æterna salute confirmet, Cœnam Domini sæpius celebrat, vt Actorum libro apparet. Sed garrulus iste, qui se perfectum hîc magno animi morbo iudicat, putat se cœlestia oculis illis suis emissitiis ac terrenis, & quidem sine Sacramentis vllis videre posse: Apage verò tantas ineptias ac blasphemias nugator.
units.tr: This sophist merely trifles here; he does not answer the question proposed, nor does he solve the argument put to him, because he cannot. Indeed he admits that the sacraments are milk suitable and fitting for nourishing us. Why, then, should we not use them, especially since Christ has commanded it, as we have shown before? Moreover, what he adds at the end of this reply, that if we still retain the sacraments of the New Testament we are to be counted among those children whom holy Scripture condemns, has already been refuted above in the sixth argument of the previous reply, and in itself it is false. For the Holy Spirit does not condemn every kind of child, since the same Spirit wills that we be children in malice; he condemns only those children who remain in the Church of God through a wilful and stubborn ignorance. And certainly, whether he likes it or not, this man must admit that all the saints, even the most perfect (except our one Lord Jesus Christ), were once, and are now still in this world (as regards eternal and heavenly things), children, weak and feeble. Therefore they have need of helps and supports, especially those instituted by God, that is, the sacraments. For what, I beg you, does Paul confess, frankly and truly, both about himself and about other faithful people? That Paul, I say, who had seen the secret things of God that cannot be told to man. "We see," he says, "in a riddle." That Apostolic Church of God, truly, if ever at any time, a perfect Church, and most skilled in the mysteries of God, in order to confirm itself in God's promises of eternal salvation, celebrates the Lord's Supper quite often, as appears in the book of Acts. But this babbler, who here judges himself perfect with a great sickness of mind, thinks he can see heavenly things with those eyes of his, which are earthly and sent out, and indeed without any sacraments at all. Away with such great foolishness and blasphemy, you trifler!

units.la: In responsione ad Quæstionem 14.
units.tr: In reply to Question 14

units.la: Nihil hic agit, nisi quod argumentum illud, Erunt omnes à Deo edocti, repetit, cui nos supra respondimus in argumento 7. Quæst. 4. Quamobrem eò reuocamus lectorem.
units.tr: He does nothing here except repeat that argument, "All shall be taught by God," to which we answered above in the seventh argument of Question 4. Therefore we send the reader back there.

units.la: In responsione ad Quæstionem 15.
units.tr: In reply to Question 15

units.la: Multa uerba & quidem obscura, iste effutit, vt doceat duplex esse hominum genus, vnum nimirum ebriorum. Ij autem sunt, inquit, qui quum veritatem Dei apprimè cognoscant, ea tamen abutuntur, quoniam non ad opera charitatis & virtutis, sed ad ineptas quasdam ostentationes ac mala opera eam cognitionem scientiámve suam conuertunt, ac impendunt. Alterum genus est eorum, qui semper sunt pueri, & nunquam ad tantam illam veritatis cœlestis agnitionem perueniunt, ad quantam primi illi. Quamobrem nunquam hi posteriores fiunt solidioris cibi capaces. Iam verò primùm genus suis, id est, suæ farinæ ac sectæ hominibus accommodat,qui illa excel-lenti Dei cognitione, qua sunt præditi, abu-tuntur adsua vitia. Itaque in eos hîc inuchi-tur,etsi tacito sectæ suæ nomine. Nos autem in altero genere comprehendit, eorum nem-pe, qui nunquam solidiorem cibum edere possunt, quia Sacramentorum à Christo in Nouo Testamento institutorum vsum & Ce-remonias à piis atque in Ecclesia Dei reti-neri debere contendimus. Quasi verò illa Christi sacrosancta Sacramenta contemnere, sit solidi cibi capacem esse.Contra verò Apo-stolus ad Hebræos,docet adultos capaces esse solidi cibi.Illos autem definit esse adultos, qui Christum vera fide agnoscunt verum & vni- cum Pontificem nostrum apud Deum,nec in sacerdotio Leuitico adhuc hærent:qui nec vi-ctimas,nec taurorum sanguinem ad expiatio-nem peccatorum suorum amplius quærunt, sed vnica Christi morte, & purissimo sangui-ne sunt contenti.Quod quum nos ingenuè ac palam agnoscamus,& ex illa Apostoli doctri-na credamus amplectamurque,certè ex Apo-stoli,id est,Spiritus sancti definitione verè su-mus adulti, licet sacramenta Christi retinea-mus: non sumus autem ex istius nugigeruli commentis pueri isto quidem nomine vel censendi vel vocandi. Itaque iam conten-ti sumus ea laude,quam nobis tribuit Spiritus ipse Dei & sanctus: istius autem conuitiatoris calumnias & probra qui nos verósque fideles omnes per contemptum pueros à sacra Scriptura damnatos vocat, secure contemnimus. Porro quod tandem ait, Qui ordinationes Ecclesiæ retinent, eos coacte seruire Deo, est supra à nobis refutatum in 6. Argumento, Responsf. duodecimæ. Nec enim coactio est quum quis lubens ordinem à Deo præscriptū sequitur & amplectitur, & ea quæ Christus præcepit, seruat, & quidem sponte, ac volens. Spontaneum enim & coactum inter sese ex diametro pugnant. Nos autem idcirco & ordinem & cætera à Christo præcepta sponte lubentésque sequimur, quoniâ Spiritum Dei accepimus per fidem in Christum, qui non est Spiritus seruitutis metus vel coactionis, sed Spiritus adoptionis, ac libertatis, vt inquit Paulus, per quem clamamus Abba, Pater. Atque ex his apparet nihil superesse iam in hac responsione, quòd non fuerit à nobis luculenter refutatum.
units.tr: This man babbles many words, and indeed obscure ones, in order to teach that there are two kinds of men, one of them being drunkards. These, he says, are those who, although they know the truth of God very well, nevertheless abuse it, since they turn and spend that knowledge and learning not on works of charity and virtue, but on certain foolish displays and evil works. The other kind is of those who are always children and never attain to that great knowledge of heavenly truth which the first kind attain; therefore these latter never become capable of more solid food. Now indeed he fits the first kind to his own people, that is, men of his own meal and sect, who abuse that excellent knowledge of God with which they are endowed for their own vices. And so he rails at them here, though under the tacit name of his sect. But he includes us in the other kind, namely those who can never eat more solid food, because we contend that the use of the sacraments instituted by Christ in the New Testament and its ceremonies ought to be retained by the godly and in the Church of God. As if to despise those most holy sacraments of Christ were the same thing as being capable of solid food! On the contrary, the Apostle to the Hebrews teaches that the mature are capable of solid food. He defines those to be mature who acknowledge Christ by true faith as our true and only high priest before God, and who no longer cling to the Levitical priesthood; who no longer seek victims or the blood of bulls to expiate their sins, but are content with the one death of Christ and his most pure blood. Since we frankly and openly acknowledge this, and believe and embrace it from that teaching of the Apostle, certainly by the Apostle's definition, that is, by the definition of the Holy Spirit, we are truly mature, even though we retain the sacraments of Christ; we are not to be counted or called children in that sense by the inventions of this bearer of trifles. Therefore we are now content with that praise which the Spirit of God himself and holy Spirit gives us, and we securely despise the calumnies and insults of this reviler, who calls us and all true believers children condemned by holy Scripture, out of contempt. Moreover, as for what he finally says, that those who keep the ordinances of the Church are compelled to serve God, this was already refuted by us above in the sixth argument of the twelfth reply. For it is not compulsion when someone willingly follows and embraces the order prescribed by God, and keeps the things Christ commanded, and indeed of his own accord and willingly. For what is spontaneous and what is compelled fight against each other in direct opposition. We, however, therefore follow the order and the other things commanded by Christ willingly and gladly, since we have received the Spirit of God through faith in Christ, who is not a spirit of bondage, fear or compulsion, but the Spirit of adoption and liberty, as Paul says, through whom we cry, "Abba, Father." And from these things it is clear that nothing remains in this reply which has not been brightly refuted by us.

units.la: In responsione ad Quæstionem 16.
units.tr: In reply to Question 16.

units.la: Qui ritus & ordinationes Ecclesiæ obseruant, patiuntur velut muli & equi frenum sibi inijci ac leges imponi. Ergo omnes ordinationes Ecclesiasticæ, nisi similes pecoribus cāpi esse velimus, sunt à nobis spernendæ atque reiiciendæ.
units.tr: Those who observe the rites and ordinances of the Church submit, like mules and horses, to having a bridle put on them and laws imposed. Therefore all ecclesiastical ordinances, unless we wish to be like beasts of the herd, must be spurned and rejected by us.

units.la: Paulus in Epistola ad Titum describens mores ac veras notas eorum, qui Ecclesiam Dei mentésque hominum falsis doctrinis ac vaniloquio suo decipiût, & corrûpunt, ait, eos ex eo maximè cognosci, quod sint refractarij & rebelles. Nec enim vlli ordini, præsertim EccleEcclesiastico & sancto, sese illi subijciunt: sed velut effrænes equi licentia carnis lasciuientes atque proterui viuunt. Itaque veram Chiftianamque libertatem (quæ in legitimo ordine omnibus in rebus seruando consistit) odio prosequentes, nullis legibus teneri, nullis repagulis coërceri se patiuntur. Quæ eadem pseudoprophetarum signa fore docet Petrus, & Iudas. Verum Ecclesia est domus illa Dei, in qua singula recte atque recto ordine, non autem confusè & perturbatè, pro cuiusque arbitratu aut impetu, fieri oportet. Quare cum illeomnem illum Ecclesiasticum ordinem, & omnes sanctasEcclesiæ ordinationes asperneatur, imò conuellendas censeat, seipsum, quali sit ingenio, ostendit, id est, ex eo hominum genere, qui pseudoprophetæ & mentium deceptores ab Apostolis appellantur. Fatemur quidem non cuicunque decreto, quod aliqui nomine Pastorum collecti sine iudicio constituerint, esse parendum: sed tamen illi etiam ipsi temerario decreto ordine & recta ratione ex ordinis Ecclesiastici legibus, non autem ex animi furore est obuiam eundum ac resistendum. Sanctis autem Ecclesiæ ordinationibus qui parendum negat, ille ex Ecclesia Dei meram populi secem: ex Dei domo, sententinam malorum: ex cœlo prope ipso, spelunca latronum facit. Sed quid pluribus opus est, quum iam toties hoc Libertinorum hæreticorum argumentum fuerit à nostris confutatum?
units.tr: Paul, in his Epistle to Titus, describing the character and true marks of those who deceive the Church of God and the minds of men with false doctrines and empty talk, and who corrupt them, says that they are chiefly recognised by this: that they are refractory and rebellious. For they submit to no order, least of all to the ecclesiastical and holy one, but live wanton and headstrong like unbridled horses, given over to the license of the flesh. Thus, hating true Christian liberty (which consists in keeping legitimate order in all things), they suffer themselves to be bound by no laws and restrained by no barriers. Peter and Jude teach that these are the same signs of false prophets. The Church, however, is that house of God in which each thing ought to be done rightly and in good order, not confusedly and disorderly, according to each person's whim or impulse. Therefore, since he spurns that whole ecclesiastical order and all the holy ordinances of the Church, and even judges them to be overthrown, he shows what sort of character he has: that he belongs to that class of men whom the Apostles call false prophets and deceivers of minds. We admit indeed that one must not obey every decree that some men, gathered under the name of Pastors, have made without judgment.
