Yet even such a rash decree must be opposed and resisted by order and right reason, according to the laws of ecclesiastical order, not by the frenzy of the spirit. But whoever refuses to obey the holy ordinances of the Church makes of the Church of God a mere sect of the people, of the house of God a den of evildoers, and of heaven itself almost a cave of robbers. But why do we need more, since this argument of the Libertine heretics has so often been refuted by our people?

units.la: Lex non est posita iustis. Ergo qui ordina-tiones Ecclesiasticas seruant,sunt iuiusti.
units.tr: Law is not laid down for the just. Therefore those who keep ecclesiastical ordinances are unjust.

units.la: Detorquetur plane sic Pauli locus à vero sensu. Docet enim illic Paulus Legem Dei esse bonam,vtpote quę nequaquam est curio-sarum quæstionum ac & genealogiarum gra-tiâ,scriptis tradita: sed vt hominum vitia dam naret coërceretque. Itaque illic agit Paulus primùm de Lege Dei, non de Ecclesiasticis ordinationibus, quæ etiam sanctè viuentibus feruntur,vt melius quid sit ipsis tanquā Chri-stianis, tum publicè tum priuatim decorum, doceatur. Deinde id dicit Paulus in ea quæ-stione,vbi homines abutuntur lege scripta ad vaniloquentiam,nec eam ad suum verùmque vsum referunt. Ordinationes autem ecclesia-sticæ nihil commune habent cum istiusmodi argumento. Quamobrem ineptissima est, & nihil ad rem quæstionémque nostram faciens Pauli locus ab isto hîc citatus.
units.tr: This passage of Paul is plainly twisted from its true sense. For Paul there teaches that God's Law is good, since it was committed to writing not for the sake of curious questions and genealogies, but to restrain and check the vices of men. So there Paul treats first of God's Law, not of ecclesiastical ordinances, which are also given to those who live piously, so that what is fitting for them as Christians, both in public and in private, may be taught. Then Paul says this in a question where men abuse the written law for empty talk and do not refer it to its proper and true use. Ecclesiastical ordinances, however, have nothing in common with that kind of argument. Therefore the passage of Paul cited here by this man is most inept and has nothing to do with the matter or with our question.

units.la: Non est vèrus Baptismus qui fit elementari aqua & manu, sed qui fit à Spiritu igneo & ar-denti amore. Ergo ille Baptismus, qui nunc fit in Ecclesiis elementari aqua,est à piis sper-nendus.
units.tr: That is not true Baptism which is done with elemental water and by hand, but that which is done by the fiery Spirit and burning love. Therefore that Baptism which now takes place in the Churches with elemental water is to be spurned by the pious.

units.la: Quàm sit ineptus scriptor iste certè quidem apparet,qui ita extrà oleas vagetur, Nam cum de Ecclesiæ ordinationibus supra agere insti-tuisset, sermonem ipsum statim abrumpens alio conuolat, atque disputat de Baptismo: quasi Baptismus etiam ille qui fit elementari aqua, tiatores,ad quos te,quum tibi erit otium, remitto.Caeterum quòd Vbique tu Vbiquitarius confundis ista duo,Christum hominem, & Christi carnem & sanguinem,seu humanam naturam, imperitè & ignoranter facis. Hominis enim vox in Christo est persone: Carnis autem est in eodem, naturæ tantùm significatio. Ergo Christum hominem vbique esse concedimus, quia hypostatica naturarum vnio in Christo nunquam dissoluitur, ac ne quidem quum essest Christi corpus in sepulcro, & anima in paradiso. Naturam autem ipsam humanam Christi esse vbique,negamus. Quæ distinctio, & veritas abs te non perceptaiinfinitos tuos tuorumque gryphos dissoluit. Quod autem Vbiquitatis,id est, Helenæ tuæ te pudet, te dignũ facis, quem etiam proprij nominis in hoc scripto puduerit. Vocas nos,Artolatras,potuisti nos,vt conuitiorum tuorũ numerum implêres, Miluios appellare, & te Erucam. Qui verò nos Artolatræ,id est,panis adoratores, Laonice, qui ne ipsam quidem Christi Domini nostri carnem,si à λόγῳ separata re ipsa esset,adoraremus,quia creatura est. Dicis nos tecum vnâ carnem Christi edere, ergo esse σαρκοφάγους. Respondeo, Non appellari à nobis σαρκοφάγως eos, qui veram ipsam Christi carnem per fidem manducant.sed qui,Capernaitarum more,eam ore & dentibus corporis à se mandi contendunt, quod vos, & Papistæ fraterculi vestri,facitis.Quod autem ad infinita illa conuitia, (quæ, vt nos orthodoxos merito damnare videreris, solito animi morbo,non iudicio,in nos euomuisti) & ad tuas
units.tr: How inept this writer is certainly appears, since he wanders so far off the point. Having set out to treat of the ordinances of the Church, he breaks off the discussion at once, flies off elsewhere, and disputes about Baptism, as if that Baptism which is done with elemental water... [Anabaptists?], to whom I refer you when you have leisure. But as to the fact that you, a Ubiquitarian, everywhere confuse these two things, Christ the man and Christ's flesh and blood, or human nature, you do so unskillfully and ignorantly. For "man" in Christ is a word signifying the person; "flesh" in the same Christ signifies only the nature. Therefore we concede that Christ the man is everywhere, because the hypostatic union of the natures in Christ is never dissolved, not even when Christ's body was in the sepulchre and his soul in paradise. But we deny that Christ's human nature itself is everywhere. This distinction and truth, which you have not grasped, dissolves your endless griffins and those of your people. As for the Ubiquity, that is, your Helen, of which you are ashamed, you make yourself worthy of it, you who in this writing were ashamed even of your own proper name. You call us Artolatrae, and you could have called us kites and yourself a caterpillar, to fill up your number of insults. But as for calling us Artolatrae, that is, worshippers of bread, Laonicus, we would not even adore the very flesh of Christ our Lord, if it were actually separated from the Word [λόγῳ], because it is a creature. You say that we eat Christ's flesh together with you, and therefore that we are sarcophagi [σαρκοφάγοι]. I reply: we do not call sarcophagi those who eat the true flesh of Christ through faith, but those who, in the manner of the Capernaites, contend that it is chewed by the mouth and teeth of the body, which you and your Papist little brothers do. As for those endless insults (which you vomited out against us, from your usual sickness of mind rather than from judgment, as if to condemn us orthodox deservedly), and your

units.la: E.j.
units.tr: E.j.

units.la: illas de ouiculis & pastoribus falsas distinctiones, quas à pag.32. vsque ad pag.36. laboriosè quidè & prolixè, sed frustra persequeris, hoc vnum tamen responsum à me accipe, quod tibi prosit, præter ea, quæ in postrema mea ad insidiosum Osiandri scriptum responsione probaui (ad quæ te reuoco.) Qui orthodoxos sic temere & ferociter damnant, qui sic blasphemant, qui sic à veritate deflectunt, vt tu hic facis, tandem in ipso corpore suo sensuros esse iustum Dei iudicium. Cuius rei vnum hoc tibi ex vera veteris & Christianæ Ecclesiæ historia narrabo. Osius ille Cordubensis Episcopus (cuius apud plerosque Christianos, Constantij Imperatoris Constantinopolitani tempore, magna autoritas fuit) cum in Sardicensi concilio Arrianæ impietati consensisset, & Cordubæ Gregorium Eliberitanum Episcopum huiusmodi blasphemiæ repugnantem ipse pro fastu Osiano & aulico dånaturus in throno Superintedetis, seu Episcopali cofedisset, in eamque suâ sententiâ condenatoriâ Clementinum Cordubæ præfectum etiam adduxisset, quo tempore erat tamen sententiâ pronùtiaturus, statim ore distorto, ceruice inflexa, ac de throno in solù decidés (miro Dei iudicio in vos omnes viros condenatos edito) illic miserè expirauit. Atque hæc non sunt, Laonice, fabulæ, non couitia: sed res gesta. Quod Osij viri Episcopi aulici exemplù ad te, & tuum Osiandrù concionatore aulicum pertinet, quod illi vt tempestiuè suggeras, etiâ atque etiâ rogo. Nam Honorichi Vvadalorum, & Hermerici Suevorum Regis, cùm vterque orthodoxos exiliis mul-
units.tr: those false distinctions about little sheep and shepherds, which you pursue laboriously and at length, but in vain, from page 32 to page 36, take from me this one answer, which may profit you, besides those things I proved in my last reply to the insidious writing of Osiander (to which I recall you). Those who so rashly and fiercely condemn the orthodox, who blaspheme in this way, who deviate from the truth as you do here, will at last feel God's just judgment in their own body. I will tell you one example of this from the true history of the old Christian Church. That Osius, bishop of Cordoba (who among many Christians, in the time of Constantius, Emperor at Constantinople, had great authority), when at the Council of Sardica he had consented to Arian impiety, and at Cordoba had seated himself on the episcopal throne as overseer, in order to condemn with courtly and haughty arrogance Gregory of Elvira, bishop, who resisted such blasphemy, and had also brought Clementinus, prefect of Cordoba, into that condemnatory sentence, at the very moment when he was about to pronounce his judgment, his mouth was suddenly twisted, his neck bent, and falling from the throne to the ground (a wondrous judgment of God, shown against all of you condemned men), there he miserably expired. These things, Laonicus, are not fables or insults, but a deed done. What the example of Osius, the courtly bishop, has to do with you and your courtly preacher Osiander, I ask you again and again to suggest in good time. For when Honoric, king of the Vandals, and Hermeric, king of the Suevi, had each punished the orthodox with exile,

units.la: Ioannes Vaffaus in Chronicis pag.526. mulctasset, qualis, & quàm tragicus fuerit exitus, quid attinet dicere? quia tu leges eam historiam, cùm tibi tantum erit otij ut rebus honestis vacare possis. Cæterum quòd tu pag. 37. & alibi me probè Pergulam mentitum esse scribis, pene demisisti gladium in gulam, vt ait ille, si vera dixisses. Verùm tu melius, & phrasi latina (quam habet Cicero in oratione pro A. Cluentio) respondere debuisti: quam, quoniam ignoras (procul dubio enim hic addidisses) eam ipse respondens, te docebo, Magnum est, & impudens mendacium. quid ais, Laonice. Ipse tu, non ego, falsarius aperte deprehenderis, qui (te ipso teste) hic neges, quod res est. Dixi enim, abs te, & tuis, Gallicas, Anglicas, Belgicas, Polonicas, Scoticas, & alias omnes orthodoxas mundi Ecclesias damnari haereseos, dum eos, qui earum doctrinam profitentur, propter eam ipsam doctrinam in exilium eiicitis. Hoc postremum de exilio tu verissimum fateris esse. Nonne enim ipse hic scripsisti, non solum nostrum dogma, sed etiam nostras personas, id est, eos omnes, qui illud docent, re vera ab Oslandro, & a vestrae illius factionis Sexuiris velut haereticos iudicari & proscribi? Quomodo igitur mentior, qui quod ipse fateris esse verum affirmo? Tu igitur potius mentitus deprehenderis, qui sciens & prudens id neges, quod verum est, & tua scripta confirmant. Profecto illud est, quod habet proverbium vetus, ἀσυλλόγιστον καὶ πρόπετες ἐστιν ἡ πονηρία, & improbus improbè conuitiatur. Nam qui sic & viuit & sentit, vt tu, Nicodeme, aliter, atque tu, loqui non poteست.
units.tr: John Vaseus, in his Chronicles, page 526. What sort of end it was, and how tragic, what is the point of saying? You will read that history when you have leisure enough to be able to devote yourself to honourable things. But as to your saying, on page 37 and elsewhere, that I have lied shamelessly, you almost let the sword down into your throat, as the saying goes, if you had spoken the truth. Yet you ought to have replied with the Latin phrase that Cicero uses in his speech for Aulus Cluentius. Since you do not know it (no doubt you would have added it here), I will teach you by answering in its place: "It is a great and shameless lie." What do you say, Laonicus? You yourself, not I, are openly caught as a forger, you who, by your own testimony, deny here what is the case. For I said that by you and your people the French, English, Belgian, Polish, Scottish and all other orthodox Churches of the world are condemned as heretical, while you cast into exile those who profess their doctrine, on account of that very doctrine. This last point about exile you yourself admit is most true. For did you not write here that not only our doctrine but our persons, that is, all who teach it, are in fact judged and proscribed as heretics by Osiander and by that faction's Sexuviri? How, then, do I lie when I affirm what you yourself admit to be true? You are rather caught lying, you who knowingly and deliberately deny what is true, and what your own writings confirm. That is surely what the old proverb means: wickedness is witless and headlong [ἀσυλλόγιστον καὶ πρόπετες ἐστιν ἡ πονηρία], and the wicked man reviles without restraint. For whoever lives and thinks as you do, Nicodemus, cannot speak otherwise than you do.

units.la: E.ij. Sed non his in me conuitiis contentus, Scelerato perturbatores, & factiosos homines vocas, quos non ipsi illustrissimi Principes Germaniæ, sed tui, tui, inquam, quidam Sexuiri e scholis, e patria, ex Ecclesiis (gregibus ipsis inuitis & gementibus) eiecerunt. Atqui conuitium istud tam graue in tot viros bonos & pios a te, præ animi impotentia, virulenter eiaculatum probandum tibi est, Laonice, nec illud impune, si perstiteris, feres. Quod si, quantum in syluis audacia potest, tantum in istis controuersiis valeret impudentia: certe plenam victoriæ spem facile ex teipso conciperes, qui tot bonos viros tam horribiliter audes calumniari. Verum his tuis tam manifestis conuitiis non respondere, vincere est. Ergo pergamus.
units.tr: E.ij. But not content with these insults against me, you call them "wicked disturbers and factious men." Yet they were not expelled by the most illustrious princes of Germany themselves but by your people, yes, your own, certain men of the six-man commission from the schools and the fatherland, who cast them out of the churches (the flocks themselves unwilling and groaning). Yet this grave insult, which you have hurled so violently at so many good and pious men out of sheer lack of self-control, you must prove, Laonice, and if you persist you will not bear it unpunished. But if audacity could do as much in the woods as impudence can in these controversies, you could certainly conceive a full hope of victory from yourself, since you dare to slander so many good men so horribly. But not to answer these insults of yours, so manifest, is to conquer. So let us proceed.

units.la: Dicis, Principibus vestris liberum esse, aut Pontificem, aut Lutherum audire. Hoc quum dicis, quid sit Christianum esse, ad hunc vsque diem, ut video, ignorasti. Cum enim Illustrissimi Germaniæ Principes (qui Protestantes appellantur) sint Christiani: iis certe neque Pontificem, neque Lutherum, neque alium quenquam ἀνθρωπον hominem sequi & audire liberum est: sed vnum modo Christum, verè Deum & verè hominem, vnicum doctorem nostrum a Patre de cœlo missum, de quo solo dixit loquens, & quidem de cœlo, Pater, Hic est Filius meus dilectus, ipsum audite. Cum enim pretioso Christi sanguine redempti simus nos Christiani, vetat Paulus ne fiamus serui hominum. Cæterum illud admodum sum miratus, & mecum pij omnes, qui tuum scriptum legerunt, quòd tam præcipiti animi perturbatione, in
units.tr: You say that your princes are free to hear either the Pope or Luther. In saying this, you have, as I see, until this day not known what it is to be a Christian. For since the most illustrious princes of Germany, who are called Protestants, are Christians, it is certainly not free for them to follow or hear the Pope, or Luther, or any other man [ἄνθρωπον]. They may hear only Christ, truly God and truly man, our one teacher, sent from the Father out of heaven, of whom alone the Father said, speaking from heaven, "This is my beloved Son; hear him." For since we Christians have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, Paul forbids us to become slaves of men. But I was greatly astonished, as were all the pious men who have read your writing, that in such a headlong disturbance of mind

units.la: hac tua Vbiquitate, quo iure, quáue iniuria defendenda, fueris abreptus, vt etiam probares Satanicam illam Synagogam, quę Constantię duos Euangelij Christi testes, duas illas oleas & candelabra (vt vocat Spiritus sanctus) Ioanne Hussium nimirum & Hieronymum Pragensem crudeliter extinxit, Hanc te coniurationem impiorum Vniuersale concilium appellare? Denique condemnationi cœlestis doctrinæ ab ea synagoga factæ tunc acquiescendum putas? Satin' sanus es, Laonice, qui hæc publicè edas & dicitis? Atqui illa ipsa Synodus Constantiensis, vt & Tridentinum concilium, si ita vocas, (cuius doctrinam tamè Kemnitius tuus, vt scis, magno volumine cofutauit) tuam & confubstantiationem, & hypostaticæ naturarum vnionis definitionem, atque Vbiquitatem manifestè damnant. Cur igitur tam cæcus es & temerarius, vt illa ipsa probes, quæ manifestè temetipsum euertunt? Porrò ad illud, quod tam anxiè quæris, Annon singulis Germaniæ Principibus licet in suis Ecclesiis, Synodos agere, ibique cum Caluinistis disputare? iam in Antiochiandro responderam. Primùm, illud ipsum nos optare, & à vobis obnixè petere, vt nobiscum legitima Synodo placidè disceptetis, atque de hac doctrina conferatis. Illum autem Dominorum Superintendentium, & Diotrephum vestrorum cum suis assessoribus in singulorum Principum ditione conuentum respondimus, neque parem esse vniuersæ Ecclesiæ orthodoxæ autoritati, & Synodo: neque de dogmate & articulo fidei contra reliquarum Ecclesiarum, præsertim
units.tr: you were carried away to defend this your Ubiquity, by what right or wrong I cannot say, so that you even approve that Satanic synagogue which at Constance cruelly extinguished the two witnesses of the gospel of Christ, the two olive trees and candlesticks (as the Holy Spirit calls them), namely John Hus and Jerome of Prague. Do you call this conspiracy of the impious a universal council? Finally, do you think that the condemnation of heavenly doctrine made by that synagogue must then be acquiesced in? Are you in your right mind, Laonice, to publish and say these things publicly? Yet that very Council of Constance, and also the Council of Trent, if you so call it (whose doctrine, however, your Kemnitz refuted at length in a large volume, as you know), manifestly condemn your consubstantiation, the definition of the hypostatic union of the natures, and Ubiquity. Why then are you so blind and rash as to approve those very things which plainly overthrow you? Furthermore, to what you so anxiously ask, "May not each of the princes of Germany hold synods in his own churches and there dispute with the Calvinists?", I have already answered in the Antiochiander. First, we ourselves wish for this very thing, and we earnestly ask you to contend calmly with us in a lawful synod and to confer with us about this doctrine. But we have answered that the assembly of your lord superintendents and your Diotrephes, with their assessors, held within the dominion of each prince, is neither equal to the authority of the whole orthodox Church and its synod, nor able to define a consensus on a dogma and article of faith against the other churches, especially

units.la: Trident Synodus sess. 3. c. 3. cā. 4.
units.tr: Trident Synod, sess. 3, c. 3, can. 4.

units.la: Antiochiandri Pag. 55. inauditarum, consensum definire posse. Itaque qui conuentus a paucis aliquot sociis vestris, Torgæ, Bergæ, Vvittebergæ, nuper acti sunt & habiti, & nunc fortasse aguntur, ne Mericæ quidem & Nationalis Synodi nome meretur, & autoritatem habent: necdum vt pro vniuersali totius reformatæ Ecclesiæ Synodo & decreto habeantur. Ergo nullum nobis inauditis præiudicium afferunt: quemadmodum in Antiochiandro luculenter demonstrauî. Sed tu totis sex paginis integris nullum non lapidem moues, nullam non calumniam in nos fingis, nulla non autoritatem tibi, tuisque tribuis, denique sudas, & æstuas: refutare tamen quod dixi, nequaquam, Laonice, potuisti: tam est nimirum aduersus omnes tuos errores potens Dei verbum, & veritas, qua in tuendo legitimo Synodorum iure & autoritate aduersus priuatas vestras de nobis condemnationes, vt vides, nitor. Nam quod ais, apud vos a pueris quadrimis Anabaptistas, & Schuecfeldianos hæreticos refutari, certè illi pueri sunt longè teipso, atque Sex illis tuis Theologis (qui tamen inter vestros censentur columnæ) doctiores, vt pote qui, quoniam Eutychetis seu Schuenckfeldij errorem confutare non potuistis, in eum consensistis. Nam in Vbiquitare stabilienda, & in deificanda, ac λόγῳ ἐχαρίζεσθαι quanda Christi carne, estis eum ambabus manibus amplexi. Quod autem ad marginem pag. 42, addidistī, quasi dixerim, Quod sine vniuersali Synodo nemo sit damnandus, hic, vt in aliis quoque meiAntiochiandri partibus, non satis euigilasti. Neque enim dico Neminem, quod
units.tr: Antiochiandrus, p. 55. Hence those gatherings, lately held and convened at Torgau, Berga, and Wittenberg by a few of your associates, and perhaps being held now, do not even deserve the name of a national or provincial synod, and they have authority only for themselves, and are not to be regarded as a synod and decree of the universal reformed Church. Therefore they bring no prejudice against us, who have not been heard, as I have clearly shown in the Antiochiandrus. But you, through six full pages, leave no stone unturned, invent every slander against us, and attribute every authority to yourself and your friends; you sweat and seethe. Yet you have not at all been able to refute what I said, Laonice; so mighty against all your errors is the word of God and the truth, on which I rely in defending the lawful right and authority of synods against your private condemnations of us, as you see. For as to your claim that the Anabaptists and the heretics of Schwenckfeld are refuted among you by four-year-old boys, those boys are certainly far more learned than yourself and those six theologians of yours (who are nevertheless counted among your pillars), inasmuch as, since you could not refute the error of Eutyches or Schwenckfeld, you have agreed with it. For in establishing Ubiquity, and in deifying the flesh of Christ, and in some sense bestowing it by the Word [λόγῳ ἐχαρίζεσθαι], you have embraced it with both hands. As for what you have added in the margin of page 42, as if I had said that no one may be condemned without a universal synod, here, as in other parts of my Antiochiandrus, you have not woken up enough. For I do not say that no one, as regards individuals,

units.la: Pag. 41. quod ad singulos pertinet, sed dico Nullum dogma, manens inter ipsas Dei Ecclesias controversum, ab vna duntaxat Ecclesia, & parte altera inaudita, damnari debere, sed à tota Dei Ecclesia in Concilio legitimo, & orthodoxo generali id fieri oportere. De vocabulo autem Superintendens (quod tu, ex meo in Pouchenium loco admonitus, in Superattendens iam mutasti) & illius origine: quod item de pinguibus & nitidis culinis (in quibus versaris) de Berengarianis, de Satana Caluinico scribis, tam sunt ea omnia & sal sa, & inepta, vt seipsa satis refutent. Atque tu ipse, nisi ea sale profano, & carmine (quod à furiis Vergilianis didicisti) condidisses, insipidum prorsus futurum esse praevidisti. Contra vero vide, qualis sit spiritus noster, quem Caluinicum inuidiosè appellas, Laonice. Pro illo enim tuo,
units.tr: Page 41. but I say that no dogma which remains disputed among the very churches of God should be condemned by one church alone, and the other party unheard, but that this must be done by the whole Church of God in a lawful and orthodox general council. As to the word superintendent (which you have now changed into superattendent, admonished by my remark on the passage concerning Pouchenius), and its origin; and likewise what you write about the fat and polished kitchens (in which you live), about the Berengarians, about the Calvinist Satan, all these are so salty and silly that they refute themselves well enough. And you yourself foresaw that they would be quite insipid unless you had seasoned them with profane salt and verse (which you learned from the Vergilian furies). But look instead at what kind of spirit ours is, which you invidiously call Calvinist, Laonice. For against that spirit of yours,

units.la: Tu potes vnanimes armare in praelia fratres:
units.tr: You can arm brothers of one mind for battle.

units.la: En tibi primum ex eodem Vergilio reponimus, & ex animo quidem, Nulla salus bello, pacem te poscimus omnes. Bella vides, quantos primus patiare labores.
units.tr: Behold, first, we answer you from the same Vergil, and truly from the heart: There is no safety in war; we all ask you for peace. You see what great labours you will first suffer in war.

units.la: Deinde istis quoque addimus, haec & potiora, & ex Dei verbo veriora, vt intelligas qualis sit Caluinistarum (quos vocas) animus.
units.tr: Then we add to these also other things, both more weighty and truer from the word of God, so that you may understand what the spirit of the Calvinists (as you call them) is.

units.la: Quam bella res est, & quam amabilis amor Fraterna iungens pectora? Non balsamum illi conferas, cuius nitet Vertex Aronis vnguine, Fragranti odore barbam, & auream togam A summo ad imum proluens:
units.tr: How good a thing it is, and how lovely, that brothers dwell together in unity! It is like the precious ointment upon the head, running down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard, down to the skirts of his garments.

units.la: Non roris vber, Hermonis herbidi iuga, Iuga & Syonis inebrians.
units.tr: Like the dew of Hermon, that falls upon the mountains of Zion.

units.la: Namque hic benigna summus effundit manu Pater vsque & vsque opes suas.
units.tr: For there the LORD commands the blessing, even life for evermore.

units.la: Vides igitur qualis sit & quàm pacificus, & à Patre pacis, Deo optimo maximo, Patre luminū profectus is Spiritus, qui nos gubernat. Quid igitur huic paci, quam quaerimus, obstat? Certè illud, quod verè hîc cum Gregorio magno, & magno cum gemitu de vobis & nobis dicimus, Peccata nostra barbaricis, nempe Turcicis, viribus sociamus, ad compescendos mundi motus pacem quaerit Ecclesia. En igitur coram vniuerso mundo testamur, quis sit & quàm desiderans pacis animus nostep, si tu miles, tuíque eam nobis concedere & vultis, & potestis. Caeterum quod toties inculcas, Religionem Anglorum, Gallorum, Belgarum nihil ad vos pertinere, certè & inhumanum est, & minimè Christianum. Nonne si vestri Christiani sunt, Christi corporis sunt membra, Laonicc, quae est vniuersa reformata, non autem tantum vna Germanica Ecclesia? Quid igitur illud Iacobi à te initio huius tui libri citatum, non ad omnes Christianos, sed ad solos eos pertinere putas qui eidem Principi Germaniae subiiciuntur? Fratres, si quis inter vos aberrarit à veritate, & converterit eum quispiam, sciat eum, qui peccatorem a- uerterit ab errore viae suae seruaturum animam à morte. Sunt tibi tam viles pretiosae illę piorum animę, pro quibus ipse Dei Filius Christus mortuus est, vt earum salutem nihil ad vestros pertinere censeas? Quàm longè alio ipse spiritu duceris, atque selectum
units.tr: You see therefore what sort of Spirit this is that governs us, and how peaceable it is, proceeding from the Father of peace, God the best and greatest, the Father of lights. What then stands in the way of this peace which we seek? Certainly that which we truly say here, with Gregory the Great and with great groaning, concerning you and us: Our sins join forces with the barbarians, namely the Turks, and the Church seeks peace to quell the disturbances of the world. Behold, then, before the whole world we declare what kind of peaceable mind we have, if you too are willing and able to grant it to us. But as to your repeated insistence that the religion of the English, French, and Belgians is nothing to do with you, this is surely both inhuman and by no means Christian. If your people are Christians, are they not members of the body of Christ, Laonice, and is not the whole reformed Church, not merely the one German church, part of that body? Why then do you think that what you cited at the beginning of this book from James applies not to all Christians but only to those who are subject to the same prince of Germany? Brethren, if anyone among you wander from the truth, and someone convert him, let him know that he who converts a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death. Are those pious souls, for whom the Son of God Christ himself died, so worthless to you that you think their salvation has nothing to do with your people? How far differently is the chosen vessel of God, Paul, led by a different spirit! For he testifies that he rejoices greatly that the truth of the gospel has reached the whole world. You say that the glory of God which lies outside the province of the Duke of Württemberg has nothing to do with you. How far this is from Osiander himself, for whom...

units.la: fcleætum illud Dei organum, Paulus? Ille enim vehementer se gaudere testatur, quòd veritas Euangelij in totum mundum peruenerit. Tu eam Dei gloriam, quæ est extra Ducis Vvirtembergici prouinciam, nihil ad te pertinere dicis. Quàm longè ab ipso iam Osiandro(pro quo pugnare videri vis)dissidesne tamen? Nam ille nuper Epistolam ad Gallicas & Belgicas Ecclesias scripsit,quòd & Gallorum,& Belgarum fidem ad se spectare iudicaret. Quantum etiam à tuo Gerlachio,qui tecum viuit, discrepas sententiâ? Ille enim, vt ipsos adeò Græcos ad Vbiquitatis doctrinam conuerteret, Constantinopolim vsque profectum se scribit. Ergo vel cum tuis consenti, Laonice, vel communem cum iis caussam tueri desine videri velle. Cæterum quod de variis nostrorum cum vestris colloquiis, Marpurgi, Heidelbergæ, Maulbrunnæ habitis, dixi, Theologos nostros in nulla collatione vnquam victos, imò eaten' victores discesisse, vt & Lutherus ipse, & vestri, mitigandas esse suas locutiones, fatentur,non refutas, quicquid pag. 46. & sequentibus vsque ad 51. æstuces. Neque etiam quod ex ipsiusmet Lutheri scriptis probaui, & è Sueuico Syngrammate (cuius proculdubio fuit autor Brentius, nondum primatum Germaniæ affectans, sed æquus & suo gradu adhuc contentus) adduxi. Item quod ostendi,Lutherum vsum esse in hoc de Coenæ argumento explicando, voce Significandi,eo ipso sensu quo nos facimus,&vestros nobiscum consensisse, id negare neque potuisti, neque in æternum, quandiu illa scripta extabunt, tabunt,poteris,quoniam illa te refutabunt. Por-rò in eo quod ais, Nostram de Cœna Domini sententiam cum pontificia opinione, id est, cum Transsubstantiatione concordare, in eo certè me misertum est tui, qui tam aperte sententias ἀπηχθισμένας ex animi cæcitate confundas,& ignem cum aqua misceas. Ergo quid sentias ipse, video te non intelligere. Nam non vides ipsam Confubstantiationem (quam vos Vbiquitarij omnes tuemini)ab homine Cardinali, & Pontificio, Petro de Aliaco, inuentam esse, atque etiam esse ex manifestis fontibus Pontificiis de Transsubstantiatione erroris profectam, illíque similimam. Illud modò discrimen inter utrunque, (id est, hunc vestrum de Confubstantiatione, & illum pontificiorum de Transubstantiatione) errorem apparet, quòd Pontificius error & minus absurditatum atque blasphemiarum habet, quàm vestra Vbiquitas: & ad verba ipsa Christi (si modò in Sacramento Sacramentalis locutio locum habere non potest) propiùs certè quidem accedere vi debitur. Absit tamen, vt ille in verbis Christi vllum habeat, vti nec vester, fundamentum. Porrò Iesuitam quendam Ingolstadiensem contra vestram Vbiquitatem iampridem scripsisse conqueruit. Quidni verò ille faceret, Laonice, & illum errorem Eutychianum pro virili euerteret, cuius etsi Sathan autor est, ipsum tamen Sathanam tam foedi erroris iam manifestè pudet? Quod vel ex eo apparet, quoniam istam Vbiquitatem tantopere antea à vobis adamatum, nunc aperte vos repudiatis ac horretis. De Lutheri cum Zvvinglio glio æquitate,post colloquium Marpurgense,de concordia inter Lutherum & Helueticas Ecclesias per piæ memoriæ virum, Dominum Bucerum conciliata, quod scripsi,vti verissimum est, ita nequaquam refutas, Laonice:ex eóque intelligis,vti tu, tuíque(qui Lutheri discipuli & imitatores videri vultis) longissimè ab illius viri æ-quanimitate& humanitate discedatis:& nihil Lutheri,nisi nimia eius fortasse bilem,quam ipse tamē detestat³ est,id est,nihil aliud quàm vitia Lutheri(fuit enim peccator MartinusLutherus)no bis representetis & recoquatis. Cæterùm quum diuinum illum virum,totius Germaniæ lumen, præceptorem omnium vestrum,Philippum Melanchthonem,qui primus Germaniam ex puerilibus Grammaticæ elementis (quæ antea duntaxat nouerat) ad summam eruditionis laudem euexit, quum, inquam, talem tu virum & ignorantiæ,& impij metus damnas, quàm te impudentem, quàm ingratum, quàm ipse te impium prodis, qui neque præceptoris tui,neque mortui hominis manes & ossa in Christo placidè quiescere, præ animi tui impotentiâ, sinis? Quid tibi dicam? Quem tibi Christianorum,quem profanorum virorum obiiciam? Saltem M.illum Tullium Ciceronem, cuius eloquentiam adumbrare videri vis: & maximum illum Macedonum Regem Alexandrum, quia nobilem & equitem te esse scribis, imitare, quorum vterque suos præceptores impesè & laudibus & omnibus honoris generibus cohonestauit. Alexander quidem,Aristotelem: Cicero verò, Poetâ Archiam. Verùm imbrem hìc in cribro gestas. Nam nemo tibi lucem tenebras vocanti credet.Sed,vt similis tui esses,hoc præclaro scilicet colophone, & impio conuitio in Philippum, primam illam tuarum in me calumniarum partem claudere voluisti. Minùs iam molestè fero igitur,me hominem extraneum omni probrorum genere abs te immerito proscindi, qui ne à præceptore quidem olim tuo, & viro illo grauissimo Philippo Melanchthone, vel nunc à viro clarissimo Ioanne-Sturmio, Germaniæ φωσφόρῳ abstinueris. Itaque quemadmodum à conuitiis librum tuum orsus es, ita in conuitia desinis,vt sit dignum videlicet patella operculum. Quam primi tui scripti partem,quia facilè & verè,vt vides,confutaui,ad alteram,quæ postrema est,accedo.
units.tr: Did he not choose that vessel of God, Paul? For he testifies that he rejoiced greatly that the truth of the gospel had reached the whole world. You say that the glory of God which lies outside the province of the Duke of Württemberg is no concern of yours. How far, moreover, do you yourself differ from Osiander, the man you seem to want to defend? For he recently wrote an epistle to the French and Belgic churches, because he judged that the faith of the French and the Belgians was his concern too. And how far do you differ in opinion from your Gerlach, who lives with you? He writes that he travelled as far as Constantinople in order to bring the Greeks themselves over to the doctrine of ubiquity. So either agree with your own people, Laonicus, or stop wanting to seem to defend a cause you share with them. As for what I said about the various conferences between our people and yours, held at Marburg, Heidelberg and Maulbronn, namely that our theologians were never defeated in any conference but in fact left as victors, and that Luther himself and your own people admit that their expressions must be softened, you do not refute it, whatever you rage about on page 46 and the following pages up to 51. Nor have you refuted what I proved from Luther's own writings and what I drew from the Swabian Syngramma (whose author was undoubtedly Brenz, who had not yet aspired to the primacy of Germany but was fair-minded and still content with his own rank). Likewise, you could neither deny nor, as long as those writings survive, ever will deny, what I showed: that Luther, in explaining the doctrine of the Supper, used the word significandi in exactly the sense we give it, and so agreed with us and not with you. Those writings will refute you. Moreover, as for your claim that our doctrine of the Lord's Supper agrees with the Papist opinion, that is, with transubstantiation, I do pity you, since you so openly confuse opinions that are hateful [ἀπηχθισμένας] through the blindness of your mind, and mix fire with water. So I see that you do not understand what you yourself think. For you do not see that consubstantiation itself, which all you Ubiquitarians defend, was invented by the Cardinal and Papist Pierre d'Ailly, and that it arose from the manifest Papist sources of the error of transubstantiation and is very like it. The only difference between the two (that is, your consubstantiation and the Papists' transubstantiation) is this: the Papist error has fewer absurdities and blasphemies than your ubiquity, and it comes somewhat closer to the very words of Christ (if indeed a sacramental expression cannot have a place in the sacrament). Yet let it be far from us to think that the Papist error has any foundation in the words of Christ, just as your error has none. Further, you complain that a certain Jesuit of Ingolstadt wrote against your ubiquity some time ago. Why would he not do so, Laonicus, and overthrow to the best of his power that Eutychian error? Even if Satan is its author, Satan himself is already clearly ashamed of such a foul error. This is evident from the fact that you now openly repudiate and shudder at that ubiquity which you once loved so much. As for what I wrote about the fairness of Luther in relation to Zwingli after the Marburg colloquy, and about the concord between Luther and the Helvetic churches brought about by that man of blessed memory, Martin Bucer: as this is most true, you in no way refute it, Laonicus. From this you understand that you and your people (who wish to seem Luther's disciples and imitators) are far removed from that man's equanimity and humanity. You offer us nothing of Luther except, perhaps, his excessive bile, which he himself nevertheless detests; in other words, you only represent and reheat the faults of Luther (for Martin Luther was a sinner). But when you condemn that divine man, the light of all Germany and the teacher of all of you, Philip Melanchthon, who first raised Germany from the childish elements of grammar (which it had known only as far as that) to the highest praise of learning, when you, I say, condemn such a man as ignorant and impious with fear, how shameless you are, how ungrateful, and how impious you show yourself to be, since in your lack of self-control you allow neither the shade nor the bones of your teacher, a dead man, to rest peacefully in Christ! What shall I say to you? Which Christian or pagan man shall I set before you? At least imitate that great Tully, Cicero, whose eloquence you seem eager to shadow, and that greatest king of the Macedonians, Alexander, since you write that you are a nobleman and a knight. Both of them honoured their teachers most generously with praise and every kind of honour: Alexander honoured Aristotle, and Cicero honoured the poet Archias. But you are carrying water in a sieve here, for no one will believe you when you call light darkness. But in order to be like yourself, you wanted to close the first part of your calumnies against me with this distinguished finale, an impious insult against Philip. So I now bear less grievously that I, a foreigner, am unjustly torn to pieces by you with every kind of reproach, since you have not spared even your former teacher, that most serious man Philip Melanchthon, nor now the most illustrious Johann Sturm, the light-bearer [φωσφόρῳ] of Germany. Therefore, just as you began your book with insults, so you end with insults, so that the lid is worthy of the dish. Since I have, as you see, easily and truly refuted the first part of your writing, I now turn to the second, which is the last.

units.la: Ad secundam Laonici Spongiæ partem, Lamberti Danæi responsio.
units.tr: Lambert Daneau's reply to the second part of Laonicus's Sponge.

units.la: Rimùm omnium repetit Laonicus nostram de S. Domini Cœna doctrinam, quam quia partim verbis ambiguis obscurat, partim quibusdam à se additis interuertit,en ipse breuiter eam repræsento. Verùm hîc antestari libet, quod contra Ioannem Constantinopolitanum (nimium iam aulicum Episcopum,& propterea primatum Ecclesiæ assectantem) verè ad Mauritium Imperatorem scripsit Gregorius primus, Non caussa mea, sed Dei:non solus ergo,sed tota turbatur Ecclesia : venerandasynodi pompatici cuiusdam sermonis (veluti de Maiestatico Christi corpore){inuentione turbaN tur. Quid igitur vniuersi orthodoxi de sacra Cœ na sentiamus, én tibi,Laonice,iterum repeto atque suggero. Ipsum quidem & essentiale Christi corpus, & sanguinem in S. Domini Cœna à solis piis,& ex fide pane & vino illo vescentibus, spiritualiter manducari: itaque Christum ipsum, etiam quatenus homo est, affirmamus piis in sua Cœna vere quidem,sed non corporalis præsentiæ modo, adesse: panem autem illum & vinum illud esse vera signa & sigilla illius essentialis carnis & sanguinis Christi, propterea-que metonymicè carnem & sanguinem Christi vocari, non autem esse ipsummet essentiale Christi corpus & sanguinem. Quare veram carnem & verum sanguinem Christi in hoc S. Cœnæ Sacramento, id est, totius actionis & ipsorum fidelium respectu, sacramentali & pactionali præsentiâ, præsentem adesse dicimus: cum ipsis autem Cœnæ signis, in signis, sub signs, quæ etiam Sacramenta nominantur, corporalis præsentiæ modo aut cohæsione, aut alligatione, vt vult Laonicus, aut cocxistentia reali adesse certè pernegamus. Hæc sententia, plana est, & perspicua, neque vllam in verbis aut sensu ἀντιφωνίαν habet, qualem tamen in ea videri vult Laonicus. Sed variam vocis huius, Sacramentum, significationem ille non percepit, & semper in hoc argumento Sacramentum, quùm sumitur pro signo, & pro tota actione confundit. Hanc autem nostram cum Dei verbo, vt sæpe probauimus, maximè consentientem doctrinam ex nouis Vbiquitariorum commentis in Anti-
units.tr: First of all, Laonicus repeats our teaching on the Lord's Supper. Partly he obscures it with ambiguous words, and partly he distorts it with additions of his own, so I will briefly set it out myself. Here I like to recall what Gregory the First truly wrote to the Emperor Maurice against John of Constantinople, a bishop already too much a courtier and therefore grasping after primacy in the Church: "The cause is not mine but God's. So it is not only one man who is troubled, but the whole Church. The venerable synod is thrown into turmoil by the invention of some pompous sermon (such as the one about the majestic body of Christ)." What all orthodox believers think about the holy Supper, I repeat and suggest to you again, Laonicus. The very essential body and blood of Christ are eaten spiritually in the Lord's Supper by the pious alone, those who eat that bread and wine in faith. We affirm that Christ himself, even as he is man, is truly present to the pious in his Supper, but not in the manner of a bodily presence. That bread and that wine are true signs and seals of the essential flesh and blood of Christ, and for that reason the flesh and blood of Christ are called by metonymy, but they are not the essential body and blood of Christ itself. Therefore we say that the true flesh and true blood of Christ are present in this Sacrament of the Holy Supper, that is, with respect to the whole action and to the faithful themselves, by a sacramental and covenantal presence. But we firmly deny that they are present with the Supper's signs themselves, in the signs or under the signs (which are also called sacraments), by a bodily presence, whether by cohesion, by attachment, as Laonicus wishes, or by real coexistence. This position is plain and clear, and it contains no contradiction [ἀντιφωνίαν] either in its words or in its sense, though Laonicus wants it to seem to. But he has not grasped the varied meaning of this word, sacrament, and in this matter he always confuses it, whether it is taken for the sign or for the whole action. Moreover, this doctrine of ours, which, as I have often shown, agrees most closely with the word of God, he tried to refute against the new inventions of the Ubiquitarians in the Anti-

units.la: Pag. ss. sturmio refutare tentauit Osiander,& octo quasdam leues machinas in acie instruxit:eas ego,quia leues erant, in Antiosiandro facilime deieci, & ita tum ex ipso Dei verbo, tum ex patribus euerti,vt ne ipse quidem Osiander eas erigere postea sit conatus. Itaque cessit,& se victum iam aperte sua taciturnitate confessus est. Quid igitur restat, nisi vt Domino Deo laudes, & epicenia de tam praeclara victoria concinam,& sic omnes adhortans,frequenter ingeminem,
units.tr: (p. ss.) Osiander attempted to refute Sturmius, and he drew up eight light engines in battle line. Because they were light, I overthrew them very easily in my Anti-Osiander, and I refuted them both from the word of God itself and from the Fathers, so thoroughly that Osiander himself afterwards did not try to raise them up again. So he yielded, and by his silence he has now openly confessed himself defeated. What remains, then, but to sing praises to the Lord God and to chant a song of triumph over so splendid a victory, and so, exhorting everyone, to repeat it often:

units.la: Victori cantate Deo, cantate triumphum.
units.tr: Sing to the victorious God, sing a triumph.

units.la: Nimirum vnus tu, Laonice, te huic Deilaudi opponis,& interstrepis vt anser sylvestris,& plenum istius pacis & victoriae fructum ipsi etiam Dei Ecclesiae adimere cogitas. Sed, Domino fauente,non fiet. Quid enim affers,cur mea refutes? Ineptis plane,& nihil nisi quod millies iam sit confutatum, dicis. Itaque nulla mea responsione egebat ista tuae quatriduane Spongiae pars: sed ne miles togato mihi insultares, en tibi ad omnia, quae magno labore & frustra conquisitisti,argumenta breue responsum. Primum ais me non totidem syllabas descripsisse, quot in ipso Osiandri scripto extant. Quis se vnquam huic legi alligauit, modo sensus & mens integra seruetur? Ac ne ipsi quidem Euangelistae in citandis Veteris Testamenti locis. Augustinus multos haereticos confutauit, multos Hieronymus: vbi sibi hanc tam seueram & iniquam legem vllus eorum vel sibi,vel alij indixit? Ac ne tu quidem in meis recitandis eam tuam legem seruas,qui nec mentem nec, verba mea recites & transcribas. Sed neque debes folicitus esse de verbo, vbi sensus est in tuto: nisi quod ipse, vt paginas impleres, & nos tuo scripto onerares, ea transcribis, quæ nihil erat necesse. Dum tu autem hic me reprehendis, ipse vbique paralogismum eum committis, qui dicitur in Scholis αὐτὴν τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ, quod probandi & respondendi genus est omnino vitiosissimum. Sed age singula tua breuiter perpendamus.
units.tr: Clearly you alone, Laonicus, set yourself against this praise of God, and you hiss like a wild goose, and you plan to take from the Church of God the full fruit of that peace and victory. But with the Lord's favour it will not happen. For what do you bring forward to refute my arguments? You say they are simply trivial and nothing but what has been refuted a thousand times already. So this part of your four-day Sponge did not need any reply from me. But lest you insult me as a soldier insults a civilian, here is a brief answer to all the arguments you have sought out with great labour and in vain. First you say I have not written down as many syllables as appear in Osiander's own text. Who ever bound himself to such a law, provided the sense and meaning are kept whole? Not even the Evangelists themselves, in quoting the places of the Old Testament. Augustine refuted many heretics, and Jerome many more; did either of them ever impose on himself or on others such a severe and unfair law? Nor do you yourself keep that law of yours when you cite and copy my words, since you neither quote nor copy my meaning or my words accurately. But one ought not to be anxious about the wording when the sense is safe, except that you, to fill your pages and to burden us with your writing, copy out things that were not necessary at all. While you rebuke me here, you yourself everywhere commit that paralogism which the Schools call "begging the question" [αὐτὴν τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ], a kind of proof and reply that is wholly faulty. But come, let us briefly weigh your points one by one.

units.la: Prima & fortissima Osiandri machina pro corporali carnis & sanguinis Christi in, sub, cum pane & vino S. Cœnæ præsentia, hæc fuit: Quia Christus distribuens panem & vinum in Cœna sua dixit, Hoc est corpus meum, hoc est sanguis meus, ergo ipsummet Christi corpus esse in, sub, & cum pane illo præsentia corporali. Negaui vero illam consecutionem. Nam quum panis ille, & vinum illud Corpus & sanguis Christi dicuntur, illa non simpliciter, sed Sacramentaliter sic appellantur. Sacramentale autem corpus Christi non est ipsummet & essentiale Christi corpus. Ergo propter ipsam panis & vini appellationem, nequaquam efficitur ipsum, & essentiale Christi corpus cum iis signis realiter adesse. Quid tu ad hæc? Dicis illa Christi verba esse sumenda ἐχ τὸ ῥητὸν, non ἐχ διανοίας. Principium vero in eo petis, mi Laonice, & fortasse nondum tibi otium fuerat, quid istud rei sit, discere à Dialecticis. Veruntamen vt tuam illam sententiam de ῥητῷ salsissimam esse ostendam, dico, hanc Christiphrasim, Hoc est corpus meum, esse eodem modo accipiendam, quo dicitur à Paulo,
units.tr: The first and strongest engine of Osiander for the bodily presence of the flesh and blood of Christ in, under, and with the bread and wine of the Supper was this: because Christ, distributing bread and wine in his Supper, said, This is my body, this is my blood, therefore the very body of Christ itself is present bodily in, under, and with that bread. But I denied that inference. For when that bread and that wine are called the body and blood of Christ, they are not so called simply, but sacramentally. But the sacramental body of Christ is not the very essential body of Christ itself. Therefore, from the mere name given to the bread and wine, it by no means follows that the very essential body of Christ is really present with those signs. What have you to say to this? You say that those words of Christ must be taken from the letter [ἐκ τοῦ ῥητοῦ], not from the sense [ἐκ διανοίας]. But, my dear Laonicus, you are begging the question there, and perhaps you have not yet had leisure to learn from the dialecticians what that matter is. Nevertheless, to show that your saying about the letter is utterly foolish, I say that this figurative saying of Christ, This is my body, must be understood in the same way as Paul says,

units.la: Petra erat Christus: a Mose, Agnus erat trajitus a Deo, Iris est foedus Dei, vbi διάνοια, non τὸ ῥητόν, sequenda est. Hisne tot testibus contentus es, Laonice? Verum perge. Dixi ex Augustino, sce-lus & flagitium a Christo praecipi, nisi tropice verba illa interpretemur. Dixerat enim Christus, Accipite, manducate. Quid tu vero, mi homo, hic tantopere a tropis omnibus abhorres, qui supra pag.22. pane tropice, pro fructu panis interpreta-tus es? Nam quod ais, illum locu Augustini a me citatum, non pertinere ad S. Domini Coenam, certe ab ipso Christo & Augustino refutatur, quoniam in sacra Coena quoque iubet diserte Christus, ut suam carnem manducemus. Augusti. autem exemplum ex Ioanne attulit, non ut suam regulam ad unum illum Ioannnis locum restrin-geret, sed ut illam ex eo tantum illustraret. Exem-pla enim regulam non limitant, ut sciunt omnes qui sunt versati in Dialecticis. Ergo nihil te tuo-que iuvat, tuum in interpretando & restringen-do Augustini loco subterfugium.
units.tr: Christ was the rock (1 Cor. 10); Moses says, The lamb is the Passover [transitus] of God; The rainbow is the covenant of God. In all these, the sense [διάνοια], not the letter [τὸ ῥητόν], must be followed. Are you content with so many witnesses, Laonicus? Go on, then. I have said, following Augustine, that it would be a crime and a shameful thing for Christ to command, unless we interpret those words figuratively. For Christ had said, Take, eat. But why, my good man, do you here so greatly shrink from all figures, you who above, on p. 22, interpreted "bread" figuratively as the "fruit of the bread"? As for your claim that the passage of Augustine I cited does not pertain to the Lord's Supper, it is refuted by Christ and Augustine themselves, since in the holy Supper too Christ plainly commands us to eat his flesh. Augustine brought the example from John, not to restrict his rule to that one place in John, but only to illustrate the rule by it. For examples do not limit a rule, as all who are practised in the dialectic know. So your evasion, by which you restrict and narrow Augustine's passage, does not help you at all.

units.la: Secundum Osiandri argumentum (quod non iam ad S.Domini Coenam, sed ad Vbiquitatem suam stabiliendam pertinet) hoc fuit, Si verum Christi corpus pluribus in locis esse non potest, sua Deo omnipotetia adimitur. Respondi paralogismum esse σοφισμα τὸ ἐπιμενον, quoniam omnipotentiam Dei, non ex humanae mentis fictione & libitu, sed ex ipsius Dei verbo, voluntate, & consensione cum eiusdem sapientia metiri debemus. Unde fit, ut citra Diuinae omnipotetiae immi-nutionem, Deus tamen multa non posse dicatur; veluti vt factum infectum reddatur, tempus prę- teritum fiat futurum. Item, vt Christus in carnem non venerit, non quia Deus non sit omnipotens, sed quia Deus est, & verax, & sapiens, & sibi ipsi constans, nunquámque contrarius. Tale quoque, & illud est, vt verum corpus, quale habuit Christus, sit ἀσυγκατάτον, & loco circunscriptū. Quid tu ad ista, Laonice, excipis? Respondes me hæc ab Aristotele didicisse. Ineptis. A teipso pag. 14. didici, qui me in veri corporis natura agnoscenda ad leges Physicas revocasti. Constes igitur ipse tibi, & inter nos consentiemus. Nam pag. quoque 67. ais, esse corporis proprium quarto modo, vt corpus sit Semper finitum & locatum. Sed quid te nomino, Laonice, cum hoc, quod de corpore dixi, ab ipsomet Christo didicerim? didicerim ab orthodoxo illo Augustino, quem tu quoque testem aliquando producis? Verùm ais, Non omne corpus esse in loco. Nam cœlu extimum esse in loco, vt alia corpora, negas ex Aristotele. Sed præclarè addis, vt alia corpora. Esse enim cœlum etiam supremum in certo vbi, & loco, certum est, quod tamen vt alia hæc inferiora corpora, alio corpore neque ambitur, neque circundatur, in quo vno tota est illa Aristotelica distinctio posita, sed abs te non intellecta. Petis vt digito demonstrem tibi locum illum in cœlo, vbi nunc est Christus. Non alligo perpetuò Christum certæ alicui cœli parti, cui infixus pedibus hæreat, vt tu signis Christi carnem alligas. Liberrimè enim in cœlo, vti in amplissima quadam, & verè regia aula, Christus versatur cum sanctis & Angelis. Preterca praeclare Augustin. Non est fragilitatis nostrae coelorum secreta discutere. Ostende tu mihi locum in signis Coenae, vbi Christi corpus sit, quemadmodum putas. Dicis denique Christum homine esse vbique. concedo illud quidem: sed nego naturam ipsius humanam propterea esse vbique. Ratio est quia aliud est dicere, Christum hominem, quo vocabulo persona designatur: aliud carnem, aut humanam naturam Christi. Nam de persona recte dicitur tota, quod tamen vni illius naturae convenit: de utraque tamen natura non dicitur recte quod vnius tantum proprium est, quale est, vbique esse, quod soli Diuinae Christi naturae competit. Itaque de eiusdem humana natura vere dici & enuntiari hoc idem non potest. Denique quam ineptus es & falsarius? quum ais, Christum adimplere omnia corporaliter. Nam illud tuum corporaliter, ad Paulum Ephes. 4. vers. 10. addis. Et quod de potentia ipsa Christi exponit Paulus ibidem, tu in praesentiam corporale ignorantissime comutas, quasi nimirum, vbicunque alicuius Regis maiestas & potentia apparet, ibidem quoque sit eiusdem persona & corpus. In summa ipsissimam Ioannis Hierosolymitani Episcopi Origenistae (merito propterea a Hieronymo reprehensi) haec resim revocas, qui negas nostra corpora fore similia corpori Christi: sed tantum illi similia, qualis fuit ante resurrectionem, & tempore exinanitionis.
units.tr: Osiander's second argument (which no longer concerns the Lord's Supper but seeks to establish his Ubiquity) was this: if the true body of Christ cannot be in many places at once, then omnipotence is taken away from God. I replied that this is a paralogism, a persisting sophism [σοφισμα τὸ ἐπιμενον], since we must measure the omnipotence of God not by the invention and whim of the human mind, but by God's own word, will, and agreement with his wisdom. Hence it follows that, without any diminution of divine omnipotence, God is still said not to be able to do many things: for example, to make what has been done undone, or to make the past future. Likewise, that Christ did not come in the flesh is not because God is not omnipotent, but because God is true, wise, consistent with himself, and never contrary to himself. Of the same kind is this too: that the true body which Christ had is uncircumscribed [ἀσυγκατάτον] and not confined to a place. What do you object to these points, Laonicus? You reply that I learned these things from Aristotle. How silly! I learned them from yourself, on p. 14, where you called me back to the laws of physics in recognising the nature of a true body. So you agree with yourself, and we shall agree between ourselves. For on p. 67 too you say that it is a property of a body, in the fourth way, that a body is always finite and located. But why do I name you, Laonicus, when I learned from Christ himself what I said about the body? I learned it from that orthodox Augustine, whom you too sometimes bring forward as a witness. But you say, Not every body is in a place. For you deny, on Aristotle's authority, that the outermost heaven is in a place, as other bodies are. But you add cleverly, as other bodies are. For it is certain that even the highest heaven is in a definite where and place, yet it is not, like these other lower bodies, surrounded or encircled by another body, and in this one point lies the whole Aristotelian distinction, which you have not understood. You ask me to point out with my finger for you that place in heaven where Christ is now. I do not bind Christ perpetually to some particular part of heaven, to which he would cling fixed by his feet, as you bind the flesh of Christ to the signs. For Christ moves most freely in heaven, as in some very spacious and truly royal court, among the saints and angels. Moreover, Augustine well says: It is not for our frailty to search out the secrets of the heavens. Show me, you, the place in the signs of the Supper where the body of Christ is, as you think. Finally, you say that Christ as man is everywhere. I grant that indeed, but I deny that his human nature is therefore everywhere. The reason is that it is one thing to say "Christ the man," a term which designates the person, and another to say "the flesh" or "the human nature of Christ." For what belongs to the one nature can rightly be said of the person as a whole, but what is proper to one nature alone, such as being everywhere, which belongs only to the divine nature of Christ, cannot rightly be said of either nature taken separately. So the same thing cannot truly be said or predicated of his human nature. Finally, how foolish and deceitful you are when you say that Christ fills all things bodily. For you add that word "bodily" to Paul, Ephesians 4:10. And what Paul there sets out about the power of Christ itself, you most ignorantly turn into a bodily presence, as if, wherever the majesty and power of some king appears, his person and body were also there at the same place. In short, you revive the very opinion of John, bishop of Jerusalem, a follower of Origen (rightly rebuked for it by Jerome), who denied that our bodies will be like the body of Christ, but only like it as it was before the resurrection and during the time of his humiliation.

units.la: Tertium Osiandri argumentu hoc fuit, signa S. Coenae fore nuda, nisi in, sub, & cum illis, praesentiae corporalis modo adsit & cohaereat ipsum essentiale Christi corpus & sanguis. Negaui consecutione, quia illa signa sunt certissimae promissio nū Dei & corporis Christi σφραγίς, quod obtestatur nobis offerri, & si credimus, dari reipsa, & a nobis percipi. Id quod certe nequaquam est elle nuda rei pictura, uti statua Herculis dicitur signum absentis Herculis. Quid tu porro? Quaeris a me, si res ipsae signatae absunt a signis, quomodo non sunt illa signa nuda? Respondeo quoniam re ipsam nobis a Deo exhiberi & offerri verisime testantur, atque, si credimus, vere percipi certius omni humano argumento demonstrant. Illa vero signa no sunt nuda, Laonice, quae re ipsam, qua signat, vere exhiberi nobis obsignat, quaeadmodum nec a spofo spofae datus annulus est nuda spofionis factae figura, sed arrhabo initi cosensus. Illa sunt signa nuda, quae nihil aliud sunt, quam rerum quouis modo abfetiu mera simulacra & imagines, qualis est pieti Lutheri in vestris templis statua. Ergo ia intelligis quid sit signum nudum, & non nudum. Nam quod de differetia Sacramentorum V. & N. Testameti multis verbis narras, quid ad rem? quū (praeter illud quod vetetis Testameti Sacramenta incarnadi Christi signa erant: N. vero Testamenti Sacramenta iam exhibiti & incarnati, sine ea ipsa re, qua nobis nostra Sacramenta significant, non fuerunt veterum Sacramenta, neque Christi carnis esu, seu communione caruerint fideles Patres sub Veteri Testamento. Eande nobiscum esca. i. carne Christi illi ederunt: eunde nobisque potu. i. sanguine Christi illi biberunt, si Paulo credis. Fide enim habuerunt, cui etiam futura Christi caro praesens erat. Sed tu nimirum in eo falleris grauissime (uti & Gerla-
units.tr: The third argument of Osiander was this: the signs of the Lord's Supper would be bare unless the essential body and blood of Christ were present with them, and cohered with them, by the manner of bodily presence, "in, under, and with them" [in, sub, & cum illis]. I denied the inference, because those signs are most certain promises of God and a seal [σφραγίς] of Christ's body. They attest that this body is offered to us, and, if we believe, it is really given and received by us. This is certainly not at all the same as the bare picture of a thing, as a statue of Hercules is called a sign of an absent Hercules. And what do you say next? You ask me: if the things signified are absent from the signs, how are those signs not bare? I answer: they truly attest that the thing itself is really exhibited and offered to us by God, and they demonstrate, more certainly than any human argument, that it is truly received if we believe. Those signs, Laonicus, are not bare, since they seal that what they signify is truly exhibited to us. Just as the ring a husband gives his wife is not the bare figure of a betrothal made, but the pledge [arrhabo] of the agreement entered into. Those are bare signs which are nothing but mere likenesses and images of things absent in whatever way, such as the statue of Luther in your churches. So you now understand what a bare sign is and what is not bare. As for what you say at length about the difference between the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments, what has it to do with the matter? For, apart from the fact that the sacraments of the Old Testament were signs of the Christ who was yet to be incarnate, the sacraments of the New Testament are of Christ already exhibited and incarnate. Without that very thing which our sacraments signify to us, the sacraments of the ancients would not have been sacraments, and the faithful fathers under the Old Testament would not have lacked the eating of Christ's flesh, or communion in it. Those men ate the same food, that is, the same flesh of Christ, that we eat, and drank the same drink, that is, the same blood of Christ, that we drink, if you believe Paul. For they had it by faith, and for them the flesh of Christ, though future, was already present.

units.la: F.ij. chius amicus meus)& pontificiorū errorē seque ris,dum existimas,signa in Sacramētis Noui Testamenti instituta, habere rem ipsam significatam in seipsis inclusam , & coniunctam, quam eandem prorsus & omnino à Veteris Testamen ti signis abfuisse censes. Ergo scribis in aqua Baptismi Vim salutificam inesse, & ab ea gratiam conferri : sed in Veteri Testamento Deum fuisse contentum fide Patrum: Rem autem ipsam Sacramenti, quam eorum fides apprehendebat,vis vel nullam fuisse, vel certè eos nequaquam eam etiam per fidem participasse, sed tantum vmbras, sine rei adumbratæ fruitione, habuisse. Quid Ser uetus ille maledictus aliud olim sensit, quum à nostris primùm merito, deinde ab omnibus Christianis teterrimus hæreticus damnatus est? Quid nostra hac ætate Iudæi aliud sentiunt? Quod ut intelligas, ex tuo collega Gerlachio, qui tandiu Constantinopoli cum iis versatus est, quære. Et tu me, qui contraria Iudæis sentio, Iudæũ appellas:te verò, qui cũ Iudæis manifestè & impiè consentias, Iudæum non nominas? Quid Paulo ipsi, quid Apostolo ad Hebræos, quid Augustino, quid patribus aliis respondebis? qui verissimè scribunt, & sentiunt, fideles patres sub Veteri Testamento, idem habuisse, quod nos sub Nouo: sed in modo duntaxat, & ratione οἰκονομίας, ac significationis fuisse inter nos & eos discrimen, quòd illi venturo Christo, nos autem iam exhibito communicamus. Vides igitur, Laonice, vt recte Osiandro responderim, ciusque argumentum
units.tr: But you are most gravely mistaken in this, as is also my friend Gerlachius, and you follow the error of the Papists, while you think that the signs instituted in the sacraments of the New Testament have the thing signified enclosed and joined within themselves, which you judge was wholly absent from the signs of the Old Testament. So you write that the saving power is present in the water of Baptism, and that grace is conferred by it; but in the Old Testament you hold that God was content with the faith of the fathers. As for the thing of the sacrament itself, which their faith laid hold of, you say either that there was no power in it, or certainly that they in no way participated in it even by faith, but had only shadows, without enjoyment of the thing shadowed. What did that accursed Servetus think otherwise, when he was condemned first by us, rightly, and then by all Christians, as a most foul heretic? What do the Jews think otherwise in our own age? To learn this, ask your colleague Gerlach, who has long dwelt among them at Constantinople. And you call me a Jew because I hold views contrary to the Jews, yet you, who clearly and impiously agree with the Jews, do not call yourself a Jew? What will you answer to Paul himself, to the Apostle to the Hebrews, to Augustine, and to the other fathers, who most truly write and hold that the faithful fathers under the Old Testament had the same thing that we have under the New, differing only in the mode and manner of economy [οἰκονομία] and of signification: that they communicated in Christ who was to come, while we communicate in him who has already been exhibited? You see then, Laonicus, how rightly I answered Osiander, and so resolved his argument that you cannot overturn my reply by any means.

units.la: Pag. 84. tum sic soluerim,vt meam responsionem euerte- re nequaquam possis.
units.tr: Page 84. ... and so I have answered it, that you can by no means overturn my reply.

units.la: Quarto loco dixerat Osiander, Ideo verum corpus, & sanguinem Christi esse in, sub, & cum pane & vino sacrae Coenae, quia Paulus ait,indi- gne accedentes esse reos corporis & sanguinis Christi.Responderam, Paralogismum esse a non consequenti: rationem addideram. Primum, quod diserte Paulus ipse dicat,indigne sumentes Accipere hunc panem, & hoc poculum, non autem accipere ipsum ac essentiale corpus & sangui- nem,Christi. Deinde quòd, vt ait Hieronymus, dum Panis iste & poculum illud Sacramenta violantur, ipse, cuius sunt,violatur: & ideo non propter praesentiam corporis Christi cum signis, sed propter contemptionem promissionis Dei fiunt indigne accedentes, rei corporis Christi, spreti nempe,non autem accepti. Quid ad haec Nicodemus Frischlinus,professor profanae poeticae Tubingae,quem suiipsius nominis, propter huius sui scripti blasphemias,puduit ?iConuitiatur,& me vocat Iudaeum, quia bona fide verba Pauli citarim, quemadmodum in eodem loco & argumento postea versans Gerlachius ipse testatur:& Osiandrum aperte falsi damnat, qui pro his verbis Panem hunc, & poculum hoc, substituit corpus & sanguinem Christi. Sed quoniam nihil eorum,quae dixi,Laonice,refutas, vel te ipso teste,vera me scripsisse,proculdubio apparet.
units.tr: Fourth, Osiander had said that the true body and blood of Christ are in, under, and with the bread and wine of the holy Supper, because Paul says that those who approach unworthily are guilty of the body and blood of Christ. I had answered that this is a paralogism of a non sequitur, and I had added reasons. First, because Paul himself expressly says that those who partake unworthily receive this bread and this cup, and not that they receive the very essential body and blood of Christ. Next, because, as Jerome says, when this bread and that cup, which are sacraments, are violated, he to whose they are is violated; and therefore they approach unworthily not because of the presence of Christ's body with the signs, but because of contempt for God's promise, so that they receive, not the body of Christ, but despise it. What does Nicodemus Frischlin, professor of profane poetry at Tübingen, say to this? Ashamed of his own name, because of the blasphemies of this writing of his, he abuses me and calls me a Jew, because I quoted Paul's words in good faith, just as Gerlachius himself later testifies when he treats the same passage and subject. He also openly condemns Osiander as a liar, since in place of these words this bread and this cup he substituted the body and blood of Christ. But since you refute none of the things I said, Laonicus, it clearly appears, even by your own testimony, that I have written the truth.

units.la: Transeo igitur ad quintum Osiandri argumentum,quod est de maiestate Christi hominis. Vult Osiander,carnem a λόγῳ,seu Filio Dei af-
units.tr: I pass therefore to Osiander's fifth argument, which concerns the majesty of Christ's human nature. Osiander wants the flesh, assumed by the Word, or the Son of God, to be everywhere, especially now that it has been received into the state of glory and majesty, and all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ as man.

units.la: F.iij. sumptam esse vbique, nunc praesertim, postquam est in statum gloriae & maiestatis recepta, & homini Christo data est omnis potestas in coelum & in terram. Respondi id nequaquam sequi. Primum, quoniam, vt docet Augustinus, ea gloria & maiestas carni Christi data est, quae naturam eius minime destruit. Christus enim carni suae gloriam dedit: naturam autem non abstulit. Item, Cauendum est, ait idem, ne ita Diuinitatem Christi adstruamus, vt veritatem corporis aufferamus. Praeterea quod consecutio a potentia ad praesentiam & situm corporis omnino est φαντασίαν & αλογίαν, ac inepta, quemadmodum in inuicto Germanorum Imperatore Viennae Austriae degente demonstrauimus, cui tamen potestatem in totam Germaniam datam esse a Deo, nemo Germanus negare audebit, vt spero. Quid ad haec Nicodemus seu Laonicus? Obmutescit, & se fatetur superatum. Tantum illud adijcit, & sequi putat, vt nisi λόγος carni suae Vbiquepraesentiam, id est, infinitatem dederit, nullam illi gratiam habitualem concessisse videatur. Verum quae ista consecutio est, obsecro? Nisi totum imperium suum & maiestatem Angelis beatis Deus dederit, ergo nihil maiestatis illis dedit. Nisi tota suam dignitate Imperator legatis suis, & in Italia vicarijs concesserit, Ergo nihil concessit. Euigila Laonice, & teipsum excita, si potes. Vide quid dicat Paulus de ea gloria, quae Christo homini concessa est, Nam omnia subiecit sub pedibus eius. Quum autem dicit, omnia esse ei subiecta, palam est hoc dici, eo excepto, qui subiecit ei omnia. Ergo non est æquata Deitati caro ἀλόγῳ assumpta. Verum Vbiquitarij nihil à Deitate λόγω in naturam assumptam collatum putant, nisi eam sibi exæquaverit, & eandem quartum quendam Deum effecerit. Id quod ex impurissimo Eutychis cœno sumptum esse, & deriuatum nemo pius negare potest.
units.tr: I answered that this does not follow at all. First, because, as Augustine teaches, that glory and majesty was given to the flesh of Christ in such a way that it does not destroy its nature. For Christ gave glory to his flesh, but did not take away its nature. Likewise, we must take care, the same father says, not so to assert the divinity of Christ that we take away the truth of his body. Besides, the inference from power to the presence and place of a body is altogether phantasia [φαντασία] and alogia [ἀλογία], and absurd, as we demonstrated concerning the unconquered Emperor of the Germans, who dwells at Vienna in Austria, to whom, nevertheless, no German will dare deny that power over all Germany has been given by God, as I hope. What does Nicodemus or Laonicus reply to this? He falls silent and confesses himself overcome. He only adds this, and thinks it follows, that unless the Logos [λόγος] gave his flesh ubiquitous presence, that is, infinity, it seems he gave it no habitual grace at all. But what kind of inference is this, I beg you? Unless God had given the blessed angels his whole empire and majesty, therefore he gave them no majesty at all. Unless the Emperor has granted his whole dignity to his legates, and to his vicars in Italy, therefore he has granted nothing. Wake up, Laonicus, and rouse yourself, if you can. See what Paul says of that glory which was granted to Christ as man: For he has put all things under his feet. But when he says that all things are subjected to him, it is plain that this is said with the exception of him who subjected all things to him. Therefore the flesh assumed by the Logos has not been made equal to the Deity. But the Ubiquitarians think that nothing has been conferred by the Logos on the assumed nature, unless he has made it equal to himself and made it a fourth God. That this has been taken from, and derived from, the most filthy mire of Eutyches, no pious man can deny.

units.la: Sextum Ofiandri argumentum fuit, Christi carnem esse Vbique, & idcirco in S.Cœna esse in, sub, & cum signis, pane & vino, quia Christus homo habet omnes thesauros sapientiæ & scientiæ re-conditos. Respondi, esse prorsus ἀσυλλόγιστον, & paralogismum σοφιστικὸν τὸ ἐπιούσιον, vti superior oratio iistius fuit. Nam vt in Christo duplex est natura, sic est duplex & scientia, & potentia, & sapientia, & voluntas. Vna enim in Christo incst, ipsi Deitati essentialis & æterna, quam Christus habet vt Deus. Hæc nequaquam est naturæ assumptæ, id est humanæ communicata vel communicabilis, nisi propter prædicationem verbalem, quoniam assumpta est in vnitatem illius personæ, quæ est Deus. Nam quum sit caro Christi creatura, non est illius essentialis Dei scientiæ, potentiæ, &c. vti neque æternitatis capax vel capabilis. Alia igitur est sapientia, scientia, potentia, creata & qualitas, cuius est reipsa caro Christi capacissima, quoniam est caro Vnigeniti. Itaque ea summa est in Christo, & quanta maxima esse in vlla creatura, aut etiam simul in omnibus, & cœlestibus, & terrestribus creaturis potest: imò ea in Christo multis gradibus alias omnes superat, estque ipsis adeò
units.tr: Osiander's sixth argument was that the flesh of Christ is everywhere, and therefore is in the holy Supper in, under, and with the signs, bread and wine, because Christ as man has all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge laid up in him. I answered that this is wholly asyllogiston [ἀσυλλόγιστον], and a sophistical paralogism [σοφιστικὸν παραλογισμόν], just as the former argument was. For as there are two natures in Christ, so there are two kinds of knowledge, power, wisdom, and will. One kind is in Christ, essential and eternal to the Deity itself, which Christ has as God. This is by no means of the assumed nature, that is, of the human nature, communicated or communicable, except by verbal predication, since it was assumed into the unity of that person who is God. For since the flesh of Christ is a creature, it does not possess the essential knowledge, power, and so on, of God, nor is it capable or receptive of eternity. Therefore there is another wisdom, knowledge, power, created and qualified, of which the flesh of Christ itself is most capable, since it is the flesh of the Only-begotten. And so the greatest measure of this is in Christ, as great as it can be in any creature, or even in all heavenly and earthly creatures together; indeed, in Christ it surpasses all others by many degrees, and is admirable even to the blessed angels themselves. Therefore, since ubiquitous presence, like infinity, is an essential attribute of God, it cannot be ascribed to the flesh of Christ without blasphemy, unless the most foul error of the Monothelites is revived. What do you say against this, Laonicus? Nothing. Indeed you assert only one power, and knowledge, and wisdom...

units.la: F.iiij. beatis Angelis admiranda. Ergo quum vbique-praesentia, vti infinitas, sit essentiale Dei attribu-tum, carni Christi tribui sine blasphemia, aut ni-si Monothelitarum errore foedissimo renouato, certe non potest. Quid tu contra Laonice? Nihil. Imo tu vnam tantum potentiam, & scientiam,& sapientiam in Christo Deo & homine esse conte-dis: nec vis tamen Monothelita censeri. Cur ve-ro illius erroris nomen & appellationem refugis aut extimescis, cuius foeditatem & dogma tam lubenter amplecteris? Obijcis porro mihi, qua-si Lyrani mentem corruperim, tanquam ea,quae cito, & quae de Christo scribit Lyranus, perti-nent tantum ad statum exinanitionis Christi. falleris. Confiderat enim Lyranus Christum non solum qualis tunc erat, quum in his terris versabatur, qui est exinanitionis Christi statu-s:sed etiam qua-lis nunc est ad dextram Patris sedens, qui est sta-tus maiestatis hominis Christi. Itaque eo verbo vtitur Lyranus,quod praesentis temporis,& prae-sentis status Christi significationem manifestam habet. Ait enim,etiam te ipso teste,SECVN-DVM vero naturam humanam HABET aliam scientiam, scilicet creatam. Vide iam & cô ferquo tempore illa scripserit Lyranus. Annon post re-ceptum Christum in coelum? Quod negare non potes,quantumuis tergiuerseris. Vixit enim Ly- ranus post annum a nato Christo 1300. Ergo de Christo etiam in coelum recepto agit & scri-bit,vt teipsum Lyrani mente nō intellexisse iam demonstres. Caetera quae tribus paginis tuis conti-nentur,sunt gerrae,quas propterea tibi relinquo.
units.tr: F.iiij. admirable to the blessed angels. Therefore, since omnipresence, like infinity, is an essential attribute of God, it certainly cannot be ascribed to the flesh of Christ without blasphemy, unless we revive the most foul error of the Monothelites. What do you say to this, Laonicus? Nothing. Indeed, you maintain that there is only one power, one knowledge and one wisdom in Christ, God and man, yet you do not wish to be counted a Monothelite. But why do you shun or dread the name and label of that error, whose foulness and doctrine you embrace so willingly? You further object that I have corrupted the mind of Lyranus, as if what Lyranus writes about Christ pertains only to the state of Christ's humiliation. You are mistaken. For Lyranus considers Christ not only as he was when he dwelt on this earth, which is the state of Christ's humiliation, but also as he now is, sitting at the right hand of the Father, which is the state of the majesty of the man Christ.
