So Lyranus uses that word which clearly signifies the present time and present state of Christ. For he says, as you yourself admit, that according to human nature Christ has another knowledge, namely created. Now consider at what time Lyranus wrote this. Was it not after Christ was received into heaven? You cannot deny it, however much you wriggle. For Lyranus lived after the year 1300 from the birth of Christ. So he also deals with and writes about Christ as received into heaven, and thereby you already show that you did not understand Lyranus' mind. The rest, which is contained in your three pages, is trifling, and I therefore leave it to you.

units.la: Septimum Ofiandri argumentum erat, Carnem Christi esse vbique, quia TOTVS Christus, id est, & Deus & homo Christus mundum gubernat. Ergo conquerebatur diuidi & separari operationes Christi, nisi Christi caro ibidem sit & sistatur, vbicunque homo Christus, id est, illa persona, quae est homo & Deus, operctur. Indesplen dide ab eo Nestoriani vocabamur, qualis est Ofiandri facundia. Respodi: Non diuidi vel personam ipsam, vel operationes Christi, etiam si caro neque sistatur vbicunque est Deitas λόγῳ, neque vbicunque operatur homo, id est, illa persona Christus, ex vna sui natura, illic quoque esse & versari, & praesens esse corporalis praesentiae modo concedatur caro Christi. Nam hoc iam sepius dixi, à potentia ad situm personae nullam esse consecutionem, quae sit legitima & firma. Praeterea etiam antea docui, aliud esse distinguere naturas, & operationes in Christo: aliud vero eas separare ac diuidere. Quae duo tamen vel sciens, vel imprudens confundit Laonicus. Non agit quidem scorsim, & in proprio ὑφιστάμενῳ subsistēs natura humana à λόγῳ assumpta: agit tamen distincte, & alia quàm λόγος, quanquam λόγῳ semper hypostaticè manēs vnita. Leo primus, quem, breuitatis causa, vnum produco, sic ait, Sicut enim Deus non mutatur miseratione, ita homo non consumitur dignitate. Agit enim vtraque forma cum alterius communicatione (id est, vnione, & hoc perpetuò M. Kemnitium fefellit) quod proprium est, Verbo scilicet operante, quod est verbi: & carne exequente, quod est carnis. Caro naturam nostri generis non relinquit. Hic est locus Leonis, què à me non esse transcriptum conquestus es, Laonice, quoniam vos in patrum scriptis notisimis versatos esse iudicabam. Ergo vt vides, aliud est naturas & operationes in Christo distinguere, quod solum facimus: aliud autem earum communicationem, id est, vnionem, vt patres loquebantur, dissoluere, quod fecit Nestorius, & nos execramur. Quamobrem cum Damasceno dicimus, naturas in Christo χωρὶς μὲν, καὶ ἀδιαιρέτως ἢ ἀσυγχύτως μίως operari. Quid tu ad haec verisima? Obuagu laris primum. Deinde vere te Nestorianum, cuius nos haereticos falso accusas, esse ostendis. In summa(ces enim hic, vt in plerisque tui huius συγγραμμ scripti locis, & obscurus, & prolixus) in summa, inquam, vis, si duae in Christo Deo & homine operationes ponantur, duos quoque Christos inducì & statui: etsi naturarum, diuinae videlicet, & humanae, proprietates, in Christo realiter (vt tu loqueris) id est, vere distinguatur, duo quoque realia ὑφεστῶτα, & duos realiter separatos Christos constitui. Nam ais, Operatio & proprietas nequaquam sine suo subiecto esse potest. Nonne tua verba, Laonice, iam agnoscis? In quibus si perstas adhuc quoque, nonne te omnes merito Monophysitam, & Monothelitam appellabunt? vtpote qui in Christo Deo & homine vnicam duntaxat operationem, non autem duas: vnicam duntaxat sapientiam, non duas: vnicam voluntatem, non autem duas esse contendas? Respice te ipsum, & quid dicas, nunc saltem à me fraterne admonitus, cogita. Hoc vnum est tuae responsionis ad mea superio-
units.tr: Osiander's seventh argument was that the flesh of Christ is everywhere, because the whole Christ, that is, both God and man, governs the world. Therefore he complained that the operations of Christ are divided and separated unless the flesh of Christ is present and stationed wherever the man Christ, that is, that person who is man and God, operates. On this ground we were called Nestorians by him, such is Osiander's eloquence. I replied that neither the person itself nor the operations of Christ are divided, even if the flesh is not fixed wherever the Deity is present [λόγῳ], nor wherever the man, that is, that person Christ, operates, and even if it is granted that the flesh of Christ is present there in the manner of bodily presence. For I have said this often already: there is no legitimate and firm consequence from power to the location of a person. Moreover, I have taught before that it is one thing to distinguish the natures and operations in Christ, and another to separate and divide them. Yet Laonicus confuses these two, knowingly or unknowingly. The human nature, assumed by the Word, does not indeed act separately and in its own subsistence [ὑφιστάμενῳ], yet it acts distinctly and differently from the Word, although it always remains hypostatically united to the Word. Leo the First, whom I cite alone for the sake of brevity, says thus: For just as God is not changed by compassion, so man is not consumed by dignity. For each form acts in communion with the other (that is, in union, and this always escaped M. Kemnitz), which is proper to the Word operating, namely what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. The flesh does not abandon the nature of our kind. This is the passage of Leo, which you complain I did not copy out, Laonicus, since I judged you to be well versed in the most famous writings of the Fathers. So, as you see, it is one thing to distinguish natures and operations in Christ, which is all that we do; it is another thing to dissolve their communion, that is, their union, as the Fathers called it, which is what Nestorius did and what we execrate. Therefore, with Damascene we say that the natures in Christ operate [χωρὶς μὲν καὶ ἀδιαιρέτως ἢ ἀσυγχύτως μίως], without separation and without confusion, in one person. What do you say to these true things? First, you wander about vaguely. Second, you show yourself to be truly the Nestorian of whom you falsely accuse us. In sum (for here, as in most places of your writing, you are both obscure and prolix), I say, you maintain that if two operations are posited in Christ, God and man, then two Christs are also introduced and established; and, if the properties of the natures, namely divine and human, are distinguished in Christ really (as you put it), that is, truly, then two really existing subsistences are also constituted, and two Christs really separated. For you say: An operation and a property can by no means exist without its subject. Do you not recognise your own words, Laonicus? If you still persist in them, will not everyone rightly call you a Monophysite and a Monothelite, since you contend that in Christ, God and man, there is only one operation and not two, only one wisdom and not two, only one will and not two? Look at yourself and consider what you are saying, now at least that you have been admonished by me as a brother.

units.la: Pag. 61. ra vitium. Alterum(neque enim omnia tua, cui amicitiæ nomine parco, velim recensere) quòd subiectum cum ὑφεσταμένῳ imperitisime hic confundis. Putas enim, quæcunque habent diuersa subiecta, habere quoque diuersa supposita, & personas. Quo quid magis falsum, atque ἀσυλλόγιστον atque ἀπλίστυτον? Animus & corpus in vnoquoque nostrum sunt vnum ὑφεσταμένον, id fateris: & tamen aliæ sunt animi nostri, aliæ corporis operationes, & vtrææque propria habent in eadem persona, & diuersa subiecta, nisi quum potat in œnopolio Nicodemus, putat esse actionem animi fui: & quum ratiocinatur in musæo, censet esse actionem fui corporis. Potatio igitur & ratiocinatio in Nicodemo seu Laonico, sunt diuersæ actiones & distinctæ, & habet quæque earum diuersa (a quibus fiunt, & in quibus insunt) subiecta. Dicetne propterea Nicodemus iftefe non esse vnum tantum hominem, ὑφεσταμένον, & personam, sed duos homines? Certe nemo alius bene mente fanus id dixerit. Ipse fortasse tum fe duplicem existimauerit, quum est in statu suæ ἐπονία σεως (scit quid dicam) & illi similis, qui (vt aliquid ipsi de suo Virgilio regeram) videt & Solem geminum, & duplices fe ostendere Thebas. Scholastici, quorum eam sententiam quoque probat laudatque horum omnium coryphæus Kemnitius lib. De Duabus in Christo naturis, pag. 243. longè quàm tu, & rectius, & doctius scribunt. Sicut idem suppositum est subiectum diuersarum proprietatum propter diuersa principia causantia illas proprietates: ita in vna persona Christi duæ sunt naturales actiones, Diuina, & humana, & tamen vna est Christi persona. Sed vt hunc locum concludam, possunt, Laonicæ,in vno & eodem hyphistameno esse duæ operationes, imò etiam duæ naturæ,& eæ quidem inconfusæ ac distinctæ,ex quo fit,vt naturarum, aut actionum vel in Christo, vel in quolibet alio homine distinctio suppositi & personæ distractionem ac separationem non inducat. Quamobrem quælibet proprietas & operatio in Christo habet, Laonice,suum subiectum proprium cui inest:actio humana, naturam humanam: Divina verò actio,Diuinam naturam:non habet tamen separatum vtraque propterea suppositum, in quo seorsim, & separatim subsistat.
units.tr: Page 61. This is the one fault of your reply to my previous points. The other (for I will not review all your points, which, for the sake of friendship, I spare) is that you here confuse the subject with the hypostasis [ὑφεστάμενον] most ignorantly. For you think that whatever has different subjects also has different supposita and persons. What could be more false, more illogical, and more absurd? In each of us, soul and body are one hypostasis; you admit this. Yet the operations of our soul are different from those of our body, and each has its proper and different subject in the same person. Unless, when Nicodemus drinks in the wine-shop, he thinks it is an action of his soul, and when he reasons in the museum, he thinks it is an action of his body. Drinking and reasoning in Nicodemus, or Laonicus, are therefore different and distinct actions, and each of them has a different subject from which it proceeds and in which it inheres. Will Nicodemus therefore say that he is not one man, one hypostasis and one person, but two men? Surely no one of sound mind would say so. He himself might perhaps then think himself double, when he is in the state of his own ἐπονία σεως (you know what I mean), and like the one who (to borrow something from my own Virgil) sees both a double sun and two Thebes appearing. The Scholastics, whose opinion the leader of all these, Kemnitz, also approves and praises in his book On the Two Natures in Christ, page 243, write far more truly, rightly and learnedly than you do: Just as the same suppositum is the subject of different properties, on account of the different principles causing those properties, so in the one person of Christ there are two natural operations, divine and human, and yet Christ's person is one. But to conclude this point: in one and the same hypostasis, Laonicus, there can be two operations, indeed even two natures, and these unconfused and distinct. From this it follows that the distinction of natures or actions, whether in Christ or in any other man, does not bring about a distraction and separation of the suppositum and the person. Therefore every property and operation in Christ, Laonicus, has its own proper subject in which it inheres: the human action has the human nature; the divine action, the divine nature. Yet neither has a separate suppositum in which it subsists apart and by itself.

units.la: Octauum Osiandri argumentum fuit: Christi carnem esse vbique, quia totus Christus est vbique. Respondi ex Augustino, Etsi totus Christus est vbique,totum tamen Christi non esse vbique. Aliud enim est Totus Christus, aliud totum Christi. Totus Christus vbique est, quia qui Christus est,vbiuis est,idem & Deus & homo. Manent enim vnione illa hypostatica naturæ inter se semper in Christo coniunctæ. Nam Deitas λόγεαm naturam,quam ex virgine Maria assumpsit,nunquam deserit. Totum autem Christi,id est singulæ naturæ Christi non sunt tamen vbique, & simul, & semper in eodem loco. Non facit enim vnio hypostatica rerum hypostaticè vnitarum coextensionem,aut exæquationem inter se. Auris in humano corpore viuo,brachiis suis & pedibus hypostaticè vnitur, quemadmodum docet Damascenus: neque tamen tam extensa & latè patens est auris istius corporis, quàm brachia pedes.Quales enim,obsecro,haberet aures Laonicus amicus meus,nempe non asininas tantum, (quales mihi praeter meas addere voluit, sed renui) sed haberet ipse aures ad terram vsque, more quorundam barbarorum & brutorum animantium, dependentes. Quid ad haec Laonicus? Primum conqueritur,Augustinum, quem refutare non potest, incommodè locutum fuisse, nimirum tibi incommodè,& inutiliter:verè tamen & confentienter Dei verbo locutus est Augustinus. Deinde veterem illam inter Vbiquitarios, & tamen palmariam,de candenti carbone similitudinem, ac cantilenam toties illis extortam reponit. Vbiquitatè postea,id est,suam Helenam, miser repudiat & reiicit. Denique fe mirum in modum sensu etiam communi priuatum esse tandem ostendit, qui scribat calorem seu ignem fumere virtutem & momentum vrendi ex ipsa materia, cui inest. Et me,qui propter & rationem, & omnium hominum experientiam , aliter credam,(nempe calorem seu ignem à fe,& in fe virtutem illam vrendi habere: materiam autem ab ipso igne & calore, quem secum defert) ad asinos remittit,iuuenile r exultat, & diu, multúmque in sua illa similitudine carbonaria desudans & laborans, vbique præ angustiis ( quibus à me premitur ) & propter acerbum illius suæ carbonariæ similitudinis fumum,nō potest distinguere hominem Christum & humanitatem Christi gratiam vnionis cum gratia habituali diuersam esse non videt: Deitatem alij , quàm Deo,communicabilem facit : Theophylacti & ætatem, & sententiam Transsubstantiationi Papisticæ sa-uentem esse non meminit. Multa hic perturbat & confundit. Denique Cyrillum ipsum carbo-nariâ illa, suavt opinor,similitudine perturbatus tandem corrumpit. Vnum vero hoc maximè & supra cætera ridiculè facit, quod ipse(quem no-minis sui puduit)qui aliena larua tectus, & post careƈta latitans, vt miser quidam poeta solitus in triuiis stridenti stipula miserum disperdere car-nem,se prodere non audet, qui in isto fumo suo carbonario seipsum non videt,speculum tamen, in quo se alij intueantur,fabricatur,& mihi obii-cit. Quanquam quæ de me narrat, illa sunt(Dei optimi maximi gratiâ) omnia salsissima. Ego non latito in tenebris, viuo in luce hominum Christianorum,in vrbe,& Ecclesia Dei totius orbis celeberrima, Geneuæ nimirum,&(si quid in his terris est sanƈtum)sanƈtissima,quod citra cuiusquam alterius reformatæ Ecclesiæ iniuriâ di-ƈtū esse volo.Ergo si essem turpis, & qualem me fingis,nec ad mometum quidē hore hic viuerem, qualis est Dei gratiâ istius Ecclesiæ reformatio.
units.tr: Osiander's eighth argument was that the flesh of Christ is everywhere, because the whole Christ is everywhere. I answered from Augustine: even if the whole Christ is everywhere, the whole of Christ is not everywhere. For the whole Christ is one thing, and the whole of Christ is another. The whole Christ is everywhere, because he who is Christ is everywhere, being both God and man at once. For by that hypostatic union the natures remain forever joined to one another in Christ. The Word never forsakes the nature which it assumed from the Virgin Mary. But the whole of Christ, that is, the individual natures of Christ, are not everywhere, and at once, and always in the same place. For the hypostatic union does not make hypostatically united things coextensive or equal with one another. In a living human body the ear is hypostatically united with the arms and feet, as Damascene teaches; yet the ear of that body is not as extended and widespread as the arms and feet. For what sort of ears, I ask you, would my friend Laonicus have, namely not merely asses' ears (which he wanted to add to mine, but I refused), but ears hanging down to the ground, like those of certain barbarians and brutish animals? What does Laonicus say to this? First, he complains that Augustine, whom he cannot refute, spoke inappropriately, namely inappropriately and uselessly for you; yet Augustine spoke truly and in agreement with the word of God. Then he brings back that old, and yet most telling, comparison of the glowing coal, which the Ubiquitarians have so often extorted from him and sung over and over. Then he wretchedly repudiates and rejects his Helen, namely ubiquity. Finally, he shows himself to be strangely deprived even of common sense, since he writes that heat or fire takes its power and momentum for burning from the very matter in which it inheres. And me, who, on account of both reason and the experience of all men, believe otherwise (namely that heat or fire has that power of burning from itself and in itself, while the matter has it from the fire and heat which it carries with it), he sends back to the asses. He exults like a youth, and, sweating and labouring long and hard over his carbon comparison, he cannot, because of the straits in which he is pressed by me and because of the bitter smoke of that charcoal comparison, distinguish the man Christ from the humanity of Christ; he does not see that the grace of union is different from habitual grace. He makes the deity communicable to anyone other than God. He does not remember that the age and opinion of Theophylact favour the Papist transubstantiation. He throws many things into confusion here. Finally, Cyril himself, being disturbed, I think, by that charcoal comparison, he at last corrupts. But this one thing he does most ridiculously and above all others: he, who is ashamed of his own name, who, covered by a foreign mask and lurking behind a curtain, like that wretched poet who used to destroy wretched flesh with crackling straw at the crossroads, does not dare to show himself, who in that carbon smoke of his does not see himself, nevertheless fabricates a mirror in which others may look at him, and throws it at me. Yet what he says about me is, by the grace of God the best and greatest, all most witty. I do not lurk in darkness; I live in the light of Christian men, in the city and Church of God most celebrated throughout the whole world, Geneva I mean, and (if anything on this earth is holy) most holy; I wish this said without injury to any other reformed Church. Therefore, if I were foul, and such as you pretend, I would not live here even for a moment, such as is the reformation of this Church by the grace of God.

units.la: Verùm obiter,Laonice, mi frater teipsum amicè monebo eorum,quæ tui fratres,& omnes qui ti-bi bene ex animo cupiunt,te meminisse,& recor-dari plurimùm iubent.Eorū enim aliquando co-ram Deo ipso,vt hominū iudicia omnia perrum-pas,ratione tamen es reddituru s.Memineris igi-tur frater (siue Nicodemus, siue Laonicus , siue Frifchlinus, siue eques,siue poeta vocari gaudes) primùm,quàm constàter tu nobilitatis equestris laudem captes,qui contra nobilitatẽ(quam & o-difti disti & contenenda docuisti)contumeliosum libru antea edideris: deinde quam falso tanta tibi dignitate tribuas, qui spurca solum, &sales profanorum poetarum tractare,non autem arma didiceris. Turpe est graue virum de seipso mentiri, falsa praesertim iactante.Nec Christum,nec Paulu imi taris. Christu quide,qui, vt ait Cyrillus,exemplum humilitatis nobis ostendit. Paulu aute,qui omnia illa,quae mundus tanti facit, pro stercoribus habuit. Tu vero etiam quae non habes,nobis iactas,& tibi tribuis,quae tua est arrogatia & ἀλαζονεία. Recordare quae sunt tuae apud illustriss. Principem V virtebergicu in ipsius conuiuiis Morionis seu scurrae partes, quas in ipsius aula(solent enim etiam grauissimi Principes morionibus delectari) satis lepide,vt audio,pro tua natura & grauitate, agis & sustines. Veniat in mentem tibi, quis, & quam plen' offendiculi fuerit tuus FriburgiBrifgoiae cum sacrificulis Pontificiis congressus. Quae tua fuerit cum ancilla tua (quo tempore ficti filius Eunuchi,Chereg Terentiani,personam & actic-nem vere,non in fabula,repraesentasti)familiaritas. Quis partus inde natus. Quae castissimae vxoris tuae, propterea fuerit iustissima de te querimonia. Quam tibi amice ad prenegandum illud tuum facinus & benigne quidam amici tui,quos, si ipsi voluerint,facile nominabo,operas tibi suas commodarint. Haec ad te pertinent, Laonice. Quae tu refutare, imo iam negare (cum tot sint testes) non potes, nisi homo omnium impudentissimus haberi gaudeas. Nam quae tu mihi degenis liuidis, auribus asininis, ore distorto &c. obiicis,teipsum certè in tuo speculo, quum haec scribebas, intuebaris. Quamobrem te, nō me, depinxisti. Sunt enim haec omnia huiusmodi, ut nemo tibi in eo de me credat, & omnes, qui me viderint, te impudenter calumniatum esse facile intelligant. Debebas tu quoque (quia te ipsum his in me conuitiis oblectare voluisti) totam famis descriptionem scurriliter tuo more transcribere ex Ouidij Metamorphosi, vt eam abs te lectam, velut Eunuchum Terentij, sciremus, ac ex ea in me vibrares quae pueri legūt in Scholis. Sed pau cula, illa nimirū ex Pisoniana quoq; Ciceronis, Rhetodiocte didiceras. Verùm verbis non contentus tu Mercurij Malcuoli signum mihi, more Centaurorū & Lapitharum tuorum (quoniam vt illi erant equites, sic tu) vulnera & caedes & bipennem Tenediam intentas, aduersus quam fidei in Christum & verae doctrinae clypeum intrepidus obiicio, quae etiam ipsius Satanae tela inflammata facile exstinguit & hebetat. Ego igitur (cui, vtpote in Ecclesia Dei, ipsius misericordia, doctoris arma, non sunt carnalia) pro bipenni Tenedia arripiam verbum ipsum Dei, & sermonem illum efficacē, qui est quouis glalio ancipiti penetrantior. Pertingit enim ad diuisionē animae simul ac spiritus, copagúmque, & medullarum, & diiudicat cogitationes & conceptiones cordis, quemadmodum docet ipse Spiritus sanctus, per quem vt ad verā de S. Domini Coena doctrinam conuertaris, Deum summis votis per Christum, vnigenitum ac vnicum mediatorem nostrum, rogo precórque. Vale.Geneuæ, Anno Domini 1581. Calend. Ianuariis pro Strenis.
units.tr: But in passing, Laonicus, my dear brother, I will kindly remind you of things your brothers and all who wish you well strongly urge you to remember and to call to mind. For you will one day have to give an account of them before God himself, who will break through all human judgements, however you may be called. Remember therefore, brother (whether you like to be called Nicodemus, Laonicus, Frischlin, knight or poet), first how shamelessly you claim the glory of equestrian nobility, when you had earlier published an abusive book against nobility, which you had taught to be despised and contemned. Then consider how falsely you ascribe such dignity to yourself, when you have learned to handle only filth and the witticisms of profane poets, and not arms. It is shameful for a serious man to lie about himself, especially when he boasts falsely. You imitate neither Christ nor Paul. Christ, as Cyril says, showed us the example of humility; Paul counted all those things that the world values so highly as dung. But you boast to us even of what you do not have, and claim for yourself what is your own arrogance and boastfulness [ἀλαζονεία]. Remember the part you play at the Virtemberg prince's banquets as his buffoon or jester, which, as I hear, you perform and sustain quite wittily in his court, in keeping with your nature and seriousness (for even the most serious princes are wont to delight in buffoons). Let it come to your mind how full of offence your meeting at Freiburg im Breisgau with the Papist priests was. Remember what your intimacy was with your maidservant, at the time when you played the part of the feigned son of the eunuch Chaereas from Terence, acting it truly and not in a play. Recall what offspring came of it, and how very just was the complaint of your most chaste wife about you. Some of your friends, whom I could easily name if they wished, kindly helped you to deny that deed of yours. These things pertain to you, Laonicus, and you cannot refute them, indeed cannot even deny them (since there are so many witnesses), unless you wish to be thought the most shameless of men. For those things you throw at me with livid eyes, asinine ears, a twisted mouth and so on, you were surely looking at yourself in your own mirror when you wrote them. Thus you have painted yourself, not me. All these things are of such a kind that no one will believe them of me on your word, and everyone who has seen me will easily understand that you have calumniated me shamelessly. You ought also (since you wished to amuse yourself with these insults against me) to have copied out, in your usual buffoonish way, the whole description of famine from Ovid's Metamorphoses, so that we could know you had read it, like Terence's eunuch, and so that you might hurl at me from it what schoolboys read in their classes. But you had learned only a few little things, namely those from Cicero's Pisoniana and the rhetoric. Yet not content with words, you brandish at me, in the manner of your Centaurs and Lapiths (since, as they were horsemen, so are you), the sign of Mercury's staff, wounds, slaughter and the Tenedian axe. Against this I fearlessly oppose the shield of faith in Christ and of true doctrine, which easily quenches and blunts even the flaming darts of Satan himself. Therefore I, who (as belonging to the Church of God, by his mercy) have weapons of a teacher that are not carnal, will take up in place of the Tenedian axe the very Word of God, and that effective speech which is more piercing than any two-edged sword. For it reaches even to the dividing of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow, and it judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart, as the Holy Spirit himself teaches. Through him I pray and beseech God with my utmost prayers, through Christ, his only begotten and unique mediator, that you may be converted to the true doctrine of the Lord's Supper. Farewell. Geneva, in the year of the Lord 1581, on the Kalends of January, for New Year's gifts.

units.tr: "Clay, unless it is ... , becomes ..." [Πλήλος, εἰ μὴ ἂν δ᾽αρῇ, κίεχμος ὁ γίνεται.]

units.la: IATROTHEI ANTILAONICI AD LAONICVM A STVRMENECK equitem nec aureum, nec auratum.
units.tr: Iatrotheus Antilaonicus to Laonicus of Sturmeneck, a knight neither golden nor gilded.

units.la: PLebeie miles, & ferox, nec aurate Equĕs, quid istud? Spongiámne, qua vulnus Nondum datum abstergas? videlicet victor Certamen ante consertum? Aut magè ignaue Pugnare certus hanc geris? Quid ignaue? Non hoc geruntur bella cum viris pacto: Cum fœminis, tute experire, quas vincens, Reminciénsque, bellus es quidem victor, Eques nec auratus. Viden' nouum vulnus? Hîc Spongiam quaras: sed ablues nunquam: Habes. Quid imbuta interim tamen fiet, Tot, qua patras, quaque helluaris, infandis Quid fiet, inquam, Spongia? aut tibi vt fiet? Nam te simul percussit ense Lambertus Verbi Dei, nec Spongia, nec vltores Vlli tibi iam proderunt, nec aurate. Prædicit ista Delphicus tibi Phœbus.
units.tr: Plebeian soldier, and fierce, not gilded knight, what is this? Are you wiping away with a sponge a wound not yet given? Are you, forsooth, a victor before the contest is joined? Or do you go into battle, more cowardly, already certain of the result? Why cowardly? Wars are not waged with men on those terms. Try it with women, whom you conquer, and garlanded, you are indeed a fine victor, a knight not gilded. Do you see the new wound? Here you seek a sponge, but you will never wash it clean. You have one. Meanwhile, what will become of the sponge soaked in so many unspeakable deeds which you commit and gorge on? What will become of it, I say? Or what will become of you? For Lambert, of the Word of God, has struck you at once with the sword, and neither sponge nor avengers will avail you any longer, nor gilding. Delphic Phoebus foretells these things to you.
