units.la: Cal. lib. 4. in Instit. Christ. cap. 17 sect 6. & 34 & in Ioan. 6. ver. 34. stum sola Sacramentali manducatione non edi in S.Cœna,nisi spiritualis mäducatio coniungatur. Itaque idem hic pene pag.53.noster est,quum ait, Sacramentalem carnis Christi manducationem esse obsignationem spiritualis mäducationis eiusdem carnis. Ex quo colligo,vel ipso Gerlachio teste,non aliter ipsam carnem Christi in S. Cœna, quàm extra Cœnam manducari, quod & verum est, & nobiscum facit,& suos aperte oppugnat.Sed homo inconstans seipsum postea euertit, quia,etsi à nostris rationibus vincitur,à suis tamen discedere non audet, metu exilij à Laonico sibi intentati.Sed & illud,quod ait pag.60. Sacramentum vnum & idem est, quoad substantiam, dignis, & indignis,quàm parum à veritate distat?dic,Sacramentu vnum & idé est, quod ad significationem, &ipsius Sacrameti naturam,dignis & indignis,& rectè dixeris, & nobiscum consenseris,& tota lis erit finita. Verum reliqua perpendamus.Ait Gerlachius,Substantia Sacramenti percipi & à dignis,& ab indignis: idque se putat confirmare ex verbis Domini. Verum verba illa Christi,vti sæpe docui mus,nequaquam intelligit, Hoc est corpus meum, quia hoc ipsum est petitio principij. Nam sunt tropica.Quod autem cŏtraria à nobis dici putat, quum asseueramus carnem Christi & absente, & pręsente esse inS.Cœna,facile ex hac distinctione verisima dissoluitur. Abest caro Christi à S.Cœna præsentiæ corporalis situ & modo, & coexistentia cum signis,qualem vos solam carnis præsentiam in S. Cœna fingitis. Adest eadem caro Christi in S.Cœna,spirituali efficacitate,pręsetia sidei, & Sacramentali, & veré nostra cum ea pcr Spiritus sansti opus communicatione ac conso‑ciatione. Vides igitur vt te istis animi anxietati‑bus leui distinctione liberemus. Paulum vero sic interpretaris, quum ait ille, Panis, quem frangi‑mus, est communicatio corporis Christi, quasi velit si‑ne discrimine digni, & indigni hominis ipsam substan‑tiam Sacramenti, id est, ipsam substantia’em carnem Christi ab omnibus ad S.Coenam accedentibus edi.Dormitasne vero quum Paulum legis, qui in eadem Epistola cap.11.non animaducer‑ris eum distinguere manifeste inter dignos & in‑dignos, & velle dignos duntaxat sumere ipsum corpus Christi: indignos autem hunc panem, & hoc poculum, vt ipse loquitur, id est, sacra tantum signa essentialis corporis, & sanguinis Christi su‑mere? vel, vt loquitur Augustinus, demonstratio‑nem gratiæ, cuius sunt isti ingrati. Perbella vero est illa tua verborum Pauli interpretatio, Poculum benedictionis est κοινωνία sanguinis Christi, id est, San‑guis Christi est cum vino, in vino, & sub vino. Tria enim illa coniungere debuisti, quoniam hæc est plana tua, & tuorum sententia, quam hic propter ἀποπόμπη perspicuè addere non es ausus. Quod ad locum autem Augustini lib. 3. de Bap‑tis. contra Donatistas cap.14.eum plane admit‑timus, & te, tuosque, si recte intelligeres, ab eo oppugnari animaduerteres. Disputans enim Au‑gustinus contra Donatistas, qui Sacramenta, id est, Actiones, & ritus ipsos à Deo institutos, nō ex ipsa Dei institutione, sed ex hominum da‑tium aut accipientium fide & probitate, Sacra‑menta, & σφραγίδας promissionum esse constitue‑bant
units.tr: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, book 4, chapter 17, sections 6 and 34, and on John 6:34. ...stum alone is not eaten in the Holy Supper by the sacramental eating alone unless spiritual eating is joined to it. So our man here is almost in agreement with us on page 53, when he says that the sacramental eating of the flesh of Christ is a sealing of the spiritual eating of the same flesh. From this I conclude, even on Gerlachius' own testimony, that the flesh of Christ is eaten in the Supper in no other way than outside the Supper, which is both true and on our side, and openly undermines his own people. But this inconsistent man afterwards overturns himself. For although he is beaten by our arguments, he still does not dare to depart from his own people, for fear of the exile threatened him by Laonicus. And how far from the truth is what he says on page 60: The sacrament is one and the same in substance for the worthy and the unworthy? Say instead that the sacrament is one and the same in its signification and in its very nature for the worthy and the unworthy, and you will speak rightly, you will agree with us, and the whole dispute will be over. But let us weigh the rest. Gerlachius says: the substance of the sacrament is received both by the worthy and by the unworthy, and he thinks he confirms this from the words of the Lord. But he does not understand those words of Christ, This is my body, as I have often taught; and that is simply begging the question, for they are tropical. As for his claim that we say contrary things when we affirm that the flesh of Christ is both absent and present in the Holy Supper, this is easily resolved by a true distinction. The flesh of Christ is absent from the Supper in respect of bodily presence, place and manner, and of coexistence with the signs, which is the only presence of the flesh in the Supper that you imagine. The same flesh of Christ is present in the Holy Supper in spiritual efficacy, by the presence of faith and by the sacrament, and by our true communion and fellowship with it through the work of the Holy Spirit. You see, then, how we free you from those anxieties by a slight distinction. But you interpret Paul wrongly when he says, The bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ, as though he wanted the very substance of the sacrament, that is, the very flesh of Christ, to be eaten by all who come to the Holy Supper without distinction between worthy and unworthy. Are you asleep when you read Paul, who in the same epistle, chapter 11, plainly distinguishes between the worthy and the unworthy, and wants only the worthy to receive the body of Christ itself, while the unworthy receive this bread and this cup, as he himself says, that is, only the holy signs of the essential body and blood of Christ? Or, as Augustine says, a demonstration of grace, of which these ungrateful men are the heirs? Your interpretation of Paul's words, The cup of blessing is the communion [κοινωνία] of the blood of Christ, that is, the blood of Christ is with the wine, in the wine, and under the wine, is very pretty indeed. You ought to have joined those three things together, since this is your plain view and that of your people, which you have not dared to state openly here for fear of ἀποπομπή. As for the passage of Augustine, On Baptism against the Donatists, book 3, chapter 14, we plainly accept it, and if you understood it rightly, you would notice that it is aimed against you and your people. For Augustine, disputing against the Donatists, who held that the sacraments, that is, the actions and rites instituted by God, and the seals of the promises, depend not on God's own institution but on the faith and goodness of the men who give or receive them, answers truly that the whole and so holy and so complete sacrament is received by the godly and by the ungodly alike. But Augustine speaks only of the receiving of the signs, not of the thing signified, as he himself testifies...

units.la: August. in Ioan. tract. 61. bant, vere respondet, & totum, & tam sanctum, & tam integrum Sacramentum a pio quàm ab impio homine accipi: sed de signorum tantùm acceptione, & non de re signata loquitur Augustinus, vel eo ipso teste in Ioan. Tract. 62. Rem enim ipsam Sacramenti ab indignis sumi negat. Atque hoc ipsum est, quod idem ait, ad salutis viam longam esse differentiam inter dignos & indignos. Etsi tamen ab ijsdem totum Sacramentum, & Christi Sacramentum accipi concedit. Id quod nos & cum Augustino dicimus, & ab eo didicimus, & vos cuertit, qui rem Sacramenti, & non tantùm ipsum signum, seu Sacramentum ab indignis sumi vultis. Legat illud ipsum cap. 14. Augustini qui volet, & habebit illic facilem sui interpretem Augustinum nobis prorsus assentientem, vobis autem contrarium. Eodem modo intelligendum est, quod Gerlachius ex codé Augustino, cap. 6. contra Fulgentium, & ex epistola 162. citat. Nam his omnibus locis Augustinus signum ipsum corporis Christi, quod Iudas sumpsit, vocat bonum corpus, & pretium, ratione Sacramentali, quia signum: quemadmodum aquam Baptismi, quam sumpsit Simon Magus, appellat idé Augustinus bonum Baptisma, quia (quatenus ea signa ex Christi institutione considerantur) hæc bona sunt, & rerum earum, quas significant, nomina accipiunt. Ad tertium autem locum Augustini Laonico iam respondi. Cæterum quod affingit mihi Gerlachius, quasi sentiam, nos in S. Cœna per fidem participare tantùm efficaciam, & virtutem carnis Christi, non autem ipsam carnem, puerilis est istius hominis hallucinatio, & iocatio, vt nihil grauius dicam. Nam praesentiam carnis Christi in S. Coena dico esse ἐνεργητικὴν: ipsam vero nostram cum ea carne communicationem, affirmo esse veram, realem, atque etiam rei ipsius, quae percipitur a nobis, ratione, non autem modo perceptionis corporalem (corpus enim ipsum Christi participamus) Non tamen eam statuo corporalis praesentiae genere, & modo praesentem. Sed iste quia non putat communicationem nostram vllam esse posse cum re quapiam, quae sit praesentiae corporalis modo ab iis terris absens, idcirco praesentiam carnis Christi & nostram cum eo communicationem confundit, & vtraque corporale facit, sed, quemadmodum antea dixi, male. Porro quod ait Augustinus apud Prosperum, Integrum Sacramentum duobus constare, nimirum signo & re signata, & vetus est, & verum, & ex Irenaeo sumptum: sed non ideo sequitur, vtrunque hoc, nempe signum, & rem signatam ab omnibus signa sumentibus capi. Indigni enim, & impoenitentes, ad S. Coenam accedentes, ex hac Sacramenti significatione, dimidiu tantum Sacramentum, nempe signa duntaxat, sumunt: poenitentes autem sibi integrum. Sacramentum, hoc Sacramenti significato. Sed quum sumitur Sacramentum pro signo tantum, & eo quidem sacro, & teste promissionum Dei (in quo integra vis signi, & natura posita est, & virtus Sacramenti, quatenus Sacramentum pro signo sumitur) certe indigni & impoenitentes sumunt integrum Christi Sacramentum, id est, illud totum, quod est promissionum
units.tr: Augustine, in Ioan. tract. 61. He answers truly that the whole sacrament, so holy and so complete, is received by the godly and the ungodly alike. But Augustine speaks only of the reception of the signs, not of the thing signified, as he himself attests in In Ioan. tract. 62. There he denies that the thing of the sacrament is taken by the unworthy. This is exactly what he means when he says that there is a long difference to the way of salvation between the worthy and the unworthy. Yet he does concede that the whole sacrament, the sacrament of Christ, is received by both. This is what we say with Augustine, and what we have learned from him. But you turn it upside down, wanting the thing of the sacrament, and not merely the sign or sacrament itself, to be taken by the unworthy. Let anyone who wishes read that same chapter 14 of Augustine. There he will find an easy interpreter, Augustine wholly agreeing with us and wholly opposed to you. The same must be understood of what Gerlachius cites from the same Augustine, chapter 6 against Fulgentius, and from letter 162. In all these places Augustine calls the very sign of the body of Christ, which Judas received, good body and price, in a sacramental sense, because it is a sign. Likewise the same Augustine calls the water of baptism, which Simon Magus received, a good baptism, because, so far as those signs are considered in terms of Christ's institution, they are good and take the names of the things they signify. As for the third passage of Augustine, I have already answered Laonicus. As for what Gerlachius attributes to me, as if I held that in the Holy Supper we participate only by faith in the efficacy and power of Christ's flesh and not in the flesh itself, that is a childish delusion and a joke on the man's part, to put it no more harshly. For I say that the presence of Christ's flesh in the Holy Supper is energetic [ἐνεργητικὴν]. But I affirm that our communion with that flesh itself is true, real, and also, with respect to the thing itself that we receive, not merely a matter of the mode of receiving, since we partake of the very body of Christ. Yet I do not hold that it is present in the manner and mode of bodily presence. But this man, because he does not think that any communion of ours can be had with a thing that is absent from this earth in the mode of bodily presence, therefore confuses the presence of Christ's flesh with our communion with it, and makes both bodily. But, as I said before, he does this wrongly. Furthermore, what Augustine says in Prosper, The whole sacrament consists of two things, namely the sign and the thing signified, is both old and true, and is taken from Irenaeus. But it does not follow from this that both of these, the sign and the thing signified, are taken by all who receive the signs. For the unworthy and the impenitent, coming to the Holy Supper, take from this meaning of sacrament only half of the sacrament, namely the signs alone. The penitent take the whole sacrament for themselves in this meaning. But when sacrament is taken for the sign only, and indeed the sacred sign and witness of God's promises (in which the whole force and nature of the sign lies, and the power of the sacrament, insofar as the sacrament is taken for the sign), then certainly the unworthy and the impenitent do take the whole sacrament of Christ, that is, that whole which is the sign of God's promises.

units.la: Dei signu. Verum has(etsi vsitatissimas)significa tiones Sacramenti,confundit Gerlachius,&vocis æquiuocatione ludit.Sic etiam spirituale mădu-cationem,cum Sacramentali postea quoque per- turbat, quu ait,spirituale manducatione habere fignorü vsum. Nec enim mere spiritualis,sed ea, quæ etiam est Sacramentalis,signorum vsum, & esum habet cum fide coniunctum: sed ista non vi det Gerlachius.Denique omnino secludit Gerla chius S.Cœnâ à communi lege reliquorü N.Te-ftamenti Sacramctorü. Quomodo igitur N.Te-ftamenti Sacramentu S.Domini Cœna iure vo-cabitur?Ait enim,Solu Cœna Sacramentum habere re signata coniuncta cum symbolis.Sed hæc exce ptio est salsissima,(petit enim principium) & o-mnis iftorū erroris magnus fons & caussa. Errat quoque puericiliter Gerlachius,quu nō videt,præ-bitionem quidē eflentialis corporis & sanguinis Christi fieri nobis ex institutione,id est,gratia,& virtute promissionis Christi : Acceptione autem illius carnis à nobis virtute fidei fieri. Nam vult iste,& scribit confuse,Communicatione fieri nobis carnis Christi,ex virtute permissionis.Sed in co-municatione, Gerlachi, præbitio, & acceptio fi-mul insunt & comprehenduntur:& diftinguen-dū tibi erat,vnde præbitio,vnde acceptio fiat,vel proprie in nobis pendeat. Perperā enim dicitur, quód quemadmodu fempcr à Deo integrū Sacra mentu omnibus offertur,ita ab omnibus integrū quoque recipitur,fi integrū Sacramentū & de fi-gno,& de re signata,vt facitis,intelligas.Nā ex ve ra necessitate,&confequetis,& non tantum con-fequetiæ(quicquid Philofoph'hic fe intelligere, sed frustra putet Gerlachius)fides requiritur ad vera essentialis Christi carnis participationem. Verum nouus iste Philosophus plane ineptus est,qui scribat,praeter vnum Deum nihil dici pof fc necessarium neccfsitate absoluta, & conse-quentis. Quid enim? Annon est neccefsitate con-sequentis, & absoluta iam necessarium, vt homines,filij Adami,peccent, Gerlachi,vt moriantur,vt edant, vt bibant, &c? Disce igitur,multa praeter Deum dici pofle necessaria neccfsitate absoluta. Vide Thomam in prima parte primae summae. Quae sequuntur autem a pag. 63.vsque ad 69. vnum habent Chryfoftomi testimonium, vnde (quia Chryfoftomus vocat signa corporis, & sanguinis Christi, corpus & sanguinem Christi) iste extruit (sed quam inaniter) suam illam confubftantiatione rei signatae cum signis S.Coenae. Quis enim nescit Chryfoftomum sic loqui, Corpus Christi cadit in terram, corpus Christi videtur, conficitur, &c. quae millies a nostris antea repetita, & explicata huic satisfacere debebant. Legat igitur quae nos ad Laonicum in hoc ipso argumento respondimus. Nam vt ille, sic iftefacratiffimam Domini nostri Iesu Christi carnem in rerum ἀδιαφόρων numero, certe quidem impie (liceat enim verum dicere) constituit, quae per fe non magis viuifica fit, quam mortifera fumentibus: sed pro illius, qui ipsa vtitur, ingenio, mortem, vel vitam per fe afferat hominibus. Obsecro,quę maior potest esse,vel audiri blasphemia?
units.tr: But Gerlachius confuses these meanings of sacrament, however common they are, and plays on an equivocation in the word. So too he later confuses spiritual eating with sacramental eating, when he says that spiritual eating has the use of signs. For eating is not purely spiritual; the eating that is also sacramental has the use and eating of signs joined with faith. But Gerlachius does not see this. Finally, Gerlachius entirely excludes the Lord's Supper from the common law of the other sacraments of the New Testament. How then will the Lord's Supper rightly be called a sacrament of the New Testament? For he says that only the Supper has the thing signified joined with the symbols. But this exception is most foolish, for it begs the question, and it is a great source and cause of all their error. Gerlachius also errs childishly when he does not see that the offering of the essential body and blood of Christ to us comes from the institution, that is, from the grace and power of Christ's promise, while the reception of that flesh by us comes through the power of faith. For this man wants, and writes confusedly, that the flesh of Christ is made ours by communication through the power of the promise. But in communication, Gerlachius, offering and receiving are both present and included together. You ought to have distinguished whence the offering comes, whence the reception comes, and what properly depends on us. For it is wrongly said that, just as the whole sacrament is always offered to all by God, so too the whole is received by all, if you understand the whole sacrament both as sign and as thing signified, as you do. For faith is required for the true and essential participation in the flesh of Christ by true necessity, and by necessity of consequence, and not merely by consequence (whatever this philosopher thinks he understands, though Gerlachius thinks it in vain). But this new philosopher is entirely inept, who writes that nothing besides the one God can be called necessary by absolute necessity and by necessity of consequence. For what? Is it not already necessary, by necessity of consequence and absolutely, that men, the sons of Adam, sin, Gerlachius; that they die, eat, drink, and so on? Learn, therefore, that many things besides God can be called necessary by absolute necessity. See Thomas in the first part of the first Summa. What follows, from page 63 to 69, rests on one testimony of Chrysostom, from which this man builds (but how vainly) his well-known consubstantiation of the thing signified with the signs of the Holy Supper. He does this because Chrysostom calls the signs of the body and blood of Christ the body and blood of Christ. For who does not know that Chrysostom speaks thus: The body of Christ falls to the ground, the body of Christ is seen, is made, and so on? Our side has repeated and explained this a thousand times before, and it ought to satisfy the objection. Let him therefore read what we answered to Laonicus on this very argument. For, like Laonicus, this man places the most sacred flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ among the things indifferent [ἀδιαφόρων], certainly impiously (for I must speak the truth), a flesh which in itself is no more life-giving than deadly to those who take it. Rather, according to the disposition of the one who uses it, it brings death or life to men. I beg you, what greater blasphemy can be imagined, or even heard?

units.la: Porro quae ex Theodoreto, Ignatio, Cyrillo, & Hilario profers, Gerlachi, nihil ad rhombum tuum faciunt. Probant enim illa, nos vere ipsi Christi carni per fidem communicare, quod nos quoque cum Patribus affirmamus: vetram autem sententiam de coexistentia carnis cum signis ipsis S. Coenae ista prorsus euertunt, cum carnem Christi per fidem, & sub Sacramento participari, vel teipso teste, Patres dicant. Fides autem procul dubio rem, id est, carnem ipsam Christi absentem esse docet, si modo Paulo credis fidem & aspectum inter se ex diametro opponenti. Sed quid si excipiam, quod ipse addis, Patres illos videri tollere signorum substantiam? Quod ostendit, te non intellectos Patrum locos, sed ab aliis emendicatos hic protulisse. Quae pagina 71. & seq. de Dei omnipotentia declamitat Gerlachius, sunt a me in responsione ad Laonicum explicata & soluta, & millies a nostris iistis inculcata, si modo cor a Deo peterent, per quod veritatem ipsius intelligerent. Locum Cyrilli ex libro 12 in Ioannem, in Antiochiandro explicavi, & bostea repetetur ab isto, ut paginas nimirum suas implicat. Concedo igitur carnem seu corpus Christi adesse in S. Coena σωματικῶς παρουσίας, si de reipsa, qua participamus, quaeritur. Ipsum enim corpus Christi in S. Coena fide percipim. Sed fide modo praesentiae illius agitur, nego σωματικῶς παρουσίας, id est, praesentiae corporalis modo eam adesse. Ergo si quaeritur, quid adsit in S. Coena illo genere praesentiae, quod dixi, concedo σωματικῶς adesse. Inde fit ut a Cyrillo dicta sit praesentia carnis Christi σωματική, nempe rem ipsam, quae nobis communicatur, intuente. Manet enim corpus Christi, quod nobis communicatur, verè corpus, & verè per fidem à nobis participatur: sed propterea tamen corporali præsentiæ situ actu do nequaquam adest, qui situs & modus admiritatem corporis stabiliendam necessariò requiritur, vt plane intolerabiles sitis, quum corporalem præsentiæ modum, non tamen localem statuitis. Neque aliter unquam, vti docui, Cyrillus sensit. Cæterum quod negas, præsentiam localem, vel corporalem Christi situm à vobis in illa ipsius cohæsione cum Cœnæ signis induci, video quidem, te præsentire illa absurda, quæ ex tua sententia sequuntur, sed nihilominus non tollere. Nam licet ea neges, & sequi ex tua sententia nolis, sequuntur tamen. Quomodo enim verum corpus esse realiter & corporaliter visquè sine situ, & vbi, & loco suo, Gerlachi, potest? Ergo & localem, & corporalem situm habeat ista vestra corporalis præsentia est necesse, quæ admodum videt omnes. Quæ multis verbis pag. 77. & sequentibus addidisti, quia nihil nisi conuitia continent, prætermitto, vti & quæ pag. 81. & sequentibus, dum nos comparas rebellibus Iudæis: & vos Prophetis Dei. Torgensem synodum postea damnas, & rectè. Nam eam verissimis rationibus à Theod. Beza confutatam esse memineras, quibus adhuc nemo vestrum respondere potuerit. Cæterum quod nos iam convictos esse erroris, nos verbis Christi contradicere, nos omnipotentiâ Christi negare ais, in eo flores tuæ eloquentiæ video, sed argumenta non audio. Nā istæ sunt veteres vestræ næniæ, & plus quàm conspuendæ nugæ, toties & hic, & alibi, & supra in nostra ad Laonicu SpngiaRefpofione refuta-tæ,vt hic eas repetere me propter teipfu pudeat. Quod autem iterū de nostris Ecclesijs vniuersis non dānatis,sed tātum de illarū Pastoribus à pa. 36.vsque 100.dicis,ius tantum vetus recoquis: vel id facis,quod ista Pastorū, qui in nostris Ecclesijs docet,condenatio mire tibi placeat: vel vt paginas impleas:vel vt nos hoc tædio oneres, & à tuis legedis arceas nimia illa tua & inutili prolixitate. Diuinas esse septẽ hominū millia in Gallia,qui vestrā Vbiquitatem amplectātur. Quis ti bi spiritus ista reuelauit? Ego vero,Gerlachi, qui nostras Ecclesias noui,id nego: & Osiādro antea verè negaui vel vnū esse. Sed me in eo medacij ac cusas. Quo iure? Quid vero,si in vtroque nostrū mędaciū est,plūsne mętitur qui in vno,vt ego·an quiin 7000.mentitus est, vt tu? Sed tu quine Gallię quidē aerē vnquā hausisti,te hisce somnijs pascis. Nā & qui amant,sibi somnia fiugut,ait ille. Sed video quid velis,Gerlachi:quia inter vos qui dā sunt,qui nostrę doctrinę.i. Veritati Dei ( etiā vobis inuitis)assetiutur,vt tu retaliare,& hoc vestrarū Ecclesiarū dānū cōpensare , ac tua doctri- nā quo iure quaue iniuria cōmedare vestris pos sis,magno animi errore,fingis esse vicifiim inter nostros,7000.hominū,qui vestru errore,& vbi- quitate probēt.Sed quādiu salsa ista diuinare per seuerabis,tibi nō credā:nec eorum quisquā, qui & nostras Ecclesias norūt,& singulos(qui sut in eis)nisi sint magni hypocrite,perspexerūt.Quæ- ris post Osiandrū,vtrum Paulus singulos,qui e- rant in Ecclesijs Corinthiaca, & Galatica, dāna- rit? Respondeo, nequaquā,quia singu!i ei errori, quem Paulus damnabat, minimè consentiebant. Nam si singuli consensissent, singulos vnâ & eâdem sententia feriret Paulus. Quanquam & verbum Damnandi, notandum tibi est apud Paulum. Reprehèdit quidem errores, vt rem malam, & redarguit ita sentientes: sed nequaquam Sathanæ tradit, neque ex Ecclesia expellit, neque anathematizat, quod vos facitis. Cesset diuinatio, quod res est, dicatur, Gerlachi. Singuli pij, & verè fideles, qui sunt in Ecclesiis Gallicis, vestram Vbiquitatem, vt manifestam hæresin, oderunt, & eam scientes prudentésque damnant. Ergo singulos Ecclesiarum Gallicarum pios, & singulas illas, quas vocatis, & excipiebatis, ouiculas iam vestra illa crudeli sententia condemnatis. Hæc conclusio vera est, & quorsum vestræ condemnationes cuadant, iam, vt opinor, vides. Nec enim quæritur, vtrùm totas Ecclesias, vel vos vel Paulus damnarit, quod putas: sed quæritur, vtrùm singulos in iis Ecclesiis errâtes, etsi nō pari pœna & iudicio, Paulus condemnarit. Quòd ego dico, tu negas, quia errorem in abstracto tantùm, & non omnes errâtes à vobis quoque feriri dicitis. iudicet Ecclesia vtri verius sentiant. Cæterùm te omnis Ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ valde imperitum demonstras, qui quemlibet in Ecclesia damnatu, putes statim ex Ecclesia esse vel eiectum, seu excommunicatum: vel eiici, ac excommunicari debere: mèque reprehendis, quòd sic scripserim, Non quicunque damnantur, iidem tamen propterea ex toto fratrum coetu statim excommunicantur. Quid igitur? ex Stoicorùmne profanorum
units.tr: Moreover, the passages you cite from Theodoret, Ignatius, Cyril and Hilary, Gerlachius, have nothing to do with your fancy. They prove that we truly communicate in the flesh of Christ through faith, which we too affirm with the Fathers. But they utterly overthrow your view that the flesh is coexistent with the signs of the holy Supper, since the Fathers say, as you yourself admit, that the flesh of Christ is partaken through faith and under the sacrament. Faith, without doubt, teaches that the thing itself, that is, the flesh of Christ, is absent, if indeed you believe Paul, who sets faith and sight in direct opposition to each other. But what if I accept what you add, that those Fathers seem to remove the substance of the signs? That shows you have not understood the Fathers' passages and have brought them forward here borrowed from others. The things Gerlachius declaims on pages 71 and following, about God's omnipotence, have already been explained and resolved by me in my reply to Laonicus, and have been pressed upon you a thousand times by our people, if only you would ask God for a heart by which to understand his truth. I explained the passage from Cyril's twelfth book on John in my reply to Antidanaeus, and it will be repeated by him, so that he may pile up his pages. I therefore grant that the flesh or body of Christ is present in the holy Supper σωματικῶς, if the question concerns the very thing we partake of. For we perceive the body of Christ itself in the holy Supper by faith. But the matter here concerns his presence by faith, and I deny that it is σωματικῶς παρουσίας, that is, present in a bodily manner. So if the question is what is present in the holy Supper in that kind of presence which I have described, I grant that it is present σωματικῶς. Hence Cyril called the presence of Christ's flesh σωματική, namely with respect to the thing itself which is communicated to us. For the body of Christ, which is communicated to us, remains truly a body, and is truly partaken by us through faith. Yet it is by no means present in the bodily manner of a place and situation, which situation and mode are necessarily required to establish the reality of a body. So you are utterly intolerable, since you posit a bodily mode of presence but not a local one. Nor, as I have taught, did Cyril ever think otherwise. As for your denial that you introduce a local presence or a bodily situation of Christ by that cohesion with the signs of the Supper, I see indeed that you foresee the absurdities which follow from your opinion, yet you do not remove them. For although you deny them and do not wish them to follow from your opinion, they follow nonetheless. For how, Gerlachius, can a body be real and corporeal and yet be without situation, and where, and in its own place? Therefore your corporeal presence must have a local and corporeal situation, as everyone sees. What you have added on page 77 and following in many words, since it contains nothing but abuse, I pass over, as also what is on page 81 and following, where you compare us to rebellious Jews and yourselves to the prophets of God. You later condemn the Torgau synod, and rightly so. For you will remember that it was refuted by Theodore Beza with the most true arguments, to which none of you has yet been able to reply. But as for your saying that we, now convicted of error, contradict the words of Christ and deny the omnipotence of Christ, in this I see the flowers of your eloquence, but I hear no arguments. These are your old dirges and trifles, more than worthy of spitting upon, already refuted so many times here, elsewhere, and above in our reply to Laonicus, that I am ashamed to repeat them here for your sake. As for your repeating that we are condemned not as whole churches but only in our ministers, from page 36 to 100, you are merely recooking your old broth: either because this condemnation of the ministers who teach in our churches pleases you wonderfully, or to fill your pages, or to burden us with this tedium and keep your readers away with your excessive and useless prolixity. You say there are seven thousand people in France who embrace your Ubiquity. What spirit revealed this to you? I, Gerlachius, who know our churches, deny it, and I earlier truly denied it to Osiander, that there is even one. But you accuse me of lying in this. On what right? Indeed, if there is a lie on both sides, does he who lies in one thing, as I do, lie more than he who lies about seven thousand, as you do? But you, who have never breathed the air of France, feed yourself on these dreams. For, as that poet says, those who are in love make up dreams for themselves. But I see what you want, Gerlachius: since there are some among you who support our doctrine, that is, the truth of God, even against your will, you want to retaliate and offset the damage to your churches with this, and by some great error of mind you pretend that among our people there are seven thousand men who approve your error and Ubiquity, so that you may commend your doctrine to your own people by whatever right or wrong. But as long as you persist in divining these salty fictions, I shall not believe you, nor will any of those who know our churches and have examined each individual in them, unless they are great hypocrites. You ask, following Osiander, whether Paul condemned the individuals who were in the churches of Corinth and Galatia? I reply, by no means, because the individuals did not agree with the error which Paul condemned. For if the individuals had agreed, Paul would have struck each of them with the same single sentence. Yet you should note the word "condemn" as used by Paul. He indeed reproves the errors as an evil thing, and refutes those who think so, but he by no means hands them over to Satan, nor casts them out of the church, nor anathematizes them, as you do. Let the divining cease; let the fact be stated, Gerlachius. The individual pious and truly faithful who are in the French churches hate your Ubiquity as a manifest heresy, and knowing it, and being wise, they condemn it. Therefore by that harsh sentence of yours you condemn the individual pious members of the French churches, and all those sheep whom you call and receive. This conclusion is true, and, as I think, you now see where your condemnations lead. For the question is not whether you or Paul condemned whole churches, as you suppose, but whether Paul condemned the individuals in those churches who were erring, though not with the same penalty and judgment. What I say, you deny, because you speak of error only in the abstract and say that you do not strike all who err. Let the Church judge which side holds the truer view. Moreover, you show yourself very ignorant of all church discipline, since you think that anyone condemned in the church is at once cast out of the church or excommunicated, or ought to be cast out or excommunicated; and you reprove me because I wrote thus: "Not all who are condemned are therefore at once excommunicated from the whole fellowship of the brethren." What then? Do you teach this from the school of the profane Stoic philosophers (I will not name them, with whom you lived at Constantinople, as you know), that all the sins of Christians are equal? Why then does Paul so plainly command that even a heretical man, though already condemned for error, be admonished once and again before we cast him out of the Church? Why does he likewise want the disobedient [ἀπειθεῖς], whom he condemns, to be marked by letter before the ministers remove them from the company and fellowship of the church and excommunicate them? Why does Christ himself direct that the Church proceed to excommunication only by certain steps, although the Church condemns all vices entirely? Why at the Nicene, Tribur, Meaux, Auvergne and countless other synods were definite grades of ecclesiastical censure, even public ones, established before the ministers came to excommunication? Let Gerlachius read Cyprian, book 1 of the Epistles, and he will understand that he is wholly ignorant of true and ancient ecclesiastical discipline, and that he has not thought or written rightly, and he will learn that he is grossly mistaken. "For not all who are condemned according to the word of God are believed, or ought to be believed, to be chosen by the Church as elect." But doubtless Gerlachius, unwisely, has here betrayed himself and his own. For he clearly shows that the ministers of the French, Helvetic, English, Polish, Scottish churches and so on are already regarded as excommunicated in their own churches, and by their own people, since we have been condemned, and indeed unheard, in that thick and newly published Ubiquitarian volume.

units.la: Pag. 105. rum Philosophorum (ne eos nominem, cum quibus Constantinopoli, vt scis, vixisti) Schola doces, paria inter se esse omnia Christianorum peccata? Cur igitur tam diserte iubet Paulus, vt etiam haereticum hominem, etsi iam erroris damnatum, semel, ac iterum moneamus, priusquam eum ex Ecclesia eiiciamus? cur idem vult ἀπαιτεῖς homines, quos condemnat, prius tamen annotari sibi per epistolam, quam eos ab Ecclesiae coetu, & consortio Pastores semoueant, ac excommunicent? Cur Christus ipse praecipit, vt certis demum gradibus ad excommunicandum accedat Ecclesia, quae tamen Ecclesia vitia omnino omnia damnat? Cur Nicena, Triburiensi, Meldensi, Auernensi, aliisque infinitis Synodis certi cesurae Ecclesiasticae etiam publicae gradus sunt constituti, priusquam ad excommunicationem veniant Pastores? Legat Gerlachius Cyprianum lib. 1. Epistolarum, & se prorsus disciplinae verae, & veteris Ecclesiasticae ignarum esse intelligit, neque recte sensisse, & scripsisse, imo se turpissime falli cognoscet. Neque enim, vt tamen ipse vult, omnes qui secundum verbum Dei damnati sunt, illi ab Ecclesia electorum electi creduntur, vel credendi sunt. Sed nimirum hic imprudens Gerlachius seipsum & suos prodidit. Ostendit enim aperte, nos Ecclesiarum Gallicarum, Helveticarum, Anglicarum, Polonicarum, Scoticarum, &c. Pastores iam pro excommunicatis prorsus in ipsorum Ecclesiis, & ab ipsis censeri, quoniam in crasso illo, & Nouo Vbiquitatis corpore nuper recens edito damnati, & quidem inauditi, sumus, ne

Why then does Paul so plainly command that even a heretical man, though already condemned for error, be admonished once and again before we cast him out of the Church? units.la: Lj. quam cum iis pacem, aut concordiam, aut communicatione speremus. Hi sunt nimirum temerariae Vbiquitariorum condemnationis, & intempestiui, & pestiferi fructus, qui totam Dei Ecclesiam perturbant. Verum eandem suam rerum Ecclesiasticarum insciitiam ostendens, postea quoque Gerlachius scribit, exempla à me prolata de Chrysostomi, Episcopi Constantinopolitani, damnatione à Theophilo Antiochiae Episcopo in Synodo facta, & per aliam Synodū reuocata: item Athanasij in Tyria Synodo, esse priuatas, politicas, & externas causas, non Ecclesiasticas: quasi nimirū Synodi, & quae in Synodo gerantur, non sint Ecclesiasticae causae & iudicia. Sed sic tutius erat per cuniculos huiusmodi euadere, quam suum factum improbare, ne in exilium eiceretur.
units.tr: ...with them we hope for neither peace, nor concord, nor fellowship. These are, to be sure, the rash condemnation and the untimely and pestilent fruits of the Ubiquitarians, which throw the whole Church of God into confusion. But in showing that same ignorance of ecclesiastical affairs, Gerlachius later also writes that the examples I cited, of the condemnation of John Chrysostom, Bishop of Constantinople, by Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch, in a synod, and its revocation by another synod, and likewise of Athanasius at the Synod of Tyre, were private, political and external causes, not ecclesiastical ones; as if synods, and what is done in synods, were not ecclesiastical matters and judgments. But it was safer for him to escape by such tunnels than to disapprove his own action, lest he be cast into exile.

units.la: Isti enim nos inauditos damnant, & in eadem causa partes & iudices, atque adeo suas in nos inimicitias publice, & aperte profesi, sedet tamen. Sed vt Pharisaeis Christum persequentibus quaeuis testimonia, & sententiae de Christo placebant, modo Christū euerterent, & grauarent: sic istis, quicquid ad nos damnandos sit, summe allubescit, & aequū censetur. Sic illa sanctos & antiquos refert Germania mores. Verum suaue fuit illius hominis inanem sudorem intueri in eleuando, restringendo, interpretando, remouendo, & tande denegando Apostolorū exemplo, qui non nisi Synodo legitime congregata, errores sui temporis publice inualescentes damnarunt. Nimirū timet Gerlachius ne nos coram Ecclesia audiant, priusquam pro haereticis habeant. Primum igitur eleuat hoc exemplum, & ait, recte à suis fuisse repre-sentatum. Nam vt in vna Hierosolyma vrbe quinque duntaxat praecipui, Petrus, Iohannes, Iacobus, Paulus, Barnabas convenerunt cum aliquot, vt iste ait, Presbyteris, & grauissimam illam controuersiam definierunt: sic Bergae sex primarij Theologi hoc de S. Domini Coena difficilimum negotiu constituerunt. Ergo Berga per Gerlachiu est beata illa Sion, & Hierosolyma: Sex illi Theologi, Vbiquitatis Apostoli, ἀντιτρίφοντες, & repraesentat quinque illos Domini Nostri Iesu Christi Apostolos: & ne nō valde res rei, & persona personae conuenire videatur, ex istis Sexuiris, & Theologis vnus etiam Iacobus, at nō ille Domini frater, appellatur, vti & vnus eorū, qui erant Hierosolymis, dicebatur Iacobus. Nonne haec est pulchra Synodi Hierosolymitanae in Bergensi pictura? Ac fortasis, vt esset maior istius Bergesis, quam illius Hierosolymitani Apostolici conuentus authoritas, Patres Bergenses voluerunt Apostolos numero superare, & Andream Musculum, illu manifeste hereticum teterrimum, secum asciuerunt, qui numerū illum maiore ac senarium (qui apud Arithmeticos perfectus quoque numerus appellatur) expleret. Haec igitur est prima illius sacrosanctę, & vere Apostolicae Synodi Hierosolymitanę ridicula eleuatio à Gerlachiofacta. Quid vero si ipse demonstre pare fraude in isto dogmate Vbiquitario inuehendo adhibita, qua Arriani in sua haeresi inter Occidentales Episcopos introduceda Mediolani seruarunt? Primū, vt τὸ ῥητὸν yrgerent, & propterea ὁμοούσιον reiiceret. Deinde vt
units.tr: For these men condemn us without a hearing, and in the same cause they are both parties and judges, and openly and publicly declare their enmity against us. Yet, just as the Pharisees, persecuting Christ, were pleased with any testimony or opinion about Christ, provided they could overthrow and burden him, so for these men whatever serves to condemn us is highly agreeable and is judged fair. Such are the holy and ancient customs that Germany brings forth. But it was a pleasant thing to watch that man sweating in vain, in raising up, restricting, interpreting, removing, and at last denying the example of the Apostles, who did not condemn the errors that were gaining ground publicly in their own time except in a lawfully convened synod. Clearly Gerlachius fears that we be heard before the Church before they regard us as heretics. First, then, he extols this example and says it was rightly represented by his people. For just as in the one city of Jerusalem only five leading men, Peter, John, James, Paul and Barnabas, met with some, as he calls them, elders, and settled that very grave controversy, so at Berga six chief theologians settled this most difficult business concerning the Lord's Supper. So by Gerlachius's account Berga is that blessed Zion and Jerusalem; those six theologians are the apostles of Ubiquity, [ἀντιτρέφοντες, mutually supporting], and represent those five Apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. And lest the comparison seem not to fit thing to thing and person to person, one of these six sextumvirs, Theologians, is called James, though not the Lord's brother, just as one of those at Jerusalem was called James. Is this not a fine picture of the Synod of Jerusalem drawn at Berga? And perhaps, so that the authority of that Berga gathering might be greater than that of the apostolic gathering at Jerusalem, the Fathers of Berga wished to outnumber the Apostles, and took in Andreas Musculus, that man manifestly a heretic and a most vile one, so that he might complete that number, greater than five and senary (which among the arithmeticians is also called a perfect number). This, then, is the first ridiculous exaltation of that most sacred and truly apostolic Synod of Jerusalem, made by Gerlachius. But what if he has introduced into this Ubiquitarian doctrine the same kind of fraud that the Arians employed at Milan to introduce their heresy among the Western bishops? First, they pressed the literal wording (τὸ ῥητὸν) and therefore rejected homoousion [ὁμοούσιον]. Then they privately extracted signatures from certain men known to them. Finally, they sent into exile those who opposed them. But afterwards Gerlachius restricts that very synod itself. For he denies that it was universal or ecumenical, and calls it merely the gathering of one city and one Church. Poor fellow, who does not understand that the Apostles there, and before Christ himself, and at the Lord's Supper, which is the occasion of this dispute between us, represented the whole Church of God, both the one then existing and the one that would exist afterwards. Moreover, he gives his own interpretation of this same synod. Surely he had learned this from his teacher Osiander, the court theologian. For he says that no general rule for rooting out and condemning errors has been prescribed to us by that event. But when he felt that I had sufficiently refuted this, at last he gave up that example and handed the Apostles over to themselves. But since I have fully answered all these points in the Antiosiander, and since such evasions are plainly empty to anyone, I pass them over. For the conjectures he draws from the two journeys of Paul to Jerusalem, mentioned in the Epistle to the Galatians, are not refuted by the fact that neither Luke in the Acts nor Paul in that Epistle to the Galatians lists all of Paul's journeys to Jerusalem. What of the fact that Gerlachius accuses the Apostles of negligence if they all took part in that Synod? Let whoever can prove this; I know that it can by no means be proved by the godly. Let us see, then, what this man adds afterwards. He says that we wish that the judicial (he meant to say ecclesiastical) process

units.la: I. ij.
units.tr: I. ij.

units.la: priuatim à quibusdam sibi notis subscriptiones corrogaret. Demum, ut sibi aduersantes in exilium mitterent. Sed cam ipsam Synodum postea Gerlachius restringit. Negat enim fuisse vniuersalem, seu œcumenicam Synodum, sed vnius tantum vrbis, & Ecclesiæ conuentum appellat. Miser homo, qui non intelligat Apostolos illic, & apud Christum ipsum, & in S. Cœna, cuius occasione hæc disputatio inter nos instituta est, vniuersam Dei Ecclesiam, & tunc existentem, & postea futuram repræsentasse. Præterea interpretatur hanc eandem Synodum. Nimirum hoc à præceptore Osiandro, Theologo aulico, didicerat. Ait enim nullam ex eo facto generale in erroribus extirpandis, & damnandis regulam nobis esse præscriptam. Sed cum hoc satis à me confutatum esse sentiret, tandem hoc exemplum abiit, & ipsos Apostolos in seipsos committit. Sed quia his omnibus abundè in Antiosiandro respondi, & ista subterfugia per se vana cuiuis apparent, omitto. Nam quas iste ex duabus Pauli profectionibus Hierosolymam, commemoratis in Epist. ad Galatas, coniecturas affert, equis non videt ex eo refutari, quod neque à Luca ipso in Actis, neque à Paulo in illa Epistola ad Galatas enumerantur omnes Pauli Hierosolymam profectiones. Quid? quod negligentiæ accusat Apostolos Gerlachius, si illi Synodo omnes interfuerint. Hæc probet, qui potest. Ego vero à piis probari nequaquam posse scio. Ergo videamus quid postea homo iste addat. Ait nos velle ut Iuridicialis, (Ecclesiasticum voluit dicere) procef-
units.tr: and the legitimate inquiry into errors should precede any doctrine being condemned in the Church. Let the accused be summoned and heard, and a lawful synod and investigation of the doctrine that is charged be held from the Word of God, and from the example of Him who himself wished to see and hear the Sodomites present before he condemned them; from the practice of the Apostles, and from the perpetual practice of every age and of the Christian Church. What could be fairer than this demand? Yet Gerlachius denies that this should be granted us. But in what fairness, or rather what evasion, he seeks this, everyone sees. For he pretends that we always demand a universal synod, and that we are not content with a particular or local one whenever some error is to be condemned.

units.la: Pag. 112. & seq. processus,& cognitio legitima de erroribus precedat, antequam in Ecclesia dogma vllum damnetur. Accusati citentur,& audiantur, & legitima synodus,ac disquisitio de dogmate, quod accusatur, fiat ex verbo Dei, & ex ipsius exemplo,qui ipse Sodomitas praesens videre voluit, & audire, priusquam damnaret: ex Apostolorum vsu·ex omnis aetatis,& Christianae Ecclesiae perpetua praxi.Quid hac postulatione æquius?Hanc tamen nobis concedendam esse negat Gerlachius.Sed in eo,quam æquitatè, aut potius quod subterfugium quaerat,videt omnes.Fingit enim, a nobis semper Vniuersalem Synodum peti, nec particulari, seu Merica esse contentos, quotiescunque de quopiam errore damnando agitur.
units.tr: Page 112 and following: the process and legitimate inquiry concerning errors. Let the accused be cited and heard; and let a lawful synod and examination of the doctrine that is charged be held from the Word of God and from the example of Christ himself, who wished to see and hear the Sodomites present before he condemned them; from the use of the Apostles, and from the constant practice of every age and of the Christian Church. What could be fairer than this demand? Yet Gerlachius denies that it should be granted to us. But in what fairness, or rather what evasion, he seeks this, everyone sees. For he pretends that we always demand a universal synod, and that we are not content with a particular or local one whenever some error is to be condemned.

units.la: Audi igitur Gerlachi,quid dicamus. Cum nunc, id est,in isto Nouo corpore doctrinae ab Vbiquitariis reliquae omnes Ecclesiae Dei damnentur, æquissimum esse contendimus,ut reliquæ omnes quoque audiantur: item cum de nouo,& inaudito ad hunc vsque diem dogmate,nempe de noua quadā Vbiquitate in Ecclesia Dei recipiēda, vel reiicienda grauis & controuersa sit quæstio, dicimus,Totius Ecclesiæ Christianæ,seu reformatæ(nec enim Papistas,vt scis, vestros & nostros hostes, imo ipsius verbi Dei deprauatores admit ti postulamus) conuentum in legitima & libera Synodo necessario congregandum esse,qui de eo nouo prorsus dogmate ex Dei verbo iudicet, non autem vos solos esse audiendos, qui nos isti reginæ nouæ, a vobis in Ecclesiam intromissæ, non parentes,& ex Dei Ecclesia,etia n inauditos, eiicitis. Hac item postulatione, quid æquius, Gerlachi? Hæc ergo nobis à vestris concedantur, & tota nostra querimonia cessabit, & hæc gravissima discordia placidè inter nos terminabitur.
units.tr: Hear, then, Gerlachius, what we say. Since now, that is, in this new body of doctrine of the Ubiquitarians, all the other Churches of God are condemned, we contend that it is most equitable that all the others too should be heard. Likewise, since on a new doctrine, hitherto unheard of, namely a certain new Ubiquity to be received or rejected in the Church of God, there is a grave and disputed question, we say that an assembly of the whole Christian, that is, reformed, Church (for we do not demand that the Papists, as you know, your enemies and ours, and indeed corrupters of the very Word of God, be admitted) must necessarily be gathered in a lawful and free synod, which may judge that wholly new doctrine from the Word of God; and that it is not you alone who should be heard, you who cast us out of the Church of God, even unheard, because we do not obey that new queen whom you have introduced into the Church. What could be fairer than this demand too, Gerlachius? Let these things be granted us by your side, and all our complaint will cease, and this most serious discord will be quietly ended between us.

units.la: Nam semper, & in quocunque dogmate damnando vniuersalem Synodū requiri, neque dicimus, neque scribimus. Quædam enim sunt dogmata iam ab orthodoxis Synodis profligata, pro quibus exstirpandis nulla alia generalis, imò sæpe ne particularis quidē, Synodus colligenda est. Quædam etiam ita manifestè impia sunt, vt, qui illa sta tim non condemnat, fundamentū ipsum fidei, & Articulos ipsos Apostolicos tollat & negetnecessefe est. Quale quicquā, Dei gratiā, neque dicimus, neque profitemur: sed vos potius id facitis, dum omnino Nouum Vbiquitatis dogma (ne dicam monstrū) multos fidei Christianæ articulos manifestè euertes inducitis, quēadmodum sæpe antea probauimus, & nunc repetere non est necesse.
units.tr: For we neither say nor write that a universal synod is required in condemning every doctrine whatever. For there are some doctrines already overthrown by orthodox synods, for the uprooting of which no other general synod, and often not even a particular one, need be called. Some are also so manifestly impious that anyone who does not condemn them at once must be considered to overthrow the very foundation of faith and the Apostles' articles themselves. We neither say nor profess anything of this kind, thank God; but rather you do it, while you introduce a new doctrine of Ubiquity (not to say a monster) which manifestly overthrows many articles of the Christian faith, as we have often proved before, and there is no need to repeat it now.

units.la: Quanquā etiam in his erroribus, qui iam damnati sunt, illud est obseruandum, vt personæ ipsæ audiantur, licèt eorū errores iam fuerint improbati, priusquā ex Ecclesia Dei ipsę eiiciantur: quia & pœnitere possunt, & noua aliqua ratione, quæ nondum refutata sit, niti, & cōfirmari.
units.tr: Yet even in those errors that have already been condemned, this must be observed: the persons themselves should be heard, although their errors have already been disapproved, before they are cast out of the Church of God; for they can repent, and rest and be confirmed on some new ground that has not yet been refuted.

units.la: Quod autem & verbum Dei, & vsum totius piæ & veteris Ecclesiæ ad meæ sententiæ confirmationē conaris euertere, à pag.115.ad pag.124.quàm id temere & frustra facias, vident omnes pij, & tu apertè pag.121:& 123.id ipsum postea cōfirmas, quod nos dicimus: & tamen ipse negare voluisti, nimirum sine legitima cognitione Ecclesiastica nec EccleEcclesiam, nec dogma vllum esse pro haeresi condemnandum. Est autem haec demum legitima cognitio, & Ecclesiastica, (non autem, vt tu putas, politicus, pragmaticus, Rabularius, & Iuridicialis processus) quum partes omnes haereseos accusatae praesentes audiuntur, nec quidem ab aduersariis tantum: sed ab aliis etiam Ecclesiasticis viris, vtriusque consensu, si fieri potest, congregatis, delegatis, & sedentibus: vt postquam vtrasque partes coram audierint, ipsi ex Dei verbo statuant, & definiant: quae congregatio Synodus appellatur. Quod si omnes Ecclesiae damnetur, vt facitis, omnes audiantur necesse est: qui iam coetus erit ex necessitate consequentiae Synodus Vniuersalis. At vos in vestris condemnationibus vtrunque praetermisistis. Nam neque nos coram vnquam audiuistis, imo ne id quidem flagitantes admisistis. Deinde neminem istarum, quae inter nos & vos agitatur, controuersiarum iudicem, praeter vos ipsos, tulistis, aut elegistis: quae prorsus est iniqua iudicandi ratio. Haeccine igitur, vt audeas tueri Gerlachi, tanquam recte atque ordine a vobis facta? Ad singulos autem homines damnandos non volumus Synodos vel vniuersales vel particulares congregari, vt antea dixi, sed ad dogmata noua, & nondum danata diiudicanda. Atque hic tuus est scopulus, in quo tanquam polypus haeres, neque ex tuis in nos figmetis ena tare potes. Caeterum aperte posthac calumniaris. Nam neque Pauli verba, neq; sententia reprehendo, dum vestros Superintendentes & D. Prepositos manifeste ambitionis accuso: sed doceo ia tyrannide
units.tr: But that you rashly and vainly try to overturn both the Word of God and the practice of the whole pious and ancient Church, in order to undermine the confirmation of my opinion, from page 115 to page 124, all the godly can see. You yourself openly confirm on pages 121 and 123 the very thing we say, and yet you wanted to deny it, namely that without a lawful ecclesiastical examination neither a Church nor any doctrine may be condemned as heretical. This lawful and ecclesiastical examination is indeed the following, and not, as you suppose, a political, pragmatic, pettifogging and legalistic process: when the parties of the accused heresy are heard in person, and not only the opponents but also other ecclesiastical men, gathered, delegated and seated with the consent of both sides if it can be managed, so that after they have heard both parties they may themselves decide and define from the Word of God. That gathering is called a Synod. But if whole Churches are to be condemned, as you do, then all of them must necessarily be heard, and that assembly would of necessity be a universal Synod. Yet in your condemnations you omitted both. For you never heard us in person, and you did not even admit us when we asked for this. Next, apart from yourselves, you have brought forward or chosen no judge of the controversies that are being argued between us and you, which is a thoroughly unjust way of judging. Is this, then, the conduct that you dare to defend, Gerlach, as done by you rightly and in good order? As for condemning individual men, we do not want Synods, whether universal or particular, to be convened for this, as I said before, but for judging new doctrines not yet condemned. And here is your sticking point, in which you cling like a polyp, and you cannot swim out of it by your fabrications against us. Otherwise, from now on, you slander openly. For I criticise neither Paul's words nor his meaning, while I openly accuse your Superintendents and Provosts of manifest ambition; rather, I teach that this is tyranny

units.la: {*} Pag 124. ab iis in suos Collegas hoc nomine, & fuco vsurpari, cum, quod omnibus Pastoribus Paulus commune esse voluit (vt sint Superintendentes, & Episcopi, quisque gregis sibi commissi) vnus tantum in quaque Principis Christiani ditione occupat, & inuadit, quæ manifestissima, & verissima fuit primum Antichristianismi, & Papalis tyrannidis stabilicndæ via, quam vos iam insistitis. Quod autem ais, vestros illos Sexuiros, & qui illis consenserunt Superintendentes, condemnasse nos ex Dei verbo, & ex Apostolorum, ac Prophetarum scriptis, & principium petis, & nugaris. Nam vel vnum apicé & iota in tota S. Scriptura recita, quod vestram Vbiquitatem confirmet: imò nulla est pagina, nullus fidei articulus, qui cam non confutet. Ergo define nobis authoritatem Verbi diuini obiicere, aut illud pro Vbiquitate profer. Verum excipis, Non omnes hæreses hoc cociliorū remedio esse sublatas. Nam & Arrianismus, & Nestorianismus, & Eutychianismus, errores teterrimi, etiam Synodis Oecumenicis damnati tamen postea pullularunt. Vnde concludis, frustra a nobis hoc remedium quæri, quod sit futurum inutile. Respondeo vero Gerachi: Non posse quidem per Synodos, etiam Oecumenicas, exstingui prorsus Sathanæ conatum inserendis erroribus, sed tamen id efficit, vt postquam illi errores Synodis legitimis damnati sunt, a quocunque tandem propagentur, & a quibuscunque recipiantur, statim hæreses esse dicantur, & a piis omnibus pro hæresi & damnentur, & agnoscantur. Sic non facit condemnatio idololatriæ triæ,etiá ab ipso Deo omnipotẽte facta,ne sint vl li iam idololatriæ: sed illa condemnatio oftedit, quod,vbicunque sit idololatria,illic sit grauisimũ peccatũ,& error,& damnáda hęresis.Quare fieri posse concedimus, vt vestra Vbiquitas ab iis Synodis, vbi nos auditi fuerimus, quásque requirimus,etiam damnata, tamen adhuc vigeat,vel inter aliquos vestrum, qui laude illa delectantur, spargatur. Verum,postquam sic erit legitimè publico totius Orthodoxæ Ecclesiæ iudicio reiecta,hæresis seu error esse vbique intelligetur,etsi a nonnullis recipiatur, a cæteris merito condemnabitur. Præclarè námque Casianus, Sufficere ergo solus ad confutandam tunc hæresin debebit consensus omnium. Itaque qui contra sentire nitatur,huius prima statim fronte non tam sit audienda assertio, quàm damnanda peruersitas. Nam ad illud quod toties inculcas,non a Sexuiris tantum, sed a pluribus Theologis eruditis fuisse perpensam vestram Vbiquitatem, & comprobatam, nostram autem doctrinam abiisdem damnatam:excipimus,nos neque ab illis Sexuiris, neque ab illis plurimis eruditis Theologis,vel in istorum (vt appellas)Eparchiis, vel alibi vnquam coram auditos fuisse. Præterea eos pro iudicibus nequaquam nos vnquam acceptaturos esse, quos etiam instituimus coram tota Ecclesia nefandarum hæresEon accusare. De Anabaptistis, Seruetanis, & aliis a nobis sine Synodo Vniuersali damnatis, quum scribit Gerlachius, partim tergiuersatur(Nam, vti diximus,illi prius abhinc auditi fuerunt,quam expulsi ex Ecclesia: neque adhuc quisquam illorum, nisi auditus,iudicatur,id quod & de nobis ficri postulamus, & de quo praetermisso vos accusamus/partim ostendit,se rerum nostra hac aetate gestarum prorsus ignarum esse,cum fuerint Anabaptistae, & Seruet',ac sectarij ipsius damnati a quanto maximo piorum coetu pro illo tempore haberi potuit:& ij errores in illis fuerint deprehensi, qui iampridem a piis Synodis saepius explosi, atque etiam aperte anathematizati fuerant, vt in iis damnandis nulla noua Generali Synodo fuerit opus. Nostrum autem dogma neque ex verbo Dei, neque ex Synodo vlla,nisi Papistica,vnquam,Dei gratia, improbatum est, aut refutatum. Nam & ipse pag.148.fateris,Publica vniuersa Ecclesia Christiana voce non fuisse damnatum dogma nostrum,adeo, vt omnino nos & coram audiri,& quidem in Synodo,id est,in coetu verae Ecclesiae,legitime congregato,sit necesse. Haec mea responsio Gerlachium luculenter refutat, & quaecunque magno, sed inutili labore a pag. 143. ad pag. 152. colligit,ac nugatur. Nam quod pag. 143. linea 4. pag. 149. linea 4. a fine scribit, nos non nisi prius auditos, atque etiam ex verbo Dei convictos fuisse damnatos,in veritatem peccat. Sed aliter quam isto insigni mendacio suorum iniquam aduersus nos sententiam tueri non potuit Gerlachius. Quod enim nos Pelagianis comparat,perinde facit, atque ipsi Pelagiani, qui Orthodoxos Manichaeis conferebant, sed vtrique ineptissime. Quod autem ex Augustino lib. 4. contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum citat ille,rarissimas haereses inueniri, propter quas quas damnandas necessitas fuerit Synodi congregan-da, ipsum refutat. Ex eo enim colligitur, Ergo ipsummet Augustinum probare hanc hæreseon euertendarum rationem, tanquam legitimam: Deinde vbi necessitas exigit, congregandas esse Synodos. At tunc in caulsa Pelagianorum nihil erat necesse eam rationem sequi, cum primus ipse erroris eorum author, Pelagius, iam in Synodo Palæstina coràm & auditus, & damnatus fuisset. Quis enim ignorat, quin Pelagius ipse iam tum errorem suum coram Innocentio, Romano Pontifice, totóque Ecclesiæ Romanæ consistorio retractasset & damnasset? Ergo quod Pelagiani Africani congregari aliam Synodum sua de caussa, & propter eundem errorem postulabant, id frustra fieret, cum iam fuissent antea ipsi legitimis Synodis sæpius damnati, à quibus minimè prouocassent. Itaque præclarè de illis prosper, qui Augustini tempore vixit, in lib contra Collator, Non ergo cum istis (de Pelagianis loquens) noua acie dimicandum est, nec quasi contra ignotos hostes, specialia sunt ineunda certamina. Tunc istorum machinæ fractæ sunt, quando beatæ memoriæ Innocentius nefandi erroris capita Apostolico mucrone percussit: quando Pelagium ad proferendam in se suósque sententiam Palæstinorum Episcoporum synodus coarctauit: quando Africanorum conciliorum decretis beatæ recordationis Papa Zosimus sententiæ suæ robur annexuit, &c Ex quibus apparet cur dixerit Augustinus, ad Pelagianos suo illo tempore, post tot legitimas sententias, damnandos noua Synodo non esse opus. Nos autem, aut nostrum dogma, quis vnquam probabit (nobis prius in aliqua Synodo coràm auditis)fuisse damnatum, adeò vt necessitas propterea esse intelligatur Synodi ob nostram caussam conuocandæ? Et quod rarissimas hæreses, huiusmodi repertas esse scribit Angustinus, propter quas Synodi fierent, id vult, hæreses, quæ fuerunt ante ipsius tempora,fuisse magnam partè tam crassas, támque aperte blasphemas, vt cum ipso Dei verbo manifestè,& statim pugnare deprehenderetur.Quo casu & nos ipsi fallì antea sumus, nullis esse Synodis ad huiusmodi errores damnandos opus.Verùm quoniam hunc Angustini locū luculeter explicauit in sua ad Pochemij virulentam criminationem responsione Iohannes Apastes, amicus meus,ad eum locú Gerlachium remittam.Certè hoc loco valde miratus sum,hominem istum, cùm hùc Augustini locum pro se proferret,non animaduertisse(tam est istorum hominum hebes ingenium ) se ab illo ipso loco euerti, quandoquidem ibi extorta subscri-ptiones disertè ab Augustino damnantur, quibus penè solis cōstat ea Nouæ doctrinæ cōfirmatio, quæ extat in Nouo illo libro, qui ab aliis Stambuch appellatur, ab istis autem Concordia. Cæterum quod iste pag.168.& 169. ad Turcas,tanquam futuros legitimos nostrarum controuersiarum iudices,toties nos remittit, meminit suæ inter eos conuersationis, ac peregrinationis, nec totum illud vitæ suæ tempus amisisse videatur, imò etiam fortasse recordatur doctrinæ,quam ab illis didicit.Sed,Gerlachi, vnum Verbum Dei& pios, & orthodoxos viros, illius intelligentes, tibi iudices ferimus:non Turcas, quos odimus: non Papistas,quos miseramur : non vllos hæreticos,Seruetanos,Anabaptistas, & Schuenckfeldianos, & cæteros , & quos ipsi ferió damnamus:nec , vti calumniaris, inter nos efle, & versari patimur. Nam vnicum vel Serueti, vel Gentilis, vel etiam Syluani exemplum tuam illam calumniam refutare fatis potest.Porrò quòd Gerlachius putat, fe belle eam sæuitiâ excufaffe, ad quam Pontificios in nos exacuat,propter no- uas condemnationes ab istis in nos prolatas, quòd iidem illi Pontificij ante hoc Nouæ doctri næ corpus editum, etiam nos affligerent, hebetem mentis ipsius aciem oftedit. Nec enim præteritarum , & ante harum damnationum editionem à Pontificiis excitatarum in nos persecutionum caufiam & culpam Vbiquitariis tribuimus: sed earum tantum,quas per istos non stabit, quo minus grauiores experiamur. Illi enim procul dubió eo furiofius ac fecurius nos aggredientur, quò nos ab istis quoque condemnatos efle, velut hæreticos, intelligent. Nec hoc ipsum ita eucenturum esse negauit ipse Pappus:sed ridiculam illam(quam commemoraui) distinctionem adhibuit, nimirum fe, & suas istas condemnationes esse tantùm earum persecutionum, quas reipfa patimur,caussam per accidens. Ita nos, vt verè dicitur, Christiani in mediis pro Christi nomine ignibus, & cruciatibus suauiter ab istis lepidis Vbiquitariis irridemur. Sed erit tandem Dominus Deus ipse tantarum in fe, & suos sannarum vindex. Ais,Gerlachi,debere & fratres,& patres, &matres a nobis damnari,si a Christo discedant. Recte dicis si modo prius audiantur, quam damnentur, quod vos in nobis omnino praetermisistis. Deinde vides,ut ex loco Deuteron. cap.13. a teipso euertantur illae tuae tam laboriose antea quaesitae distinctiones. Primum, quum ais,quando damnantur errores,tamen personas eos errores sequentes non comprehendi, seu damnari.
units.tr: {*} Page 124. They use this title and pretence among their own colleagues, although Paul meant it to be shared by all ministers (so that each one is a superintendent and bishop of the flock committed to him). Instead, one man in each Christian prince's territory seizes and claims it for himself. This was the clearest and truest first step toward establishing Antichristianity and papal tyranny, and it is the path you are now pursuing. As for your claim that the Sexviri and the superintendents who agreed with them have condemned us by the Word of God and by the writings of the Apostles and Prophets, you are taking a starting point and talking nonsense. Recite even a single letter or iota from the whole of Holy Scripture that confirms your Ubiquity. Indeed, there is no page and no article of faith that does not refute it. So stop throwing the authority of the divine Word at us, or produce it in support of Ubiquity. But you object: Not all heresies have been removed by this remedy of councils. Arianism, Nestorianism and Eutychianism, most foul errors, were condemned even by Ecumenical Synods, yet they sprouted up again afterwards. From this you conclude that the remedy we seek is useless and will be of no effect. My reply, Gerlach, is this: it is true that Satan's attempt to sow errors cannot be wholly extinguished by synods, even ecumenical ones. Nevertheless, a synod achieves this: once those errors have been condemned by lawful synods, then wherever they are spread and by whomever they are received, they are at once called heresies, and are condemned and recognised as such by all the godly. Thus the condemnation of idolatry, even though it was made by almighty God himself, does not mean that there is no idolatry left. Rather, that condemnation shows that wherever idolatry exists, there is a grievous sin, an error, and a heresy that must be condemned. So we grant that your Ubiquity may still flourish, or be spread among some of you who delight in that praise, even after it has been condemned by those synods where we, whom we ask to be heard, have been heard. Yet once it has been lawfully rejected by the public judgement of the whole orthodox Church, it will be understood everywhere to be a heresy or error, even if some people accept it, and the rest will rightly condemn it. For Cassian wrote admirably: The agreement of all alone will then be sufficient to refute the heresy. Therefore the assertion of anyone who strives to think otherwise ought not so much to be heard at the very first glance as to be condemned as perversity. As for your repeated insistence that your Ubiquity was weighed and approved not only by the Sexviri but by many learned theologians, we reply that we were never heard before those Sexviri, nor before those many learned theologians, either in your so-called eparchies or anywhere else. Moreover, we shall never accept as judges those whom we have ourselves already accused, before the whole Church, of unspeakable heresies. As for the Anabaptists, the Servetians, and the others whom we have condemned without a universal synod, when Gerlach writes about them he partly evades the issue (for, as we have said, they were heard by us before they were expelled from the Church. Nor is any of them judged without being heard, which we ourselves request for us, and which we charge you with having omitted). And partly he shows that he is entirely ignorant of the events of our own time. The Anabaptists, the Servetians and their sectarian companions were condemned by as great an assembly of the godly as could be gathered at that time. The errors found in them were ones that had long ago been often rejected by godly synods and even plainly anathematised, so that no new general synod was needed to condemn them. Our doctrine, however, has never, by God's grace, been disapproved or refuted either by the Word of God or by any synod except a Papist one. For you yourself admit on page 148: Our doctrine was not condemned by the public voice of the whole Christian Church, so that it is absolutely necessary for us to be heard, and indeed in a synod, that is, in an assembly of the true Church lawfully gathered. This reply of mine thoroughly refutes Gerlach, and whatever he gathers and trifles with at great but useless labour from page 143 to page 152. For when he writes, on page 143 line 4 and on page 149 line 4 from the end, that we were condemned without first being heard, and even convicted by the Word of God, he is wrong. But Gerlach could not defend his unjust sentence against us by any means other than this notorious lie of his supporters. For his comparison of us with the Pelagians is as foolish as the Pelagians themselves were when they compared the orthodox with the Manichaeans, and both comparisons are utterly inept. As for his citation from Augustine, book 4 against the two letters of the Pelagians, that very rare heresies are found for which a synod must be called to condemn them, it refutes him. For from it one may gather that Augustine himself approved this method of overthrowing heresies as lawful: when necessity demands it, synods must be called. But in the case of the Pelagians there was no need to follow that method, since Pelagius himself, the first author of their error, had already been heard and condemned in the synod of Palestine. For who does not know that Pelagius had already retracted and condemned his error before Innocent, the Roman bishop, and the whole consistory of the Roman Church? Therefore the African Pelagians' demand for another synod on their own account and for the same error would have been pointless, since they had already been condemned many times by lawful synods, to which they had never appealed. And so Prosper, who lived in Augustine's time, wrote admirably in his book against Collator: Therefore we must not fight these men with a new battle line, nor undertake special contests as if against unknown enemies. Their machines were broken when Innocent of blessed memory struck the heads of the unspeakable error with the apostolic sword; when the synod of the bishops of Palestine forced Pelagius to set out his opinion and that of his followers; when Pope Zosimus of blessed memory added the strength of his judgement to the decrees of the African councils, and so on. From these things it is clear why Augustine said that, after so many lawful judgements, no new synod was needed to condemn the Pelagians of his time. But as for us, who will ever prove that our doctrine has been condemned (after we have been heard in some synod), so that a synod must be called on account of our cause? And as to Augustine's statement that very rare heresies of this kind were found, for which synods were held, he means that the heresies which existed before his time were for the most part so gross and so plainly blasphemous that they were at once seen to clash openly with the Word of God itself. In such a case we ourselves were also once deceived, and there was no need of synods to condemn errors of this kind. But since John Afterman, my friend, has explained this passage of Augustine admirably in his reply to Pochemius's virulent accusation, I shall refer Gerlach to that place. I was truly amazed that this man, while bringing forward this passage of Augustine in his own favour, did not notice (so dull is the wit of such men) that he is overthrown by that very passage. For there Augustine expressly condemns extorted subscriptions, and it is almost only by these that the confirmation of this new doctrine is established, which is found in that new book that others call the Stambuch and they call the Concordia. Furthermore, when on pages 168 and 169 he keeps referring us to the Turks as future lawful judges of our controversies, he recalls his own association and wandering among them. Nor does he seem to have wasted all that time of his life; indeed perhaps he even remembers the teaching he learned from them. But, Gerlach, we bring before you as judges the one Word of God and the godly and orthodox men who understand it: not the Turks, whom we hate; not the Papists, whom we pity; not any heretics, the Servetians, the Anabaptists, the Schwenckfeldians, and the rest, whom we ourselves strongly condemn; nor do we allow them, as you falsely charge, to be or to live among us. For the single example of Servetus, or of Gentilis, or even of Silvanus, is enough to refute that calumny of yours. Furthermore, Gerlach thinks he has well excused the cruelty with which the Papists are whetted against us, on account of the new condemnations pronounced against us by them, on the ground that the same Papists were persecuting us even before this new doctrinal book was published. That reveals the dullness of his mental sight. For we do not attribute the blame and cause of the persecutions stirred up against us by the Papists before these condemnations and their publication to the Ubiquitarians. We attribute to them only those persecutions which, by their own doing, will not be prevented from becoming more severe. For the Papists will undoubtedly attack us all the more furiously and confidently when they understand that we have also been condemned by these men as heretics. Pappus himself did not deny that this would happen, but employed that ridiculous distinction I mentioned: namely, that he and his condemnations were only an incidental cause of the persecutions we actually suffer. So, as is truly said, we Christians are mocked pleasantly by these charming Ubiquitarians, in the midst of fires and torments for the name of Christ. But the Lord God himself will at last be the avenger of such great mockeries against himself and his people. You say, Gerlach, that brothers, fathers and mothers ought to be condemned by us if they depart from Christ. You are right, provided they are first heard before they are condemned, which you have altogether omitted in our case. Then you see how, from Deuteronomy chapter 13, those distinctions of yours, so laboriously sought out before, are overturned by yourself. First, when you say that, when errors are condemned, the persons who follow those errors are not thereby included or condemned.

units.la: 2. Etiamsi personae quaedam errantes damnari possint(quod ab Osiandro discedens nobis concedis) eos tantum damnandos esse,qui sunt Pastores,nō oues in Ecclesia. Atqui Deuteronomij Lex generaliter loquitur tam de Pastore, quam de oue, tam de viris quam de mulieribus (quae Pastores esse nō possunt in Ecclesia Dei.) Quemlibet enim in Lege Dei errantem (etiam teipso interprete) damnari praecipit Dominus ipse. 3.
units.tr: 2. Even if certain erring persons can be condemned (as you concede, departing from Osiander), you say that only those who are ministers should be condemned, not the sheep in the Church. Yet the law of Deuteronomy speaks generally, both of the shepherd and of the sheep, of men and of women (who cannot be ministers in the Church of God). For the Lord himself commands that whoever errs in the law of God be condemned, even on your own interpretation. 3.

units.la: Quum damnantur eae quaedam personae (quas damnandas esse, vi veritatis coactus, nobis tandem assentiris) tamen a vobis,non vt Magistratui tradendas damnari,sed sine poena relinquendas. Quasi vero, quum tu, & Laonicus contenditis,quos in Nouae vestrae doctrinae corpore damnastis, esse in exilium a Magistratu pellendos, eos ipsi Magistratui non tradatis. An vobis aut Superintendentibus vestris in Germania data ia est, vti Pontificijs Episcopis, ea potestas & iurisdictio, vt homines in exilium mittant, suis sedibus & gradibus expellant? Ego enim credidi Magistratus Germanicos in vestris Ecclesijs eam sibi potestatem referuasse, quoniam ad eos pertinet. Quod si vos Pastores illam exercetis, certe te illud, quod est Cæsaris, vsurpatis, quantumuis vobis ab ipsis magistratibus delatum, & concessu hoc ius fuerit. Quod autem negas, quenquam apud vestros religionis caussa in vitæ periculum incurrisse, obliuiosum te tuæ, & Germanicæ historiæ ostendis, siue sciens & prudens, siue quod ea gesta sunt, quum adhuc cum Turcis suauiter habitares.Nam de clarissl. illo viro, Caspar Peucero, magno sui seculi ornamento, nihilne, Gerlachi, vnquam inaudisti? Quem Laonicus ipse sibi nominandum putauit. Funestum etiam toti Christianitati testamentum Brentij defenden-dum, (qua te putas esse eloquentiâ) suscipis, sed frustra. Illud enim Testamentum efficiet, vt, nisi Dominus maturè prouideat, sit etiam propediem futura ipsius Germaniæ insepulta sepultura. Sed tu M. Antonius Cæsaris tui Brentij, qui tibi, & tuis istam Vbiquitariam controuersiam suo testamento, tanquam opimam hæreditatem reliquit, ex qua Præsidatus & Præposituras Eparchiarum, vt vocas, & Gentium in Germania vestra speras & expectas) merito, & pro tuæ gratitudinis officio, defendis.
units.tr: Although certain such persons are condemned (whom, forced by the power of truth, you at last agree should be condemned), you condemn them not so that they may be handed over to the magistrate, but so that they may be left unpunished. As if, when you and Laonicus contend that those whom you have condemned in the body of your new doctrine should be driven into exile by the magistrate, you did not hand them over to the magistrate itself! Or is that power and jurisdiction, by which men are sent into exile and expelled from their seats and offices, granted to you or to your superintendents in Germany, as it is to the Papist bishops? For I have believed that the German magistrates reserved that power to themselves in your churches, since it belongs to them. But if you ministers exercise it, you certainly usurp what belongs to Caesar, however much that right may have been delegated to you by the magistrates themselves and conceded.
