As for your denial that anyone among your people has incurred danger to life for the sake of religion, you show yourself forgetful of your own and of German history, whether knowingly and deliberately, or because you were living pleasantly among the Turks when these things were done. For have you never heard, Gerlach, of that most distinguished man, Caspar Peucer, the great ornament of his age? Laonicus himself thought he ought to be named. You also take up the deadly testament of Brenz to Christendom as a whole, to defend it (with the eloquence you think you have), but in vain. For that testament will bring it about that, unless the Lord soon provides, Germany itself will soon have an unburied burial. But you, Master Antonius, defend (rightly, and as a duty of your gratitude) your Caesar Brenz, who left you and yours this Ubiquitarian controversy in his testament, as a rich inheritance, from which you hope and expect (as you call it) the presidencies and provostships of the dioceses and the nations in your Germany.

units.la: Ad Secundam libelli Gerlachiani partem.
units.tr: To the Second Part of Gerlach's Booklet.

units.la: Rgo prima verbosissimi tui scripti parte facile, vt vides, expeditus venio ad alteram. Negas primum meam confessionem esse apertam, quia dico ipsam Christi carnem, licet corporalis præsentiæ situ à signis absentem, tamen præsentia Sacramentali esse
units.tr: Having therefore easily dispatched, as you see, the first part of your very wordy writing, I come to the second. You deny first that my confession is open, because I say that the flesh of Christ itself, though absent from the signs by the situation of bodily presence, is nevertheless present to the faithful by sacramental presence.

units.la: fidelibus præsentem.Quare verò hâc orationem tam perspicuam vocas tu obscuram? Quoniam nimirum nullam credis esse posse rerum cœlestium(qualis est caro illa dignissima Christi,& in cœlum euecta) præsentiam, nisi corporalem. Itaque fidei præsentiam cum corporali præsentia,Sacramentalem cum locali imperitè confundis.Quod quoniam apparet per scipsum ineptissimum,diutius in eo confutando non morabor. In reliquis autem tuæ huius responsionis partibus breuior ero, partim quoniam iis omnibus, quæ hîc affers,abundè in superiore meaad Laonicum Spongiam responsione iam satisfeci: partim quia ipse tu Gerlachi, eam disputatione,etsi primariam,fugis, & ingredi formidas. Dicis enim septem priora Osiandri argumenta nihil ad hoc de Vbiquitate argumentum ab eo susceptum pertinuisse.In quo insignem tuo illi clienti Osiandro iniuriam,tu ipsius patrone,facis,quam illi factam esse nollem.Queris à me,unde ex verbis Testamenti Christi probem,ipsum corpus, & sanguinem Christi ,non corporalis præsentiæ situ adesse Dominicæ Cœnæ. Quanquam antea respondi, tamen in tuam gratiam(te enim verè diligo) Gerlachi, repeto. Tam enim gratificari hic tibi cupio, quàm antea Laonico,quoniam me non paucioribus conuitijs,pro tua eloquentia, quàm ille, proscidisti, id est, apud Deum benedictionibus non paucioribus me cumulasti.Dico enim, & respondeo, quum hæc verba Testamenti Christi sint institutio Sacramenti omnium nobilissimi, & excellentissimi, esse quoque in illis Testamenti Christi verbis sensum, & significationem Sacramentalem: & propterea praesentiam Sacramentalem. Sacramentalia enim Sacramentis sunt accommodanda. Praesentia vero Sacramentalis est certe ἐντρυπτικὴ, pa-stionalis, & rerum, corporalis praesentiae situ absentium, praesentia. Habes igitur dilucidum responsum ad id, quod ex me quaerebas. Quo ipso responso refutatur tua ex Basilij in Asce-teriis, & Iurisconsultorum regulis argumentatio. Concedimus enim non esse dubitandum de ipso Dei verbo, cum sit verissimum: sed Dei verbum non est, vt ait idem Basilius, sonus, sed sensus, & mens. Leges enim & scripturas scire, non est earum verba tenere, vt tibi aliquid replicem de Iurisconsultis, sed vim & mentem earum, quam nos hoc loco tuemur. Quare quod alibi dixit Paulus, vere hic quoque quadrabit, vos literam sequimini, nos vero spiritum. Concedimus etiam hoc, in testamentis sequenda esse verba testatoris, sed qua mente, & sensu illa testator ipse intellexit. Alias enim fit summa ipsis testatoribus iniuria, & vis Testamenti verbis. Nam, vt ait non Bartolus, sed lex ipsa, in testamentis dominatur testantium voluntas. Et in eo ipso stupor vester apparet vel caecis ipsis, qui sigillum pro ipso diplomate: & Coenam pro ipsa ordinatione testamenti stolidissime accipere perpetuo consueuistis, vt & vobis ipsis, & aliis os sublinatis. Hoc autem Christi Testamentum, vt & Patrum veterum, scatet tropicis locutionibus, quemadmodum in mea ad Selneccerum responsione
units.tr: Why do you call this statement so clear obscure? Because you evidently believe that there can be no presence of heavenly things (such as that most worthy flesh of Christ, raised into heaven) except a bodily one. Thus you clumsily confuse presence by faith with bodily presence, and sacramental presence with local presence. Since this appears to be most absurd in itself, I will not linger long in refuting it. In the remaining parts of your reply I will be briefer, partly because I have already fully answered all the things you bring up here in my earlier reply to Laonicus's Sponge, and partly because you yourself, Gerlach, shun and fear to enter that disputation, though it is the main one. For you say that the first seven arguments of Osiander did not pertain to this argument about Ubiquity that he took up. In doing so you, the patron of that famous client of yours, Osiander, do him a great wrong, one I would not wish done to him. You ask me from what words of Christ's testament I prove that the body and blood of Christ are present at the Lord's Supper, not by the situation of bodily presence. Although I answered this before, I will repeat it for your sake, Gerlach (for I truly love you). I want to do you this favour just as I did to Laonicus, since you have torn me to pieces with no fewer insults, relying on your eloquence, than he did; that is, you have heaped upon me no fewer blessings before God. I say, and answer, that since these words of Christ's testament are the institution of the most noble and excellent of all sacraments, there is also in those words of Christ's testament a sacramental sense and meaning, and therefore a sacramental presence. For sacramental things must be adapted to sacraments. Now sacramental presence is certainly [ἐνεργητική] energetic, passional, and the presence of things absent by the situation of bodily presence. So you have a clear answer to what you asked of me. By this same answer your argument from Basil's Ascetica and from the rules of the jurists is refuted. For we grant that there must be no doubt about the word of God itself, since it is most true; but the word of God is not, as Basil says, a sound but a sense and mind. For to know the laws and writings is not to hold on to their words (to say nothing further of the jurists to you), but to grasp their force and mind, which we here defend. Hence what Paul said elsewhere will fit here too: you follow the letter, but we the Spirit. We also grant that in wills the words of the testator must be followed, but in the sense and meaning in which the testator himself understood them. Otherwise the greatest wrong is done to the testators themselves and to the force of the testament's words. For, as not Bartolus but the law itself says, in wills the intention of the testators rules. And in this very matter your stupidity is apparent, even to the blind, since you have always been accustomed most foolishly to take the seal for the document itself, and the Supper for the very ordinance of the testament, so that you smear mud on your own faces and on those of others. Now this testament of Christ, like that of the ancient Fathers, is full of tropical expressions, as I taught from the very word of God in my reply to Selnecker, the Saxon Exegesis, to which I refer you for the sake of brevity.

units.la: K.j.
units.tr: K.j.

units.la: pro Exegesi Saxonica, ex ipso Dei verbo docui, ad quam te breuitatis caussa remitto. Caeterum quod ais, multas ἀντιφυσικὰς prærogatiuas carni Christi propter vnionem hypostaticam datas esse, certè & corde credimus, & ore cõfitemur, etiam eas, & tantas in eam esse collatas, quæ sint ipsis adeo beatis Angelis incomprehensibiles, & illi carni etiam inhæreant subiectiuè. Verum vllas ἀντιφυσικὰς propter eam vnionem illi datas esse, id est eas, quæ carnis ipsius assumptæ essentiam, & naturam euertant, negamus, quale est, vt vnicum corpus & verum pluribus in locis, imò vbique sit. Quod vos tamen Christi carni attributum esse reipsa dicitis. Iudicet in Synodo de vtriusque dogmate Orthodoxa Ecclesia. Tu dicis, quòd hoc carni insit, esse diuinæ omnipotentiæ Christi opus. Nos negamus. Neque enim Dei omnipotentia salutem nostram, id est, veram Christi carnem euertit, sed stabilit. Iudicet in Synodo orthodoxa Ecclesia, nobis & vobis vocatis, & coràm auditis. Quæ potest æquior tibi dari optio, & lex imponi? quam tu tamen acceptare non audes, ne ex edictis abs te procuratis in exilium à toto tuo collegio Theologico, à quo tam pulcram laudationem venatus es, expellaris. Nam quòd sentis, veram illam Christi carnem vbique esse posse, quoniam etiam excellenti illa gloria prædita est, vt viuifica & sit, & appelletur, quid carni Christi dari possit, quid non possit: quomodo item viuifica sit, aut non sit, non intelligis. Quædam enim Deitatis attributa sunt prorsus rebus
units.tr: Moreover, as to your claim that many prerogatives contrary to nature [ἀντιφυσικὰς] were given to the flesh of Christ on account of the hypostatic union: we certainly believe in our heart and confess with our mouth that many such prerogatives, and such great ones, were conferred upon it, prerogatives that are incomprehensible even to the most blessed angels, and that inhere in that flesh as subject. But we deny that any prerogatives contrary to nature were given to it on account of that union, that is, prerogatives that overturn the essence and nature of the flesh assumed. Such would be that one and the same true body should be in many places, indeed everywhere. Yet you say in fact that this is ascribed to the flesh of Christ. Let the Orthodox Church judge in a Synod concerning the doctrine of both of us. You say that this, which is in the flesh, is a work of the divine omnipotence of Christ. We deny it. For the omnipotence of God does not overturn our salvation, that is, the true flesh of Christ, but establishes it. Let the Orthodox Church judge in a Synod, with us and you called and heard face to face. What fairer option can be given you, or what law imposed? Yet you do not dare to accept it, lest by edicts procured by you you be expelled into exile from your whole Theological college, from which you hunted such fine praise. For as to your view that that true flesh of Christ can be everywhere, since it is endowed with that excellent glory so that it is and is called life-giving, you do not understand what can be given to the flesh of Christ and what cannot, or how it is life-giving, or is not. For some attributes of the Deity are altogether unshared with created things, such as to be eternal, to be infinite, and, as a consequence, to be everywhere.

units.la: Pag.191. rebus creatis ἀκοινώνητα, veluti æternum esse, infinitum esse, &, quod consequens est, Vbique esse. Quædam autem sunt κοινωνητά, veluti esse seu existere, viuere, viuificare, docere, &c. In quibus tamen longa est inter Deum ipsum essentialiter, & à se hæc habentem, & creaturas hæc participantes differentia. Vnum enim est essentiale: altera autem sunt effecta & qualitates creatæ. Exempli gratia, Caro Christi est viuifica illa quidem, & longè potiori ratione, quàm ipsum etiam Euangelium, seu Dei verbum prædicatum: quàm Sacramenta seu signa: denique quàm fides ipsa, qua in Christum credimus, quoniam hæc caro vnita λόγῳ, est ipsissimus & proximus inter nos, & Deum canalis, & nexus, per quem à Deitate λόγος, non autem ab ipsa Christi carne fluit, & manat in nos viuificus ille æternæ vitæ vigor, & succus. Est igitur hæc caro qualis illa scala, quæ Iacobo apparuit, qua terrena cum cœlestibus coniungebantur. Reliqua autem, quæ cum hac Christi carne comparaui, velut est prædicatio Euangelij, Sacramentorum ex fide vsus, & fides ipsa, sunt tantùm huius carnis Christi apprehendendæ, & eius nobiscum coniungendę media & organa. Quomodo igitur fit caro Christi viuifica vides, Gerlachi, vt non ab ipsa carne Christi, vitam æternam in nos fluere, sed à Deitate λόγῳ proprie per carnem immitti, & in ipsa, & per ipsam in nobis operante, videas. Quod autem & Deo corpus tribuis, (quod est corpus
units.tr: Pag.191. Others, however, are shared with created things, such as to be or to exist, to live, to give life, to teach, and so on. In these, however, there is a long difference between God himself, who has them essentially and from himself, and creatures who participate in them. For the one is essential; the others are effects and created qualities. For example, the flesh of Christ is life-giving, and with far greater reason than the gospel itself, or the preached word of God; than the sacraments or signs; and finally than faith itself, by which we believe in Christ. For this flesh, united to the Word, is the closest and nearest channel and link between us and God, through which the life-giving vigour and sap of eternal life flows and streams into us from the Deity through the Word [λόγῳ], not from the flesh of Christ itself. So this flesh is like that ladder which appeared to Jacob, by which earthly things were joined to heavenly. The remaining things, which I have compared with this flesh of Christ, such as the preaching of the gospel, the use of the sacraments in faith, and faith itself, are only the means and instruments of apprehending this flesh of Christ and of joining it with us. So you see, Gerlach, how the flesh of Christ is life-giving: not that eternal life flows into us from the flesh of Christ itself, but that it is sent into us properly by the Deity through the Word, acting through the flesh and in it, and through it in us. As for your attributing a body to God too (which is the view of the Anthropomorphite heretics), and contending that one and the same body can be [ἀπειρόπαπλον] and [ἀπεὶρόπαπλον], that is, present in innumerable places and in no place (which is the invention of the Papists, who hold that the body of Christ can be in many places by way of substance, but by way of quantity only in one place), and that some body without…

units.la: Anthropomorphitarum haereticorum) corpus vnum & idem ἀπειρόπαπλον & ἀπεὶ-ρόπαπλον esse posse contendis (quod est Pontificiorum commentum, qui corpus Christi per modum substantiae pluribus in locis esse posse sentiunt: per modum autem quanti vno tantum in loco) & corpus aliquod sine loco statuis, (quod plane repugnat Augustino) sentis Gerlachi, quot quantosque errores hic paucis verbis foueas, & complectaris. Sed fortasse imprudens ista scribebas. Illa vero similitudo de ferro, quod miraculose aquis innatauit: & de aquis ipsis, quae velut rupes & murus, populo Dei transeunte, cōstiterunt, certe nihil omnino te iuuat: primum, propterea quod illa miracula fuerunt. Sacramenta vero non sunt miracula. Nam, quemadmodum inquit Augustinus, bonum habere possunt, vt religiosa: stuporem autem, vt mira, habere non possunt. Deinde, quia in illis miraculis virtus quidem proprietatis ferri & aquae ad tempus suspensa est, & a Deo retenta: ipsa vero eorum natura, & κοινωνία proprietas non fuit per illud miraculum annihilata, vt ita loquar, & sublata. Verum si corpus aliquod vel vbique, vel pluribus in locis simul esse statuatur, eius natura ac essentia prorsus annihiletur, & tollatur, necesse est. De signis autem S. Coenae, quae ais a nobis nuda statui, quoniam luculenter & in Antiofiandro confutaui, & in responso ad Laonicu meam sententiam confirmaui, nihil repetere hoc loco puto necesse. Veruntamen, vt vno verbo perspicuam ad omnia tua argumenta, & breue responsionem habeas, sic habeto, Christi verum corpus, & sanguine praesentiae corporalis situ,& modo a signis Coenae abesse: fidei & vera,& spirituali,& mystica praesentia credentibus adesse,quia per fidem verum illud Christi corpus,& sanguinem vere participamus, non vt substantia carnis Christi,& nostra vllo contractu vniantur: sed vt nos per illam vera fide apprehensam spiritualiter viuificemur. Caeterum calumniaris manifestissime,quum ais me scripsisse, Non magis exhiberi nobis corpus & sanguinem Christi in S. Coena, quam Veteri populo in sacrificiis. Dixi quidem Veterum Sacramenta non fuisse illis credentibus tantum nuda signa,& nudas picturas & figuras (quod tu Serueto assentiens scribis) sed rem quoque ipsis illis communicatam fuisse affirmo,& antea affirmaui,quoniam fides est ἐλπίς ... Nam quae nondum sunt, tamen velut praesentia videt. (Abraham vidit diem Domini, vt ait ipsemet Christus,& Patres in Manna eandem nobiscum spiritualem escam, nimirum ipsam Christi carnem, comederunt,(vt ait Paulus) sed in eo discrimen est,quod eam ipsam viderunt futuram in suis Sacramentis Patres, quam nos in nostris videmus iam exhibitam,& reipsa existentem. Ergo hac ratione maior & efficacior est nostrorum,quam illorum Sacramentorum vis & exhibitio,quia clarior, quia facilior, quia augustior, & nobis visibilius dispensata est. Ex quo fit,vt huius dispensationis ratione Patres σκιὰν habuisse dicantur,nos autem εἰκόνα & Christus ipse melioris foederis ac Testamenti Mediator,seu sponsor appelletur. Reliqua porro quae hic habes, sunt satis adversus Laoni-
units.tr: You also ascribe a body to God (which is the body of the heretical Anthropomorphites), and you contend that one and the same body can be infinitely extended [ἀπειρόπαπλον] and boundless [ἀπεὶ-ρόπαπλον]. This is a fiction of the Papists, who think Christ's body can be in many places at once by way of substance, but in only one place by way of quantity. You also posit some body without place, which plainly contradicts Augustine. Gerlachius, you can see how many and how great errors you foster and embrace in a few words. Perhaps you wrote these things without thinking. That comparison with the iron that miraculously floated on the water, and with the waters themselves, which stood like a rock and a wall while the people of God passed through, certainly does not help you at all. First, because those were miracles, whereas sacraments are not miracles. For, as Augustine says, they can have goodness, as sacred things do, but they cannot have wonder, as marvels do. Second, because in those miracles the proper power of the iron and the water was suspended for a time and held back by God, but their nature itself and their communion [κοινωνία] property was not annihilated or, so to speak, taken away by that miracle. But if some body is held to be everywhere, or in many places at once, its nature and essence must necessarily be utterly annihilated and destroyed. As for the signs of the Lord's Supper, which you say we hold to be bare, I think there is no need to repeat here what I have clearly refuted in the Antiosiandrus and confirmed in my reply to Laonicus. Nevertheless, so that you may have a clear answer to all your arguments in one word, take this: the true body and blood of Christ are absent from the signs of the Supper in their bodily presence, place and manner, but to believers a true, spiritual and mystical presence is present, because through faith we truly partake of that true body and blood of Christ. This does not mean that the substance of Christ's flesh and ours are joined by any contact, but that we are spiritually quickened by it, when it is apprehended by true faith. Moreover you clearly misrepresent me when you say that I wrote, Christ's body and blood are no more offered to us in the Lord's Supper than to the people of old in their sacrifices. I did indeed say that the sacraments of the Old Testament were not, for those who believed, merely bare signs, bare pictures and figures (as you write, agreeing with Servetus). I affirm, and affirmed before, that the thing itself was communicated to them too, since faith is hope [ἐλπίς]... For it sees things that are not yet as if they were present. (Abraham saw the day of the Lord, as Christ himself says, and the Fathers ate in the manna the same spiritual food as we do, namely Christ's very flesh, as Paul says.) But the difference is this: the Fathers saw in their sacraments as future that very thing which we see in ours as already offered and actually existing. On this reasoning, therefore, the power and offering of our sacraments is greater and more effective than theirs, because it is clearer, easier and more majestic, and has been dispensed to us more visibly. From this it follows that the Fathers are said to have had the shadow [σκιὰν], but we the image [εἰκόνα], and Christ himself is called the Mediator and surety of the better covenant and testament. The rest of what you say here is sufficiently answered against Laonicus,

units.la: K.iij. cum antea confutata, ad quem te remitto. Quae ad stabiliendum quartum Osiandri argumentum profers, partim] & ipsa iam sunt ibidem explosa, partim sunt ipsa per se inepta, & tibi ipsi contraria. Inepta quidem, veluti quod ais, Panem & vinum, S.Coenae nimirum, absque corpore & sanguine Christi realiter praesente non esse Sacramentum, id est, signum sacrum Coenae. Quid enim ineptius, quum idcirco sint panis ille, & vinum illud in sacra Coena Sacramenta,& signa, quoniam ipsum Christi corpus, & ipse sanguis praesentiae corporalis situ absunt? Item incepte & illud, quod apud Augustinum non intelligis, ipsa signa S.Coenae tum Sacramentali locutione, tum ut commendaren-tur populis, appellari Dominicum corpus, Domini corpus, sanctas carnes Christi, cum ipsemet Augustinus ibidem ea ipsa signa antea Panem & calicem Domini nominasset. Chrysostomus quoque, quem citas, aperte testatur se de credentibus agere, qui non signa tantum, sed rem quoque signatam sumunt. Tu vero contra, ipsummet Christi corpus absque fide edi posse scribis & sentis. Haec igitur in tua illa Osiadri defensione incepta sunt. Tibi autem ipsi, & Osiandro, & tuo proposito contraria sunt, quum aperte fateris, Osiandrum pro his verbis Pauli, Panem hunc, Poculum hoc, substituisse (nimirum ut suo errori inseruiret) Corpus & sanguinem Domini. Quod autem diserte Manna, & carnem Christi inter se velut contraria opponis, primum contradicis Paulo 1. Cor. 10. deinde locum Ioannis ex cap. 6. quae affers, minime te intelligere manifeste declaras. Sed ad commenta-rios
units.tr: K.iij. which I refer you to, since it was refuted earlier. As for the arguments you bring forward to support Osiander's fourth argument, some have already been exploded in the same place, and others are in themselves absurd and contrary to your own position. They are absurd, for instance, when you say that bread and wine of the Lord's Supper, namely, without the body and blood of Christ really present, are not a sacrament, that is, a holy sign of the Supper. For what could be more absurd? Are that bread and that wine sacraments and signs in the holy Supper, precisely because the body of Christ and his blood are absent in their bodily presence? Equally inept is what you do not understand in Augustine: that the signs of the Lord's Supper are called, both in sacramental language and so that they may be commended to the people, the Lord's body, the body of the Lord, the holy flesh of Christ, although Augustine himself had earlier named those same signs the bread and cup of the Lord. Chrysostom, whom you cite, also clearly testifies that he is speaking of believers, who receive not only the signs but also the thing signified. You, on the contrary, write and hold that the body of Christ itself can be eaten without faith. These things, then, are the mistakes in your defence of Osiander. But they are contrary to yourself, to Osiander and to your own purpose, since you openly admit that Osiander, for these words of Paul, this bread, this cup, substituted (no doubt to serve his error) the body and blood of the Lord. As for your clear opposition of manna and the flesh of Christ as if they were contrary, first you contradict Paul in 1 Cor. 10, and then by your own declaration you clearly show that you do not understand the passage of John from chapter 6 that you cite. But I refer you, my Gerlachius, to the commentaries of our men, rather than filling pages with other men's writings as you do.

units.la: Pag.208. Pag.209. Pag.211. rios nostrorum,mi Gerlachi, ne paginas alienis scriptis,vt tu,implea,tc remitto. Nam Manna fe pe,vt signum tantum,& per fe,quemadmodum à nor credentibus sumebatur: saepe autem vt cum re à fe signata coniunctum, & vt à credentibus edebatur,in S.Scriptura consideratur. Primo modo Christus considerat Manna:fecundo modo Paulus:sed tu ista ignoras.
units.tr: Pp. 208, 209, 211. Commentaries of our men: I refer you to them. For manna is sometimes considered in Scripture as a mere sign, by itself, as our believers took it. Often, however, it is considered as joined to the thing it signifies, and as eaten by believers. Christ considers manna in the first way, Paul in the second, but you do not know these things.

units.la: Ad quintum autem Ofiandri argumentum propugnandu accedis, & primum teipsum impru densugulas,&tamen verum dicis,& quia verum dicis, nobiscum facis. Ais enim, Humanitatem Christi, qua natura sua est potentia finita, habere omnem potentiam sibi communicatam per gratiam V-nionis. Quid verius? si modo quid sit gratia V nionis, intelligas. Est autem haec loquendi ratio sup-ti Sholasticis: quae Gratia Vnionis non quic quim realiter humanitati tribuit, sed tantum persoiae Christi adscribit, quae sic, id est per gratiā vnionis dicuntur, & attribuuntur, quia vni natur: istius personae id, quod dicitur, competit, vt Filius hominis dicatur aeternus, & Creator mundi, quia personae λόγος (qui est Creator) est vnitis, est haec praedicatio seu gratia vnionis in conceto, non in abstracto: quia abstracta significant naturas per se: concreta vero hypostatice vnita. Itaque nulla ex eo communicationis genere praedicatio fieri potest, vt ipsi iidem fatentur nisi Dialectica, & verbalis. Quod tamen pstea negas, quia reipsa eadem illa humanitati haerere putas, atque ita teipsum euertis, & hac postrema tua sententia falleris.
units.tr: As for Osiander's fifth argument, you come forward to defend it, but you first unwittingly cut your own throat. Yet you say what is true, and because you say what is true, you agree with us. For you say: The humanity of Christ, which by its own nature has finite power, has all the power communicated to it through the grace of union. What could be truer, if only you understood what the grace of union is? This way of speaking is taken from the Scholastics, who do not really attribute the grace of union to the humanity, but ascribe it only to the person of Christ. In this way, that is, through the grace of union, things are said and attributed because what is said belongs to the one person of this nature. Thus the Son of man is called eternal and the Creator of the world, because the Word [λόγος], who is the Creator, is united to the person. This predication or grace of union is in the concrete, not in the abstract, because abstract terms signify natures in themselves, but concrete terms signify what is hypostatically united. Therefore no predication of this kind of communication can be made, as they themselves admit, except a dialectical and verbal one. Yet you later deny this, because you think those same things really cleave to the humanity, and so you overthrow yourself, and you are deceived by this last view of yours.

units.la: Nihil enim per gratiam istam Vnionis habet cæmi. Sed cur nō tua improbares discipulus, qui summi omnium Vbiquitarij, Brentij tui (quem tanquam topere laudas) & primi Vbiquitatis Apostoli Iacobi Andreæ sententia, vt hæresin grauissimam, & tamen merito vna litura manifeste in tuo cripto damnas? Illi enim manibus pedibusque tien tur, Diuina attributa, & proprietates Deitatis omnes in humanitatem Christi esse effusas. Tu, & quidem recte, (si modo in ea tua sententia permanueres) hoc falsum esse ais. Itaque à Tubingenium Doctorum rubricis discedens in Brunsuicensum, vel M. Kemnitij partes & pulpita transis, qui in libro de duabus Christi naturis non obscure Iacobum Andream, vt hæreticum propter istam proprietatum effusionem sæpius flagellat. Sed croris illius recens pigmentum, & interpolationem nouam vocabulo Communicationis tecta Kemnitius proponit. Verùm quemadmodum est in mire appetens nouitatis vestra Germania, quæ est Vbiquitaria, explosa priore illa Iacobi Andreæ sententia, nouam Kemnitij amplecti coit, & eam nunc tu quoque cum communi, & vigo, vt loquuntur, sequeris. In quo, quantum tibi præiudicium facias, non sentis, Gerlachi, qui te à Iacobo Andrea, Magnifico Domino Præposito, separes, eumque tibi inimicum reddas, quinus omnia ad Superintendentias obtinendas & in Saxonico, & in VVittenbergesi Ducatu in potest. Cæterùm in reliqua tui ad Osiandrargumentum fulcimenti parte dupliciter peccas. Primùm quum ais, Carnem Christi ipsâ eadem & illâ omnipotenomnipotētia,qua est Verbi,esse omnipotētem.Ergo & scientia illā,&eādem,qua verbum erit sapiens,& volens,& operās caro Christi,quod etiam sentit Kemnitius: & ita proculdubiò Monothelitarum teterrimum errorem ab inferis revocatis. Hoc primum tuum manifestissimum est peccatum, quod ipse agnoscens, postea damnati, pag.221. & ais in Christo secundum diuersas naturas duplicem quoque esse scientiam, & per consequens potentiam,& maiestatem. Alterum tuum hīc quoque peccatum est, quòd æque infinitum Christi meritum facis, atque Deus perse,& suā naturā est infinitus. Itaque duo reipsā infinita constituis. Quæ si vera sunt,non tantùm duo ponere cogeris,sed plura infinita, quia & vita, & operatio, & virtus hominis Christi erunt quoque per te eundem, vt ipsius meritum,vere infinita, & tantùm, quantum Deus ipse est infinitus. Atque ita infinities erunt infinita:quod &Dei prærogatiuam, & rerum naturam euertit. Vt autem habeas ipse breuissimam ad omnia tua, quæ & hîc,& in reliqua tui scripti parte sequuntur,responsionem,sic dico,inter has duas propositiones tuas, Humana natura nihil habuit sibi à Deitate λόγῳ, à qua suit assumpta, communicatum: & Humana natura habuit omnia Deitatis idiomatafibi realiter communicata, esse hanc tertiam, ac mediam propositionem, Natura humana à λόγῳ assumpta habet quadam sibi realiter à Deitate λόγῳ communicata, quedam autem non habet.Habet omnia,quæ in naturam creatam cadere possunt : non habet ea, quæ sunt ipsius Deitatis proprietates essentiales,& à rebus creatis verum ipsius discrimen, qualis æternitas, infi-nitas, & quæ ex ea necessario sequitur, Vbiquepræsentia. Priores igitur duas propositiones tuas falsas esse contendo. Hanc autem meam & tertiam duntaxat veram esse palam cum tota Ecclesia affirmo. Tu nega si potes. Quod si verum esse negas, iudicet de hoc dogmate nostro, nobis auditis, in Synodo Ecclesia Dei. Hancne conditionem, Gerlachi, etiam recusabis ipse, ut vestri solent?
units.tr: For it has nothing from this grace of union. But why do you not reject your own view, as a disciple of the chief of all the Ubiquitarians, your Brenz (whom you praise so highly), and of the first apostle of ubiquity, Jacob Andreae, which you clearly condemn in your writing as a most grievous heresy, though you strike it out with one line? For they hold with hands and feet that all the divine attributes and properties of the Deity are poured out into the humanity of Christ. You, and rightly so (if only you had remained in that view), say this is false. So, departing from the rubrics of the Tübingen doctors, you pass into the parts and pulpit of the Brunswick men, or of M. Kemnitz, who in his book On the Two Natures of Christ openly and repeatedly lashes Jacob Andreae as a heretic for this pouring out of properties. But Kemnitz offers a fresh coat of paint on that old error, and a new interpolation covered by the word communication. Indeed, as your Germany is wonderfully eager for novelty, and is Ubiquitarian, once the earlier view of Jacob Andreae was exploded, it has now gone after Kemnitz's new one, and you now follow it too, as they say, with the common and vigorous crowd. You do not see, Gerlachius, how much harm you do yourself in this, since you separate yourself from Jacob Andreae, the Most Honourable Provost, and make him your enemy, although he controls everything for obtaining superintendencies in both the Saxon and Wittenberg duchies. But in the rest of your support for Osiander's argument you err in two ways. First, when you say that the flesh of Christ is omnipotent by the very same omnipotence which belongs to the Word. Then the flesh of Christ, by the same knowledge by which the Word will be wise, willing and working, is also wise, willing and working, which Kemnitz also holds, and so, undoubtedly, the most foul error of the Monothelites is called back from the dead. This is your first and most manifest error, which you yourself recognise when you later say, on page 221, that in Christ, according to the different natures, there is also a twofold knowledge, and consequently power and majesty. Your second error here is that you make the merit of Christ equally infinite as God is infinite in himself and by his nature. Thus you posit two things that are really infinite. If these are true, you will be forced not only to posit two but many infinites, since the life, operation and power of the man Christ will also, by your account, be infinite in the same way as his merit, and as infinite as God himself. And so infinities will be infinite many times over, which overturns both the prerogative of God and the nature of things. To give you yourself a very brief answer to all your arguments here and in the rest of your writing, I say this: between your two propositions, The human nature received nothing communicated to it from the Deity of the Word, by which it was assumed, and The human nature has all the properties of the Deity really communicated to it, there is this third and middle proposition: The human nature assumed by the Word has some things really communicated to it by the Deity of the Word, but other things it does not have. It has everything that can fall within a created nature. It does not have those things which are the essential properties of the Deity itself and the true difference of it from created things, such as eternity, infinity, and what necessarily follows from these, omnipresence. I therefore contend that your first two propositions are false. I openly affirm, with the whole Church, that this my third proposition alone is true. Deny it if you can. But if you deny it is true, let the Church of God in Synod judge this doctrine of ours, after both sides have been heard. Or will you yourselves refuse this condition, Gerlachius, as your people usually do?

units.la: Ad sextum Ofiandri argumentum accedis. Quod vt quocunq; pacto tandem fulcias (agnoscis enim ineptissimum esse, & prorsus elumbe) quem non lapidem moues? Quid non tentas? Quid non audes? Et quum alia te via elabi posse non cerneres, quam si mihi obscuritatem ascribe-res, eam in meis verbis tuo ore recitandis affinxisti, vt ne memet quidem ipsum apud te recognoscerem, qui tamen in meis scriptis perspicuus, & meus a quouis facile possim agnosci. Sed quid dicas perpendamus, quoniam ne teipsum quidem hic intellexisti. Dixi aduersus Ofiandrum, vt in Christo sunt & manent duæ naturæ etiam post glorificationem Christi carnis in confusione; ita duas esse & permanere operationes, potentias, scientias, voluntates, maiestates, glorias &c. vna increata & æterna & infinita, quæ est ipsius Christi Deitatis essentialis ac propria: altera vero creatam, in tempore sumptam, & finitā, quæ est carnis Christi, etiam glorificatæ & sedentis ad dextram Patris omnipotentis propria. Neq; per, & propter vnioVnionem hypostaticam, vel propter carnis & hominis Christi glorificationem, humanam ipsius naturam reipsa factam esse participem, & susceptricem, aut susceptibilem Diuinæ & essentialis λόγῳ potentiæ, maiestatis, &c. Tu vero hæc omnia, quæ probaui ex verbo Dei, suntque toti piæ & eruditæ vetustati consentanea, conaris euertere. Ac primum ais, quia Christus petiit à Patre, vt glorificaretur ea gloria quam ante mundi creationem apud Patrem habuerat, ipsam carne Christi realiter accepisse, sed in tempore, ipsam illam omnem Deitatis maiestatem, gloriam, potentiam infinitam, increatam, æternam, quæ ipsius Deitati λόγῳ est essentialis.
units.tr: Now you come to Osiander's sixth argument. How will you prop this up, however you manage it? You admit it is most inept and utterly feeble. What stone do you not turn? What do you not attempt? What do you not dare? Since you could see no other way to slip out, you ascribed obscurity to me and wrapped it into my words as you recited them, so that I hardly recognized myself in your version, though my writings are clear and anyone can easily recognize them as mine. But let us weigh what you say, since you did not even understand yourself here. I said against Osiander that, as two natures are and remain in Christ even after the glorification of Christ's flesh, without confusion, so there are and remain two operations, powers, knowledges, wills, majesties, glories, and so on: one uncreated, eternal and infinite, which is the essential and proper property of Christ's own deity; the other created, taken up in time, and finite, which is the proper property of Christ's flesh, even glorified and seated at the right hand of the Father Almighty. Nor, through or because of the hypostatic union, or because of the glorification of Christ's flesh and man, has his human nature in fact been made a partaker of, and a recipient of, or capable of receiving, the divine and essential power, majesty, and so on of the Logos [λόγῳ]. But you try to overturn all these things, which I have proved from the word of God and which are wholly consonant with pious and learned antiquity. And first you say that because Christ asked the Father to be glorified with the glory he had with the Father before the creation of the world, the flesh of Christ really received in time that very whole majesty of deity, that infinite, uncreated and eternal power, which is essential to the deity of the Logos [λόγῳ].

units.la: Primum satin' sanus es, Gerlachi, qui potentiam à carne Christi in tempore, vt tu fateris, acceptam, æternam tamen esse putes? qui finitam & creatam naturam (qualis est, scipso hic teste, etiam glorificata caro Christi) capacem infinitæ, & increatæ maiestatis esse existimes? & continens minus contento esse assueueres? Deinde, quæ sit vis illius Christi sententiæ, & postulationis à Christo factæ, ignoras.
units.tr: First, are you sane, Gerlachius, that you think power received in time by Christ's flesh, as you admit, is nevertheless eternal? That you think a finite and created nature (such as, by your own witness here, even the glorified flesh of Christ is) is capable of infinite and uncreated majesty? And that what contains is accustomed to be less than what is contained? Then, you do not know what force lies in that saying of Christ, and in the request made by Christ.

units.la: Audi igitur ex ipso Cyrillo (quem hic citas) quæ sit vera mens illius loci. Cum propter carnem, & eam quidem vilem, & in formam serui à Christo assumptam imminuta Deitatis Christi gloria videretur: imo quidpiam dedecoris, vt loquitur Cyrillus, incidisse in eam censeretur, postulat à Patre Christus, vt illius sibi primæ naturæ, & æternæ gloriæ splendor restituatur, illæ velut nubes abstergantur, atque adeo in ipsa illa (quàm Christus iam habet, & in æternum habiturus est) Mediatoris persona illa sua gloria, & maiestas perspicuè & palàm omnibus eluceret, refulgeret, ac in ipsa etiam eius carne postea radiaret. Id quod est factum, quum in cœlum recepta est caro Christi, & ad dextram Patris, id est, in altissimam supra omnes cælos, & creaturas gloriam est euecta. Ergo quod ait Cyrillus Christum nihil aduentitium sibi postulasse, quemadmodum alij homines faciunt, quum glorificari à Deo petiit, verè dixit ille quidem, quia Christus est homo & Deus: quod de nullis aliis hominibus dici potest, & habet illam gloriam natiuam, non aduentitiam: ab æterno, non ex tempore, quâ Deus: sed quam in ipsa Mediatoris persona elucere quoque Christus cupit. Atque id sentit Cyrillus, cuius hæc sunt verba lib. 9. in Ioan. cap. 20.
units.tr: Hear then, from Cyril himself (whom you cite here), what the true meaning of that passage is. When, on account of the flesh, and that a lowly flesh assumed by Christ in the form of a servant, the glory of Christ's deity seemed diminished, nay, as Cyril puts it, it was thought to have incurred some dishonor, Christ asks the Father that the splendor of that first nature and eternal glory be restored to him, that those clouds be wiped away, and that his glory and majesty, in that very person of the Mediator which Christ now has and will have forever, might shine forth clearly and openly to all, and afterwards blaze also in his very flesh. This was done when the flesh of Christ was received into heaven and carried up to the right hand of the Father, that is, raised to the highest glory above all heavens and creatures. Therefore, when Cyril says that Christ asked for nothing accidental to himself, as other men do when they ask to be glorified by God, he spoke truly, since Christ is both man and God. This can be said of no other men: he has that glory natural, not accidental, from eternity and not from time, as God; yet Christ also desires it to shine forth in the very person of the Mediator. Cyril holds this, and these are his words in book 9 on John, chapter 20.

units.la: Non in nouam quandam dignitatem ascendit, qui natura Deus erat (nihil enim nouum in Filio Dei potest inueniri) sed habebat omnia naturaliter, vt Deus, etiam antequam formam serui acciperet: factus igitur homo, quoniam ad dignitatem pristinam cum humanitate rediit, glorificationem accepisse dicitur. Quod autem idem scribit, λόγον adduxisse templum suum, id est, carnem in gloriam, quæ sibi, vt Deo, semper adest, verum quoque ille & sensit, & scripsit: sed propterea tamen neque vult, neque tradit Cyrillus, templum illud in æqualem ipsi Deitati gloriam euectum, & proprietates Deo essentiales realiter
units.tr: He did not ascend into some new dignity, who was God by nature (for nothing new can be found in the Son of God), but he had all things naturally, as God, even before he took the form of a servant; having therefore become man, since he returned with humanity to his former dignity, he is said to have received glorification. That he also writes that the Logos brought his temple, that is, the flesh, into glory, which is always present to him as to God, Cyril both truly felt and wrote. Yet for that reason Cyril neither means nor teaches that this temple was carried up into a glory equal to deity itself, and actually attained the properties essential to God,

units.la: Greek words in the text: λόγον (Logos), printed in Greek letters. realiter esse consecutum, quod & vos dicitis, & ex illius verbis perperam colligitis. Hoc enim & naturas in persona Christi confundit, quas accu-rate à S. Scriptura fuisse dispulas ipse profiteris, & Cyrillus, contra Nestorium illam naturarum Christi exæquationem, perpetuo oppugnauit, quemadmodum ipsius liber de Incarnatione Vnigeneti, vbique testatur. Ergo petit Christus, vt sibi natiuæ illius gloriæ, quam semper habuit, lux & splendor per illam exinanitionem suam apud homines proculdubiò obscuratus restituatur: vti & nos quotidie petimus, vt nomen Dei sanctifi- cetur, & Christus ipse patrem sic rogauit, Pater glorifica nomè tuum: & Paulus testatur exinanitionem illa Christi fuisse quasi illius gloria λόγῳ natu-ralis obiectionem, ex qua Pater eum postea extulit, & dedit ei nomen supra omne nomè. Ergo neque Iohannis locus, neque Cyrilli testimonium quicquam te iuuant, qui vis vnam & eandem esse potentiam, & maiestatem, & gloriam, & scientiam carnis, & Deitatis Christi, non autem distinctas, quanquam tamen non diuersis personis separatas, sed duabus diuersis naturis, vti diuersis subiectis, inhærentes. Quæ sit autem hæc glorificatio, vel gloria, explicat Augustinus, nempe vtna-tura humana, in qua est Filius hominis, quæ à Verbo æterno susceptâ est, etiam immortali æternitate domi-netur. Cyrill. lib. 9. in Ioan. cap. 20. Qui homo nu-dus ab omnibus putabatur, sic exaltatus est, vt verus Deus esse demonstretur. Idem lib. 2. cap. 73. fidus homo, vt homo incepit dominari, quo cum carne ad id, quod semper est, homo filius ascendit. Item lib. 10.
units.tr: which you also say, and wrongly gather from his words. For this also confounds the natures in the person of Christ, which you yourself profess were accurately distinguished by Holy Scripture. Cyril also, against Nestorius, constantly opposed that equalization of Christ's natures, as his book On the Incarnation of the Only-begotten testifies everywhere. Therefore Christ asks that the light and splendor of his natural glory, which he always had and which was doubtless obscured among men by that emptying of himself, be restored to him, just as we too daily ask that the name of God be sanctified, and Christ himself asked the Father thus: Father, glorify your name. Paul testifies that that emptying of Christ was, as it were, an obstruction to his natural glory of the Logos [λόγῳ], from which the Father afterwards raised him up and gave him a name above every name. Therefore neither John's passage nor Cyril's testimony helps you at all, you who want one and the same power, majesty, glory and knowledge in the flesh and in the deity of Christ, not distinct, though not separated into different persons, but inhering in two different natures as in different subjects. What this glorification or glory is, Augustine explains: namely that the human nature, in which is the Son of man, which was assumed by the eternal Word, reigns even with immortal eternity. Cyril, book 9 on John, chapter 20: He who was thought by all to be a mere man was so exalted that he is shown to be true God. The same, book 2, chapter 73: the faithful man, as man, began to rule, when the Son of man ascended with the flesh to that which he always is. Likewise book 10.

units.la: cap. 9. Thesauri, Glorifica me, exponit, Largiaris talem opinionem, & fidem de me, ut non pro verme, sed pro Deo me agnoscant. Item lib. 10. in Iohannem cap. 9. Sed cum ad humanam, ut ita dicam, in-gloriam descenderit, ad gloriam rursus rediit suam. Verum ais carnem habere eam gloriam per & propter Vnionem hypostaticam. Respondi vero iam antea, illam vnionem neque tollere naturas in Christo, neque confundere earum essentiales proprietates. Ergo si per vnionem intelligis Gratiam Vnionis, & vis hac ratione recte dici ac tribui personae toti Christi, aeternam omnipotentiam, omniscientiam, &c. id tibi iam pridem, & prolixe concessimus. Vere enim dicitur, Homo Christus ab aeterno est omniscius, & omnipotens, & Patri aequalis. Vere etiam dicitur, Hic homo est aequalis Deo Patri, quia de persona dicitur. Est enim huius propositionis hic sensus, haec persona, quae est homo, est omniscia, & Deo aequalis, non qua homo tamen, sed qua Deus, &c. Verum nequaquam vere dicitur, Haec Christi humanitas est aequalis Deo Patri, quoniam non nisi de natura per se considerata, hoc dicitur. Sed excipis, sanguinem Christi mundare nos, iustificare nos, carnem Christi nos viuificare. Recte sane id dicitur, quoniam & sanguis ille, & caro illa (quatenus Vnigeniti caro est, & sanguis) verissimum est, primarium, & immediatum iustificationis nostrae, viuificationis, purgationis a nostris peccatis instrumentum, a Deo ordinatum, cui nobis applicandae reliqua, vt diximus, omnia a Deo instituta subseruiunt, veluti Euangelij prædicatio, Sacramentorum celebratio, ipsa denique fidei in nobis creatio. Quamobrem iam vides, quemadmodum & piisimè, & sanctisimè de Christi carne sentiamus, illíque suam gloriam relinquamus. Cæterum quòd ais, Dona, quæ sunt in carne Christi, non esse finita, refutatur à teipso, qui postea, & quidem statim, negas exæquandas esse in Christo naturas, & supra scripsisti, Christi carnem esse finitam potentiam. Atque exæquantur, si infinita potentia, & increata, (quæ Deitati proprie conuenit) carni quoque per te detur. Item antea concessisti vi veritatis victus, Duplicem in Christo secundum diuersas naturas scientiam esse. Id quod est nostrum dogma, idémque etiam tuum plane euertit, quod tu ipse supra pag.214. commemorasti, linea 8. à fine. Quòd ais Christum hominem OMNIA nouisse, Excipe quæ ipsemet Christus excepit, Marc.13. verf. 22. & his similia, quæ Pater in sua vnius potestate posuit. De die illo, ac hora nemo scit, ait, Christus ille, ne Angeli quidem, qui in cœlo sunt, nec ipse Filius: sed solus Pater: nisi Christum vel sibi contrarium, vel mentitum (abest ab utroque verbo blasphemia) esse dixeris, Gerlachi, Quod ne Turcæ quidè senserint. Præterea quòd putas, quia sedet Christi humanitas ad dextera Dei, eam omnisciente esse, vti ipsam Deitatem, plane hic falleris. Sedere enim ad dexteram Dei non est Deo exæquari: sed est carnem illam etiam in statu gloriæ Deo minorem esse. Id quod ipse ex Ambrosio, & Augustino verum esse concedis, ut mirer te tam & tot pugnantia tecum scribere. Denique quod obiicis mihi, quasi errem, dum dona (quæ habet Christi humanitas) ipsi fonti & plenitudini quæ autem nos habemus, exiguis tantum, & iis etiam turbidis, riuulis comparo, ipsemet erras, quum in eo manifestam Iohannis sententiam sequar. Ait enim Iohannes, Ex plenitudine eius omnes accepimus. Ergo in eo certè differentiam inter dona Christo homini, & nobis data secundum plus & minus constituo, præter diuersam habendi rationem, per quam ea dona Christus habet, nimirum & à se, & vt homo Deus: nos autem aduentitia, & ab alio, non à nobis (vtpote meri homines) habemus, non natura, vt ille, non per Vnionē hypostaticā Deitatis nobisēum factæ, vt ille: sed per solam Deitatis in nobis χάριν, quod est infinitum inter nos, & Christum hominem discrimen. Quare dicimur hæredes Dei, & coheredes Christi. Porrò quod varias huius loci ex Paulo sumpti protulì interpretationes, In Christo insunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ, & scientiæ, idcirco feci vt intelligeretis, multis modis eum Pauli locum à Patribus ipsis esse iam pridem explicatum, ne vestram illam interpretationem de exæquata carne Christi Deitati, tanquam quæ sola, & vnica vere ad eum locum afferri posset, nobis in posterum obtrudatis. Habes, vt opinor, ad omnia fulcimenta, quæ ad Osiandri argumenta adhibuisti, eam responsionem meam, ex qua illa ipsa tua per se ruere intelligis, & te in idem (atque Osiander incidit) praecipitium deuolui pulchrè iam sentis. Pergamus tamen.
units.tr: cap. 9. Thesauri, on the words "Glorify me," explains: You grant him such an opinion and faith about me that they acknowledge me not as a worm but as God. Likewise in book 10 on John, chapter 9: But when he descended to human, so to speak, dishonour, he returned again to his own glory. You say, however, that the flesh has that glory through and on account of the hypostatic union. But I have already answered before that this union neither removes the natures in Christ nor confuses their essential properties. Therefore, if by union you mean the grace of union, and wish that on this ground eternal omnipotence, omniscience, and so on, be rightly said and attributed to the whole person of Christ, we have long since conceded this to you, and at length. For it is truly said that Christ the man is omniscient and omnipotent from eternity and equal to the Father. It is also truly said that this man is equal to God the Father, because it is said of the person. The sense of this proposition is: this person, who is man, is omniscient and equal to God, not as man, however, but as God, and so on. But it is by no means truly said that this humanity of Christ is equal to God the Father, since that is said only of the nature considered in itself. But you object that the blood of Christ cleanses us, justifies us, and that the flesh of Christ quickens us. This is rightly said, since that blood and that flesh (insofar as they are the flesh and blood of the Only-begotten) are truly the primary and immediate instrument of our justification, quickening, and cleansing from our sins, ordained by God. To this instrument all the other things instituted by God serve, as we have said, in applying it to us: the preaching of the Gospel, the celebration of the sacraments, and finally the very creation of faith in us. Wherefore you now see how devoutly and holily we think of the flesh of Christ, and how we leave to it its glory. As for your saying that the gifts which are in the flesh of Christ are not finite, you refute it yourself, who afterwards, and immediately, deny that the natures in Christ are to be made equal, and who wrote above that the flesh of Christ has finite power. And they would be made equal if infinite and uncreated power, which properly belongs to the Deity, were also given to the flesh by you. Likewise, earlier, overcome by the force of truth, you conceded that there is a twofold knowledge in Christ according to the different natures. This is our doctrine, and it plainly overthrows your own, which you yourself recalled above on p. 214, line 8 from the end. As for your saying that Christ the man knew ALL things, make the exception that Christ himself made, Mark 13:22, and similar things, which the Father has placed in his own power alone. Of that day and hour no one knows, says that Christ, not even the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son himself, but only the Father. Unless you say that Christ was either self-contradictory or lying (blasphemy is absent from both words), Gerlachius, which not even the Turks have thought. Moreover, where you think that because the humanity of Christ sits at the right hand of God it is omniscient, as the Deity itself is, you are plainly mistaken. For to sit at the right hand of God is not to be made equal to God; rather, the flesh itself, even in the state of glory, is less than God. You yourself concede this is true on the authority of Ambrose and Augustine, so that I marvel you write things so many and so contrary to one another. Finally, as to your charge that I err in comparing the gifts which the humanity of Christ has to the fountain and fullness itself, while the gifts we have I compare to small and even muddy streamlets, you yourself are mistaken, since in this I follow the clear saying of John. For John says: Of his fullness we have all received. Therefore I certainly establish in this a difference between the gifts given to Christ the man and those given to us, by more and less, besides the different manner of having them. Christ has those gifts both from himself and as man God; we have them as adventitious, and from another, not from ourselves (being mere men), not by nature as he has them, nor by the hypostatic union of the Deity made with us as he has them, but only by the Deity's grace in us [χάρις]. This is the infinite difference between us and Christ the man. Hence we are called heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ. Moreover, that I have set forth various interpretations of this passage taken from Paul, In Christ are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, I did so that you might understand that this passage of Paul has long since been explained by the Fathers themselves in many ways, so that you may not henceforth press upon us your interpretation about the flesh of Christ made equal to the Deity, as if that alone could truly be brought to that passage. You have, I think, my answer to all the props you applied to Osiander's arguments, from which you understand that those very things of yours fall by themselves, and you already clearly perceive that you are sliding down into the same precipice into which Osiander fell. Nevertheless, let us go on.

units.la: In septimo Osiandri argumento calumniaris me Nestorianum esse, quoniam naturas distinguere, & naturas in Christo separare aliud esse affirmo: & illud in Christo recte fieri, hoc impiè, contendo. Quid tu igitur, Gerlachi, vel ista duo Distinguere, & separare esse duo negas, vel confundis, vel de nihilo esse putas? Maximus Episcopus in lib. de duabus Christi naturis, Qui porrò & distinctionem & vnitatem in Christo dicit is nec differentiam diuidit, nec confundit vnitatem.
units.tr: In Osiander's seventh argument you accuse me of being a Nestorian, because I affirm that to distinguish the natures and to separate the natures in Christ are different things, and I contend that the former is rightly done in Christ, the latter impiously. What then, Gerlachius? Do you deny that these two, to distinguish and to separate, are two things, or do you confuse them, or do you think them to be nothing? Maximus the Bishop, in his book on the two natures of Christ: Whoever says in Christ both distinction and unity neither divides the difference nor confuses the unity.

units.la: Cur igitur me Nestorianum vocas? Imò vt mihi tantùm inuidiam, tanquam nimium scrupuloso Grammatico, creares, ipse horum vocabulorum vim ignoras, ea quae te hic pungüt maximè & vrget, leui cubito agitas, & praeterfilis. Sed tibi, qui nihil hoc loco contra me afferas, minimè est opus responsione mea. Ceterum aduersus Laonicum eam illam inter distinguere & separare sententiam, vt videbis, luculenter confirmaui. In summa verò ipse vis propter vnionem duarum in vna Christi persona naturarum hypostaticam, omnes Deitatis λόγου proprietates communes & contributas esse realiter assumptae humanitati. Quid igitur? Socias, vt ita dicam, ὁμοοδρόνους, & ὁμοούσιος, vbique συνεργούς, eas naturas in Christo, iam facis, vt ipsa adeò operatio Diuina (id quod etiam scribit Kemnitius) veluti ipsius aeternae viuificationis, spiritus regenerantis, infusio, ἐνέργεια & efficacitas sit communis Carni & Deitati Christi.
units.tr: Why then do you call me a Nestorian? Indeed, in order to create hatred against me as an overly scrupulous grammarian, you yourself are ignorant of the force of these words. You wave with a light elbow those things which sting and press you most here, and you pass them by. But you, who bring nothing against me in this place, have no need at all of my answer. Moreover, against Laonicus, as you will see, I clearly confirmed that very opinion about to distinguish and to separate. In sum, you yourself maintain that, on account of the hypostatic union of two natures in the one person of Christ, all the properties of the divine Word are really common to, and communicated to, the assumed humanity. What then? You now make those natures in Christ, so to speak, homodromous [ὁμοδρόμους] and homoousios [ὁμοούσιος], everywhere synergoi [συνεργούς], co-workers, so that the divine operation itself (which Kemnitz also writes about) is common to the flesh and to the Deity of Christ, as if it were an infusion of eternal quickening and regenerating Spirit: energeia [ἐνέργεια] and efficacy.

units.la: L.j. virtus, operatio & efficacitas. Falleris. Nam ὑπο- λείψματα quidé ipsa, vt loquitur Damascenus, sunt vtriusq; naturę cōmunia, velut salus ipsa nostra, Vita æterna, reconciliatio: ipsæ vero ἐνέργειαι & operationes, ex quibus nascuntur illa ὑπο-λείψματα, sunt cuiusque naturę proprię, nec κοινωνητά. Nam proprietates sua subiecta non egrediuntur, vt recte dicitur in Scholis. Verbi gratiâ, Vita æterna est ὑπολείψμα, ad quod explendum vna ἐνέργεια, seu operatio est propria solius Deitatis λόγος, nempe ipse ille Christi Spiritus, nostras animas viuificas, & pascens succo viuifico in æternum. Is enim ex sola eius Deitate fluit in nos. Altera ἐνέργεια est ipsius Christi humanitatis, & quidem solius, propria, nempe sanctitas illa, quæ propter ipsius plenam odedientiam nobis ita, eòque Christi Spiritu pascendis omnino necessaria est. Illa enim sanctitas, seu obedientia hominis Christi, nobis imputata, altera est illius æternæ vitæ pars nobis ne cessaria, quæ est carnis Christi propria operatio, & ἐνέργεια. Quare etiam si ὑπολείψματα naturarum communia esse concedimus: ἐνεργείας tamen, seu operationes ipsas naturarum ad illa ὑπολείψματα concurrentes negamus esse communes, sed dicimus manere proprias cuiusque naturę. Nam si earum operationum cuiusque naturæ propriarum communicatio aut confusio statuatur, naturarum quoque ipsarum confusio & commixtio introducatur necesse est: quoniam cùm pendeant propriæ ἐνέργειαι, seu operationes ab ipsa φύσις, vti operationes ipsæ communes fiunt, ita & φύσεις quoque ipsę erunt communes. Ergo si natura Diuina communicat municat humanæ propriam ἐνέργειαν, eidem quo- que θεότητα suam, & propriam, i. diuinam communi- cet, necesse est: atque ita fiet caro Christi Deitas, seu Deus, præter Trinitatem, quod vel sentire est impiissimum, nedum dicere. Sic enim, & Damascenus (quem profers) & Basilius, & Athanasius ab ἐνεργείας ad θεότητα, & ab θεότητος ad ἐνέργειαν, seu operationem reciprocatione necessaria argumentantur, ut cui una ex iis communicatur, velut ἐνέργεια Deitatis, eidem quoque θεότης ipsa λόγῳ donetur, & tribuatur. De quo quia plura in nostro ad Kemnitij libru De duabus in Christo naturis responso dicemus, quæ repetere hoc loco nequaquam est operæpretium, ad illud te remitto. Cæterum quod Damascenum & Cyrillum citas, qui unamquamque naturam cum alterius communione, & περιχώρησιν propriam operationem agere scribunt, & Communes facere operationes, item carnem suscepisse totam verbi operationem, dicunt, quis tam parum est in eorundem scriptis versatus, ut non intelligat illic communionem, & περιχώρησιν significare Vnionem, & reciprocationem, non autem immeationem naturarum siue naturalium proprietatum συνέργειαν, seu cooperationem, quemadmodum tamen tu censes. Itaque quia illæ duæ naturæ (quæque propria sibi operans) manent in illa hypostatica vnione vnitæ, dicuntur habere communes, i. in vnica hypostasi, non in diuersis personis, actiones. Dicitur etiam natura Christi humana suscepisse totum λόγον sibi vnitum, id est, non suscepisse ex parte tatum, sed inte grum: non autem propterea dicitur in societatem ac
units.tr: As to your virtus, operatio et efficacitas: you are mistaken. For the hypoleimmata [ὑπολείψματα], as Damascene calls them, are indeed common to both natures, like our very salvation, eternal life, and reconciliation. But the energeiai [ἐνέργειαι] themselves, the operations from which those hypoleimmata arise, belong to each nature and are not communicable [κοινωνητά]. For properties do not go beyond their subjects, as is rightly said in the Schools. For example, eternal life is a hypoleimma, and to bring it about, one energeia or operation is proper to the Word of the Deity alone, namely that very Spirit of Christ, who quickens our souls and feeds them with life-giving sap forever. For this flows into us from his Deity alone. The other energeia belongs to the humanity of Christ alone, and is its own: namely that holiness which, through his full obedience, is wholly necessary to us, so that we may be fed by the Spirit of Christ. For that holiness or obedience of the man Christ, imputed to us, is the other part of that eternal life which is necessary to us, and it is the proper operation and energeia of the flesh of Christ. Therefore, even if we concede that the hypoleimmata are common to the natures, we deny that the energeiai, the operations of the natures themselves which concur to those hypoleimmata, are common; we say they remain proper to each nature. For if a communication or confusion of the proper operations of each nature is established, a confusion and mixing of the natures themselves must necessarily be introduced. Since the proper energeiai, or operations, depend on the physis [φύσις] itself, as the operations become common, so the natures themselves will also become common. Therefore, if the divine nature communicates its proper energeia to the human nature, it must also communicate to it its own theotēs [θεότης], that is, its divinity. And thus the flesh of Christ becomes Deity, or God, besides the Trinity, which is most impious even to think, let alone say. For both Damascene (whom you cite), and Basil, and Athanasius argue from energeia to theotēs, and from theotēs to energeia, by a necessary reciprocation: whichever of the two is communicated to something, such as the energeia of the Deity, the theotēs itself is also given and attributed to that same thing. Since we shall say more about this in our answer to Kemnitz's book On the two natures in Christ, and it is not worth the effort to repeat it here, I refer you to that. Moreover, as for your citing Damascene and Cyril, who write that each nature acts in communion with and by perichōrēsis [περιχώρησις] of the other, and who speak of making operations common, and of the flesh having assumed the whole operation of the Word: who is so little versed in their writings as not to understand that there communion and perichōrēsis signify union and reciprocation, not an intermingling of the natures or a synergeia [συνέργεια], that is, a cooperation of natural properties, as you suppose? Thus, because those two natures, each acting its own proper action, remain united in that hypostatic union, they are said to have common actions, that is, in the one hypostasis, not in different persons. The human nature of Christ is also said to have assumed the whole Word united to it, that is, not to have assumed it in part but entirely; yet it is not for that reason said that the human nature was admitted into fellowship and

units.la: effectionem eius operationis (quæ verè Diuinæ naturæ propria est) naturā humanam assumptam esse, ascitam, & consociatam λόγῳ. Gloriam enim suam nemini dabit, qui verè est Deus. Est autem λόγος verè Deus. Quod postremo loco scribis me hanc, quæ est inter totum Christi, & totum Christum, distinctionem, hausisse ex Lombardo, fratre, ineptis. Nam ea ex Augustino & Damasceno sumpsi: sed quasi hoc solo nomine, quod ex Lombardo sumpserim, satis refutaretur (tantum enim Augustini in te telum contortum cuitare non potes) ex sola Lombardi mentione abs te inuecta, victorem te ipsum pronuntias. Porrò quod sic λόγῳ Deitatem assumptæ carni communicari posse sentis, quemadmodum dulcedo, & calor aliis rebus communicari a melle & igne poteit, falleris in hac rerum dissimilimarum comparatione imprudentissime, atque grauissime. Deitas enim nulli alij rei, præterquam ipsa sibi, id est, Deo soli, est communicabilis, & ut loquitur Bernardus, capabilis, quoniam est essentia singulariter vna. Calor autem & dulcedo sunt qualitates Physicæ, & naturales, ideoque facile aliis quoque rebus communicantur. Nisi enim Deitatem ipsam uti dulcedinem, accidens esse statuatis, certè ita, ut illa, communicari non poterit. Nam si Communicationis nomen pro vnione hypostatica accipis, concedo communicari, id est, vniri assumptæ carni Deitatem λόγῳ. Sin communicationem pro participatione sumis (id quod certè facis) nego Deitatem ab assumpta carne participari. Itaque prorsus inepta est ad hoc argumentum tua de melmelle, & igne suas qualitates aliis quoque rebus communicante similitudo. Reliquum argumentum, quoniam & à me recte conceptum fateris: & nihil affers ipse, quod meam illius refutationem euertat: denique quoniam, quæ in tuo scripto sequuntur, sunt omnia aduersum Laonicum iam euicta, ne inani repetitione paginas impleam, finem dicendi faciam, Dominum Deum precatus, vt Gerlachio saniorem mentem, & placidiorem agendi rationem largiatur. Quod ad me verò nostrósque omnes attinet, sic statuito, Gerlachi, te, tuósque de nobis illud esse verum experturos, quod habet prouerbium vetus, Palma pressa fit valentior. Vale. Calend. Ianuariis 1581. Geneuæ.
units.tr: The effecting of that operation (which is truly proper to the divine nature) is that the human nature was assumed, taken up and joined to the Word [λόγῳ]. For he who is truly God will not give his glory to another. The Word is truly God. As for your last point, that I drew this distinction between the whole of Christ and the whole Christ from Lombard, brother, you are being foolish. I took it from Augustine and Damascene. But as if it were sufficiently refuted by this name alone, that I took it from Lombard (for you cannot dodge the shaft of Augustine turned against you), you declare yourself the victor merely from the mention of Lombard that you have brought in. Moreover, in thinking that the Deity can be communicated by the Word to the assumed flesh, just as sweetness and heat can be communicated to other things by honey and fire, you are most imprudently and gravely mistaken in comparing things so unlike. The Deity can be communicated to no other thing except itself, that is, to God alone, and, as Bernard says, it is capable of it, since it is a single essence, one in a unique way. But heat and sweetness are physical, natural qualities, and so they are easily communicated to other things too. Unless you hold that the Deity itself is an accident like sweetness, in which case it certainly could not be communicated in the same way. For if you take the word communication for hypostatic union, I grant that it is communicated, that is, that the Deity is united by the Word to the assumed flesh. But if you take communication for participation (which surely you do), I deny that the Deity is shared with the assumed flesh. So your comparison of honey and fire, which communicate their qualities to other things too, is utterly pointless for this argument. As for the remaining argument, since you admit I have stated it correctly, and you bring nothing yourself that overturns my refutation of it; and finally, since whatever follows in your writing has already been overcome in the case against Laonicus, I will not fill pages with empty repetition. I will bring my discussion to an end, praying the Lord God to grant Gerlach a saner mind and a more peaceable way of conducting himself. As for me and all of ours, be assured, Gerlach, that you and yours will find true of us what the old proverb says: A pressed palm becomes stronger. Farewell. Geneva, the Kalends of January, 1581.

units.tr: LAMBERTUS DANÆUS TO NICOLAUS SELNECCERUS: mercy, peace, and a turning to the true doctrine of the Lord's Supper, and grace, from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: CCEPI epistolam tuam, charissime Selneccere, in qua responsdes meæ defensioni ad tuam in Excegesin (quam Saxonicam appellavi) repetitionem. Quoniam vero in hoc quoque scripto, quemadmodum in superiore à me propterea iustè reprehensio, ὑσπρν ᾳεῖ-προν (vt ipse animadvertisti) facis, non quidem Rhetorum præceptis, sed animi tui splendidæ bili obsecutus: in hac mea responsione sequar eũ ordinem, quem ipse tibi in scribendo delegisti. De re quidem ipsa, quanquam omnium maxima, & præcipuo fidei nostræ fundamento nihil agis, quemadmodum ingenuè fateris ipse, id est, de Christi gloria, & ipsius doctrinæ, quam profiteris, veritate, nulla tibi cura est: de te autem, & tui nominis existimatione solicitudo multa, ne nouæ illi Domini Superintendentis dignitati, (quam te recens consecutum Lipsiæ scribis) M. j. minùs suus honos suáque dignitas fortasse con- staret. Verùm Iohannis Baptistæ exemplum potius veris Ecclesiæ pastoribus id sequendum docet,vt ipsi minuantur, crescat autem vnus Christus. Paulus selectum illud Dei organon, ac verum nobis propagādæ Christi gloriæ exemplar, pro minimo habet, si ab hominibus iudicetur, modò salua Deo sua gloria,& ipsius cælestis doctrinæ,quam annuntiabat, veritas maneat. Verùm tu de tam bonorum & fidelium Pastorum numero nequaquam es, neque præ Christo reliqua pro stercoribus ducis, quemadmodum idē Paulus fecit,Philip.3.v.8. Equidem magnum à te meæ huius admonitionis Christianæ fructum non expecto,(quis enim,vt inquit Ieremias, Æthiopem dealbare se posse speret) sed vt videant pii, quàm in mea illa ad scriptum tuum responsione,ab omni tum mentiendi, tum calumniandi animo(quem mihi Selneccere,toties,quasi nihil aliud habeas, quod respondeas, in recenti hac epistola tua,& tamen falsò,& ipse mentiens obiicis) fuerim alienus, & me propter sparsa illa tua in me conuitia, quicquam detrimenti veritas Dei, & doctrina de Sacra Domini Cœna (quam asserui) patiatur, en tibi breue ad omnia mihi obiecta crimina responsum. Scio enim, vt ait ille,grauem esse iniuriam sacra præsertim tractanti,si veritati seruiens,fallax credatur. Præterea tu me ad scribendum prouocas, qui tamen non terres eloquentia. Flocci enim pendo titulos tuos, vmbrásque laruarum, quarum hæc est, (vt ait Hieronymus)natura, vt paruulos terreât, & in tenebrosis angulis garriant.
units.tr: I have received your letter, dearest Selneccerus, in which you reply to my defence of my reply to your repetition in the Exegesis (which I called the Saxon one). But since in this writing too you do what I rightly rebuked in the earlier one, a hysteron proteron [ὕστερον πρότερον] (as you yourself noticed), not from the rules of the rhetoricians but following the bright bile of your temper, I shall follow in this reply the order you chose for your writing. As to the matter itself, though it is the greatest of all and the chief foundation of our faith, you accomplish nothing, as you frankly admit yourself. That is, you have no concern for the glory of Christ or for the truth of the doctrine you profess. But you have much anxiety about yourself and your own reputation, lest that new dignity of Superintendent of the Lord (which you write that you recently obtained at Leipzig) should perhaps lose some of its honour and its standing. Yet the example of John the Baptist teaches that true ministers of the Church should follow him in this, that they decrease while Christ alone increases. Paul, that chosen instrument of God and true model for us of spreading Christ's glory, counted it as nothing if he was judged by men, provided that God's glory and the truth of the heavenly doctrine he preached remained safe. But you are by no means among the number of such good and faithful ministers, nor do you count all else as dung compared with Christ, as the same Paul did (Philippians 3:8). Indeed, I do not expect much Christian fruit from you from this admonition of mine (for who, as Jeremiah says, could hope to make the Ethiopian white?). But let the godly see how, in my reply to your writing, I was free from any spirit of lying or calumny (which you, Selneccerus, so often and so falsely charge me with in this recent letter of yours, as if you had nothing else to answer, while yourself lying). And let them see that, despite your scattered insults against me, the truth of God and the doctrine of the Lord's Supper (which I have maintained) suffer no harm. Here, then, is a short reply to all the charges brought against me. For I know, as that writer says, that it is a grave wrong, especially for one handling sacred matters, to be believed when he is deceitful while serving the truth. Moreover, you challenge me to write, though you do not frighten me with your eloquence. For I care not a fig for your titles and the shadows of bugbears, whose nature, as Jerome says, is to frighten little children and chatter in dark corners.

units.la: Mones autem me primum, vt,si deinceps re- sponderē voluerim, vera dicam. Habeo gratias, Selneccere, tam boni & salutaris consilij nomine: sed tamen & id feceram abs te non monitus, nec erat necesse vt per totum annum hoc in me scomma meditareris. Ergo audi quàm omnia verè (etiam te ipso teste) antea scripserim, & vt de via in semitam me frustra hac tua admonitione reuocaueris.
units.tr: You advise me first, that, if I should wish to reply afterwards, I should tell the truth. I thank you, Selneccerus, for this good and wholesome advice. But I had already done this without your admonition, and it was not necessary for you to spend a whole year meditating this jibe against me. So listen to how everything I wrote earlier was true (even by your own testimony), and how in vain your admonition has called me back from the path to the byway.

units.la: Postea vero meum scriptum pro Exegesi Sa- xonica examinans reprehendis, quòd Exegesin illam appellaui Saxonicam. Certè Saxonicam dici posse existimaui, & quidem rectè, quæ in Saxonia edita, & inde ad nos perlata, & à bonis viris omnibus (qui in Saxonia rectè de Sacra Domini Cœna sentiebant) fuerat mirum in modum probata: nisi forte & ipsius Martini Lutheri prima scripta aduersus Antichristum Romanum Germanica dici non posse exististimes, quoniam refragante summo Germaniæ magistratu, nimirum Imperatore Carolo Quinto, fuerunt ab illo edita ac promulgata.
units.tr: Afterwards, examining my writing on the Saxon Exegesis, you find fault because I called that Exegesis Saxon. Certainly I thought it could rightly be called Saxon, since it was published in Saxony, brought from there to us, and greatly approved by all good men who held sound views on the Lord's Supper in Saxony. Unless perhaps you think that even the first writings of Martin Luther against the Roman Antichrist cannot be called German, because they were issued and published by him although the chief magistrate of Germany, namely the Emperor Charles V, opposed them.

units.la: Dicis te nolle confutare nænias, vel muscas meas abigere. Itáne verò, Selneccere, sacrosancta illa de Cœna Domini veritas tibi, & res nihili videtur? Certè ita te muscæ illæ meæ pupugerunt, vt quanuis à te contemni dicantur, earum tamen puncturam in ὑσίῳ tuo dissimulare non potueris. Et certè sic te ipse gessisti, vt omnes bonos abs te tam procul propter ambitionem tuam abegeris, vt ne musca quidem bona iam sit tecum.
units.tr: You say that you are unwilling to refute my trifles or to drive away my flies. Is it really so, Selneccerus, that that most sacred truth about the Lord's Supper seems to you a trifle and a small matter? Certainly those flies of mine have stung you so much that, although you say you despise them, you could not hide their sting in your [ὑσίῳ]. And indeed you have conducted yourself in such a way, driving away all good men so far from yourself because of your ambition, that not even a good fly is with you now.

units.la: Scribis Philippum Melanchthonem nec æquum, nec amicum vnquam fuisse Iohanni Caluino, nec ipsius doctrinam probasse. Quis vero tibi homini inconstanti potius, quàm ipsi illi Philippo, viro (omnium bonorum iudicio optimo, & verissimo, habebit fidem? cuius scripta & priuata & publica tuam illam calumniam refellunt: cum in ipso sinu Iohannis Caluini, tanquam viri sibi amicissimi deponere etiam animam ipsam exoptarit? At tu quaedam priuata, si Deo placet, testimonia pro te affers. Nempe impudenter nugas dicis. Sed est haec nimirum tua canina, ut cum Hieronymo loquar, facundia, quae, ut optimum quaeque arrodat, strenuè mentiri didicit. Nam quae citas, vbinam, quaeso, locorum extant? & ea ipsa, quae collegisti, potius te copotationum tuarum verum, quàm scriptorum tuorum recetium memorem ostendunt, quae contra tuam Vbiquitatem, pro nobis aliquando edidisti. Denique nihil in his ipsis praeter rumusculum tenuem, & incertum, nil praeter auditum habes. Quod enim scribis Philippum anno domini 1550. in promotione Schurstabii dixisse, hic te tam veracem esse prodis, atque postea p.9.& 11.& 13.fuisti, vbi quid pro nobis scripseris, & de ipso illo Philippo, eiusque scriptis damnandis, ipse cum caeteris Bergae constitueris, prorsus non meminis ti.
