Ad illa vero tua, quibus scribis, te optare ut Philippus forti animo suam constantiam expressisset, & ne quid humani passus esset, non modò risi ipse (quemadmodum & tu ad illa mea, quae tamen ex ipso Philippo, præceptore tuo, didiceram, a verbis ad verbera risum non continuisse scribis) sed etiam mecum ridebunt, & te irridebunt omnes, qui illa legent, si qui forte legent. Nū vero tu, tuiq; similes, Dij & ἀναμάρτητοι sitis, quivirtutū vestrarū splēdore mūdo præluceatis? Philippus autē, præceptor vester, & homo nescio quis, & inconstans fuerit. An nō potius fuit Philippus sui ipsi? seculi lumē: vos autē huius ætatis, vestrarūmque ciuitatum ac Ecclesiarum Germanicarum carcinomata estis? Quamobrem teipsū postea refutas, & animi tui hypocrisin ostendis. Nam scribis & te, & Osiandrum, & alios tuos maximè cupere, vt Philippi præceptoris vestri authoritas salua, sarta, tectàque maneat. Quomodo enim vt Philippi (hominis, vt dicitis, in fide fluctuantis & incerti) sententia valeat tantopere desideratis, cùm fides nostra certissima & constantissima doctrina esse debeat. Itaque te quoque Selneccere, aperte cōfutat impurus ille impuri patris filius, Osiander, ingratus discipulus, qui Philippum & Bucerum, lumina Germaniæ, hæresεos aperte in Antisturmio damnauit: & tu ipse, & Ienenses Theologi Torgensem Synodum alioqui probantes, de hoc vno tamen estis aducrsus eam grauiter conquesti, quòd Philippum, & illius scripta non reiecissēt. Cæteræ, quæ pagina septima scribis, cùm nihil itidem, nili auditas à te fabulas, contineant, iudicaui prætermittēda. Nam te primatū in Ecclesiis Germanicis expetere, vti Diotrephes ille à Iohanne propterea dānatus in Ecclesiis Asiaticis
units.tr: You write that Philip Melanchthon was never fair or friendly to John Calvin, and never approved of his doctrine. But who would give you more credence than Philip himself, a man (by the judgement of all good men) the best and most truthful? His writings, both private and public, refute your slander, since in the very bosom of John Calvin, as of a man most dear to him, he longed even to lay down his very soul. You bring forward certain private testimonies in your favour, if God pleases. Indeed, you shamelessly tell trifles. But this is surely your doglike eloquence, as I say in Jerome's words, which has learned to bite at all that is best and to lie boldly. For where are the passages you cite, I ask? And the very things you have collected show more the memory of your drinking parties than the true record of your writings, which you once published on our side against your own Ubiquity. In the end you have nothing in these matters but a thin and uncertain little rumour, nothing but hearsay. For what you write, that Philip said in the year of our Lord 1550, at the promotion at Schurstab, shows you to be such a truthful man. Yet you have quite forgotten what you wrote for us afterwards, on pages 9, 11 and 13, and how you yourself, with the others, at Berga, condemned Philip himself and his writings. As for those words of yours, in which you write that you wished Philip had expressed his constancy with a brave spirit and had suffered nothing human, I not only laughed (just as you, in reply to my remarks, which I had indeed learned from Philip himself, your teacher, write that you could not keep from laughing at words that turned to blows), but all who read those words, if any happen to read them, will laugh with me and mock you. Are you and men like you then gods and sinless [ἀναμάρτητοι], who shine before the world with the splendour of your virtues? Yet Philip, your teacher, was, I know not who, and inconstant? Was not Philip rather a light of his own age? And you are the cancers of this age, of your cities and of the German Churches. Therefore you later refute yourself and reveal the hypocrisy of your own mind. For you write that you and Osiander and your other friends most earnestly desire that the authority of your teacher Philip should remain safe, intact and undamaged. For how do you desire so greatly that the opinion of Philip (a man, as you say, wavering and uncertain in faith) should hold weight, when our faith ought to rest on the most certain and constant doctrine? Therefore, Selneccer, that impure son of an impure father, Osiander, an ungrateful disciple, also openly refutes you. He condemned Philip and Bucer, the lights of Germany, openly as heretics in his Antisturmius. And you yourself, and the Jena theologians, who otherwise approve the Torgau Synod, have complained bitterly against it on this one point alone, that it did not reject Philip and his writings. The rest, which you write on page seven, since it likewise contains nothing but tales heard from others, I have thought fit to pass over. For that you seek the primacy in the German Churches, as that Diotrephes whom John therefore condemned, who sought the first place in the Asian Churches, the matter itself makes plain, and every effort of yours shows it, as you now differ most bitterly from that little brother of yours, Jacob Andreae, formerly your dearest friend, whom you never again call by name in your writings.

units.la: Pag. 7. ambiebat, res ipsa manifeste loquitur, & tuus omnis conatus oltendit, qui infestissime a tuo illo fraterculo Iacobo Andrea, antea tibi charissimo, iam propterea dissentias, quem nusquam amplius in tuis scriptis appellare soles. Festiua vero est illa tua ex idololatrico cultu Francisci Franciscanorum Monachorum idoli transcripta, & scurriliter in me vibrata oratio, An verum loquaris, quis dubitat, nisi totus mundus. Fortasse tu puer a Monachis literas istas didicisti, quas tu iam vetulus & grandaeuus Theologus obliuisci non potuisti: in quo tibi parum cum Kemnitio (quem vnum in deliciis habes) conuenit. Ille enim, & merito quidem, Iesuitas & caeteros monachos odio plus quam vatiniano prosequitur: tu vero φιλομόναχος ineptissima eorum verba, etiam de ipsamet foedissima Missa repetita, pro floribus orationis tuae inepte nobis cuomis, & regeris. Quae quòd spurca sint, omitto. Venio igitur ad Camerarium, virum illum optimum, qui vestras insanias sua authoritate, frendentibus etiam vobis, tamen coercuit. Nam vt Camerarius (quā fuit animi modestiā) intra suae vocationis & artis fines se continuerit, propterea tamen non mentior, dum affirmo ab illo, quandiu vixit, vestros furores fuisse sua grauitate, tanquam fraeno validissimo, ad tempus cohibitos. Cur tu igitur id negas Seineccere, nisi vt nullam vnquam reuerentiam & honorem vlli hominū mortalium, vel praeceptori, vel seni (quod tamen fieri iubet diserte Lex Dei) abs te fuisse exhibitum demonstres? Caeterum quod fidem & doctrinam (quam de S. Domini Coena profiteor, quamque non ex hominis Lutheri scriptis, sed ex ipso Dei verbo verissime didici) appellas Phanaticas, alibi diabolicas opiniones, certe tuum illud conuitium non in me, Selneccere, sed in ipsum Deum, cuius veritatem sequor, & coelum torquetur. Deum enim huius meae doctrinae authorem habeo. Sed praeterea totam piam, atque orthodoxam vetustatem, quae procul dubio mecum facit, feris, & flagellas, eamque Phanaticae opinionis, id est haereseos hoc loco damnes necesse est. Sed praeterquam quod insignis conuitiator es, etiam impudens deprehenderis, qui pag. 9. aperte neges, Vvittenbergensem Cathechisin publico Lipsiensis & Vvittebergensis Academiae, ac trium etiam consistoriorum, atque adeo omnium Superintendentium Ecclesiarum Saxonicarum consensu conscriptam, ac in lucem aeditam fuisse, anno Domini videlicet 1571. De quo quoniam nuper Aspasces amicus meus in doctissima illa sua ad Pochemium Lubecensem Superintendentem responsione copiose scripsit, ad eam te, breuitatis causa, remitto. Spero enim eam tibi, & tuis (ut potest quae vestrae & in Philippum praeceptorem vestrum ingratitudinis, & apertae in Ecclesias Germanicas tyrannidis fidem facit) fore iucundissimam. Quod etiam addis eadem pagina, meplura, quae vera non sunt, dicere, certe illa refutare debebas, quod tamen non fecisti: sed facile est cuiuis alii
units.tr: Page 7. That witty speech of yours, copied from the idolatrous cult of Francis, the idol of the Franciscan monks, and hurled at me in a buffoon's manner, "Do you speak the truth? Who doubts it, except the whole world?" is perhaps something you learned as a boy from the monks, which you, now an old and aged theologian, could not forget. In this you agree poorly with Kemnitz, whom alone you hold dear. For he, and rightly so, pursues the Jesuits and the other monks with more hatred than Vatinius did. But you, a friend of monks, repeat their most foolish words, even those about that most foul Mass, and clumsily throw them at us as the flowers of your eloquence, and hurl them back. That they are filthy I pass over. I come therefore to Camerarius, that excellent man, who nevertheless restrained your madness by his authority, though you gnashed your teeth. For although Camerarius, with the modesty of his spirit, kept himself within the limits of his calling and art, I do not lie in affirming that, as long as he lived, your frenzies were held in check for a time by his gravity, as by a very strong bridle. Why then do you deny this, Selneccer, unless to show that you never showed any reverence or honour to any mortal man, either teacher or old man, which nevertheless the Law of God expressly commands? Moreover, as for your calling the faith and doctrine that I profess concerning the Lord's Supper (which I learned most truly not from the writings of the man Luther, but from the very Word of God) fanatical, and elsewhere diabolical opinions, surely that reproach of yours is aimed not at me, Selneccer, but at God himself, whose truth I follow, and at heaven itself. For I have God as the author of this my doctrine. But beyond that you must strike at and scourge the whole pious and orthodox antiquity, which without doubt agrees with me, and condemn it here as the fanatical opinion, that is, heresy. But besides being a notable reviler, you have also been caught being shameless, since on page 9 you openly deny that the Wittenberg Catechism was composed and published with the common consent of the public Academies of Leipzig and Wittenberg, of three consistories, and indeed of all the superintendents of the Saxon Churches, namely in the year of the Lord 1571. Since my friend Aspasius recently wrote copiously about this in his most learned reply to Pochemius, superintendent of Lübeck, I refer you to that, for the sake of brevity. For I hope it will be most pleasing to you and yours (as it bears witness to your ingratitude toward Philip, your teacher, and to your open tyranny over the German Churches). As for your further addition on the same page, that I say many things which are not true, surely you ought to have refuted those things, which you did not do; but it is easy for anyone else to measure by his own nature...

units.la: M. iiij. ex suo ingenio metiri, quemadmodum me ex tuo mendacem iudicas.
units.tr: M. iiij. to measure me by your own character, just as you judge me a liar by yours.

units.la: Imprimis autem tu ipse iam manifeste mentitus argueris, quum Typographum (qui Exegesin Saxonicam edidit) scribis fugâ sibi à vobis vestrisque consiliis consuluisse, quum tamen nullum esset periculum. Quid, tu, Selneccere, putasne nos esse tam obliuiosos, quàm tu es, vt quæ proximis hisce annis gesta sunt, iam non meminerimus? Falleris. vestra haec historia est recens, & animis hominum inhaereret, nec tam est vetus, quàm Cataclysmus ille Deucalionis, de quo tamen adhuc certa narrantur. Quis enim nescit eum miserum Typographum tuis, tuorumque crudelibus consilijs fuisse omnibus suis bonis spoliatum, & ea pecuniæ summa mulctatum & emunctum, vt vix ipsam suam vitam ac pellem etiam fugiens à vobis pro spolio abstulerit? In quo, cum tot modis ille à vobis vexatus ad vestros tamen errores non descenderit amplectendos, insignem & constantem fidei suæ confessionem cum retinuisse, & illius rationem aperte, non clàm (vt tu accusas) reddidisse vides. Saltem cum teipso fortiorem fuisse, fatearis necesse est, cùm mihi narres te propter alapam duntaxat, & Grammaticam criminationem (quam propter studium concordiæ cum nobis ineundæ scilicet ab illo Sextumuiro, & collega tuo inhumanissimo, Iacobo bo Andrea, accepisti) quū mihi narres(inquāⁱ)te propter tam leuia incommoda mutum ita iam euasisse, vt de concordia ne hiscere quidem nūc audeas inter tuos.
units.tr: Above all, you have already been caught in a plain lie when you write that the printer (who published the Saxon Exegesis) saved himself by flight from you and your counsels, although there was no danger at all. What do you think, Selneccer? Do you suppose we are as forgetful as you are, that we no longer remember what was done in these recent years? You are mistaken. That affair is recent, it still clings to people's minds, and it is not so old as the flood of Deucalion, of which certain accounts are still told. For who does not know that the wretched printer was stripped of all his goods by the cruel schemes of you and yours, was fined and fleeced of such a sum of money that, fleeing, he barely carried off his own life and skin as plunder from you? In this matter, although you harassed him in so many ways, he did not give way to embrace your errors, and you see that he kept a notable and steadfast confession of his faith and set out his reasons openly, not secretly (as you accuse him). At least you must admit that you were weaker than he was, since you tell me that you were moved only by a slap and a grammatical charge (which you received, forsooth, from that inhuman Sextumvir and your colleague, Jacob Andreae, out of zeal for forming concord with us), and, while telling me this, you say that over such trifling troubles you have become so mute that you do not dare even to breathe a word about concord among your own people.

units.la: Porrò quòd me dicis nomen viri boni mentien-do amittere,dum affirmo te nobis nostraque doctrina, etiam aperte,antea fauisse, ipse illud, quod in me criminaris, praestas, Tune enim, Selneccere, id verum esse negare audeas, cùm aduersum te tot testes possim producere, si fuerit necesse? Ecce i gitur quàm tui sis memor, & eorum, quae paucis ante annis feceris. Imò inde apparet, quàm magnus etiam hypocrita, & nostrorum illo tempore fueris assentator, Quemadmodum neque in eo ipso satis tibi, tuorumque collegarum existimationi caues, dū ais, Exegesin Saxonica prius extraneis principibus, quàm vobis Saxonicarum Ecclesiarum pastoribus innotuisse, & per exteros illos commonefactū de ea fuisse Inclytum Dominum Electorem Saxoniae. Nae tu mihi teipsū Doctorem Ienensem, inspectorem Brunsuicensem, & aulicum concionatorem, nimiùm stertentem & negligentem hic describis, cuius fuerit tam supina & vacors in ijs rebus, & libris (qui ad doctrinam pertinent) inuestigandis negligentia, vt extranei prius, quàm tu, tuisque Superintendentes, quid in Saxonia, tibique vicina ciuitate de Religione Christiana ederetur, & docceretur, cognouerint: & de eo ipso prius illustrissimum Electorem tuū admonuerint. Certè venit hìc mihi in mentem vera il la comici sententia, Qui alienum agrum arat,familiarem deserit. Nam tu dum aulica & reliqua βίωτικά curas, munus tuum strenuè neglexisti. Quamobrem te amicè moneo, Selneccere, vt in posterum diligentior ac vigilantior sis, & illud ad te pertinere existimes, etiamsi es dominus Ecclesiarum Lipsicarum Superintendens, quod est ab Homero sapienter dictum, vt videas nimirum,
units.tr: Moreover, as for your saying that I lose the good name of a good man by lying when I affirm that you once favoured us and our doctrine, even openly, you yourself do the very thing you charge me with. For, Selneccer, how do you dare to deny that this is true, when I could produce so many witnesses against you, if it were necessary? See then how mindful you are of yourself and of what you did a few years ago. Indeed, from this it appears how great a hypocrite you were, and how much of a flatterer of our people at that time; nor do you take sufficient care for the reputation of yourself and your colleagues in this same place, when you say that the Saxon Exegesis became known to foreign princes before it became known to you, the pastors of the Saxon churches, and that the most illustrious Elector of Saxony was first warned about it by those outsiders. Indeed, you describe yourself here to me as the Jena doctor, the inspector of Brunswick, and a court preacher who snores too much and is careless; and your negligence was so lazy and idle in investigating those matters and books which pertain to doctrine, that outsiders learned what was being published and taught about the Christian religion in Saxony and in the neighbouring city of Brunswick before you and your superintendents did, and they first warned your most illustrious Elector about it. Certainly that true saying of the comic poet comes to my mind: "He who ploughs another's field neglects his own." For while you attended to court affairs and the rest of your temporal [βίωτικά] concerns, you vigorously neglected your own duty. Therefore I kindly warn you, Selneccer, to be more diligent and watchful in future, and to consider it your business (even though you are superintendent and lord of the Leipzig churches) to heed what Homer wisely said, namely that you should see

units.la: Ædibus in propriis quae prava, & quae tecta gerantur,
units.tr: What is wrong and what is going on in one's own house

units.la: ne sis ἀλλοτριεπίσκοπος, & ea, quae nihil ad te pertinent, tam solicitè cures. Nam dum sic aliis animum intendis, parùm ipse tibi attendis. Caeterùm pro scommate interpretaris, quòd libri tui, ad quem respondebam, inscriptionem secutus, te Doctorem Electoralem vocaui. Illo ergo scommate te tuus ille M. Hermannus Rostochiensis, tàquam sale Baltico, primus aspersit, qui hûc immerito tibi titulum voluit adscribere. Neque verò illud (tam es ambitiosus) etiam recusabas, vt quamcunque vitae tuae nobis praedicandae occasionem arriperes, & laborum, id est, discursitationum tuarū lepidam illam historiam nobis narrares. Ex qua apparet quàm sis μεγαλόψυχος, & vir animi elati, qui Imperatores summos, nempe L. Syllam, & Augustum Caesarem, vtrunque hominem & profanum & ambitiosissimum imitaris, dum, quemadmodum illi, sic tu de vita tua breuis commentarios conscribis. Verū Selnecc-breues re, hæc tua te historia parum commendat, cum ex ea cernamus, te nullibi stabile (quemadmodu inquit ille) stabulum habuisse. Primum igitur prædicas te Aulicum concionatorem fuisse. Quis hoc de te facile non credat quamvis nō dixeris, cum ne nunc quidem, dum ab aula abes, mores illos aulicos exuere & dedisce potueris? Et certè pulcher ille tuus libellus prorsus aulicus, quem Germanicè contra Theodorum Bezam scriptū Damiselis Illustrissimæ Electricis Saxoniæ dedicasti, te verè suauissimum aulicum hominem esse arguit & te aulicam, ut vocant, religionem sequi: sed vide, mi Selneccere, ne quia per octennium illud (quod commemoras) in Aula versatus es, illud verum esse iam ostendas, quod de Principū suæ ætatis aulis scripsit Lucanus,
units.tr: so that you are not a meddler in other men's affairs [ἀλλοτριεπίσκοπος], and so that you do not so carefully attend to things that have nothing to do with you. For while you direct your mind so much to others, you pay little attention to yourself. Moreover, you interpret as a jibe that, following the title of your book to which I was replying, I called you Electoral Doctor. That jibe was first thrown at you by your Mr Hermann of Rostock, as if with Baltic salt, since he wrongly wanted to attach this title to you. Nor, being so ambitious, did you refuse even this, so that you might seize any occasion of your life to proclaim yourself to us, and tell us that charming story of your labours, that is, of your rushing about. From it one sees how magnanimous [μεγαλόψυχος] you are, and a man of lofty spirit, who imitate the greatest commanders, namely Lucius Sulla and the Emperor Augustus, both of them profane and most ambitious men, since, like them, you write commentaries on your own life, though brief ones. But, Selneccer, brief as they are, this story of yours does little to commend you, since from it we see that you never had a firm stable (as the saying goes). First, then, you proclaim that you were a court preacher. Who would not readily believe this of you, although you have not said it, since not even now, while you are away from the court, have you been able to shed and unlearn those courtly manners? Indeed, that fine little book of yours, wholly courtly, which you wrote in German against Theodore Beza and dedicated to the most illustrious Electress of Saxony, proves that you are truly a most charming courtier and that you follow the courtly religion, as they call it. But take care, my dear Selneccer, lest, because you spent those eight years at court which you mention, you now show that what Lucan wrote about the courts of the princes of his own age is true:

units.la: --Exeat aula,
units.tr: --Let him leave the court,

units.la: Qui volet esse pius. Sed amplificas, ipse laudes tuas, & qua summa potes eloquentia, diligenter narras, te ultra ducentos discipulos privatos habuisse. Expectabam ut decies aut tricies mille auditores diceres: quem fuisse ordinariū aurei illius Constantinopoleos Episcopi, Iohannis Chrysostomi, dum in aula Arcadij concionaretur, auditorum numerum, ipsius historia testatur: sed, quemadmodum video, longè adhuc ab eo numero abes. Quorsum verò ista tua de ducentis auditoribus tuis tam ambitiosa iactantia, nisi ut raritatem & infrequentiam auditorij tuis collegis Saxonicis ex probres: vel ambitiosè te magnū quendam & doctum Alanum fuisse (de quo vulgò iactatum est, sufficiat vobis vidisse Alanū) nobis ipse de te prædices? Atqui vel puer illud didicisse debueras, Non te laudet os tuum, Proverb. 27. Item illud Catonis, Nec te collaudes, nec te culpaueris ipse: vel grandior illud Ciceronis, Laus in ore proprio sordescit. Sed ista nō meminisi, vt tete nobis ostentes. Nā in tota hac narratione tua quid aliud describis, ineptissime Suffene, quàm dignitates tuas & Doctoratus, Ienensem videlicet, Lipsiensem, ac Electoralem, & Præposituram Brunsuicensem, postea etiam Superintendentiam iterum Lipsiensem, vt tanquam Atlas totius Mundi, sic tu totius Germaniæ onus, & tamen homuncio, & tam paruus sustinere videaris. Itaque nec ipse tu ambitiosum illū tuum animum iam celare potes, imò etiam postremam hanc tuam Præposituram & Archiepiscopatum Lipsiensem ad te per mortem alterius, aut alio quocunque modo devolutum κοψλῶς nobis commemoras & describis, quæ mirifico Dei ductu tibi obla tū esse ais. Restabat vt manifesto etiā Dei miracu lo tibi, velut Ambrosio, delatum diceres. Verum si dixisses, blasphemum & mendacem esse te omnes statim percepisse: sed tamen etiam percipiunt, quum id Dei ductu factum esse scribis, quandoquidem apertissima coniuratione cum Iacobo Andrea tuo, & Monopolio illo vestro Bergensi (vt omnes recte de Cœna Domini sentientes, toto Lipsiensi agro tandem exturbaretis) à vobis astutè & fraudulenter id gestū esse negare non potes, vel audes. Iámne intelligis, Selneccere, quænam sit illa tua ad hanc Superintendentiam Lipsiensem vocatio? Nec hoc ipsum nega-
units.tr: Who wishes to be pious. But you yourself magnify your praises and tell them carefully, with all the eloquence you can muster, that you had more than two hundred private pupils. I expected you to say ten or thirty thousand hearers, as the history itself testifies was the usual number of hearers of that golden bishop of Constantinople, John Chrysostom, when he preached in the court of Arcadius; but, as I see, you are still far from that number. Why, then, this ambitious boasting of yours about two hundred hearers, except to reproach the rarity and thinness of the audience of your Saxon colleagues, or to proclaim yourself to us as some great and learned Alanus (of whom it was commonly said, it is enough for you to have seen Alanus)? Yet even as a boy you ought to have learned that "your own mouth should not praise you" (Prov. 27), and that saying of Cato, "Do not praise yourself, nor blame yourself," or the grander saying of Cicero, "Praise sounds foul in one's own mouth." But you do not remember these things, so that you may display yourself to us. For in this whole narrative of yours, what else do you describe, most foolish Suffenus, than your dignities and doctorates, namely at Jena, Leipzig and as Electoral Doctor, and your provostship at Brunswick, and afterwards your superintendency at Leipzig again; so that you seem, like Atlas bearing the whole world, to bear the burden of all Germany, and yet you seem a little manikin, and so very small to sustain it. Thus you cannot even conceal your ambitious spirit now; indeed, you also recount and describe in a witty way this last provostship and archbishopric of Leipzig, which fell to you by the death of another or by some other means, smartly [κομψῶς], saying that it was offered to you by the wonderful guidance of God. It remained for you to say that it had been brought to you by a plain miracle of God, as to Ambrose. But if you had said this, everyone would at once have perceived that you were blasphemous and a liar; yet they perceive it even so, since you write that it was done by the guidance of God, when you cannot deny, or dare to deny, that it was cunningly and fraudulently done by you, in most obvious conspiracy with your Jacob Andreae and that Bergen monopoly of yours (so that you might at last drive out of the whole Leipzig region all of us who think rightly about the Lord's Supper). Do you now understand, Selneccer, what your calling to this Leipzig superintendency was? Nor can you deny this very thing.

units.la: Pag.12. negare potuisti. Nam te inuitis obtrusum esse non dissimulas: sed addis te in ipso feruore Sacramentaria luis vocatum. Sacramentariae lucis dicere voluisti. Ergo fateris te à Papa Vbiquitariorum Jacobo Andrea, & à cæteris factionis tuæ hominibus in eum locum ex minoribus ordinibus ordinatum & promotum fuisse, quum lux cælestis, & vera de Sacramentis doctrina excitari Lipsiæ coepisset, vt eam nimirum tu (tanquam obscura quædam terræ vmbra) obscurares, vel prorsus, si posses, extinguores. Hic igitur fuit illius tuæ ad Superintendentiam, seu Archiepiscopatum Lipsiensem vocationis, vt omnes intelligant, finis.
units.tr: Pag. 12. You could not deny this. For you do not hide that you were thrust upon the unwilling, but you add that you were called in the very heat of the Sacramentarian light. You meant to say "of the Sacramentarian light." So you admit that Jacob Andreae, the Pope of the Ubiquitarians, and the other men of your faction raised you from the lower orders and promoted you to that post when the heavenly light and the true doctrine of the sacraments had begun to shine at Leipzig. Your task was to obscure that doctrine, like some dark shadow of the earth, or, if you could, to extinguish it altogether. This, then, was the purpose of your call to the superintendency, or archbishopric, of Leipzig, as everyone can see.

units.la: Quod autem toties me mendacem, me in mendacijs (quoniam alio modo, quàm conuitio, te tueri non potes) cumulandis perseuerare, mendacijs rum pi, & cætera huiusmodi inculcas, ea certè quidè est mera & perpetua tua in me calumnia, etiam teipso teste. Nam ea ipsa, quæ dico, vera esse fateris, & nihil habes quod contra afferas. Dixi te nostræ doctrinæ, id est, veræ, quam hodie inconstantissimè deseruisti, antea fuisse: Dixi, te ingratissimum discipulum scripta Philippi Melàchthonis præceptoris tui & damnare, & damnasse: Dixi te anno 1574. Responsionem ad Exegesin scripsisse, quam quadriennium postea, id est, 1578. edideris, quid in his omnibus, Selneccere, sum mentitus? Nam ex his tribus, quæ dixi, postremum omnino verum esse ipse concedis.
units.tr: As for your repeated charges that I am a liar, that I persist in piling up lies, that I break faith with lies, and similar things, which you can only defend by abuse, this is plainly and constantly your own slander against me, and your own witness proves it. For you admit that the things I say are true, and you have nothing to offer against them. I said that you were once of our doctrine, that is, the true doctrine, which you have so inconstantly abandoned today. I said that you, the most ungrateful pupil, both condemned and have condemned the writings of your teacher Philip Melanchthon. I said that you wrote a reply to the Exegesis in 1574, which you published four years later, in 1578. In all of this, Selneccer, what have I lied about? For you yourself concede that the last of these three things is entirely true.

units.la: Vide igitur quàm falsò me Sycophatam voces?
units.tr: See, then, how falsely you call me a sycophant!

units.la: Quod autem de Philippo scripsi, cum à vobis hæresεos damnari, non negas tu quidem, sed tantùm σοφιστικῶς eludis. Ais enim vestros monere tantùm lectores de erroribus Philippi cauendis. Næ tu mirus artifex, & subtilis videris, eíque similis, qui, quû equû furatus esset, eúmque domum abduceret, & in ipso furto deprehensus ad iudicem deduceretur puniendus, astuto cauillo & festiuo diluit totam accusationem. Dixit enim se non vt ad se à domino abduceret, sed vt aquatum tantùm deduceret, equum iltum accepisse. Sic tu non vt damnes, ais, sed vt serues Philippi scripta, illa inconstantię & hæreseos publicè notas, & proscribis. Sed tu quoque es mirè sapiens discipulus Selneccere, quem non pudet, etiam contra Christi verba, iactare, esse te scilicet supra magistrum tuum. Verùm enim verò Noua nouæ fidei vestræ cófessio (quam alij Noua biblia Vbiquitariorum, vos autem Nouam formulam concordiæ vocatis) me verum dicere, te autem mendacem esse testatur: quemadmodū & in eo quoque, quod ais, te prorsus insciò, & inconsulto, & tamè iam Superintendentem Lipsiæ agente, editam esse à Marco Hermanno Rostochiensi in eadem ciuitate Lipsiæ tuam aduersus Exegesin criminationem, cuius nullum apud te exemplar etiam retinueris. Quis hoc de te homine ambitiosissimo crederet? te tuos fumos ita neglexisse, & donasse, nisi qui te non norit. Et vt verum esse quis concedat, quomodo id fateri audes, nisi te negligentissimum Ecclesiæ tuæ inspectorem esse, & prorsus munere tuo indignum, ipse declares? Quamobrem iudico te ex ore tuo.
units.tr: As for what I wrote about Philip, that your people condemn him as a heretic, you do not deny it, but you dodge it with sophistry. You say that your people only warn their readers to beware of Philip's errors. But you are a clever trickster and a subtle fellow, like the man who stole a horse, led it home, and, caught in the act and brought before a judge to be punished, dissolved the whole charge with a sly and witty quibble: he said he had not led the horse away from its owner, but had only taken it to water. So you say that you do not condemn Philip's writings, but preserve them, while publicly marking them as inconstant and heretical and posting notices against them. But you are a wonderfully wise disciple, Selneccer, who is not ashamed to boast, even against Christ's words, that you are above your master. Indeed, the New Confession of your new faith (which others call the New Bible of the Ubiquitarians, but you call the New Formula of Concord) testifies that I speak the truth and you are a liar. The same holds for your claim that Marcus Hermann of Rostock published your attack on the Exegesis in this very city of Leipzig, "entirely without your knowledge or consent," even though you were already acting as superintendent there, and that you kept no copy of it. Who would believe this of you, the most ambitious of men, that you neglected and gave away your own writing so carelessly? Unless one does not know you. And who would concede that it is true, when you dare to admit it? Do you not reveal yourself to be a most negligent overseer of your church, and utterly unworthy of your office? So I judge you out of your own mouth.

units.la: Verùm post superiorem illam vitæ tuæ hifto- riam ad me redis, & quàm te pulchrum & formosum, & magnum quendam Homerum, tam me & tetrum, & deformem hominé, & Margirum quendam pingis.Appellas enim me homici- dam, furem maledicum, καχοπολύτα, ἀλλοτριόπλεκτον alibi Satanam, alibi Diabolicum, alibi etiam Latronem. Quid amplius? Aliquid prætermisisti. Nam me etiam Mariam Magdalenam appellare debebas, vt in me postea septem dæmonia fuisse probabiliter metireris. Prætermitto enim, quod non me duntaxat, sed omnes nostros, pro virulentæ illius tuæ eloquetiæ floribus, & Ἰουδαίους, Turcas, & Epicureos, & Atheos, & Mahumetanos (ipse factus & beatus: ipse inquam solus scilicet claues scientiæ & veritatis & promissionum Dei penes te habens) appellas & declamitas. Vbinâ verò, Selneccere, hæc in me crimina vel vidisti, vel ab alijs inesse audiuisti? Quisquam hæc tibi de me narrauit, qui me nouerit, vel Gallus, vel Germanus? Est hîc, Dei gratiâ, magistratus, & is quidem (fiquis in mūdo alius) in suo munere fūgendo diligentissimus, qui fi me aut omnium horum, aut vnius tantùm ex his criminibus conuiċtum, imò etiam legitima aliqua suspicione grauatum videret, tandiu non paterctur in hac ciuitate viueret atque etiam sanċto illo, & meis humeris longè quidem (quemadmodum ingenuè agnosco) graviore munere, in tam honesto cœtu, à quo sum cooptatus, ornatū esse. Sed ais me animas occidere & furari, nempe vt ad nomen Selneccere, tuū (Sehlthoter) alluderes, & quid ipsce facias,ostéderes. Nam illud, quod mihi falso obiicis,cōpetit inte verè,vel nominis tui etymo id testante,Selneccere. Et recte illud hoc loco, Cōueniūt rebus nomina sœpe suis. Verū istáne me exceptio, quòd animas occidā,à crimine excusaret. Estne leuius flagitiū animarū quàm corporū homicidiū,& furtū? Verùm ita res est,quicunque vestrum illud Vbiquitatis monstrū non amplectuntur,& Nestorianismū simul cum Eutychismo, id est, horrendas duas hydras simul cum vobis non coniungunt,ij & fures,& homicidæ,& inexpiabiles homines à vobis (qui nihil nisi maledicere bonis viris didicistis) appellátur. Sed audi, Selneccere, quid de te ex teipso didicerim. Dicis vocationis tuæ tibi curam esse. Sed nō ostendis nec addis exequutionis quoque, quam ea vocatio desiderat,solicitudiné & curam tibi esse. Hoc enim oblitus es,& certè qui in tot loca per totam vitam discurrit,& Wittenbergam in aulam,& ex Aula Ienā,Ienā Lipsiā,Lipsia Brūschuigū, Brunschuigo iterum Lipsiā redit, & aliquot annos in singulis istis discursationibus consumit (quod te fecisse ipse scribis) quomodo pastoris Ecclesiastici vocationem exequi & verè exercere,obsecro,potest? Nam, aut te tuíque similes esse nouos quosdam Germaniæ Apostolos oportet, nulli certo loco vel Ecclesiæ addictos: aut,si certę cuipiā Ecclesię eras præpositus(qualem verum & Euangelicum Pastorem ex Pauli præcepto esse oportet) quomodo munere tuo fūgi sic vagus & erro,in certo vllo loco potuisti? Ergo eaten' vocationis tibi cura est Selneccere, niminimirū vt spatiādi,&animigratiā aliquò voceris: quod cùm facis,quis te ipsum non merito vel furem, vel allotrioepiscopum, vt tuis verbis vtar, appellet, qui Ecclesiæ tuæ operam & præsentiā fureris & substrahas : & aliena ambitiosè speculari velis? Et certè, vt verū dicam, quid aliud sunt vestræ istæ in vnius persona perpetuæ(quan diu ille viuit) Superintendentiæ & Præposituræ, quàm Episcopatus ille humanus præter Dei verbum institutus,ex quo tandem Episcopatus Satanicus,id est, miserrima illa Episcoporum in Ecclesiam Dei tyrannis nata est? Itaque quid ipsis Germanicis Ecclesiis sit ex istis Præposituris euenturu m,facilè iam vident prudentes, & pij viri omnes. Sed si,qui fratrem suum Racha appellarit, Selneccere, iudice etiam ipso Christo,reus est confessus, & censendus homicida, profecto qualis sis,ipse vides,qui me &Sycophantam, & Dolium Danaidum tam conuitiosè nominés, idque quia de te,& tua in Philippum præceptorem tuum ingratitudine verum dixi, & contra Helenam vestram,Vbiquitatem, merito sum inuectus. Egóne Sycophanta, Selneccere? qui,vt meū temperametū, & palati mei gustum noris, illud genus cibi (à quo Sycophantæ sunt appellati) nunquam equidem edere vel possum vel soleo:verum etiam tam odi, quàm qui maximè. Sed teipsum obleƈtare hoc tuo in me conuitio à nimia illa tuæ Superintendentiæ fortasse molestia voluisti. Saltem si tu me Israelitam ex tribu Dan,(quia Danæus vocor) quemadmodum N.j.
units.tr: But after that history of your life, you turn to me, and you paint yourself as a beautiful and handsome, great Homer, and me as a foul, deformed man, a sort of Margites. You call me a murderer, a thief, a slanderer, a bad citizen [kakopolyta], a meddler [allotriopleikton], elsewhere Satan, elsewhere a devil, and elsewhere even a robber. What more? You have left something out, for you ought to call me Mary Magdalene too, so that you could then plausibly measure out seven demons in me. I pass over the fact that you call not only me but all our people, by the flowers of your venomous eloquence, Jews, Turks, Epicureans, atheists and Mahometans (you who have become blessed by yourself, you alone, I say, who hold the keys of knowledge and truth and the promises of God in your own hands). Where, Selneccer, did you see these charges against me, or hear that they belong to me from others? Did anyone who knows me, Frenchman or German, tell you such things about me? Here, by God's grace, is a magistrate, and surely (if anyone in the world) most diligent in discharging his office, who, if he saw me convicted of all these crimes, or even of any one of them, or burdened with some lawful suspicion, would not let me live in this city, nor allow me to be adorned with that holy office, which is indeed heavier on my shoulders (as I freely acknowledge) than in so honourable a company, to which I was co-opted. But you say that I kill and steal souls, clearly alluding to your name, Selneccer, (Sehlthoter, that is, soul-killer), and showing what you yourself do. For what you falsely charge me with truly belongs to you, and your name's etymology testifies to it, Selneccer. And rightly here: "names often agree with their things." But does the excuse that I kill souls free me from the charge? Is the crime against souls lighter than murder and theft of bodies? The truth is this: whoever of you does not embrace that monster of Ubiquity, and does not join with you the Nestorianism together with Eutychianism, that is, the two horrible hydras, is called by you (who have learned only to revile good men) a thief, a murderer, and an unpardonable man. But hear, Selneccer, what I have learned about you from yourself. You say that the care of your calling is yours. But you do not show, nor add, that you have also the concern and care for carrying out the work that such a calling demands. For you have forgotten this, and surely a man who runs about through so many places all his life, going to the court at Wittenberg, from the court to Jena, from Jena to Leipzig, from Leipzig to Braunschweig, and from Braunschweig back to Leipzig, and spends some years in each of these wanderings (as you yourself write that you did), how, I ask, can he perform and truly exercise the calling of an ecclesiastical minister? For either you and your like must be some new apostles of Germany, attached to no fixed place or church, or, if you were set over a particular church (as a true and evangelical minister must be, by Paul's precept), how could you, wandering and straying like this, perform your office in any fixed place? So the care of your calling is yours, Selneccer, namely that you are called to wander and to gratify your mind somewhere else. And when you do this, who would not rightly call you a thief, or, in your own words, an allotrioepiscopus (a bishop of other people's affairs), since you steal the work and presence of your own church and wish to spy on the affairs of others out of ambition? And truly, to tell the truth, what else are your perpetual superintendencies and provostships, held by one person for his whole life, than that human episcopate instituted apart from God's word, from which the satanic episcopate was finally born, that is, the most wretched tyranny of bishops over the church of God? Thus the prudent and all the godly already easily see what will result for the German churches themselves from these provostships. But if whoever calls his brother Raca, Selneccer, is by the judgment of Christ himself liable and deserving to be counted a murderer, then surely you can see what kind of man you are, you who so abusively name me a sycophant and a cask of the Danaids, and this because I spoke the truth about you and your ingratitude toward your teacher Philip, and rightly inveighed against your Helena, the Ubiquity. Me a sycophant, Selneccer? You, who know my temperament and my palate's taste, know that I can never eat, and am not accustomed to eat, that sort of food from which the sycophants got their name; indeed I hate it as much as anyone. But perhaps you wished to amuse yourself with this insult against me out of the excessive annoyance of your superintendency. At least, if you had called me an Israelite of the tribe of Dan (because I am called Danaeus), just as N.j.

units.la: dum ille Laonicus,Germana spongia,& Osian-dricus eques,nominasses. Quòd autem me Dolium Danaidum, alludens fortasse ad meum cognomen,sestiue, vt tibi quidem videtur, vt autè bonis omnibus,scurriliter,vocas,falleris, in tuo isto scommate,toto cælo. Nam neque ego sum ex Danais: sed potiùs è Troianis: siquidem ego sum Francus: Franci verò à vetustissimis illis,& nobilissimis Troianis sunt oriundi, non autem ab illis mendacissimis Danais,quorum naturam tu refers.Dolium autem qui possim esse, cùm id neque corporis mei statura,neque vitæ ratio patiatur, qui ebrietatem & vinolentiam vestram (qua cantaros istos in stomachum, tanquam in vtrem & ocreas demittitis) toto pectore, quod sciunt omnes, execror. Verùm addis me inter diuos collocare Berengarium. Nequaquam Scilneccere. Imagines enim nec colo, Dei optimi gratiâ(sum enim ab istis idololatriæ tenebris summo Christi beneficio, liberatus) nec eos in templis Christianorum seruo,vel probo. Nec verò quia veram Berengarij laudem ex vera illius temporis historia, contra tuam insctiam protuli,qui illum,tragicum vitæ exitum habuisse scripseras.propterea conuitiis abs te proscindi debui. Equidem Berengarianum me, si modò rectè illius sententia (qualis primùm fuit) intelligatur,esse malim, quàm Lanfrancianum, qualis tu es. Berengarius enim veram de Sacramentis Domini doctrinam, ex Augustino tuebatur, docebátque & signa à rebus signatis differre, & rem ipsam signatam nobis spirituali modo per fidem communicari. Denique Christi carnem iuxta articulos symboli Apostolici in cælo esse, non in his terris quærendam. At Lanfrancus Pontificum Romanorum assecla pessimus, & homo ignorantissimus, omnia illa ex Eutychetis, & Monophysitarum errore (quem hodie renouatis) euertere conabatur. Nam & Transsubstantiationem defendebat, & carnem Christi in his terris, quemadmodum & vos, collocabat. Denique idololatriam illam (unde horrendum Missæ sacrificium postea fabricatum est) propagabat. Quæ pluribus describerem, nisi iam tempus esset, ut finem dicendi facerem. Illud modo à te peto, Selneccere, ut cum in hoc de sacra Cœna, tum in aliis fidei Christianæ articulis, ex ipso Dei verbo sapere velis. Est autem Dei verbum, doctrina ipsa, & mens spiritus Dei, quæ iis vocabulis, quibus ipse vtitur, continetur. Non autem illud, quod carnalis sensus & ratio (quæ mysteria Dei nequaquam capit) crasse imaginatur, & illi affingit. Nam qui τὸ ῥητὸν in Sacramentali Scripturæ locutione vrget, is verbum Dei certè quidem non habet: sed in eam, quam miserrimā vocat Augustinus, seruitutem incidit, ut signa pro rebus ipsis colat ac veneretur. Quis enim dubitat, quin Sacramentalis locutio (qualis est hæc, HOC EST CORPVS MEVM) sit sacramentaliter intelligenda, propterea quòd Sacramenta sunt rei sacræ & cœlestis, ac denique corporali situ à nobis absentis σϕραγίδες, testimo-
units.tr: while you named that Laonicus, German sponge, and Osiandrian knight. But as for your calling me Dolium Danaidum (a barrel of the Danaids), perhaps alluding to my surname, wittily as it seems to you but scurrilously in the eyes of all good men, you are wrong by the whole sky in that jibe. For I am not of the Danaans; I am rather of the Trojans, since I am a Frank, and the Franks are descended from those most ancient and noble Trojans, not from those most lying Danaans whose character you describe. But how could I be a barrel, when neither my bodily stature nor my way of life allows it? I who, as everyone knows, abhor with my whole heart your drunkenness and winebibbing, by which you pour those tankards down your gullet as though into a wineskin or a boot. But you add that I place Berengarius among the gods. By no means, Selneccer. For I neither worship images, by the grace of the best God (for by the supreme benefit of Christ I have been freed from those shadows of idolatry), nor do I keep them in the churches of Christians or approve of them. Nor ought I to be torn apart by your insults merely because I put forward Berengarius's true praise, drawn from the true history of that time, against your ignorance, you who had written that he had a tragic end to his life. Indeed, I would rather be a Berengarian, provided his opinion is rightly understood as it was at first, than a Lanfrancian, which is what you are. For Berengarius defended the true doctrine of the Lord's sacraments from Augustine, and taught both that the signs differ from the things signified and that the thing signified is communicated to us in a spiritual manner through faith. Finally, he taught that Christ's flesh is in heaven, according to the articles of the Apostles' Creed, and is not to be sought on these earthly lands. But Lanfranc, the most wicked follower of the Roman Pontiffs and a man most ignorant, tried to overturn all those things with the error of Eutyches and the Monophysites, which you renew today. For he both defended transubstantiation and placed Christ's flesh on these earthly lands, just as you do. Finally, he propagated that idolatry from which the horrible sacrifice of the Mass was afterwards fashioned. I would describe these matters at greater length, were it not already time to make an end of speaking. This only I ask of you, Selneccer: that you be willing to judge, both in this matter of the Holy Supper and in the other articles of the Christian faith, from the very Word of God. Now the Word of God is the teaching itself and the mind of God's Spirit, contained in the words that he himself uses. It is not what carnal sense and reason (which by no means grasp the mysteries of God) crudely imagine and attach to it. For whoever insists on the literal sense [τὸ ῥητόν] in the sacramental language of Scripture certainly does not have the Word of God, but falls into that slavery which Augustine calls most wretched, so that he worships and venerates the signs in place of the things themselves. For who doubts that sacramental language, such as this, THIS IS MY BODY, must be understood sacramentally, because the sacraments are seals [σφραγίδες], testimonies and signs of a holy and heavenly thing, and of one who is absent from us in bodily location?

units.la: N.ij. nia & signa? Ergo ad διάνοιαν nobis recurrendum est, Selneccere, quam qui sequitur in Sacramentis, ille Dei spiritum & sequitur & habet, atque etiam idē totā vetustatē orthodoxam suæ fidei testem laudare potest. Et quia de re ipsa in aliud tempus disputationem differs, & nos quoque ad illud nos reseruabimus, in quate à Dei spiritu illustrari, Selneccere, summis ab ipso votis precor postuólq;. Vale. Dominus oculos mentis tuæ illuminet, ut veritatem ipsius, sepositis omnibus præiudiciis, tandem intueri, & verè amplecti possis.
units.tr: So we must return to the sense [διάνοια], Selneccer, and whoever follows that in the sacraments both follows and has the Spirit of God, and can also commend the whole orthodox antiquity as a witness to his faith. And since you defer the discussion of the matter itself to another time, we too will reserve ourselves for it. In the meantime, Selneccer, I pray and beseech with the highest prayers that you be enlightened by the Spirit of God. Farewell. May the Lord illuminate the eyes of your mind, so that, setting aside all prejudices, you may at last look upon his truth and truly embrace it.

units.la: Ad Τὸ ἀπέγεν Ἀπόγεν Selnecceri.
units.tr: To Selneccer's "Τὸ ἀπέγεν Ἀπόγεν" [Τὸ ἀπέγεν Ἀπόγεν]

units.la: ET hic quoque Selneccerus, quāuis à me admonitus, se sano mentis iudicio carere ostendit, qui quæ priora sunt natura, posteriora tamen, contra omnium mortaliū sensum, faciat, nec ab eo etiam errore revocari possit. Verum quid dicas, videamus. Ais, Selneccere, nonnullos persuasione peculiaris eruditionis turgidos se omnia esse existimare. Quos autem alios hic perstringas, nescio, nisi quod teipsum, & Iacobum Andream his verbis graphicè depingis. Vis autē de re ipsa cum Danæo isto coram conferre. Certè nec Danæus iste recusat, si modò non ex scriptis Lutheri, idest hominis minimè Apostoli, miniméque irrefragabilis Prophetæ, (qualem tamen vos cum eum esse censetis) sed ex ipso Dei verbo conferre volueris. Caeterum quae,(ut probes etiam indignos ipsum Christi corpus sumere, & non tantum signa corporis Christi)affers,illa nequaquam sunt solida (ut tibi videntur)vel ex Christi verbis vel ex vera omnipotentiae Dei cognitione ducta argumenta,sed errores vestri tantum, qui facile vel ex eo refelluntur, & exufflantur,quod neque Christus id dixit, quod ais, neque qualis sit omnipotentia Dei,intelligis. Itaque vexillum illud, quod adscriptis,maiori charactere his verbis,HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, tam magnifice iactas, & erigis, a Christo ipso dejicitur.Neque enim ille dixit,CORPVS MEVM EST IN, SVB, & CVM HOC PANE, quod tamen vos dicitis: sed, HOC EST CORPVS MEVM. Itaque illud, quod in oratione Christi praedicatum est,vos facitis subiectum, cotraque. Quamobrem & Brentius, & Iacobus Andreas ipse aperte illud, quod ex verbis Christi ducis, fundamentum in hac disputatione prorsus dejiciunt, tanquam manifeste nullū. Aliud autem ipsi,nimirum ex hypostatica duarum in Christo naturarum vnione,magnis laboribus,& tamen infaustis, substruere conantur. Nec vero dubiū est, quin,si nulla sit in his Christi verbis, Hoc est meum corpus, accipite, edite, figura,flagitium praecipiatur, quemadmodum recte scribit Augustinus:& verior Papistarum, quam Vbiquitariorū sit futura sententia.Et haec quidē quod ad verba Christi. Quod autem ad Omnipotentiam Dei, illa nequaquam Dei misericordiam ,& veritatē eius destruit, cum hæ omnes virtutes sint vna Dei essentia, nec ex his virtutibus vna alteri contraria esse possit. Quare non facit omnipotentia Dei vt vera illa caro Christi, per quā Deo reconciliati sumus, & in qua manet nolter in æternū mediator, vnquam aboleatur. Si enim id fieret, quod ex vestra tamen sententia necessario sequitur, certè desineret Christus esse Christus, & frater noster & Mediator. Manere autē vera caro, & qualis nobis ex Dei verbo descripta est, non potest, nisi sit nobis ὁμοούσιος & quod ad essentiam, & quodad essentiales eius proprietates, inter quas vna hæc est præcipua, vt sit ipsa ἀπέρατος, id est, loco circumscripta, non autem sit vel pluribus locis, vel cum λόγῳ Deitate coextensa, id quod vos manifeste vultis. Vides igitur, Selneccere, vt tua te duo illa potissima fundamenta destituant. Verùm tu hominum seruus, nimirū illius (quem, etsi non nomino, satis tamen intelligis) quo iure, quáue iniuria sententiam (quam semel imbibisti) tueri vis. Præclarè verò Hieronymus, Quæ est tàta pertinacia, sic laudare alicuius doctrinam, vt sequare blasphemiam? Sed pergamus.
units.tr: Here too Selnecker, although I have admonished him, shows that he lacks sound judgment, since he makes what is prior by nature posterior, against the common sense of all mortals, and cannot be called back even from that error. But let us see what you say. You say, Selnecker, that some men, puffed up by the persuasion of their peculiar learning, think that they know everything. Whom you mean to hit here, I do not know, unless it is yourself and Jacob Andreae, whom you depict vividly in these words. You want to confer with this Daneau about the matter face to face. Certainly Daneau does not refuse, provided you do not confer from the writings of Luther, that is, of a man by no means an apostle and by no means an irrefragable prophet (though you Lutherans think him such), but from the Word of God itself. But the arguments you bring forward, to prove that the unworthy receive the body of Christ and not merely the signs of Christ's body, are by no means solid (as they seem to you), nor are they drawn either from the words of Christ or from a true knowledge of the omnipotence of God. They are only your errors, which are easily refuted and blown away by this very fact, that Christ did not say what you claim, and you do not understand what the omnipotence of God is. Therefore that banner which you have inscribed, in larger letters, with these words, THIS IS MY BODY, which you boast of and raise so magnificently, is thrown down by Christ himself. For he did not say MY BODY IS IN, UNDER, AND WITH THIS BREAD, which nevertheless you say; he said THIS IS MY BODY. Thus you make the subject what in Christ's utterance is the predicate, and conversely. Therefore both Brenz and Jacob Andreae himself openly abandon the foundation of this dispute, which you derive from the words of Christ, as manifestly none at all. Instead they labour, with great effort and yet without success, to build on another foundation, namely the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ. Nor is there any doubt that, if there is no figure in these words of Christ, This is my body, take, eat, then a crime is commanded, as Augustine rightly writes; and the opinion of the Papists will be more correct than that of the Ubiquitarians. And these things concern the words of Christ. As for the omnipotence of God, it by no means destroys the mercy of God and his truth, since all these attributes are one essence of God, and of these attributes one cannot be contrary to another. Therefore the omnipotence of God does not cause that true flesh of Christ, through which we have been reconciled to God and in which our Mediator remains for ever, to be abolished. For if that happened, which nevertheless necessarily follows from your opinion, Christ would certainly cease to be Christ, and our brother and Mediator. But true flesh, such as it has been described to us from the Word of God, cannot remain unless it is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with us, both in its essence and in its essential properties, among which this one is chief: that it is uncircumscribed [ἀπέρατος], that is, circumscribed in place, and not either in many places or coextensive with the Deity of the Word [λόγῳ], which you plainly want. You see, then, Selnecker, how those two chief foundations of yours fail you. But you, a slave of men, namely of that man (whom, though I do not name him, you understand well enough), by what right or wrong do you want to defend the opinion which you once imbibed? Jerome wrote admirably: What obstinacy is this, to praise someone's doctrine in such a way that you follow his blasphemy? But let us go on.

units.la: Obiicis quod dixerim non constare de voluntate Christi. Imò verò, Selneccere, vel meum scriptum non legisti, vel malignè præuaricatus es, & interpretatus. Constare enim, atque adeo aperte de ipsius Christi sententia affirmo: & tuā etiam de his verbis interpretationem ex ipsa Christi sententia tolli & refutari dico. Quid igitur tur hic mihi & falsò, & inepte obiicis?Addis autem, male à me concludi, si caro Christi sit corporali(vt tu vis)præsentiæ modo in cœna,beatos quoque defunctos ibidem sisti oportere. Hæc in mea responsione grauiter accusas. Atqui non hæc mea:scd ipsius Sp. Sancti, & postea Hieronymi ad Ruffinum oratio, & ratiocinatio fuit. Sequuntur enim beati Agnum quocunque ierit, in- quit S. Sanctus:& dixit Christus ipse,Pater volo, vbi sum ego,& illi sint mecum. Aut igitur Christus falsum dixerit,aut verum est quod ex ipsius verbis vna cum ipso Hieronymo colligo. Obiicis porrò,quasi dixerim quòd cordatis viris non satisfiat si quid Christus dixerit. Falleris. Impij enim sunt,etiam me iudice,qui vel solo Christi verbo conteti non sunt. Quid igitur dixi? Viris nimirum bonis & piis non satisfieri, vbi hoc vnum, HOC EST CORPVS MEVM,perperā à vobis intelle ctum pro vestrorum errorum fundamento semper occinitis. Falsò enim dicitis : hoc Christum dixisse,quod vos sentitis. Denique quòd negaui vnquam à nostris appellari Christi corpus ἀλληγορικόν, καὶ νοητὸν, καὶ μεταφορικόν, id iterum dico. Nec enim idem est dicere,locutionem ipsam esse metaphoricam,& rem ipsam,de qua agitur,& de qua locutio est tropica seu metaphorica, esse metaphoricam. Hæc igitur locutio & phrasis, HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, est ipsa quidem metaphorica. Sed nec res ipsa,nec signum, de quo hoc dicitur, propterea vel metaphora est, vel Christi corpus metaphoricum:imo & panis ille verus est naturalis Panis,& corpus illud, cuius est signum,est verum,naturale, seu essentiale ipsius Christi corpus pro nobis olim crucifixi. Manet enim vere res eadem, quae prius erat,nec in attributo, nec in subiecto huius locutionis, sed in ipso modo attributionis, vel in verbo est, nimirum tropus iste, seu figurata locutio versatur. Et hoc quidem de hoc vocabulo Metaphoricum. Quòd autem ad ἀλληγορικὸν, νοητὸν , &c. nusquam apud nostros ista, Selneccere, legisti, quemadmodum nec hoc , quod postremo loco pro colophone addis, dici nimirum Christum corpore suo tam esse remotum in Coena a nobis,quam calum ipsum est a terra. Quid igitur? Mentiendo rumperis,& antiquum tuum obtines, ut & sensum, & verba nostra perpetuo immutes. Nam ingenuè profitemur,& toto corde credimus, Christum ipsum nobis fide ad sacram Coenam accedentibus esse etiam corpore ipso suo, quod tamen in caelis manet,praesentissimum.Fides enim nostra illud etiam in caelo & quaerit, & reipsa apprehendit, adeò ut fiamus illius corporis Christi vere,& reipsa quoque participes. Itaque ne de hac nostra sententia amplius, Selneccere, dubites , & vt, quod dicimus, in posterum melius legas,& memoriae infigas, en tibi nostram sententiam grandiusculis elementis descriptam.
units.tr: You object that I said it is not established what the will of Christ is. Rather, Selnecker, either you have not read my writing, or you have wickedly misrepresented and misinterpreted it. For I affirm that it is established, indeed openly so, from the very judgment of Christ; and I say that your interpretation of these words is removed and refuted by the very judgment of Christ. Why then do you falsely and foolishly object this to me? You add that I reason badly if the flesh of Christ is present in the Supper in a bodily manner (as you want), so that the blessed departed too must be placed there. You gravely accuse this in my reply. Yet this was not my argument, but the argument and reasoning of the Holy Spirit himself, and afterwards of Jerome in his letter to Rufinus. For the blessed follow the Lamb wherever he goes, says the Holy Spirit; and Christ himself said, Father, I will that where I am, there they also may be with me. Either Christ therefore spoke falsely, or what I gather, together with Jerome himself, from his words is true. You further object, as if I had said that men of sense are not satisfied if Christ has said something. You are mistaken. For those who are not content with the word of Christ alone are impious, even in my judgment. What then did I say? Namely that good and pious men are not satisfied when you always sing this one phrase, THIS IS MY BODY, wrongly understood by you, as the foundation of your errors. For you falsely say that Christ said what you think. Finally, as to my denial that our people ever call the body of Christ allegorical, intelligible and metaphorical [ἀλληγορικόν, καὶ νοητὸν, καὶ μεταφορικόν], I say so again. For it is not the same to say that the locution itself is metaphorical and that the thing itself of which the locution is tropical or metaphorical is metaphorical. This locution and phrase, THIS IS MY BODY, is indeed metaphorical. But neither the thing itself nor the sign of which this is said is therefore a metaphor, or is a metaphorical body of Christ. Indeed that bread is true natural bread, and that body of which it is the sign is the true, natural, or essential body of Christ, once crucified for us. For the same thing truly remains as it was before, not in the predicate or the subject of this locution, but the trope, or figurative locution, lies in the mode of predication itself, namely in the word is. And this is what I say about the word "metaphorical." As for allegorical, intelligible, etc., you have never read these terms among our writers, Selnecker, nor have you read what you add last, as a colophon, namely that Christ in the Supper is said to be as far from us by his body as heaven itself is from earth. What then? You break yourself by lying, and you maintain your old habit of constantly changing both our meaning and our words. For we frankly profess, and believe with our whole heart, that Christ himself, while he is present in his very body, which nevertheless remains in heaven, is most present to us, when we approach the holy Supper by faith. For our faith seeks him in heaven, and in fact apprehends him, so that we truly and really become partakers of that body of Christ. Therefore, Selnecker, that you may doubt no more about this our opinion, and that you may read better in future what we say and fix it in your memory, here is our opinion set out for you in rather large letters: CHRIST IN THE SUPPER IS AS FAR REMOVED FROM US BY HIS BODY, NOT FROM THE SIGNS, AS HEAVEN ITSELF IS FROM THE EARTH.

units.la: CHRISTVM IN COENA CORPORE SVO A SIGNIS, NON A NOBIS, TAM ESSE REMOTVM, QVAM COELVM IPSVM A TERRA EST.
units.tr: CHRIST IS IN THE SUPPER AS FAR REMOVED FROM THE SIGNS, NOT FROM US, AS HEAVEN ITSELF IS FAR FROM THE EARTH.

units.la: Cuius rei ratio est,quòd signa ipsa,nempe panis & Vinum S. Coenae, in sese fidem non habeat,qua sola ipsu & essentiale Christi corpus fit alicui rei præsens, & coniunctum.Intellextin' iam Selneccere?Quare in posterum à mendacijs & calumnijs istis in nos (si vir bonus videri velis abstine. Porrò liceat mihi hanc epistolam,Selneccere,hac pulcherrima Augustini sententia claudere,Senti de Danæo quicquid libet,sola me in oculis Dei conscientia non accuset. Quàquam me vehementer hoc affligit, vt cum alio Patre loquar ,quòd inde falsitatis crimen tolero, vnde quotidie vires hostium immaniter excrefcūt,&Ecclesia Dei laceratur.Cæterum doleo ex animo(quamuis enim te diligā, Selneccere , tamen verum dicam , ὁ γρ ἀφρόν τῆς ἀληθείας πμιτος ἀνὴρ, vt ait Plato ) doleo inquam, quòd te(quem virum alioqui haud omnino ineptum nostrûm quidam existimabant) stolidum tandem non coniecturis tantùm,non signis, nō leuibus argumentis, sed certissimis ἐκμαρτύρια, & omni demonstratione firmioribus ostendisti, dum nobis insulsa quædam mittis carmina, quæ cum tuam in pangendo versu ἀντίαν, tum etiam tuum desparso iam per totam Germaniam à vobis Sex viris ἐριδὸς ac discordiæ μῆλον, gaudium testantur. Sed quid aliud à te fieri potuit, quàm vt de re mala,ipse quoque malus,vt video, poëta malos versus scriberes. Verùm vt tibi gaudium & cachinnum compensem,quem nobis gloriosa ista tua versificatio attulit,en tibi alia carmina, quæ,vt ad te mitterem,boni aliquot viri, tui studiosi,& amantes(quibus tua ostendi,rogarūt)& ad te libentissimè remittunt. Ipsi autem ne de eorum erga te benevolentia dubitares, sua manu in αὐτοσεσφῳ nomè suo ascripserunt. Vale,Dominus Deus per Vnigenitum Filiū suum, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum mentis tuæ oculos sanet,quemadmodum illius à natiuitate cæci hominis & corporis,& mentis lumina restituit,vt depulso omni metu Pharisæorū (quos fortasse adhuc times,quoniam alapâ tibi,vti scribis,inflixerunt) Christum verè agnoscere,ac inter homines Selneccere,profiteri & ausis, & possis. Vale.
units.tr: The reason for this is that the signs themselves, namely the bread and wine of the Holy Supper, do not have in themselves the faith by which alone Christ's very and essential body is made present to and joined with anything. Do you understand now, Selneccerus? So in future, abstain from these lies and slanders against us, if you wish to seem a good man. Furthermore, Selneccerus, allow me to close this letter with that very beautiful saying of Augustine: "Think what you like about Daneau, let only the conscience before the eyes of God not accuse me." Although this grieves me deeply, so that, to speak with another Father, I bear the charge of falsehood from the very quarter where the strength of our enemies grows enormously every day and the Church of God is torn apart. Otherwise I grieve from my heart (for although I love you, Selneccerus, I shall still speak the truth: "for the man who is a stranger to truth [ὁ γὰρ ἀφρόν τῆς ἀληθείας πμιτος ἀνὴρ], as Plato says") I grieve, I say, that you, whom some of our people did not judge to be altogether a fool, have at last shown yourself a fool, not merely by conjectures, signs or light arguments, but by most certain proofs [τεκμήρια] and demonstrations firmer than any. You send us some silly verses, which testify both to your contradiction [ἀντιλογία] in composing verse and to the apple of discord [μῆλον ἔριδος] that you and the six men with you have now scattered throughout all Germany, which is a source of joy. But what else could you do than write bad verses, being yourself, as I see, bad, on a bad subject? Yet, so that I may repay you with the joy and laughter which that glorious versifying of yours has brought us, here are other verses. Some good men, your admirers and friends, who were shown your work, asked me to send them to you, and they most willingly send them back to you. That you may not doubt their goodwill towards you, they have written their names in their own hand, as signatures. Farewell. May the Lord God, through his Only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, heal the eyes of your mind, just as he restored the light of sight and mind to the man born blind; so that, with all fear of the Pharisees put aside (whom perhaps you still fear, since they struck you on the cheek, as you write), you may both dare and be able to acknowledge Christ truly and to profess him, Selneccerus, among men. Farewell.

units.la: Verè in Domino sapere,& sanctè viuere.
units.tr: To be truly wise in the Lord and to live holily.

units.la: IN EDITIONEM PANDORÆ A BERGENSIBVS Patribus æditæ.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE EDITION OF THE PANDORA PUBLISHED BY THE BERGEN FATHERS.

units.la: RIdiculus tandem ecce cauis mus prodit ab an-Quem grauidi Montes parturiere diu. (tris, Ille prius totis spirans pulmonibus ignes, Qui nunc conspicui nil nisi fumus erunt: Attamen haud paucis perstringens lumina cæcis, Rursum ipsis donec lux micet ex tenebris.
units.tr: Look, at last a ridiculous mouse comes forth from the hollow mountain, the one that the pregnant mountains laboured over so long. That creature, which at first breathed fire from full lungs, will now be seen to be nothing but smoke. Yet, dazzling the eyes of not a few blind people, it will flash before them again, until light gleams for them out of the darkness.

units.la: Quorsum etenim tristes cælo fulgere Cometæ, Pallida quos pauidis Cynthia vidit equis? Sensimus & Solem æstiuos geminasse calores, Et micuere nouæ claraque per astra faces.
units.tr: For why did the sad comets blaze in the sky, those that pale Cynthia saw with her frightened horses? We felt the sun doubling its summer heat, and new torches blazed through the stars.

units.la: Quinetiam pariens monstrosa hæc dogmata Berga, Berga quoque est motu bis pauefacta grauí. Scilicet hæc cladem, funestaq; bella notarunt, Quæ nouus hic toto nuntiat orbe liber.
units.tr: Moreover, Berga, bearing these monstrous dogmas, Berga too was shaken twice by a heavy quake. Surely these portents marked slaughter and deadly wars, which this new book announces to the whole world.

units.la: Sed pariter Christus libro sua fata minatur, Et vix nascenti nuntiat exequias.
units.tr: But at the same time Christ threatens its fates with the book, and scarcely announces funeral rites to it as it is being born.

units.la: Ioannes Venantius.
units.tr: Ioannes Venantius.

units.la: NICOLAI SELNECCERI Epigramma in Pandorae Bergensis commendationem.
units.tr: Epigram of Nicolaus Selneccer in praise of the Bergic Pandora.

units.la: CHristus ait: Sine me tenebrae sunt omnia mundi, Qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris. Lux ego sum mundi, Dux vita, Iustitia Sol, Qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris. Hoc, pie Christe, pij grata pietate notantes, Imponent super altare tuum vitulos. Hoc tibi nunc offert Concordia voce Lutheri, Fundata in verbo, Maxime Christe, tuo.
units.tr: Christ says: "Without me all the world is darkness; he who follows me does not walk in darkness. I am the light of the world, the Leader of life, the Sun of Righteousness; he who follows me does not walk in darkness." O gracious Christ, those who mark this with a pious devotion pleasing to a pious man will place calves upon your altar. Now Concord offers this to you, O greatest Christ, with the voice of Luther, founded on your word.

units.la: Ad illud Epigramma, carmen ἀμοιβαῖον L. Danaei.
units.tr: To that epigram, an antiphonal poem by L. Danaeus. [ἀμοιβαῖον]

units.la: PAnis ego vita coelo delapsus ab alto, Christus ait, vita, credite, Panis ego. Hac mea verba capit fidei, non corporis, auris. Nam caro nil prodest, spiritus intus alit. At te carnea gens, Christe, aspernata docentem Carnales tandem decidit in tenebras, Et quam tu carnem coelesti sede locasti, Pergit adhuc imis quaerere caca locis: Quinetiam auctorem te, Selneccere, sequuta, Imponit super altare novum vitulos. At tu stulte cave, ῥητὸν ne forte sequuta Sic reliquos inter te iugulent vitulos. Aut vituli saltem fac isti usque superstint, Pro vitulis asinos vel iugulare veta.
units.tr: "I am the bread of life, come down from high heaven," Christ says. "Believe it: I am the bread. Only the ear of faith, not of the body, takes in these my words. For the flesh profits nothing; the spirit nourishes within." But you, Christ, the fleshly race has spurned your teaching and at last has fallen into fleshly darkness. The flesh which you placed in your heavenly seat still seeks you, blind, in the lowest places. Indeed, following you, Selnecker, as its author, it places calves upon the new altar. But you, fool, take care lest, following the literal words [ῥητὸν], they slaughter the other calves among you. Or at least make sure that those calves stand firm for ever, and forbid the slaughter of asses in place of calves.

units.la: IN VITVLATIONEM N. Selnecceri.
units.tr: Against the Calf-Offering of N. Selneccer.

units.la: Mente Deum placa, vitulum sine crescat aratro, Et vera Christum quaerere disce fide. Sin vitulos offerre libet, ne quaerito longè, Selneccerus adest, en tibi ter vitulus.
units.tr: Appease God in your mind, let the calf grow up unyoked to the plough, and learn to seek Christ with true faith. But if you are minded to offer calves, do not look far: here is Selneccer, lo, a calf three times over, ready for you.

units.la: Antonius Appius.
units.tr: Antonius Appius.

units.la: VENERABILI DOMINO, Domino Superintendenti Lipsiæ, Nicolao Selneccero.
units.tr: TO THE VENERABLE LORD, the Superintendent of Leipzig, Nicolaus Selneccer.

units.la: Cauillator caulicus, Prædicator aulicus, Doctor Electoralis, Et spe iam Cardinalis, Et nunc Superintendens, Nuper Superpraesidens, Hac fuistis omnia, Quod tot testimonia,
units.tr: Caviling cabbage-man, court preacher, electoral doctor, and already a cardinal in hope, and now superintendent, lately super-president: you have been all these things, as so many testimonies show,

units.la: Probant, atque maligni, Mores his rebus digni, Sanus esse non potes, Ni multum vinum potes, Caula sordibus scatet, Aula fraudibus patet, Fallit sæpe Electio, In spe fit deceptio, Quare vt quidlibet sies, Vir bonus nunquam fies.
units.tr: Prove it, and the malicious add that your morals are worthy of such things. You cannot be sound unless you can drink a great deal of wine. The sheepfold swarms with filth, the court lies open to fraud, election often deceives, and hope often ends in disappointment. So whatever you may be, you will never become a good man.

units.la: Iacobus Didumimus.
units.tr: James Didymus.

units.la: VENERABILI DOMINO,
units.tr: TO THE VENERABLE LORD,

units.la: Domino Superiori Abbati Cisterciensi,
units.tr: To the Lord Superior Abbot of Cîteaux,

units.la: Nicolao Schrecero.
units.tr: Nicolaus Schrecerus.
